items.body:
Every durable community has lore: the inside jokes, the shared stories, the names for things only the group uses, the legends about the early days. Lore is not decoration. It is one of the things that makes a community feel like a community rather than a meeting.

This framework draws on writing by **Mia Quagliarello** and others at the [grouphug](https://grouphug.substack.com/) Substack on the role of lore in healthy community.

## What lore is

Lore is the accumulated cultural material that's distinctive to your community. It can include:

- **Inside jokes.** The thing that's funny because we were all there.
- **Founding stories.** How this gathering started. What the first meeting was like. The legend of the first attendee who's now an institution.
- **Names for things.** "The big potluck." "The night we ran out of chairs." "Mike's chair." Group-specific shorthand.
- **Recurring characters.** The person who always brings the dog. The neighbor who's always early. The kid who's grown up at these gatherings.
- **Rituals.** A specific way you open meetings. A song you always sing. A toast that's traditional. A specific dish someone always makes.
- **Catchphrases.** Things people in the community say that wouldn't make sense outside it.
- **Symbols.** A flag, a logo, a t-shirt, a particular kind of name tag, a special chair.

Lore accumulates over time. You can't manufacture it on day one. You can create conditions for it to grow.

## Why lore matters

Three functions.

**It produces "we-feeling."** Lore is the difference between a group of strangers and a group with a shared identity. When you can refer to "remember the time" and people remember, you are not strangers anymore.

**It welcomes regulars while protecting against extraction.** Regular participants get to enjoy the lore as their own. They become carriers of it. The lore creates a soft boundary: visitors are welcome, but regulars are home.

**It documents what matters.** What a community remembers about itself is what it values. Lore preserves the moments that taught the community who it was. New members learn the values by learning the stories.

## How lore forms

Mostly by accident. A few patterns that help:

**Repeated gatherings produce more lore than one-offs.** The first time something happens, it's a thing that happened. The fifth time it happens, it's "what we do." The tenth time, it's tradition.

**Telling stories builds lore.** When a regular tells a new member about "the time we tried to..." they're transmitting lore. Create space at gatherings where these stories get told. A retrospective at the end of the year. An informal "tell the newbies about" segment. Stories that get told become canonical.

**Naming things builds lore.** The unnamed gathering is harder to remember. The Front Yard Friday. The Stoop Crew. The Tuesday Soup. Naming makes a practice into a thing the community can carry.

**Photos and artifacts help.** Albums of past gatherings, a notebook where people write notes, a flag for the block party. The artifacts become evidence and reminders of the lore.

**Welcoming the wild moments.** The chaotic, weird, unexpected things that happen become lore. The time it rained on the block party and everyone moved inside. The time a stranger showed up and turned out to be a long-lost neighbor. Lore loves accidents.

## How to seed lore intentionally

You can't fake lore, but you can make space for it.

1. **Make your gathering recurring.** Lore needs repetition.
2. **Use the same physical space when possible.** The space accumulates meaning.
3. **Mark the milestones.** Five gatherings, one year, fifty meetings. The anniversaries themselves become lore.
4. **Document lightly.** Photos, brief journal entries, a community Slack or text thread. Just enough record to remember.
5. **Tell stories at gatherings.** When natural moments come up, retell the history. New members learn; old members feel seen.
6. **Welcome the weird.** Don't sanitize the funny, awkward, surprising moments. They become the gold of the lore.

## When lore goes wrong

Two failure modes.

**Lore that excludes.** Inside jokes that go on too long, references that new people can never understand, lore that's used as a way of signaling who's in and who's out. The corrective: practice explaining the lore when new people are present. Brief unpacking turns lore from a barrier into an invitation.

**Lore that ossifies.** Lore that prevents change. "We've always done it this way" can be a strength or a constraint. The corrective: occasionally revisit which traditions still serve the community and which are dead weight. Some lore should die when its time comes.

## The simple test

Could a regular tell a new neighbor a few stories that capture what your community is like? If yes, you have lore. If not, you haven't been at it long enough yet, or you haven't been telling the stories.

The fix in both cases is the same: keep showing up; keep telling the stories.

## Where to read more

- The [grouphug.substack.com](https://grouphug.substack.com/) essays on lore and community design
- Priya Parker, *The Art of Gathering* (on the role of ritual and meaning)
- Adjacent recipes: [Block Party](../recipes/01-knowing-your-neighbors/block-party.md) (a recurring gathering produces lore well), [Story-Sharing Potluck](../recipes/01-knowing-your-neighbors/story-sharing-potluck.md), [Sunday Assembly](../recipes/11-civic-rhythms/sunday-assembly.md)

attribution.name: Relational Technology Project
attribution.source: Drawing on reporting about Nextdoor's 2016 redesign, 311-equity research, and mutual aid data practices

items.body:
Neighborhood technology has a documented shadow. Nextdoor's early 'crime and safety' posts became a notorious channel for racial profiling — neighbors reporting people, not incidents — until organized pressure (notably from Oakland's Neighbors for Racial Justice) pushed the company to redesign the posting flow in August 2016, forcing reporters to describe behavior rather than appearance; the company claimed the new form cut racial-profiling posts by about 75% in its test markets — Nextdoor's own figure (its CEO had told NPR roughly 50% the day before launch, and reporting a year later found profiling persisted). Peer-reviewed research on 311-style reporting finds the same shape from both directions: requests are over-reported in higher-income, higher-homeownership, whiter tracts (Minkoff 2016, *Urban Affairs Review*), while low-income and minority neighborhoods under-report street problems relative to actual need (Kontokosta & Hong 2021, *Sustainable Cities and Society*) — so complaint data is never a neutral map of conditions (White & Trump 2018, *Urban Affairs Review*). And 'report a problem' features aimed at encampments or 'suspicious activity' convert civic energy into enforcement against the most vulnerable neighbors. SeeClickFix's own record carries the critique that anonymous reporting can disproportionately target homeless residents.

The design responses, drawn from projects on this shelf:

- **Report conditions and needs, never people.** A map can hold broken streetlights and icy ramps; it must not hold 'suspicious person.' (Taiwan's Disfactory went further: anonymity *protecting the reporter's village relationships*, for reports about land, not people.)
- **Add friction where harm is easy.** Nextdoor's multi-step form is the proof that a well-placed speed bump changes behavior.
- **Route reports to care first.** 'Ms. Ruth's ramp is icy' goes to the neighbor with the salt, not to code enforcement.
- **Collect the minimum, and know who could subpoena it.** COVID mutual aid networks learned to treat neighbor data as a liability to minimize, not an asset to grow.
- **Name a human steward.** Moderation is a relationship, not a filter.

The test for any build: imagine the tool in the hands of the block's most punitive resident, pointed at its most vulnerable one. If that picture worries you, redesign before you ship.

metadata.verification_note: Citations verified 2026-08-13. Nextdoor: coverage of the Aug 24, 2016 launch (BuzzFeed News, Slate, CBS — 75% company-claimed in test markets; NPR quoted ~50% pre-launch; BuzzFeed News May 2017 found profiling persisted). 311 equity: Minkoff 2016, Urban Affairs Review 52(2), doi:10.1177/1078087415577796; Kontokosta & Hong 2021, Sustainable Cities and Society 64, doi:10.1016/j.scs.2020.102503; White & Trump 2018, Urban Affairs Review 54(4), doi:10.1177/1078087416673202.

items.summary: Every 'report a problem' tool can become 'report a neighbor.' The design line that keeps neighborhood tech on the right side: point it at conditions and needs, never at people — and add friction where harm is easy.
items.title: Design for Care, Not Enforcement

items.body:
A common pattern in neighborhoods: people see a thing that should exist, agree someone should do it, and wait for that someone to show up. The someone never shows up. The thing never exists. Everyone is frustrated, then resigned.

High agency is the opposite move. *I see the thing. I am the someone. I will start.*

This isn't about being a hero. It's about a specific orientation that the strongest community builders share. The framework here draws on writing by **Casey Rosengren** and others in the "high-agency person" tradition, applied specifically to neighboring.

## What high agency looks like in neighboring

A few specific moves:

**Skip the permission ask.** Most things you'd want to do in your neighborhood don't actually need permission. A porch hang, a block walk, a potluck, a newsletter, a Buy Nothing group, a tool library, a community fridge: none of these require approval. Some require permits (street closures, large events on public land), but most of the actual community-building work needs only a host and a couple of friends.

**Send the first invitation.** The most powerful sentence in neighboring is *I'm hosting X, come.* Not *would you be interested in X*. Not *we should do X sometime*. The specific, scheduled invitation.

**Be willing to host an empty room.** The first time you do almost anything in your neighborhood, attendance will be lower than you hoped. Maybe two people. Maybe nobody. High agency means doing it anyway, noting what you learned, and trying again. The second time has more people. The fifth time has regulars.

**Start before you're ready.** The information you need to do something well comes mostly from doing it. Waiting until you feel ready is waiting forever. Start the practice with what you know; refine as you go.

**Own the small things.** When you notice a need (a path that's broken, a flyer that's misleading, a neighbor who's missing, a meeting that needs better facilitation), the high-agency move is to take it on. Not all of it. Just the next piece.

**Make it easy for others to join.** High agency is not solo work. It's starting in a way that makes participation easy: clear invitation, low barrier, specific role. The high-agency person doesn't carry the whole load. They make the load joinable.

## Where this is different from "leadership"

Traditional leadership models often assume:
- You have a title or position.
- You direct others.
- You have a vision and bring people to it.

High-agency neighboring inverts most of this:
- No title required.
- You start; others may or may not follow.
- You hold a question or curiosity; you don't impose a vision.

The recipes in this book mostly require high-agency hosts and almost never require formal leadership. A [block party](../recipes/01-knowing-your-neighbors/block-party.md) doesn't need a president. It needs someone who orders the snacks and sends the texts.

## Common failure modes

**Mistaking talking about it for doing it.** Conversations about hosting a thing, planning meetings about a thing, brainstorming the thing: all of this can substitute for actually doing the thing. High agency notices when planning has become a substitute for action.

**Burning out by carrying too much.** The high-agency person is also at risk of becoming the only person doing anything. The corrective is to design participation in from the start: roles, rotations, distributed hosting, multiple conveners.

**Mistaking activity for impact.** Hosting many events is not the same as building durable community. Sometimes the high-agency move is to slow down, attend other people's gatherings, listen, and adjust before doing more.

**Performing high agency.** The point is the practice, not the persona. Some "high-agency" online discourse has become performative. Notice when "high agency" has become a brand rather than a tool.

## The simplest test

If you've been thinking about hosting something for more than a week, send the invitation today.

If you've been thinking about it for more than a month, the question has changed: *what's stopping you?* Often the answer is fear of low attendance, fear of being weird, fear of being seen trying. Name that fear. Then send the invitation today.

## Where to read more

- *On the Importance of Being a High-Agency Person* — [Casey Rosengren](https://medium.com/@caseyrosengren/on-the-importance-of-being-a-high-agency-person-d4f877c9aeec)
- *The Minimum Viable Community* (and related grouphug.substack essays)
- Adjacent practices: [Block Party](../recipes/01-knowing-your-neighbors/block-party.md), [Porch Conversations](../recipes/01-knowing-your-neighbors/porch-conversations.md), [Block Stewards](../recipes/01-knowing-your-neighbors/block-stewards.md)

attribution.name: Relational Technology Project, drawing on the Civic Tech Field Guide's Graveyard (Micah Sifry & Matt Stempeck)

items.body:
The Civic Tech Field Guide's Graveyard commemorates hundreds of dead civic tech projects 'for research and field learning.' Its stewards name the uncomfortable patterns: most innovation projects fail; funding success doesn't guarantee project success; and social networks for local information fail *repeatedly*.

The hyperlocal row, with lessons attached:

- **EveryBlock** (2007–2013): Adrian Holovaty's block-level news feeds — Knight-funded, widely admired, shut down by its corporate parent NBC with no notice. Data feeds about neighbors aren't community, and corporate parents kill hyperlocal on a whim.
- **Neighborland** (2011–2019): a beloved participatory-planning platform used by 200+ agencies — acquired by Nextdoor and closed. Communities that don't own the platform lose the archive of their own participation.
- **PledgeBank** (mySociety, 2005–2015): 'I'll do it if N others join me' — mutual commitment productized. It worked at small scale, repeatedly, and still couldn't sustain itself as a destination site. Commitment mechanics want to live *inside* an existing community, not on their own island.
- **The sharing-site cluster** (StreetBank, OpenShed, Favabank, OurGoods): stand-alone borrow-a-ladder platforms die of empty-marketplace loneliness. Sharing thrives where a trusted forum already exists — Front Porch Forum's borrowed ladders outlived every dedicated sharing site.
- **The disaster-born tools** (Red Hook Hub, Recovers.org): coordination tech born in crisis evaporates between crises unless it gets a peacetime job.

The survivors share a shape: owned by or accountable to their community (Front Porch Forum's public benefit corporation, Loomio's worker co-op, Decidim's association, Amsterdam's Gebiedonline cooperative), paid stewardship rather than pure volunteerism (Detroit's digital stewards, City Bureau's paid Documenters), and modesty of scope. Before building anything, visit the graveyard and find your idea's headstone — then design against its cause of death.

metadata.source_note: Graveyard framing and project fates per the Civic Tech Field Guide (CC BY-NC-SA); EveryBlock and Neighborland details per Holovaty's own post-mortem and CTFG's entries.
survivor_patterns: modest scope with a peacetime job
embed in existing trust rather than build a destination

items.summary: The Civic Tech Field Guide keeps a cemetery of dead projects, and hyperlocal tech fills a whole row. The patterns behind the headstones are the most useful design guidance this shelf has.
items.title: Learn from the Graveyard

items.body:
A counter-intuitive insight from community builders: more structure often produces more community, not less.

The popular intuition is the opposite. We imagine community as warm, spontaneous, free-flowing. Structure feels formal, bureaucratic, the opposite of relational. So community builders often try to keep things light: no rules, no roles, no schedules, no expectations.

The result is usually disappointment. A gathering with no structure attracts the people who'd be friends already and excludes everyone else. The unspoken norms become the actual norms; newcomers can't read them. The work concentrates in a few hands.

The opposite move: just enough structure to make participation easy and clear, and no more.

This framework owes most to writing by **Mia Quagliarello** and others at the [grouphug](https://grouphug.substack.com/) Substack, alongside long traditions in organizational design and group facilitation.

## What "just enough" looks like

A minimal viable structure has a few specific elements:

**A clear purpose.** Why are we gathering? What is this for? "Get to know neighbors" is fine. So is "share grief" or "plan the block cleanup" or "have fun playing weird games." Vague purposes attract vague participation.

**A predictable rhythm.** When does it happen? Where? How often? The strongest community gatherings recur on a fixed schedule. The third Thursday. The first Sunday. Every other Saturday. Predictability lets people plan; it also makes the gathering easier to remember.

**Clear roles.** Who is hosting? Who is making sure new people feel welcome? Who's bringing what? Even informal gatherings benefit from someone explicitly playing host. The host doesn't have to be charismatic; they have to be present and attentive.

**Light rituals.** A consistent opening (a check-in question, a moment of silence, a song). A consistent closing (a round of gratitude, a goodbye ritual). The bookends help people enter and exit the gathering with intention.

**A clear way in.** New people should know how to join. Is there a sign-up? A "first-timers welcome" message? A specific person who introduces them? The threshold matters more than the content for new participants.

That's it. Five elements, each minimal. Add only what you need.

## What "too much structure" looks like

Structure becomes counter-productive when:

- It serves the structure rather than the community. Rules become more important than the people they were meant to serve.
- It exists to manage anxiety. Hosts who feel uncertain sometimes over-structure to feel in control. The structure may not serve the participants.
- It excludes new energy. Long-standing structures can become barriers to newcomers who'd contribute differently.
- It substitutes for relationship. Process becomes a way of avoiding the actual messy work of being with each other.

## What "too little structure" looks like

The more common failure in community building. Symptoms:

- People aren't sure if the gathering is happening. Last-minute confusion about whether to come.
- One person is doing everything. They're burning out. Nobody else knows how to help.
- New people don't know how to participate. They come once and don't return.
- Conflict has no path to resolution. Tensions accumulate until they break out.
- The gathering depends on one personality. When that person is gone, the gathering ends.

If you're seeing these symptoms, more structure is the medicine.

## The principle: structure for what's actually hard

Structure should solve specific problems, not exist for its own sake.

- *Hard: getting people to come.* Solution: predictable rhythm and clear invitations.
- *Hard: new people feeling welcome.* Solution: a greeter role and a ritual for introductions.
- *Hard: one person carrying everything.* Solution: distributed roles and rotation.
- *Hard: conflict.* Solution: community agreements (see [Community Agreements](../recipes/04-gathering-design/community-agreements.md)) and a process for addressing tension.
- *Hard: knowing when to stop a thing that's run its course.* Solution: explicit end-of-season check-ins.

Each new structural element should solve a hard problem you actually have. If it doesn't, leave it out.

## In practice

When you're starting a new gathering or practice:

1. Pick the purpose. One sentence.
2. Pick the rhythm. Frequency and time.
3. Pick the host. Even if it's you, name it.
4. Pick the simplest opening ritual you can. A name round, a check-in question, a song.
5. Run it three times before evaluating. Patterns become visible in repetition.
6. Add structure when a problem emerges. Don't add it preemptively.

The result is a gathering that's easy to start, easy to join, and easy to sustain. Not because it has no structure, but because it has just enough.

## Where to read more

- *More Structure, Not More Community* and related essays at [grouphug.substack.com](https://grouphug.substack.com/)
- Priya Parker, *The Art of Gathering*
- *The Tyranny of Structurelessness* by Jo Freeman (a foundational 1970s essay on why no-structure organizations develop hidden hierarchies)
- Adjacent recipes: [Art of Hosting](../recipes/04-gathering-design/art-of-hosting.md), [Community Agreements](../recipes/04-gathering-design/community-agreements.md), [Block Stewards](../recipes/01-knowing-your-neighbors/block-stewards.md)

attribution.name: Relational Technology Project, after Marshall Ganz
attribution.source: Organizing: People, Power, Change (2014), adapted from the work of Marshall Ganz, the Leading Change Network & the New Organizing Institute

items.body:
Organizing is leadership that enables people to turn the resources they have into the power they need to make the change they want (Marshall Ganz). At neighborhood scale, that arc becomes six questions, asked roughly in order and then asked again:

1. **Who are my people?** The first question an organizer asks — not "what is my issue?" This is expansive: in a place, your people are the people who live there with you, not just the ones who agree with you. You find them one conversation at a time.

2. **What do we care about?** Values, not issues, come first. We find shared values by trading stories — especially the choice points in our lives — and weaving a story of self, us, and now.

3. **What resources do we have?** Every neighborhood is built on the gifts of its people. Before asking what's missing, map what's there: skills, spaces, associations, institutions, stories (asset-based community development).

4. **What could we do together?** Strategy is turning what you have into what you need to get what you want. Pick a goal that is concrete, winnable, and builds capacity — then say your theory of change out loud in one sentence.

5. **What commitments do we make to each other?** Power comes from commitment, and commitment is made person to person: a hard ask, a clear role, a date on the calendar, mutual accountability.

6. **After our collective action: how did it go? Are we stronger now?** Win or lose, debrief and celebrate. The test of an action is not just whether it worked — it's whether the community that took it is now larger, more skilled, and more connected than before.

Each question has practices on this shelf that answer it, stories that show it, and tools you can build for it.

questions: What commitments do we make to each other?

attribution.name: Marshall Ganz
attribution.source: Organizing: People, Power, Change (2014), adapted from the work of Marshall Ganz, the Leading Change Network & the New Organizing Institute

items.body:
Three load-bearing definitions from the organizing tradition:

**People.** The first question an organizer asks is "who are my people?" not "what is my issue?" Organizing is not solving a community's problems or advocating on its behalf — it is enabling the people with the problem to mobilize their own resources to solve it, and keep it solved. The organizer's job is to turn a *community* (people who share values or interests) into a *constituency* (people standing together, committed to act).

**Power.** Martin Luther King Jr. described power as "the ability to achieve purpose." In organizing, power is not a thing someone possesses — it is the influence created by the relationship between *interests* (what people need or want) and *resources* (what they hold: people, time, skills, money, relationships, votes). There are two kinds: **power with** — organizing our resources alongside others (a community credit union, a neighborhood childcare co-op); and **power over** — when others hold decisions or resources we need, and we must organize our power-with first to make a claim. Five questions when facing power-over: What change do we want? Who has the resources to make it? What do they want? What resources do we have that they need? How could we organize those resources into leverage?

**Change.** In organizing, change must be specific, concrete, and significant — not awareness raised but a goal achieved, on a date, with a number. "Stop the dam" is a wish; "get one-third of town residents to sign, and council to vote, within four months" is a goal.

Five practices turn these definitions into work: telling stories, building relationships, structuring teams, strategizing, and acting. The first three build power; the last two wield it.

metadata.source_note: Definitions from 'Organizing: People, Power, Change' (Dogwood Initiative, Leadnow, One Cowichan, David Suzuki Foundation, Stonehouse Institute, 2014), adapted from Marshall Ganz / Leading Change Network / New Organizing Institute. MLK quote from 'Where Do We Go From Here?' (SCLC, 1967).

items.summary: The Ganz organizing framework in miniature: organizing starts with people (not issues), understands power as interests × resources, and aims at change that is specific, concrete, and significant.
items.title: People, Power, Change

items.body:
Most civic technology is built for cities, countries, or the whole world. Almost all of it can be *used* smaller.

Ushahidi was built for crisis mapping across Kenya — and it can map the third places of one neighborhood. FixMyStreet was built for reporting potholes to councils across the UK — and its pattern (see something, report it, watch it get fixed in public) works for a block's broken streetlights or a park's maintenance backlog. Participatory budgeting was born across Porto Alegre — and it works on a single ward's discretionary fund, or a block association's $500.

Three kinds of remixable material:

1. **Open-source platforms** — software you can run for your own place (Ushahidi, Decidim, LocalWiki, Loomio). The license is the permission slip; the neighborhood use case is yours to invent.
2. **Patterns** — designs proven somewhere and rebuildable anywhere, even in an afternoon with an AI builder: adopt-a-hydrant's 'civic objects with volunteer stewards', FixMyStreet's public issue ledger, a timebank's hour-for-hour exchange.
3. **Stories** — what neighbors in other places actually did, which is where the judgment lives: what they built, what they skipped, why it worked.

Two disciplines keep the remix honest. First, the technology is the smallest part — the map is the 10%, the door-knocking is the 90%; every tool on this shelf assumes organizing around it (that's the other shelf). Second, learn from the graveyard: civic tech has a rich history of dead projects, and the Civic Tech Field Guide keeps the cemetery well-labeled. The pattern behind most headstones: tech that substituted for relationships instead of strengthening them, or maintenance nobody committed to. Remix accordingly.

disciplines: the tech is the 10% — organizing is the 90%

items.summary: The thesis of this shelf: civic tech doesn't have to be built for your neighborhood to work in your neighborhood. Global open-source platforms, proven civic patterns, and other places' stories are all remixable at block scale.

attribution.source: Synthesized from the documented stories on this shelf

items.body:
Six patterns recur across this shelf's stories, each earned somewhere specific:

1. **Phone-first beats app-first.** Bed-Stuy Strong's intake was a Google Voice number, deliberately — 'if we were depending on an app or online form submissions we would miss a huge swath of people in need,' as a fellow COVID network's engineer put it. The neighbors who most need the tool are least likely to install it.

2. **Paper and doorsteps are part of the stack.** E-Democracy's Twin Cities forums became inclusive through 129 in-person outreach events, door-knocking in ten languages, and three thousand paper sign-ups. Front Porch Forum started as paper flyers. 596 Acres zip-tied signs to lot fences. If the stack has no offline layer, it has a class filter.

3. **Pay local stewards.** Red Hook's mesh network and Detroit's Equitable Internet Initiative both survived because trained neighborhood residents were *paid* to build and maintain them. Infrastructure that must persist can't run on volunteer enthusiasm alone.

4. **Small, single-relationship apps remix best.** Adopt-a-Hydrant encoded one relationship — 'this civic object is mine to care for' — and was re-skinned within months for sirens and storm drains. Big platforms spread only when a local institution adopts them.

5. **Subtract friction from existing rights before adding features.** Chicago's Large Lots reduced a byzantine city land-purchase process to a one-page application — and blocks bought over a thousand lots. The highest-leverage build is often a deletion.

6. **Measure relational outcomes.** Front Porch Forum's 13,000-user study (more informed, more likely to volunteer and talk with neighbors) and Large Lots' crime findings (biggest drops when *near neighbors* bought the lots) are the proof pattern: the question is never 'did people use the tool' — it's 'do neighbors know each other better because of it.'
items.summary: Cross-cutting lessons from the documented wins: phone-first beats app-first, paper is part of the stack, pay local stewards, small apps remix best, subtract friction before adding features, and measure relational outcomes.

items.body:
Most people approach loneliness and disconnection as an individual problem. *I need to make more friends. I should put myself out there. I should be less awkward.* The structural-thinking move is to ask different questions: *what arrangements in my neighborhood, my workplace, my city make connection easy or hard? What infrastructure exists or doesn't exist? What patterns govern who meets whom?*

This shift, from psychology to structure, opens up a different toolkit. You can't will yourself into friendships at scale. You can build infrastructure that produces friendships.

The framework here owes most to **Sam Pressler** and the **Connective Tissue** project. The thinking pulls together strands from Robert Putnam's social capital research, Eric Klinenberg's work on social infrastructure, the asset-based community development tradition, and many practitioners in the field.

## The structural lens

A structural question replaces an individual one.

Individual: *Why am I lonely?*
Structural: *What in this neighborhood produces or prevents connection?*

Individual: *How do I make friends as an adult?*
Structural: *What recurring practices in this community let strangers become friends?*

Individual: *I'm too busy to be social.*
Structural: *What designs of my workplace, my commute, my family life squeeze out time for relationships?*

Individual: *My neighbor and I have nothing in common.*
Structural: *Where could we be in the same room repeatedly, doing something together?*

The structural lens doesn't deny individual responsibility. It puts individual responsibility into context. A person responsible for their own connection in a neighborhood designed against connection will mostly fail. The same person in a neighborhood designed for connection will mostly succeed, often without trying.

## What counts as "structure"

Several layers.

**Physical infrastructure.** Sidewalks, porches, parks, plazas, third places, community centers, libraries. Whether you walk past your neighbors or never see them. Whether there is a place to be a regular.

**Social infrastructure.** Recurring practices that make connection predictable: weekly farmers markets, monthly meetings, daily morning runs at the same park. Predictability matters; people develop relationships in the second, third, and tenth encounter, not the first.

**Economic infrastructure.** Whether you have time, money, and energy to participate. Whether your work schedule allows evening or weekend involvement. Whether you can afford to host even modestly.

**Institutional infrastructure.** Whether your neighborhood association exists. Whether your library hosts community events. Whether your local government supports or blocks block parties, street closures, public gatherings.

**Cultural infrastructure.** Whether your community values being known by neighbors, or values privacy. Whether it's normal to drop in unannounced, or weird. The cultural defaults shape everything else.

All five layers interact. Strong cultural defaults can compensate for weak physical infrastructure (some apartment buildings produce community against the odds). Strong institutional support can build new cultural defaults (cities that fund block stewards see more neighbor-knowing).

## Why structural thinking helps community builders

Three reasons.

First, it identifies leverage. If your neighborhood lacks third places, no amount of asking people to "be more social" will fix what's missing. Build or borrow a third place; the social will follow. The recipes in this book are mostly structural interventions disguised as gatherings.

Second, it resists blame. When connection fails, the temptation is to blame people for not trying hard enough. Structural thinking says: the people are responding rationally to the structures. If the structures change, behavior changes.

Third, it scales. Individual approaches don't scale beyond the people you can personally befriend. Structural approaches scale to everyone the structure touches. A weekly community dinner reaches more people every year than a thousand individual coffee invitations.

## Where it connects to the recipes

Most recipes in this book are structural interventions. The names of the categories alone tell the story:

- *Gathering design* (the structure of how groups meet)
- *Placemaking* (the structure of physical space)
- *Civic rhythms* (the structure of time and recurrence)
- *Shared land and home* (the structure of housing and tenure)

The principle running through all of them: don't ask people to behave differently. Build the structure that makes the behavior natural.

## Limits of structural thinking

Structure isn't everything. Two cautions.

Structure without culture fails. A perfect cohousing development with residents who treat each other as adversaries will not produce community. The relational work still matters.

Structure without justice can entrench harm. Some communities have rich social infrastructure that operates by exclusion: country clubs, gated neighborhoods, racially restrictive covenants of various kinds. Strong structure for the included, harder isolation for the excluded. Structural thinking has to be paired with attention to who's inside and who's not.

## Where to read more

- Sam Pressler's [Substack](https://samuelpressler.substack.com/) and the **Connective Tissue** writings
- Eric Klinenberg, *Palaces for the People* (on social infrastructure)
- Robert Putnam, *Bowling Alone* (foundational, now dated)
- Marisa Franco, *Platonic* (on friendship as adult practice)
- **Surgeon General's 2023 Advisory on Loneliness**
items.title: Structural Thinking About Connection

items.body:
A simple framework for assessing the strength of a community. Five qualities, each useful on its own, more useful together:

- **Connection**
- **Conversation**
- **Care**
- **Creativity**
- **Continuity**

This framework appears in various forms across community-design literature. The version here is shaped to apply at neighborhood scale.

## Connection

Do people in this community actually know each other? Names, faces, basic context, kids' names, work, what they're going through?

Connection is the floor. Without it, the other Cs can't develop. Most neighborhoods are weak on connection, often without realizing how weak. People know the neighbors on either side and almost nobody else.

**Test:** Could you, walking around your block, greet ten neighbors by name?

**Build it with:** [Block Party](../recipes/01-knowing-your-neighbors/block-party.md), [Welcome Wagon](../recipes/01-knowing-your-neighbors/welcome-wagon.md), [Porch Conversations](../recipes/01-knowing-your-neighbors/porch-conversations.md), [Map Your Neighborhood](../recipes/07-resilience/map-your-neighborhood.md)

## Conversation

When people in the community talk to each other, do they talk about real things? Or only weather and surface pleasantries?

Conversation is what turns connection into relationship. A community where everyone knows each other but nobody has ever had a meaningful exchange is shallow. A community where there's a way to talk about what matters (joy, grief, fears, dreams, conflict) is deep.

**Test:** Is there a recurring practice in your community where people talk about real things?

**Build it with:** [Story-Sharing Potluck](../recipes/01-knowing-your-neighbors/story-sharing-potluck.md), [Death Cafe](../recipes/02-small-groups-for-support/death-cafe.md), [Microsolidarity Crew](../recipes/02-small-groups-for-support/microsolidarity-crew.md), [Talking Circle](../recipes/04-gathering-design/talking-circle.md)

## Care

When someone in the community is struggling (illness, loss, hardship), does the community show up?

Care is the practical demonstration that the community is more than social. It is one of the strongest signals of community strength, and one of the hardest things to build artificially. Care emerges from connection and conversation, not the other way around.

**Test:** When the last neighbor on your block had a baby, lost a parent, or went through a medical crisis, did the community respond?

**Build it with:** [Meal Train](../recipes/02-small-groups-for-support/meal-train.md), [Mutual Aid Pod](../recipes/02-small-groups-for-support/mutual-aid-pod.md), [Dinner Party Grief](../recipes/02-small-groups-for-support/dinner-party-grief.md), [Block Stewards](../recipes/01-knowing-your-neighbors/block-stewards.md)

## Creativity

Does the community make things together? Art, food, music, performances, gardens, repairs, celebrations, traditions?

Creativity transforms a community from a service unit into a generative one. Communities that make things together also know each other in different ways than communities that only manage logistics. Making is a form of conversation.

**Test:** In the last year, did your community produce something together: a party, a garden, an art project, a tradition?

**Build it with:** [Repair Cafe](../recipes/03-mutual-aid/repair-cafe.md), [Community Garden](../recipes/06-placemaking/community-garden.md), [Community-Built Playspace](../recipes/06-placemaking/community-built-playspace.md), [Come Out & Play](../recipes/10-play-and-joy/come-out-and-play.md), [Intersection Repair](../recipes/06-placemaking/intersection-repair.md)

## Continuity

Does the community persist across years? Across leadership changes? Across membership changes?

Continuity is the test of whether the community is a living thing or a personality cult. A community that depends entirely on one charismatic person has not yet built continuity. A community that has weathered the departure of original conveners and continued has.

**Test:** If the most active person in your community moved away tomorrow, would the gatherings continue?

**Build it with:** [Neighborhood Association](../recipes/11-civic-rhythms/neighborhood-associations.md), [Front Porch Forum](../recipes/01-knowing-your-neighbors/front-porch-forum.md), [Sunday Assembly](../recipes/11-civic-rhythms/sunday-assembly.md), [Block Stewards](../recipes/01-knowing-your-neighbors/block-stewards.md), [Community Land Trust](../recipes/12-shared-land-and-home/community-land-trusts.md)

## How to use the framework

A simple practice: once a year, rate your community on each of the five Cs from 1 to 5. Then ask: which one would most strengthen the whole? Spend the next year working on that one.

The Cs are not independent. Connection enables conversation. Conversation deepens care. Care expresses through creativity. Creativity, sustained, becomes continuity. Each strengthens the others.

But they're also distinct. You can have a community with strong connection and weak conversation (an active block club where nobody talks about anything real). You can have strong creativity and weak care (an art collective that doesn't show up for each other in hard times). The diagnostic helps you see which thread is thin.
items.title: The 5 Cs of Community

items.body:
A framework from **John McKnight** and **Peter Block**, articulated in their 2010 book *The Abundant Community*. The book argues that healthy neighborhoods are organized around the gifts, skills, and assets that already exist within them, not around the deficits that need to be filled by professionals and institutions.

This framework underlies much of the asset-based community development (ABCD) tradition. It is one of the most important reference points for any neighborhood organizer.

## The core argument

Most contemporary communities have outsourced the work of community to institutions. Health to the medical system. Safety to police. Education to schools. Aging to retirement homes. Food to grocery chains. Care to professionals.

The result is a "consumer community" where neighbors are clients rather than participants. We pay for services that used to be reciprocal among neighbors. The institutional alternatives are often genuinely useful, but they have not replaced the community functions they substituted for. They have hollowed out community while leaving the underlying needs unmet.

McKnight and Block argue for the *abundant community*: a neighborhood where the gifts and capacities of residents are recognized, mobilized, and connected, and where institutions are partners to the community rather than substitutes for it.

## Three core moves

The abundant community framework proposes three shifts.

### From deficits to gifts

Most community planning starts with what's wrong: the poverty rate, the crime rate, the health disparities. This framing produces "needy" communities that wait for outside intervention.

The asset-based move: start by mapping the gifts. Every person has skills, knowledge, relationships, and resources. Every neighborhood has institutions, associations, physical assets, and stories. The strongest community development surfaces and connects these.

This is not naive positivity. Real problems exist. The point is that solutions usually emerge from the assets, not from the deficits. A community that knows its own capacities can address its own problems.

### From clients to citizens

In a consumer model, residents are clients of services. In a citizen model, residents are participants in their own community. The shift involves practical changes: who decides, who hosts, who organizes, who is paid.

Block writes about this as the "citizen way" vs. the "consumer way." The consumer way is faster and more passive. The citizen way is slower and more demanding. The citizen way produces deeper community.

### From institutions to associations

Institutions (hospitals, schools, government agencies, large nonprofits) deliver services. They are good at certain kinds of work and bad at others. They cannot produce community; only people in relationship can.

Associations (block clubs, faith groups, neighborhood committees, mutual aid networks, [microsolidarity crews](../recipes/02-small-groups-for-support/microsolidarity-crew.md), [microgrant gatherings](../recipes/11-civic-rhythms/microgrant-gathering.md)) are the form in which neighbors organize themselves. They have less capacity than institutions in many ways and more capacity in others. They produce belonging.

The abundant community treats institutions as partners and associations as the engine.

## The four properties of an abundant community

McKnight and Block identify several properties of healthy communities. A simplified version:

**Visible gifts.** People know each other's skills, talents, and offerings. The gifts are surfaced through conversations, gatherings, and intentional asset-mapping.

**Hospitable space.** Neighbors gather in shared physical spaces (homes, community centers, libraries, parks) regularly enough that strangers become familiars and familiars become friends.

**Productive associations.** Residents form small groups for support, problem-solving, and joy. The groups don't require permission from institutions; they emerge from neighbor relationships.

**Mutual generosity.** When someone has a need, neighbors respond. When someone has something to give, they give it. Generosity is normal, not exceptional.

## The hidden gifts in any neighborhood

Most asset-mapping exercises surface gifts most people didn't know were there. Common categories that turn up:

- **Skill gifts.** Cooking, carpentry, repair, gardening, music, teaching, listening, language fluency, financial literacy, child care, elder care.
- **Knowledge gifts.** History of the neighborhood, knowledge of available resources, technical expertise, professional knowledge.
- **Time gifts.** Retirees with time. Stay-at-home parents with time. Students with time. People between jobs with time.
- **Connection gifts.** People who know everyone. People who can introduce. People who hold the social map of the block.
- **Space gifts.** Backyards, basements, garages, porches, dining rooms that can host. Tools, equipment, vehicles that can be shared.

The same mapping that identifies these gifts produces relationships. The asset-mapping process is itself an act of community building.

## How to start

A simple practice rooted in the framework:

1. **Make a list of your own gifts.** Skills, knowledge, time you could share, things you'd be willing to host or lead. Most people, when asked, can list 15 to 30 things they could offer.
2. **Ask three neighbors what they're good at.** Frame it casually. *I'm curious, what are you actually good at that most people don't know?* The conversations themselves are valuable.
3. **Hold a gift-mapping gathering.** Five to ten neighbors. Each person shares two or three gifts they could offer the block. Look at the list together. Surprises will emerge.
4. **Connect one giver to one receiver.** Someone's gift matches someone's interest. Make the introduction.
5. **Repeat.** The practice compounds. After a year of gift-mapping conversations, your neighborhood has become a different place.

## Limits and cautions

A few honest qualifications.

**Asset-based approaches can become an excuse for state withdrawal.** "The community has assets" can be used as cover for cutting public investment. The framework should be paired with continued advocacy for public goods, not used to replace them.

**Some communities have been so depleted that asset-mapping alone won't restart them.** Long-term displacement, generational trauma, and active disinvestment require more than community organizing. Honest practitioners hold both: asset-based community building plus continued demand for systemic resources and justice.

**Gifts must be invited, not extracted.** The framework can be misused as a way of getting volunteer labor from people who need paid work. Reciprocity is the principle. Gifts circulate; they are not harvested.

## Where to read more

- John McKnight & Peter Block, *The Abundant Community: Awakening the Power of Families and Neighborhoods* (2010)
- [Asset-Based Community Development Institute](https://resources.depaul.edu/abcd-institute/Pages/default.aspx)
- Peter Block, *Community: The Structure of Belonging*
- Adjacent recipes: [Appreciative Inquiry](../recipes/04-gathering-design/appreciative-inquiry.md), [Block Stewards](../recipes/01-knowing-your-neighbors/block-stewards.md), [Microgrant Gathering](../recipes/11-civic-rhythms/microgrant-gathering.md), [Time Banking](../recipes/03-mutual-aid/timebanking.md)

items.body:
A four-word audit for any community effort — including any tool you're about to build:

- **To**: done to communities, without consent. Coercive, however well dressed.
- **For**: done for communities — benevolent and well-intentioned, but professionals and outsiders stay in the driver's seat, and residents learn to be clients.
- **With**: done alongside communities, in more equal and reciprocal relationships.
- **By**: communities as the architects and drivers of their own change, with outside support playing a supplementary role.

Asset-based community development's home is *by*. The discipline that keeps it there is an ordering rule from John McKnight and Cormac Russell: first ask what residents can do themselves; then what they can do with a little outside help; and only then what they need outside agencies to do for them. The order is critical — start with the third question and you preclude citizen power before the work begins.

Russell's summary of the whole stance: if we want to help people in a way that does no harm to their capacities, start with what's strong, not with what's wrong.

For builders: every feature can be sorted with the same four words. A dashboard about a neighborhood is *to*; a service portal is *for*; a co-designed tool is *with*; a tool neighbors can run, change, and own is *by*.

metadata.source_note: The four modes per Russell's community-driven development framework; the ordering rule verbatim in spirit from 'The Four Essential Elements of an ABCD Process' (CC BY-NC 4.0).
ordering_questions: What can communities do best themselves?
What do communities require help with?
What do communities need outside agencies to do for them?

items.summary: Cormac Russell's four modes of change: things done TO communities, FOR them, WITH them, and BY them. Community power lives in 'by' — and the ordering of help matters more than the amount.

*Identify which civic need (agency, belonging, or well-being) is most urgent in your community, and what assets already exist to build on.*

*When to use:* The front door. Run this before choosing a recipe.

1. **Listen to Your Community** — Go listen: take a walk, visit a community space, scroll local groups, sit in a coffee shop and eavesdrop. Note which signals you hear.
2. **Identify Patterns** — Which category had the most checks? Which statements resonated most? Which observations felt most acute? What surprised you?
3. **Asset Mapping** — What does your community already have? (You have more than you think.)
4. **Notice What's Already Happening** — Which of the eight patterns do you already see in your community? What's working about those efforts, and what's missing?
5. **Match Needs to Recipes** — Based on your assessment, which recipes might serve your community?

**Closing prompts**
- Your Starting Point: Which recipe calls to you? What pattern could you build on? What's the smallest test you could run in a week?
- Reality Check: Who else needs to be in this conversation? Who might resist, and why? Who's already doing something similar? What could you try tomorrow with $0 and three people?

items.body:
*Track whether your civic media recipe is actually meeting the community's needs.*

*When to use:* After launch, on whatever timeline fits the project. For a fuller approach, see Hearken's Return on Engagement (ROE) framework, which measures impact through connection, amplification, recognition, and care.

1. **Before You Start** — Write 3 specific, realistic changes you hope to see.
2. **Check In: Early Signs** — Who's showing up (how many, who came back, who's new, who's missing)? What energy do you see (people asking when the next one is, bringing friends, suggesting ideas, taking ownership, showing up without reminders)? When will you follow up?
3. **What's Actually Changing?** — At your follow-up point, check the signals for your need type.
4. **Collect 3 Stories** — For each: who, what small thing changed, and a quote if you have one.
5. **What's Not Working?** — What resistance are you seeing, from whom, about what (and what could overcome it)? What's harder than expected? Who's not participating, and why?
6. **Quick Assessment** — Keep doing (what's working enough to continue), stop doing (what wastes energy without value), try next (what small adjustment might help).
7. **Some Harder Questions** — Is this meeting a real need or just keeping people busy? Would participants do this without you? Who benefits most, the community or the institution? Be honest.
8. **Share What You're Learning** — With participants, and with others trying similar work. How?

*Get real about what you can actually do: assemble your team, inventory resources, and right-size your scope.*

*When to use:* After Worksheet 1, once you've picked a recipe to adapt.

1. **Pick the Recipe and Need** — Which recipe are you adapting, and which civic need (agency / belonging / well-being) does it address? Give it a working project name.
2. **Your Cooks** — Who's making this happen? Lead organizer(s), a core team of 3-5 (name, role, hours/week), community partners who've said yes, people who could help if asked.
3. **Reality Check on Time** — Who are you asking to participate? What competes for their time? What's the minimum viable commitment? Can you offer childcare or pay for time? If not, what's the value exchange?
4. **Your Ingredients** — What do you actually have? Budget, technology (group text, social, email list, website, phones, printer, or none, going analog), and existing relationships and trust.
5. **Your Scope** — Right-size honestly.
6. **Your Format** — How will people participate (in person, SMS, online, social, print, phone, mixed) and when (one-time, weekly, monthly, as needed)?
7. **Time Frame** — Planning starts; first test/pilot; full launch; first evaluation.
8. **Adaptations** — Adjust for your community: language and translation, accessibility (physical and tech), cultural considerations (traditions to build on, norms to set, whose blessing you need), trust-building (why people should trust this, what proof you'll offer, how long it takes), and safety (physical, emotional, privacy).
9. **Action Timeline** — Build the foundation (confirm team, test with 5 people, name the biggest barrier); small test (run the smallest version, document, get feedback); iterate (adjust, expand slightly, build rhythm); evaluate and decide (measure against needs not metrics; stop, continue, or expand; document lessons).
10. **Success Indicators** — You'll know it's working when ___. Red flags that mean pause and reassess: ___.

items.title: Recipe Builder

items.body:
Relational tech is a practice with four dimensions:

## 1. Purpose
Reconnect with people and the place where we live, cultivating healthy
relational soil — the conditions in which agency, belonging, and trust
can grow.

## 2. Process: Embedded Design
Spend less time building in isolation and more time in the messiness and
beauty of community life. Dreams emerge from accountable relationships,
time spent in the world together, and local needs identified through deep
listening. The result is small, meaningful software that fits its community.

## 3. Math: 1:100
Fewer "users," more co-creators. One primary builder to 100 neighbors who
rely on and co-create the tools. This reflects the emerging profession of
"local relational technologist" — people who practice their craft in service
of place.

## 4. Path: Scale Deep, Spread Horizontal
Scale deep in place and spread horizontally, neighborhood to neighborhood,
through remixing rather than replication. Each place carries its own histories,
wounds, wisdom, and gifts. Relational technology is crafted locally, through
attunement and shared discernment.

items.body:
Embedded design is RTP's core methodology for building relational tech.
It inverts the typical software development process.

## The Inversion
Traditional: Identify problem → Design solution → Build → Ship → Get users
Embedded:    Be in community → Notice what's needed → Build with neighbors →
             Iterate together → Tool earns its place

## Before You Build Anything
1. Spend time in the place. Walk the neighborhood. Go to events. Be a
   neighbor first, a builder second.
2. Listen for recurring themes. What do people wish existed? What's hard?
   What's beautiful?
3. Map what already exists. There are always existing assets — people,
   spaces, channels, traditions. Build on these, don't replace them.
4. Find co-builders. If you can't find at least one person who wants to
   build this with you, you might be solving the wrong problem.

## While You Build
1. Build the smallest useful thing. Not an MVP — a "minimum relational
   thing." Something that creates one connection that didn't exist before.
2. Test with real neighbors, not personas. The people on your block, at
   your café, in your group chat. Real feedback from real relationships.
3. Let the tool earn its place. Don't promote it. Let it spread through
   the relationships it serves. If people share it, it's working.
4. Stay accountable. The 1:100 ratio means you know the people using what
   you build. You see them at the store. This accountability is a feature.

## Design Principles
- Simple over feature-rich
- Accessible over sophisticated
- Local over universal
- Accountable over scalable
- Open over proprietary
- Remix over replicate

## Common Mistakes
- Building in isolation, then "launching" to the community
- Optimizing for growth instead of depth
- Adding features instead of deepening relationships
- Assuming digital = better
- Copying what worked elsewhere without local adaptation
items.title: Embedded Design: A Guide for Builders

items.body:
Relational tech isn't measured by users or engagement metrics. It's measured
by what grows in the soil it helps cultivate.

## Agency
People experience themselves as capable stewards of their community.
- How many people are building relational tech?
- What are their stories of capability and action?
- Are people solving local problems with local tools?

## Belonging
People feel that they — and their dreams and gifts — matter where they live.
- Are people co-creating tools together?
- Do builders report their own sense of belonging changing?
- Are diverse voices and perspectives present?

## Trust
People feel motivated to engage in generalized reciprocity and shared care.
- Are relational tech tools helping people connect more deeply?
- Are neighbors engaging in mutual aid and shared care?
- Is trust growing across difference, not just within groups?

These three outcomes reinforce each other. Agency without belonging becomes
isolation. Belonging without trust becomes a bubble. Trust without agency
becomes dependence.
items.title: Measuring What Matters: Agency, Belonging, Trust

items.body:
## Trust Building
Show up consistently. Start with listening. Be transparent about intentions.
Deliver on small promises. Bridge across difference — the hardest trust to
build is often the most valuable.
Red flags: Rushing to organize before relationships exist. Assuming digital
connection equals trust.

## Burnout & Sustainability
Co-build from day one. Rotate roles. Set boundaries. Celebrate small wins.
Rest is not failure — if things stop when you rest, the infrastructure wasn't
sustainable.
Red flags: "I'll just do it myself." Checking group chats constantly. Guilt
about time off.

## Scale & Complexity
Deepen before you widen. Use the pod model (5-15 people with bridges between
groups). Layer your channels. Delegate whole domains, not just tasks. Accept
messiness — the "river, not the gardener" means letting go.

## Digital Literacy & Access
Always maintain an analog channel. Choose lowest-barrier tools. Offer gentle
onboarding. Design for phones. Translate if multilingual.
Red flags: Assuming "everyone is on WhatsApp." English-only defaults.

## Language & Cultural Barriers
Learn the landscape. Find bridge-builders who move between communities.
Translate key infrastructure. Respect different organizing traditions.
Show up at their events before inviting them to yours.

## Conflict & Disagreement
Normalize disagreement. Create structured spaces for hard conversations.
Focus on shared interests. Don't take sides as a builder. Know when to
step back and refer to mediation.

## Maintaining Momentum
Rhythm over events. Rituals matter. Regularly invite new people. Evolve
the offering. Celebrate milestones.
items.title: Navigating Common Challenges

items.body:
## The RTP Network
- RTP Studio: Structured learning platform with cohort-based curriculum.
  Best for builders at "Building" or "Sustaining" stage.
  URL: studio.relationaltechproject.org
- Civic Label Network: 50+ cross-sector civic practitioners. Cooperative
  model that reframes civic culture workers as artists deserving collective
  backing.

## Connection Patterns for Builders

### New Builders
- Find your local equivalent — every neighborhood has informal connectors
- Join before you build — participate in existing groups for a month first
- Look for adjacent builders in nearby neighborhoods

### Established Builders
- Document and share what's working
- Host a visiting builder from another neighborhood
- Contribute patterns to the knowledge commons
- Mentor a newer builder

### Builders Feeling Isolated
- You're not alone — this work is hard and invisible. That's normal.
- Even one peer in another neighborhood is transformative
- Join a cohort for structured peer connection
- Lower the bar — scale back to one practice until energy returns

## Adjacent Movements
- Block club / block captain networks
- Mutual aid networks (many formed during COVID, still active)
- Code for America brigades and civic tech meetups
- Community land trusts and cooperative housing
- Restorative justice circles
- Time banks and skill shares

items.title: Open Space Technology

items.body:
## Start a Neighborhood Communication Channel
1. Identify 5 anchor neighbors already informally connected
2. Have 1-on-1 conversations first — don't just add people to a group
3. Choose the simplest tool (WhatsApp, group text)
4. Set the tone with the first message — introduce yourself, name a
   specific purpose
5. Seed early activity in the first 48 hours
6. Invite gradually — 2-3 people per week
7. Establish norms by modeling the behavior you want to see

Pitfalls: Starting too big, not setting norms, builder doing all the posting.

## Host a First Gathering
1. Low-barrier format — coffee on the sidewalk, potluck, porch hangout
2. Choose a time that works for your street's rhythm
3. Invite personally — door knocks, hand-written notes, texts
4. Have a simple prompt ("What do you love about living here?")
5. Show up 15 minutes early
6. Capture contact info
7. Follow up within 48 hours
8. Name the next gathering before people leave

Pitfalls: Too formal, no follow-up, waiting for perfect conditions.

## Launch a Neighborhood Calendar
1. Audit what exists (bulletin boards, Facebook groups, word of mouth)
2. Start a shared Google Calendar
3. Seed with 10-15 events (recurring + one-time)
4. Recruit 2-3 co-curators (café owners, librarians, PTA parents)
5. Share widely through existing channels
6. Consider automation for scraping event sources
7. Keep it alive — update weekly

Scaling: Calendar → Weekly digest → Custom alerts (Sunset Signals model).

## Build a Mutual Aid Pod
1. Start with existing trust — don't organize strangers into a pod
2. Keep it small (5-15 households)
3. Define what kinds of help you'll share
4. Dedicated communication channel
5. Weekly check-in rhythm
6. Rotate coordination monthly
7. Practice before crisis with small exchanges

Pitfalls: One-directional giving, no practice, too formal.

## Map Neighborhood Assets
1. Physically walk every block
2. Talk to 10 people ("Who should everyone know?" "Where do people gather?")
3. Map people, places, and organizations
4. Look for connection gaps between existing assets
5. Share what you find — even rough lists create immediate value

## The Builder Loop (Meta-Pattern)
Listen → Connect → Build → Reflect → Adapt → Share → Repeat
This is not a project with an end date; it's a practice.
items.title: Playbooks for Common Builder Needs

items.body:
People come to community building at different stages. Meet builders where
they are, not where you wish they were.

## Curious
"I wish my neighborhood felt more connected."
→ Join existing local channels. Don't build yet. Listen.

## Experimenting
"I started a group chat / hosted a gathering."
→ WhatsApp group + shared Google Calendar. Keep it simple.

## Building
"I'm setting up systems and recruiting co-builders."
→ Newsletter + calendar + one action channel. Find co-builders.

## Sustaining
"How do I keep this going without burning out?"
→ Field guide + signals + mutual aid structure. Rotate roles.

## Scaling
"How do I share what's working with other neighborhoods?"
→ Studio platform + cross-neighborhood connections. Document and remix.
items.title: The Builder Spectrum

items.body:
## Layer 1: Relational Layer (Foundation)
Who knows whom? Where does trust live? This is the bedrock.
Most builders want to skip to Layer 2, but the strongest infrastructure
builds this layer first.

## Layer 2: Information Layer
How do people learn what's happening? Calendars, channels, newsletters,
directories — the connective tissue of neighborhood awareness.

## Layer 3: Action Layer
How do people help each other? Mutual aid, shared resources, collective
projects, tool libraries, cooperative care.

## The Outer Sunset Ecosystem (Reference Implementation)

### Neighborhood Scale (Public)
- Outer Sunset Today — Community calendar & daily digest (outersunset.today)
- Community Guide — Directory of local groups (outersunset.us)
- Field Guide — Walking exploration app with past/present/future (outersunset.place)

### Block Scale (Semi-Public)
- Cozy Corner — 48th Ave block hub for events, ideas, links (cozycorner.place)
- Community Supplies — Tool, gear & book lending library (communitysupplies.org)
- Block Party Planner — Event coordination
- Flyer Map Maker — Design tool for outreach

### Private Channels (Invite-Only)
- Mutual Aid Pod (25 members)
- Block Neighbors (35 members)
- Affinity groups (parents, etc.)

These three scales — neighborhood, block, private — form a pattern that can
be adapted to any place.
items.title: Three Layers of Neighborhood Infrastructure

items.body:
Build a simple mobile web app called The Cafe Guestbook.

Overview:
Build a mobile web app that acts as a 24 hour digital guestbook for a local cafe. The goal is to capture the collective consciousness of the people in the space through intentional, local sharing rather than global passive scrolling. It should encourage people to look up from their screens, feel connected to the strangers around them, and perhaps strike up a conversation.

Core Features:
Daily Prompt: Every day, the app features one thoughtful question at the top of the screen. Examples: What is a book that changed your mind? What is the best thing that happened to you this week? What are you daydreaming about today?

The 24 Hour Stream: Below the prompt is a feed of answers from people who have visited the cafe today. All posts automatically expire and disappear after exactly 24 hours to keep the space rooted in the present moment and protect people from leaving a permanent digital footprint.

Gentle Identity: Users do not create complex accounts. When answering the prompt, they simply enter their first name or an initial. They also select a Status Emoji to gently signal their physical openness in the cafe. A coffee mug means they are open to a quick hello. Headphones mean they are deep in focus. A waving hand means they would love a real life conversation.

Location Check In: To keep the boundary of the third place sacred, users simply tap a button that says I am in the Cafe right now before they can read the stream or post their thought. Keep this high trust and simple for the first version.

Design and Tone:
The design should feel cozy, warm, and minimal. Think of the texture of a real paper guestbook sitting on a wooden cafe counter.
Use a color palette of warm paper off whites, soft espresso browns, and deep ink blues.
Typography should be highly readable, using a gentle serif font that feels slightly nostalgic or literary.
Do not include any endless scrolling, push notifications, or engagement metrics like likes, hearts, or follower counts. This is about quiet presence, not optimization or virality.
items.summary: A prompt for a mobile web app that acts as a daily digital guestbook for a local cafe, encouraging intentional sharing and real life connection over passive scrolling.
items.title: 24 Hour Cafe Guestbook

items.body:
Block Party Organizing

A neighborhood block party site that helps organize, celebrate, and document block parties. The site can either live as a page within a larger Neighbor Hub or stand alone at a custom URL for a specific block and year (e.g. 48thAveBlockParty2025.org).  
Memory & Momentum: After the party, the site serves as a joyful record and keeps the spark alive for next year.  

Public-Facing Features
Hero Section: Block party name, date, and a short celebratory note (before: "Join us!" / after: "What an incredible day!").  
Event Details: Key logistics like time, date, location, and description.  
Site Plan: Visual diagram of the street layout, stations, barricades, and schedule (uploadable image).  
Volunteer Sign-Ups: Cards for each role (e.g. Setup, Food, Activities, Support), each showing:  
Role name + emoji/icon  
Time commitment or shift details  
Spots available / filled  
Sign-up button with fields for Name, Email, and optional Notes (what you can bring/offer)  
Acknowledgements: Partners, funders, and thank-yous.  
Photo Gallery: Space for sharing highlights after the party.  
Stay Tuned Section: Invitation to connect about next year.  

Steward/Admin Features
Admin Login: Password-protected steward dashboard.  
Sign-Up Roster: List of all volunteer sign-ups by role, exportable as CSV.  
Draft Day-of Schedule: Auto-generated table that assigns roles and shifts based on sign-ups. Editable by steward.  
Email List View: One-click to copy all participant emails (comma-separated or bcc-ready).  
Notes Field: Each volunteer's optional notes are visible to help with coordination.  

Relational Touches
Use emojis for roles to add warmth (e.g. 🎤 Emcee, 🍕 Pizza Setup, 🪩 Dance Class Rally Team).  
When someone signs up, they see a thank-you message like: "You're part of the magic! We'll be in touch with details."  
Public page updates in real-time to show when slots are filled — celebrating collective effort.  
After the event, steward can flip site content to a "reflection mode" with photos, gratitude, and next-year teaser.  

Example User Stories
As a parent with kids, I want to see the site plan so I know where the bounce house and art supplies will be.  
As a neighbor, I want to sign up to bring folding tables so the organizers don't have to track me down.  
As the steward, I want a copy-paste email list so I can write thank-yous to everyone who pitched in.  
As a visitor after the event, I want to relive the day with photos and know how to join next year.
items.summary: Create tools for neighbors to organize memorable block parties with sign-ups, task coordination, and event planning features.

items.body:
In 2011, Code for America fellow Erik Michaels-Ober built Adopt-a-Hydrant for Boston: a simple map where residents claimed a fire hydrant to shovel out after snowstorms — and named them. The pattern got remixed within months: storm drains, tsunami sirens in Honolulu. The insight wasn't hydrants; it was that *small civic objects + personal claim + a name* turns maintenance into relationship.

Build it for your block: a map of the things that need a person — tree wells that need summer watering, storm drains that need leaf-clearing before rain, a bench that needs paint, the little free library that needs restocking. A neighbor taps one, adopts it, names it ('Drainy McDrainface has a steward now'), and gets gentle seasonal nudges tied to real conditions (heat waves for trees, storm forecasts for drains).

Show the whole block's care at a glance: every adopted thing, every steward first-name, every 'this thing needs a person' gap. Celebrate streaks at the block party.

Constraint: adoption is an offer, not an enforcement — the tool never shames lapsed stewards, it just quietly reopens the adoption. And it works without an account for viewing; the barrier to seeing your block's care should be zero.

guardrails: adoption is an offer, not an enforcement
viewing requires no account
names and delight are features, not decoration

items.summary: A starter build: the Adopt-a-Hydrant pattern, remixed — a map of small civic objects (tree wells, storm drains, benches, little libraries) that neighbors claim, name, and care for.
