items.body:
Participatory budgeting usually means cities and millions. The pattern shrinks beautifully: a block association's dues, a community garden's plot fees, a mutual aid fund's surplus — anywhere neighbors hold shared money, they can decide together how to spend it.

Build the cycle at block scale: (1) **Propose** — any neighbor submits an idea with a guess at cost ('paint the fire hydrant garden', 'bulk-buy sidewalk chalk', 'a proper coffee urn for meetings'). (2) **Develop** — ideas get budget-checked by two volunteer 'delegates' and merged where they overlap; every idea gets a real cost and a named doer before it reaches the ballot. (3) **Vote** — every household gets a ballot, digital or paper, same weight; a week to vote; results public the moment polls close. (4) **Do** — winners get done, with photos posted to the same tool, closing the loop that makes people believe the next cycle.

The tool's job is legibility: anyone can see every idea, every cost, every vote count, and every receipt. Trust in tiny democracy is built by boring transparency.

Constraint: paper ballots count equally and are enterable by a steward — the neighbors with the strongest opinions about the coffee urn may never touch the app. And keep the cycle short: six weeks from first idea to finished project teaches more democracy than six months of process.

guardrails: paper ballots count equally
every winner gets done and photographed — the loop must close
six weeks, not six months

items.summary: A starter build: run real participatory budgeting on a block association's actual money — propose, develop, vote, do — sized so the whole cycle fits in six weeks and $500.
items.title: Build: Participatory Budgeting for a Very Small Budget

items.body:
Build the fifth question — what commitments do we make to each other? — into a tool a small team actually keeps open.

The core object is a commitment: who committed, to what specific action, by when, asked by whom, and its current state (asked / committed / done / renegotiated). Around that core, encode the handbook's retention discipline: a follow-up queue that flags any new commitment not confirmed within 48 hours; event planning that assumes half of yeses will no-show (need four? the tool tells you to schedule eight); and a 'nobody leaves without a next date' check on every gathering's attendee list.

Make the mutual-accountability visible: the ledger shows commitments in both directions — including the ones leaders made to members ('find childcare for Thursday', 'get the flyers printed'). A team where only volunteers have rows is doing hierarchy, not organizing.

Dashboard: commitments kept rate over time (celebrate it at debriefs), and a gentle escalation view — who's followed through repeatedly and might be ready for an escalation 1:1 and a bigger role.

Constraint: renegotiated is a first-class state, not a failure. The three nos — not now, not that, not ever — all deserve a graceful path.

guardrails: commitments run both directions — leaders' rows too
renegotiation is a state, not a shame
no-show math is planned, not punished

items.summary: A starter build: a team tool where every commitment has a person, a date, and a follow-up — with the 48-hour rule and plan-for-half built in.
items.title: Build: The Commitment Ledger

items.body:
Build a debrief tool for the sixth question. It runs a team through the after-action ritual in one sitting, projected on a wall or passed around phones.

Section one — Did it work? The measurable goal (pulled from the campaign's organizing sentence), what actually happened, and an honest verdict: won, lost, or mixed — with the handbook's guardrails displayed ('never claim a victory that's not yours; never pretend a loss is a win').

Section two — Are we stronger? Structured counts: first-time participants; people who took a bigger role than last time; new 1:1 relationships formed; skills the team now has that it didn't; what we learned about our own leverage. Show these alongside the same counts from previous debriefs, so the group can see its own strength curve across campaigns.

Section three — Celebration: specific contributions recognized by name, captured so they can be read aloud.

Section four — Three lessons and one next step, saved where the next campaign's kickoff can pull them in automatically.

Constraint: the tool works after losses. Its language never assumes victory, and the strength section renders first in the loss path — because that's when the second question matters most.

guardrails: works after losses — strength counts render first on the loss path
celebration is named and specific
lessons feed the next kickoff automatically

items.summary: A starter build: an after-action tool that scores the goal honestly AND counts whether the community got stronger — new people, new leaders, deeper relationships — then turns lessons into the next campaign's inputs.
items.title: Build: A Debrief That Asks Both Questions

attribution.name: Relational Technology Project, after Front Porch Forum
attribution.source: Local Civic Tech shelf starter prompt

items.body:
Front Porch Forum's software is proprietary, but its constitution is four rules, and the studied effects (members more likely to volunteer, attend local events, and talk to neighbors) flow from the rules, not the code. Build the rules:

1. **Real names, real addresses.** Members are verified neighbors — by the moderator knowing them, which at block scale is the whole verification system.
2. **One geography.** This digest serves these three blocks. There is no 'nearby areas' toggle. Growth means helping the next three blocks start their own.
3. **One send a day.** Posts queue; the digest goes out at 6pm; nothing is urgent by design. (Actual emergencies have actual channels.)
4. **A human moderator.** A neighbor — rotating quarterly so it stays a chore shared, not a fiefdom — reads everything before it ships, and knows the difference between a hard conversation and a harmful one.

The build: a submission form (email-in works too), a queue the moderator approves, a daily digest email, and a public archive page. Posts are the FPF genre mix: borrowed ladders, lost cats, contractor recommendations, meeting announcements, thanks.

Constraint: resist every feature that makes it faster. The pace is the product. If a neighbor asks for push notifications, the correct response is a porch conversation.

guardrails: the pace is the product — one send a day
moderation rotates
growth means seeding new digests, not expanding this one

items.summary: A starter build: fork Front Porch Forum's constitution, not its code — real names, one geography, one email a day, a rotating neighbor-moderator.
items.title: Build: A Front-Porch Digest for One Block

attribution.name: Relational Technology Project, after Kretzmann & McKnight
attribution.source: Local Civic Tech shelf starter prompt

items.body:
Asset-based community development starts from what a neighborhood has, not what it lacks: the gifts of individuals (head, hands, heart), the associations people already belong to, the institutions, the physical places, the local economy, the stories. This build gives that inventory a living home.

The map has layers: **people's gifts** (only ever self-declared or gathered in a real conversation with consent — 'Maria: sourdough, spreadsheet wizardry, listening'), **associations** (the block club, the domino regulars, the church choir — with a named connector for each), **places** (the community room nobody knows they can book, the church kitchen with the 40-quart pots), and **stories** (what this corner used to be; who to ask about it).

Its most important view isn't the map — it's the match: someone plans a repair café and the tool surfaces 'four neighbors declared fixing gifts, the church has tables, the tool library is six blocks away.' Assets that never get asked for are assets the neighborhood still doesn't have.

Constraint: this is the anti-directory. No scraping, no imports, no profiles anyone didn't write about themselves. An asset map is a gift exchange, and gifts are given, not taken. Track the asking: the map's success metric is connections made, not pins collected.

guardrails: self-declared gifts only — no scraping, no involuntary profiles
success metric is connections made, not pins collected
every association gets a named human connector

items.summary: A starter build bridging both new shelves: an asset-based community development map where the assets are neighbors' own declared gifts, associations, and places — collected in conversations, not scraped.
items.title: Build: A Living Asset Map

attribution.name: Relational Technology Project, after Ushahidi
attribution.source: Local Civic Tech shelf starter prompt

items.body:
Ushahidi is a global open-source platform for crowdsourced mapping; this build borrows its soul at block scale. Make a map where neighbors pin the third places of one neighborhood — the spots that are neither home nor work where life actually happens: the good stoop, the café that lets you sit, the pickup court, the library steps, the taco truck corner, the community fridge.

Each pin carries a neighbor's words: what happens here, when it's alive, who you'll meet, one story. Submissions are moderated by a named neighbor-steward (the Ushahidi lesson: every good deployment has one). Views: the map itself; a 'alive right now' filter by time of day; and a printable one-pager for the laundromat corkboard — because the neighbors who most need third places may not be on the map's own third place, the internet.

Extra credit: a 'missing places' layer — where neighbors mark the third place that *should* exist ('this vacant lot wants to be a plaza') — which quietly becomes an organizing map: each cluster of wishes is a constituency waiting for a first meeting.

Constraint: map conditions and places, never people — no 'suspicious activity' layers, ever. That road leads somewhere neighborhoods regret.

guardrails: map places and conditions, never people
a named neighbor-steward moderates
a printable path for offline neighbors

items.summary: A starter build: a local Ushahidi — neighbors collectively map the porches, stoops, cafés, courts, and corners where the neighborhood actually happens, with stories attached to every pin.
items.title: Build: A Third-Places Map for Your Neighborhood

attribution.name: Relational Technology Project, after Bed-Stuy Strong & MAMAS
attribution.source: Local Civic Tech shelf starter prompt

items.body:
Build the intake-and-dispatch layer for a small mutual aid network, honoring the two hardest-won lessons of the COVID networks.

**Phone-first.** The front door is a phone number (voice and text) plus a paper flyer that says so. A web form exists but is the secondary door. Every request — 'a week of groceries,' 'ride to the pharmacy,' 'someone to shovel' — becomes a ticket with a rough location (block, not address, until claimed), needs, and language preference.

**A claimable board.** Volunteers see open tickets near them and claim one — the Bed-Stuy Strong mechanic that made 30 deliveries a day feel human: one neighbor takes responsibility for one neighbor, start to finish, with a check-in when it's done.

**Data minimization as architecture, not policy.** Collect only what fulfillment needs; addresses visible only to the claiming volunteer; tickets auto-purge after completion; export is a decision two stewards make together, not a button. The COVID networks learned that a spreadsheet of vulnerable neighbors is a liability to protect, not an asset to grow — design as if the least trustworthy future volunteer will someday have the password.

Dashboard: open needs, average time-to-claim, and thanks — read aloud at the monthly meeting, because the ledger of care is also a story of us.

guardrails: phone number in front, app in back
block-level location until claimed
auto-purge completed tickets
two-steward rule for any export

items.summary: A starter build: the Bed-Stuy Strong pattern at pod scale — a phone number in front, a claimable ticket board behind, and data minimization as a founding principle.
items.title: Build: Phone-First Mutual Aid Intake

items.body:
Build a collaborative canvas version of the 'Tracking Down the Power' exercise, for a leadership team meeting (in one room or remote).

Screen one — Map the Actors: sticky notes sorted into five zones (constituency, leadership, supporters, competitors, opposition). Screen two — Field of Play: a spectrum from 'greatest interest in change' to 'greatest interest in the status quo', with sideline areas above and below; the team drags each actor into position and marks whether they're actively in play or watching. Screen three — Debrief: the handbook's questions, answered as decisions ('Which sideline supporter will we pull in, and who's having that 1:1? Which competitor could become an ally? Which opposition move must we neutralize — and which can we ignore?'). Each decision becomes a card with an owner and a date.

For each high-priority actor, prompt the two power questions: what do they want, and what do we hold that they need?

Constraint: this maps public roles and institutional interests, not private lives — no dossiers on individuals, no data beyond what's publicly known about an actor's stated position. Include an export that drops straight into a team agenda.

guardrails: public roles and stated interests only — no dossiers
every debrief answer becomes a commitment with an owner and a date

items.summary: A starter build: a shared digital wall for the power-mapping exercise — map the actors around your issue, drag them across the field of play, and capture the debrief decisions.
items.title: Build: A Tracking-Down-the-Power Canvas

items.body:
Build a tool that walks someone through crafting their public narrative, using the worksheet structure from the organizing handbook.

Flow: (1) Story of Self — prompts for choice points ('When did you first care about being heard? When did you first experience injustice? What did you do?'), then a challenge / choice / outcome canvas for the one moment they pick. (2) Story of Us — the same canvas, but the character is the community: shared values, shared challenges, and at least one success that gives hope. (3) Story of Now — the urgent challenge, the fork between nightmare and dream, and a hard ask with a date, time, and place. (4) Weave — assemble the three into one draft, displayed for practicing out loud, with a timer (two minutes is a good discipline).

Include a coaching mode for a partner: the listener's questions from the handbook ('What values did the story convey? What was the challenge, the choice, the outcome? What is the speaker moving people to do?') and space for notes — questions, not verdicts.

Constraint: the tool never generates the story. Neighbors write their own words; the tool only holds the structure, the prompts, and the practice clock. A narrative an AI wrote for you is exactly what public narrative is not.

guardrails: the tool structures, the neighbor writes — no generated stories
coaching mode asks questions, not verdicts

items.summary: A starter build: walk a neighbor through the Story of Self / Us / Now worksheets — choice points, challenge-choice-outcome, and a hard ask — and end with a draft they can practice out loud.
items.title: Build: A Public Narrative Workshop

items.body:
Build a small, private-first tool for the first question of organizing: who are my people?

It holds a card per neighbor you've actually talked with: their name, what you learned they care about (their words, not categories), gifts they mentioned, the date of your last real conversation, and the next commitment either of you made. It surfaces two lists: follow-ups due (nothing older than two weeks for your active five) and 'haven't met yet' — the doors, porches, and third places on your block where you haven't had a first conversation.

Constraints that keep it relational: it tracks conversations you've had, not data you've scraped — every entry is something a neighbor told you face to face. Cap the active-relationship list at five (the handbook's part-time ratio) so the tool pushes depth, not collection. Include a gentle export so the map can be handed to a co-organizer when a team forms — with each neighbor's knowledge.

Stretch: let two organizers merge maps when they launch a team, and mark which conversations were recruitment, maintenance, or escalation 1:1s.

guardrails: consent-first: only what neighbors told you directly
private by default
depth over collection: active list capped at five

items.summary: A starter build: a consent-respecting tool for answering 'who are my people?' — track your 1:1 conversations, what people care about, and whose follow-up is due.
items.title: Build: A Relational Map for Your Block

items.body:
Build a community clubs platform modeled on BuildIRL, a club management platform created in San Francisco (est. 2025) by Saumya Gupta and Colton Heward-Mills (founders, vision, and design) with Michael Li (lead developer), Kiran Prasad, and Erin Beachkofski — open-sourced in 2026 and stewarded by the Relational Tech Project. It's a place where organizers start real-world clubs and neighbors find their people. The platform handles the unglamorous parts of running a club — applications, dues, member emails — so leaders can spend their energy on actually gathering. It should feel celebratory and personal, like being welcomed into a club run by a friend, not like enterprise membership software. Everything points toward meeting in real life.

Core Features

Discover Clubs
- A public discover page — "Find your people, build meaningful connections" — with searchable club cards by name and location.
- Every club gets a warm public profile: photos, a tagline, "Who We Are," "How We Hang" (when, where, and how often they meet), values, FAQs, and member count.
- Visitors can follow a club they're curious about without committing. And if nothing fits: "Don't see what you want? Build one!"

Joining Is an Application, Not a Checkout
- Clubs offer membership tiers — free or paid (monthly, quarterly, and so on) — each describing its benefits and what the contribution makes possible, in plain words.
- The application flow is encouraging from the first screen ("Let's see if we're a fit!"): the club's own custom questions, an opt-in toggle to share your email with club leads, then payment details with a reassurance: "Don't worry — you won't be charged until you're officially in."
- Club leads review every application personally. Clubs are curated communities, not open signups.
- Acceptance is a celebration: confetti, "YOU'VE BEEN APPROVED!", and a shareable "proud member" page with the new member's name and face that doubles as an invitation for friends to apply.

Club Leadership Tools
- Start a club in under a minute: name, location, web address.
- A management dashboard in plain tabs: edit the public page, set up membership tiers, write application questions, review pending applicants (read their answers, accept or decline), and see active members.
- Connect a payment account (e.g., Stripe) so dues go straight to the club; members can change tiers or leave anytime — easy exit is part of trust.
- Communication: customizable acceptance, decline, and farewell email templates, plus one-off email blasts to all members.
- Sign in by emailed one-time code, no passwords. Email sharing with leads is opt-in; profiles show only what members choose.

Neighborhood Remix Ideas (from Sunset IRL, Josh Nesbit's Outer Sunset remix of BuildIRL)
- Not everything is a "club": let groups pick a type — crew, club, pod, block network, one-off, seasonal — each with sensible defaults for privacy, size, and dues. The tone to set: "You don't need permission to gather."
- "Start something — three people and a date": starting a group should take a minute, not a board meeting.
- Campaigns: any group — or the neighborhood itself — can rally toward a goal (a bench fund, zine printing) or a founding-member drive ("5 neighbors needed to launch"), with a public progress bar everyone can watch.
- A community calendar across every group, and gatherings with simple RSVPs ("yes / maybe / no").
- A quiet live activity ticker — "🌿 Maria joined the Mahjong Club" — so the neighborhood can feel its own momentum.
- A second payment rail: alongside automated dues, let groups choose person-to-person payments (Venmo/Zelle links that the steward marks as received). Dues are a commitment ritual, not a transaction — "the steward saw your Venmo and said thanks at the next gathering" is a feature, not a shortcut.

UI / UX Guidelines
- Style: warm and a little bold — beige background, strong black borders with hard offset shadows (a friendly zine-print feel), a lilac accent, celebratory illustrations at milestone moments.
- Typography: a geometric display font for headings (e.g., Unbounded), a clean sans for body (e.g., Work Sans). Let each club pick its own theme fonts and colors so its page feels like its own.
- Tone: exuberant and human — "YOU ROCK!", "Let's Do This!", confetti at the finish line. Joining is "applying," dues are "contributions," and every approval is a moment.
- Mobile-first: most people arrive from a link a friend shared.

Example User Stories
- A newcomer searches clubs in her city, follows two, applies to a run club, and gets the confetti welcome two days later.
- An organizer starts a supper club, writes three application questions ("What would you cook for six strangers?"), sets a $10/month tier, and approves her first eight members from her phone.
- A new member shares his "proud member" page in a group chat; two friends apply through it that week.
- Three neighbors on 47th Avenue start a block network in a minute — no dues, just a name and a first date — and it shows up on the neighborhood calendar that night.
- A club rallies toward "50 members by December 1" with a public progress bar showing that dues cover the meeting space.
items.title: Community Clubs Platform

items.body:
Build a community income sharing app modeled on the Community Guaranteed Income Club, started in Baltimore in spring 2025 — concept by Alex Zhu, platform co-created by Alex Zhu, Tyler Heath, Deborah Tien, and Josh Nesbit, and stewarded by the Relational Tech Project. It's the home base for a small club of neighbors (a few dozen to ~150 people) who each contribute a percentage of their monthly income and redistribute it equally — directly, person to person. There's no pooled fund, no middleman, no means testing, and no money moving through the app itself: it does the math, makes the introductions, and keeps the record. It should feel warm, human, and trustworthy — closer to a neighborhood potluck than a fintech product. Money is the glue, not the point.

Core Features

A Welcoming Front Door
- A public landing page that explains the model in plain words: every member contributes a set percentage of post-tax income (Baltimore's pilot used 7%); on the 1st of each month a steward runs the calculation; payments travel neighbor to neighbor by Venmo or Zelle.
- An interactive calculator — "What would your month look like?" — where a visitor enters their income and sees whether they'd send or receive, and roughly how much.
- Honest numbers from the club's track record. Baltimore's pilot: 50+ members, $23k+ moved, monthly gatherings, 100% payment completion.
- Honor the lineage: income-sharing circles exist across many cultures — susu, tanda, hui, kye, tanomoshi — "we're carrying it forward."

Joining
- Simple signup (email sign-in link or password) with a short profile: name, neighborhood, what you do, a bio, a favorite "third space" (café, park, corner), payment handles, and monthly income — asked for gently, with a clear note about who can see it.
- New members wait to be welcomed in by a steward, who gets an email whenever someone applies.

The Monthly Cycle (the heart of the app)
- On the 1st, the steward presses one button. The app calculates each member's contribution, adds it all up on paper, divides it equally, and pairs senders with receivers so every dollar travels directly between two people.
- Each sender's home screen shows "Your connection this month": one neighbor's name and photo, the amount, their favorite third space, and a box for a short note — "a small victory, a question about their favorite spot, anything human." A "Send via Venmo" button opens Venmo pre-filled; then one tap: "I've sent this." ✓
- Receivers see care, not a transaction: "[Name] showed up for you with $200. Maybe say thanks at the next gathering."

Beyond the Money
- A roster of members with photos, bios, and favorite spots — the club should feel like people, not rows in a table.
- Gatherings: anyone can post a potluck, skill share, or Sunday coffee. "RSVP so the host knows to make enough food."
- An offers & needs board with three kinds of post: offer ("spare crib, free"), need ("looking for a dentist"), lead ("freelance gig open").
- A membership card with a referral code: "share it with neighbors you'd vouch for."

Steward Tools
- A plain dashboard: welcome new members, see the monthly math laid out transparently (who sends, who receives, who breaks even), run the calculation with a confirmation step, watch payment confirmations come in, and edit the site's FAQs and welcome emails.

Trust & Privacy
- Income is visible only to the member and the steward — never on the roster.
- The app never touches the money; it arranges and records direct payments between neighbors.
- Accountability is relational, not contractual: confirmations in the app, names and faces everywhere, gatherings every month.

UI / UX Guidelines
- Style: warm and bold — cream background, a sunny yellow hero, green for receiving, orange for sending and for needs; rounded corners, friendly cards, real faces.
- Typography: a confident geometric display font for headings (e.g., Space Grotesk), a clean readable sans for body.
- Tone: intimate and plain. "Hey, [first name]." "Not a charity. Not an app. A circle of neighbors who quietly carry each other through." A touchstone quote: "All flourishing is mutual." (Robin Wall Kimmerer)
- Interaction language: "Join the Club," not "Sign up." "I've sent this," not "Confirm transaction."
- Mobile-first with bottom-tab navigation: a member should finish their monthly send from their phone in under a minute.

Example User Stories
- A curious neighbor plays with the calculator, learns she'd send about $90 a month, reads how it works, and applies.
- On the 3rd, a member sees he's sending $140 to Marcus, writes "heard you love Café Neon — coffee soon?", taps through to Venmo, and confirms with one tap.
- A member between jobs receives $210 with a kind note and thanks the sender in person at the potluck listed on the events page.
- The steward runs the monthly math in five minutes and watches confirmations roll in over the week.
- Someone posts "need a bike for my commute" on the board; a neighbor has a spare.

items.body:
Community Supplies — Detailed Prompt

A neighborhood-powered sharing system where neighbors lend and borrow supplies to make parties and gatherings stress-free, joyful, and low-cost.\n\nPublic-Facing Pages & Features
Landing Page
Hero Section:  
Headline: "Share supplies, build community 🎉"  
Subtext: "From bounce houses to birthday banners—we've got you covered."  
CTA buttons: Join the Party (primary) + Sign In (secondary).  
Why Join (3-column icons):  
Share & Save – Why buy when you can borrow?  
Meet Neighbors – Help each other out.  
Great Parties – Stress-free celebrations.  
How It Works: Three illustrated steps (Share → Browse → Celebrate).  
Footer: "Built by neighbors, for neighbors" with contact email.  
Registration & Login
Sign-up Form:  
Full name, email, password.  
Optional: "Who referred you?" to seed trust.  
Lightweight captcha (simple math question).  
Privacy Note: Assure users their info is only shared for coordination.  
Browse Supplies
Search + Filter Bar:  
Categories (tables, decorations, games, tents, etc.).  
Condition (excellent, good, fair).  
Party Type tags (birthday, block party, graduation, etc.).  
Zip code filter.  
Grid/List View Toggle.  
Item Cards:  
Title + thumbnail.  
Condition + availability tags.  
Owner's first name + block.  
CTA: View & Contact.  
Item Detail Page
Large image gallery (up to 4 photos).  
Description: What's included, condition, special notes.  
Owner Info: First name + approximate location.  
Party Tags: Quick categories (birthday, block party, holiday).  
Contact Form:  
Name, email or phone, message.  
Default message template: "Hi! I'm interested in borrowing your [item]. When would be a good time for pickup?"  
Share a Supply
Form Fields:  
Supply name, description, photos (up to 4).  
Condition dropdown.  
Category + party type tags.  
Zip code + cross-street/landmark.  
Contact email/phone.  
House Rules:  
Section for lender guidelines (e.g., return clean, handle with care).  
Option to load default community rules.  
Steward/Admin Features
Admin Dashboard:  
Approve or flag new supply listings.  
Edit/remove inappropriate items.  
Track user participation (active lenders, frequent borrowers).  
Community Settings:  
Block-level vs. neighborhood-level visibility.  
Add moderators/stewards.  \n\nDesign Guidance
Visual Style: Gradient headers (orange → pink → purple), festive icons, and soft rounded cards.  
Tone of Copy: Friendly, communal, and celebratory. Example: "Teamwork makes the dream work."  
Accessibility: Mobile-first, large buttons, alt text for all images.  
Playful Details: Confetti or balloons animations on key actions (sharing an item, borrowing success).  \n\nAutomated Emails
Welcome Email – "Thanks for joining the party! Here's how to start sharing and borrowing."  
New Listing Confirmation – Sent when someone adds a supply.  
Borrow Request – Notifies the owner when someone reaches out.  
Reminder Emails – Gentle reminders for return deadlines (configurable by steward).  
Thank You Email – Encourages borrower to send a quick thank-you note after using.  \n\nExample User Stories
A parent borrows a bounce house and tables, saving $200 while meeting two new families.  
A renter who doesn't own much joins by volunteering to transport items with their van.  
A block organizes a "party commons" pool, coordinating shared decorations for monthly celebrations.

items.body:
Build a mobile-first community web app for [NAME OF FAITH COMMUNITY] in [CITY/LOCATION].

The goal is to create a digital extension of our foyer—a warm, safe space for members to coordinate care, share resources, and organize gatherings without relying on top-down broadcasts.

AESTHETIC & VIBE
- Visuals: Peaceful, grounded, and organic. Use colors from our local landscape.
- Typography: Clean serif headers (welcoming, slightly traditional) paired with highly readable sans-serif body text.
- Interaction: Gentle and human. Using the app should feel like a deep breath, not a dopamine hit.

CORE FEATURES
1. The "Care Board" (Heart of the App): A peer-to-peer board for specific needs (Meal Trains, Rides to service, Help with house projects). Needs are visible to the community, but contact details are private until a helper accepts.
2. The "Abundance Exchange": A marketplace for free sharing (gift economy). Categories for "Have" (extra garden produce, items) and "Seek" (moving boxes, recommendations). 
3. "Service & Stewardship": Low-pressure volunteering. Instead of a roster, show "Open Opportunities" for the upcoming service with one-tap sign-up.
4. "Gatherings": A user-generated feed for members to post pop-up social events (hikes, potlucks) separate from the official calendar.

TECHNICAL & DATA
- Authentication: Simple passwordless login (email magic link) for members only.
- Privacy: No tracking, no ads.
- Mobile First: Must work perfectly on phone browsers.
items.summary: Contributed by a community member in Ann Arbor, MI. A prompt for spiritual communities to build a peer-to-peer care app. This tool focuses on mutual aid ('Abundance Exchange', meal trains, ride sharing) and member-led gatherings rather than top-down broadcasts.

items.body:
Remixable Prompt: Hyperlocal Neighbor Hubs

Prompt:  
Build a Hyperlocal Neighbor Hub: a small, cozy website for a single block or micro-neighborhood. The hub helps neighbors coordinate care, plan events (like block parties), share needs and offers, and celebrate what makes their corner of the world special. This hub should feel neighborly, not corporate — more like a bulletin board at the corner café than a tech platform.  \n\nCore Features
Block Party Planning Flow
Featured Banner CTA: a big, friendly banner at the top ("Block Party Coming Up!" with playful art).  
Party Dashboard:  
Task list with signups (e.g., bring snacks, set up chairs, host a lemonade stand).  
Status indicators (green check for filled, open slot for needs).  
Visual icons (🎸 for music, 🪑 for chairs, 🍪 for snacks).  
Easy Contribution: allow neighbors to claim tasks with one click — no login required.  
Progress Bar: shows the block "coming together" as tasks get filled.  
Story Moments: after the party, stewards can upload a few photos or quotes to reinforce shared memory.  
Neighbor Coupons Module
Coupon Concept: coupons are invitations neighbors create and others can redeem. Examples:  
"Borrow my surfboard for a day."  
"Gardening tips over tea."  
"Try an e-bike around the block."  
Coupon UX:  
Display as colorful, perforated-edge cards, like old-school paper coupons.  
Each coupon shows the offer, who it's from (first name/neighborly nickname), and how to redeem.  
Button: "I'd like this" → notifies the steward, who facilitates a warm intro.  
Careful Stewardship: coupons aren't transactions — they are conversation starters and reciprocity loops.  
Street Cleaning Reminders
Set timed notifications (e.g., 8am on cleaning days).  
Language should feel like a neighborly nudge: "Hey Cozy Corner — street cleaning today, let's keep our block shining."  
Events Feed
Simple calendar with only block-specific events.  
Visual layout: like a friendly bulletin board or chalkboard.  
Submission form: neighbors suggest events with title, date, optional note.  
About Section
Tone: "Built by neighbors, for neighbors."  
State commitments: no surveillance, no logins unless needed, no ads.  
Name the block with warmth and specificity (e.g., "Cozy Corner," "Lincoln Street Loops").  
Contact & Steward Connection
Show steward name/photo (if desired).  
Multiple options: steward email, phone, optional group chat link, suggestion form.  
Call-to-action: "This hub belongs to us — help shape it."  \n\nUI / UX Guidelines
Visual Style:  
Pastel gradients and hand-drawn-style icons (Ocean Beach zine aesthetic).  
Rounded corners, soft drop-shadows, zine-like typography (sans-serif with playful headings).  
Emphasize warmth and belonging, not slick minimalism.  
Interaction Design:  
Keep forms short and friendly.  
Replace "Submit" with neighborly language ("Share it," "Float it," "I'll help").  
Accessibility: simple responsive design, readable fonts, high-contrast for reminders.  
Low Admin Burden: steward dashboard should feel like filling out a shared Google Sheet, not running a platform.  \n\nExample User Stories
A renter who's never joined a block event clicks the block party banner, claims "bring lemonade," and feels included.  
A parent redeems a neighbor coupon to borrow toys for a playdate, leading to a new friendship.  
A street cleaning reminder sparks 3 neighbors sweeping leaves together.  
A new family moves in, scans a QR code on a flyer, and instantly sees the upcoming block party and coupons.

items.body:
Microgrants Tool

A site to help streamline microgrants for neighbors to host gatherings, cover small costs, and spark connection. This tool provides an end-to-end flow: from applying, reviewing, and approving, to reflecting and sustaining momentum.   \n\nSite Identity & Tone
Branding: Friendly, civic, and trust-building. Warm typography (Inter, Nunito, Source Sans) and grounded palette (blues, oranges, neutrals).  
Tone of Copy: Encouraging, straightforward, neighbor-to-neighbor.  
Logo Space: Allow organizers to upload their own logo.  \n\nHomepage
Hero Section:  
Headline: "Gather your neighbors. Get support."  
Sub-headline: "Apply for a $50 microgrant to bring people together in your shared place."  
Prominent CTA: Get Support.  
Secondary CTA: Donate (to fund more microgrants).  
How It Works: 3-step flow with icons.  
Apply – "Tell us your idea for bringing neighbors together."  
Get Support – "We'll select hosts and send $50 microgrants."  
Gather – "Host your event and share back what happened."  
Timeline: Rolling or fixed windows (Applications open → Selection → Gatherings → Reflections).  
Stories/Reflections Carousel: Photos, pull quotes.  
Footer: Partner logos, mission note, remix link ("Remix this tool to run your own microgrants program").  \n\nApplication Flow (Public)
Multi-step form with progress bar.  
Basic Info: Name, email, ZIP, optional phone.  
Your Gathering:  
Date (calendar picker).  
Short description (prompt: "In a few sentences, describe your gathering and how it helps neighbors imagine what's possible together.").  
Expected attendees.  
How funds will be used (checkboxes: food, supplies, space, other).  
Commitment: Checkbox agreeing to reflection afterward.  
Confirmation Page: "Thanks! You'll hear from us soon."  

Automations:  
Email to applicant confirming receipt with copy of submission.  
Email to admin notifying of new application.  \n\nAdmin Dashboard
Password-protected with tabs:  
Applications Table: Columns for name, email, event date, funding request, status.  
Qualification: Mark as qualified/unqualified.  
Selection: Randomized or manual approval.  
Bulk Email Copy: One-click to copy all emails in a status view for BCC.  
Notes Field: Add steward notes.  
Reflections Tracking: Mark received; link to reflections.  
Payment Tracking: Manage disbursements.  
Export: Applications and reflections exportable as CSV.  \n\nReflections Page (Public Form)
Headline: "Share your gathering story".  
Fields: Name, email, attendees, short narrative ("What happened? What was most meaningful?"), optional photo upload.  
Submit triggers:  
Confirmation screen + thank-you email.  
Admin notification.  \n\nResource Library
Tips for hosting gatherings.  
Sample invitations.  
Example event ideas (block clean-up, potluck, story circle).  
Budget template.  \n\nCopy Suggestions
Application: "Don't overthink it — simple ideas are welcome!"  
Reflection: "Even a short note helps future neighbors imagine their own gatherings."  
Admin: "These tools are here to make it easy for you to support connection."  
Success/thank-you: include encouragement to keep connecting.  \n\nDesign Guidance
CTA Buttons: Contrasting colors (blue for support, orange for donate).  
Forms: Progress bars, plainspoken language.  
Icons: Party popper, handshake, coffee cup.  
Photos: Real neighborhood gatherings.  
Accessibility: Mobile-first, high contrast, large touch targets.  \n\nAutomated Emails
Email automations are sent for:  
Application Received – recap submission.  
Grant Decision – approval or decline with warm copy.  
Reminders –  
1 week before event,  
1 day before event,  
1 day after event (prompt to submit reflection).  
Reflection Confirmation – thank-you with encouragement to keep building.  \n\nExample User Stories
As a parent, I want $50 for snacks and art supplies to host a sidewalk playdate that sparks conversations about reclaiming the park.  
As a renter, I want to host tea for my apartment neighbors to break the ice after years of not knowing each other.  
As a student, I want to co-host an intergenerational storytelling night with an elder in my neighborhood.  
As a steward, I want a dashboard to track applications, approvals, and reflections in one place.

items.body:
Neighbor Story Sharing

Build a local web platform for Neighbor Story Sharing: a lightweight, emotionally warm tool for collecting and sharing personal stories from community members to build trust, connection, and belonging. It should balance simplicity, consent, and relational design with a UI that feels welcoming, calm, and human — not like social media.\n\nCore Features
Homepage
Tagline (centered, bold): "The shortest distance between two people is a story."
Neighborhood Label: prominent pill-shaped button with neighborhood name (e.g. "Outer Sunset").
Call-to-Action: "Express interest in stories below! You can select multiple. We're covering coffee for the first 5 gatherings in our neighborhood."
Filters: collapsible "Show Filters" button for searching/sorting (by language, topic, recency).
Story Grid: display story cards in a 2–3 column layout, scrollable.
Story Cards
Each story card should include:
Title (short, bold).
Intro snippet (first 1–2 lines of the story).
Language tags: e.g., "English," "Mandarin." If translation support exists, add a tag: "Translator available."
Author line: e.g., "by Maria S." (allow pseudonyms).
Interest counter: shows how many neighbors clicked "Interested."
Primary Button: "Express Interest."
State Change: when selected, card border highlights (blue) and button changes to "Selected."
Optional Badges: e.g., "We're organizing a gathering soon."
Express Interest Flow
Step 1: Confirmation modal (Join Multiple Story Circles).
List all selected stories with title + author.
Explain how it works:
We'll notify authors of interest.
When 2–3 neighbors express interest, authors may choose to organize a meetup.
Meet at a local coffee shop/library to share and connect.
Button: Next.

Step 2: Your Information.
First name field.
Contact preference toggle (Email or Text).
Input field for email or phone number.
Button: Next.

Step 3: Privacy & Consent.
Checkbox: "Keep my identity private (story will show as Anonymous)."
Checkbox: "Notify me when people want to hear my full story."
Contact method confirmation.
Button: Submit.
Share a Story Flow
Trigger: "+ Share Story" button in top-right nav.

Step 1: Inspiration Modal.
Prompts with icons:
Share something you want others to know about our neighborhood.
Tell us about your family's journey.
Share something surprising about your life.
Button: Start Writing.

Step 2: Story Basics.
Title field.
Short intro (1–2 sentence) field.
Button: Next.

Step 3: About You.
Name field (text).
Story language (dropdown).
Checkbox: "I can help translate for non-English speakers."
Translation language (dropdown).
Button: Next.

Step 4: Privacy & Meetups.
Checkbox: "Keep my identity private (show as Anonymous)."
Checkbox: "Notify me when people want to hear my full story."
Contact method (Email/Text) + field for address/phone.
Button: Submit Story.
Admin & Steward Features
Dashboard for stewards to:
See submitted stories (with or without attribution).
Track interest counters.
Export contact list of people who opted in for meetups.
Option to pin or feature certain stories on the homepage.
Localization controls: easily swap in neighborhood name, copy, and visuals.\n\nUX / UI Design Guidelines
Tone: warm, approachable, neighborly — not corporate or transactional.
Color palette: soft pastels and gradients (like Outer Sunset sky). Use warm orange/pink for CTA buttons, calm blue for selections.
Typography: large, friendly headers (sans-serif), clean body text. Avoid overly sleek or "techy" fonts.
Spacing: generous padding, breathing room between cards. Focus on legibility.
Buttons: rounded, tactile, with hover/selection states that feel alive.
Accessibility: support for multilingual text entry and RTL scripts.\n\nCopy Guidelines
Always frame participation as an invitation, not extraction.
Examples:
Instead of "Submit Content," say: "Share Your Story."
Instead of "Register Interest," say: "Express Interest."
Remind people: "Stories are acts of care. Share only what feels safe."
Include community-specific hooks like: "We're covering coffee for the first 5 gatherings."\n\nAutomation Notes
Set up email and/or SMS automations for:
Story submission confirmation ("Thanks for sharing your story").
Express interest confirmation.
Meetup reminders: 1 week before, 1 day before, 1 day after.
Story owner notification when neighbors express interest.
items.summary: Build a platform where neighbors can share their stories, dreams, and visions. Perfect for strengthening community bonds through personal narratives.
items.title: Neighbor Story Sharing

items.body:
Neighborhood Association Hub

Build a modern, community-friendly website template for a Neighborhood Association Hub.  
It should serve as a digital front porch for established neighborhood associations, supporting connection, organizing, and storytelling.  \n\n🎯 Purpose & Goals
Enhance neighborhood associations' ability to communicate programs, events, and opportunities.
Showcase both legacy stewardship and new energy—balancing history with accessible invitations.
Create easy paths for membership, volunteering, and contact.
Strengthen trust with warm design, live metrics, and local storytelling.
Serve as a model that can be reused and remixed by other associations.\n\n🖥 Pages & Features
Homepage
Hero Section
Association name + tagline/mission (e.g. Enhancing and enriching neighborhood life through youth programs, events, and connections.)
Buttons: Join Our Community (primary CTA), Community Events (secondary CTA).
Live metrics bar showing:
✅ `200+ Active Members`
⏳ `20 Years Serving`
📅 `Year-Round Programs`
Our Community Programs Overview
Grid of cards (6 max):  
Membership  
Youth Programs  
Family Activities  
Business Partnership  
Newsletter / Stay Connected  
Volunteer Opportunities
Each card with icon, 2–3 sentence description, and CTA button.
Community in Action
Featured event/program with large photo (e.g., Farmers Market).
Side-by-side: photo + text block explaining impact.
Membership & Volunteer Callout
Banner with $10/year membership messaging.
CTA: Become a Member.
About Us
Mission Statement section: clear and concise, framed as "why we exist."
Board Members grid:
Each profile: Name, Role, Bio (2–3 sentences), and start year.
Community Focus Cards (4):  
Safety Patrol  
Youth Programs  
Family Activities  
Neighborhood Pride (economic health + local business support).
Legacy storytelling:
Highlight years of service, milestones, and historic community photos.
Membership
Membership Info
$10/year, benefits include: newsletters, events access, volunteer opportunities.
Simple Signup Form
Name, Address, Email, Phone, Household details.
Payment integration placeholder (Stripe/PayPal).
Option: "Sign up as a business partner."
Newsletter Opt-In checkbox.
Volunteer Interest checkbox (with categories).
Events
Integrated calendar view.
Event list with:
Name, Date/Time, Location (map link).
Short description (≤ 40 words).
CTA: Sign Up / RSVP.
Seasonal event highlights (e.g., Halloween Block Party with volunteer needs).
Volunteer Opportunities integrated into event details:
Each opportunity shows role, time slot, of volunteers needed/remaining, and sign-up button.
Safety Patrol
Info page on neighborhood safety programs:
Block watch groups, park watch groups.
How to get involved.
Contact links to coordinators.
Callout box with "Sign up for a neighborhood walk."
Farmers Market
Dedicated section for neighborhood farmers market.
Photo-driven layout highlighting vendors, seasonal produce, and volunteer opportunities.
"Vendor Info" CTA for local businesses.
Member Hub (Logged-in Area)
Tabs:
Halloween Event (or Featured Event) → with sign-up slots, volunteer tracking.  
Member Directory → Grid with Name, Role, Email, Phone, Member Since.  
Resources → Cards linking to:
Community Calendar
Meeting Minutes
Emergency Contacts
Community Guidelines
Volunteer Dashboard
Track your sign-ups, hours, and upcoming opportunities.
Footer
Contact info:
Address, PO Box, Phone, Email.
Quick links: About Us, Membership, Events, Safety Patrol, Farmers Market.
Mini "About Our Community" blurb.
Copyright + year.\n\n📩 Automations
Email Notifications:
Membership confirmation.
Event sign-up confirmation.
Volunteer reminders (1 week out, 1 day out).
Post-event thank you.
Newsletter Automation:
Monthly digest of events and updates.\n\n🎨 Design Guidance
Warm, trust-building aesthetic.
Header navigation: sticky, clean, with icons.
Color palette: grounded greens, whites, and community-friendly accents.
Local photos as anchors (events, parks, houses, markets).
Typography: bold headers + clean, readable body text.
Iconography for clarity (membership, safety, youth, family, etc.).
Responsive across mobile, tablet, desktop.\n\n✨ User Stories
A new resident Googles the association, finds the hub, and joins as a member the same day.
A parent discovers youth programs and registers their child for a summer activity.
A student looking for volunteer hours signs up for a cleanup event.
A longtime resident checks the safety patrol section and joins a walk.
A local business reaches out via the partnership contact form after learning about the association's mission.\n\n🔑 Builder Notes
Use a CMS or Google Sheets backend for easy continuity (leadership rotates often).
Balance legacy (years serving, photos, milestones) with open invitations to new members.
Show live metrics (member count, years serving, active programs).
Integrate external resources instead of duplicating (city services, mutual aid groups).
Make it feel like the neighborhood: use quotes, photos, and local vibes.

items.body:
Build a simple, welcoming, content-first website called [NeighborhoodName]people.org.

Purpose:
Help people who live in or near [Neighborhood Name] meet each other through real, existing groups and low-pressure ways of showing up locally.

Tone:
Warm, neighborly, slightly playful, not techy. Feels like someone waving from across the street and saying “oh hi.” Avoid jargon. Avoid hype. This is about showing up, not optimizing.

Core idea:
Friendship happens through shared places, repeated presence, and doing ordinary things together. This site curates those paths.

### Site structure

Single-page site with clear sections and anchored navigation.

Top navigation (simple text links):
* how to make friends in [neighborhood]
* local groups
* more fun
* contact

### Hero section

Large headline:
oh hi, people of [Neighborhood Name]

Subheadline:
A friendly guide to meeting people and finding community in [Neighborhood Name].

Optional short line:
You do not need an app. You just need a place to show up.

Hero imagery:
Wide, calm local visuals. [Describe local landscape features, e.g., Dunes, ocean light for Sunset; Trees, stoops for Brooklyn]. Not busy. Not posed.

### “How to make friends in [Neighborhood]” section

Short, grounded guidance in plain language. This should feel like advice from a neighbor, not a self-help article.

Example structure:
* Show up more than once
* Go to the same place at the same time
* Say hi first, even if it feels awkward
* Join something that already exists
* Let it be slow

Keep this section short and scannable.

### Local groups section

Headline:
local groups

Subhead:
A growing list of groups that make it easier to meet people in [Neighborhood].

Design:
Accordion or expandable list by category. Categories should be visually distinct blocks.

Suggested categories:
* Outdoors & Movement
* Care & Mutual Aid
* Making & Creativity
* Neighborhood & Civic Life
* Faith & Spiritual Life
* Food, Markets & Gathering
* Walking, Running & Low-Key Sports

Each group entry:
* Group name
* One-line description focused on how to show up
* Optional link out

[Provide specific local examples here like 'Beach Clean Up', 'Community Garden', 'Run Club']

Descriptions should emphasize:
When it happens, where it happens, and what it feels like to show up the first time.

### More fun section

Headline:
more fun

Content:
A clear callout pointing people to local event calendars or newsletters if they exist.

### Add a group / contribute section

Explicit invitation to participate.

Headline:
know a group we should add?

Copy:
This list is better when more people help shape it.
If you know a group, club, or recurring gathering in [Neighborhood], we would love to include it.

Simple form:
* Name
* Email
* Group name
* Link (optional)
* Short note

Low friction. No account creation.

### Contact section

Friendly, human closing.

Copy example:
Questions, ideas, or just want to say hi?
We would love to hear from you.

### Footer

Minimal.
* [neighborhood]people.org
* A small line like: Made by neighbors, for neighbors.

---

## Visual Design

### Overall feel
[Describe the vibe of the neighborhood - e.g. Coastal, spacious, calm, OR Vibrant, brick, energetic].
This should feel like [Neighborhood], not “Tech Startup.”

### Color palette
Primary:
* [Background color typical of the area]
* [Soft distinct divider color]
* [Accent color]

Secondary accents:
* [Local nature colors]

### Typography
Large, friendly sans-serif headline font. Rounded, generous letter spacing.
Body text should be highly readable and calm.
Headlines should feel confident but not loud.

### Interaction style
* Smooth, subtle transitions
* No flashy animations
* Plus icons for expandable lists
* Everything should feel easy and forgiving

### Emotional goal
The site should make someone think:
“Oh. I could do this.”
and then
“I might actually go.”

items.body:
"Build me a neighborhood community guide website for [YOUR NEIGHBORHOOD NAME] in [YOUR CITY]. The purpose of this site is to help residents find local groups, recurring gatherings, and low-pressure ways to meet people in person.

Core Philosophy
The site should feel welcoming and non-promotional. The tone should be plain language, factual, and warm — like a neighbor giving you advice over coffee. It is not trying to sell anything or be transactional.

Main Content: Local Groups Directory
The heart of the site is a curated directory of local groups organized by category. Each category should have a distinct color scheme. Suggested categories:
1. Outdoors & Movement
2. Care for People & Place
3. Making & Creativity
4. Neighborhood & Civic Life
5. Faith & Spiritual Life
6. Food & Gathering

For each group, include: Name, brief friendly description, website link, and optionally meeting times.

Visual Design
The site should reflect the local landscape and feel approachable. Use a warm color palette derived from the local environment (e.g., if coastal: sandy tones and ocean blues; if urban: brick warm tones and park greens). Use friendly display fonts, plenty of whitespace, and clear accordion-style listings.

Additional Sections
1. Tips for Making Friends: Genuine advice like 'show up more than once,' 'say hi first,' and 'let relationships build slowly.'
2. Events Link: Prominent link to external local calendars.
3. Suggest a Group Form: Simple form with spam protection.
4. Contact Form.

Technical Considerations
- Fast and mobile-friendly
- Schema markup for local resources
- CRITICAL: Include an AI-friendly text file at a public URL that summarizes the site's purpose and lists all groups. This helps AI assistants accurately recommend these local resources to neighbors asking questions.

Data Architecture
Keep group data in a central location that feeds the visual display, the search schema, and the AI-summary file simultaneously.

Start by asking me about my neighborhood context, and I will provide the specific list of groups."

items.body:
Neighborhood Today

Build a Neighborhood Today site: a hyperlocal events and community calendar that helps neighbors see what's happening, make small plans, and feel part of a shared rhythm. The site should feel warm, light, and human, not like an institutional app. It's a calendar that celebrates local life—civic care and cultural joy side by side.  \n\nCore Features  
Curated Daily Feed  
Homepage shows what's happening today and soon—no endless lists.  
Each card includes title, time, location, tag (music, family, hidden gem, civic care), and short description.  
Tags should feel community-shaped, not corporate. Examples: "hidden gem," "community fave."  
My Plan Builder  
Visitors can click "Add to My Plan" on any event.  
Side panel stores their personal picks with the option to:  
reorder,  
add notes,  
export/share (text, calendar file, QR).  
No login required; plan persists in browser storage.  
Add playful touches like surfacing a neighborly note: "🌊 Also, 8 neighbors are surfing OB today."  
Event Submission Flow  
Quick Submit: simple form with title, time, place.  
Detailed Submit: option to add description, type, recurring info, or upload a flyer.  
Accessible to everyone—no barriers for small or informal events.  
Steward or small group reviews before publishing.  
Community-Civic Blend  
Calendar should celebrate both joy and care.  
Examples: open mics, farmers markets, cleanup days, food distribution, block parties, sunrise walks.  
Position civic maintenance as equally worth showing up for as cultural events.  
Privacy & Community Care  
No tracking, no data sales, no cookies beyond function.  
Clear, human privacy policy ("we only use your info to follow up on your event submission").  
Community care note: if conflict arises, stewards can help talk it through and repair.  \n\nUI / UX Guidelines  
Style: minimal, warm, and legible. Light background, rounded edges, pastel accents.  
Typography: friendly sans-serif with soft weight; headings slightly playful.  
Layout: grid of cards for events, simple planner sidebar, mobile-first design.  
Interaction language: replace "Submit" with "Share your event" or "Float it." Replace "Export" with "Take it with you."  
Accessibility: mobile-optimized, large touch targets, high contrast.  
Tone: community-first, never commercial.  \n\nExample User Stories  
A newcomer to the neighborhood browses the feed and quickly finds a farmers market, a jam session, and a cleanup—all in walking distance.  
A parent builds a weekend plan with their child, adding one cultural event and one civic event.  
A neighbor posts a casual "sunset skate meetup" that three others join after seeing it.  
A steward uses the site to remind people about a block potluck, and QR codes link directly to the event page.  
A long-time resident notices "20+ neighbors are going to poetry night" and decides to finally show up.

items.body:
Privacy & Terms Page Prompt

Create a warm, clear, and human-centered Privacy & Terms page for relational tech sites and apps. Use simple language, avoid legal jargon, and keep the tone community-first. The structure and copy should follow the examples provided.

Page Structure

Header
Title: Privacy & Terms
Subtitle (optional): short description of the project or site (e.g., "NeighborStories.org is a project run by the people who live here.")  
  → This text should be editable for each project.

Sections

Privacy
Bulleted list (orange dots):  
We don't sell or share your data.  
We don't use tracking cookies.  
If you give us your contact information, we'll only use it for the purpose you expect (like notifying you about a meetup where a story will be shared).  
You can ask us to delete your information at any time.  
This site is intended for people 14 and older.  

→ The bulleted list should be editable and remixable.

Terms of Use
Bulleted list (pink dots):  
Please use this site with care and respect.  
You are responsible for your own actions when participating in gatherings.  
We don't endorse user content.  
We accept no liability for what happens in and around this tool.  
This site is operated in [Location, e.g. CA, USA] and any disputes are subject to its laws.  
We may update these terms if needed, but we'll keep them simple and human.  

→ Allow site owners to edit the legal location and adjust the list to fit their community context.

Community Care (optional section)
Short paragraph:  
  "We know things don't always go perfectly. If a misunderstanding or conflict arises, our volunteers are happy to help neighbors talk it through and find repair."

→ Make this optional but recommended for relational tech projects. Tone should emphasize repair and care.

Contact Box
Section titled Questions?  
Contact method:  
Email: hello@relationaltechproject.org (editable per site)  
Display in a soft, friendly callout box.  

Design Guidance

items.body:
App Title: Street Beat Newsletter Tool

Context:
Build a mobile-first web app for a neighborhood curator (human-in-the-loop). The goal is to walk around a neighborhood, capture information from physical posters AND text notes, and export it all into a single, formatted HTML email newsletter at the end of the week.

Core Features:

1. THE CAPTURE INTERFACE (Home Screen)
Create two distinct 'Input' buttons at the top:
A. 'Scan Poster' (Camera Action)
- Opens camera.
- Captures photo.
- Uses AI Vision (e.g. GPT-4o) to extract Title, Date, Time, Location, Description.
- Saves the cropped image of the poster.

B. 'Stoop Talk' (Text Note Action)
- A simple text field for quick observations (e.g., 'The cherry blossoms on 6th Ave are popping', or 'Street cleaning is canceled tomorrow').
- A 'Category' dropdown (General, Alert, Appreciation, Lost & Found).
- No image required.

2. THE REVIEW DASHBOARD (The Editor)
A list view of all items captured this week.
- Allow me to edit the text for both Posters and Notes.
- Allow me to delete/archive items that are spam or duplicates.
- Allow dragging and dropping to reorder.

3. THE NEWSLETTER GENERATOR (Export)
A button that says 'Copy Email HTML.' It should generate code compatible with standard email clients (Gmail/Substack).

Layout Structure:
- Header: 'This Week in [Neighborhood Name]'
- Section 1: 'Stoop Talk' (The Text Notes)
-- Display these as a clean, bulleted list or small text cards.
-- Use a light background color to separate them from events.
- Section 2: 'On The Board' (The Posters)
-- Display each event with the full-width image of the poster.
-- Below the image, put the Title, Date, and Location in clear, bold text.
- Footer: 'Curated by a human neighbor.'

STYLE GUIDE:
- Aesthetic: High contrast, utilitarian, 'Street smart.'
- Typography: Clean sans-serif (Inter or Roboto).
- Accent Color: Neon Yellow or Safety Orange.

TECHNICAL STACK:
- React / Next.js
- Supabase for database (preserves drafts efficiently).
- OpenAI API (or similar) for the Vision/OCR tasks.
- Tailwind CSS for styling.
items.summary: Contributed by Grant from Inner Richmond, SF. A tool for a neighborhood curator to turn photos of street posters and neighbor observations ('stoop talk') into a curated weekly email newsletter. It prioritizes 'street data' and human curation over algorithmic feeds.

items.body:
## What it is

A community development methodology developed by David Cooperrider and Diana Whitney that shifts conversation away from problem-finding and toward strength-finding. Groups gather stories of moments when the community was at its best, identify the conditions that made those moments possible, and design forward from there.

The framework moves through four phases (the "4-D Cycle"): **Discover** what's working. **Dream** what could be. **Design** the propositions and structures that move toward it. **Destiny** the commitments and actions that make it real.

## Why it works

Most community processes start by asking "what's wrong here." That framing trains people to see deficits, blame, and lack. It also tends to disempower the people closest to the situation, who become "problems to solve" rather than authors of solutions.

AI inverts the question. People become experts on the times their community was at its best. The stories they tell carry the specific conditions, relationships, and choices that produced those moments. The forward design grows out of evidence of what's possible because it actually happened.

It's not naïve. AI doesn't deny problems. It just sequences the conversation differently: strengths first, then aspirations, then design.

## What you need

- **Time:** 3 to 12 months for a full cycle. Often a 2 to 4 day "summit" anchors the intensive work.
- **People:** 30+ community members representing diverse perspectives. Trained interviewers.
- **Space:** Interview spaces (one-on-one or small group). A summit venue with breakout areas.
- **Materials:** Interview guides, recording equipment, flip charts, story synthesis tools.
- **Skills:** Appreciative listening, strength-spotting, facilitation of visioning, asset mapping.
- **Energy level:** Moderate. Builds momentum through story collection.

## How to host it

### Phase 1: Discover (4 to 8 weeks)

1. **Craft the appreciative interview question.** The question should prompt stories of peak moments. Examples: *Tell me about a time when this neighborhood felt most alive. Describe a moment when you knew this community could do anything. When have you seen our institutions at their best?*
2. **Train interviewers.** Often community members themselves. They learn to listen for the texture of the story, the specific conditions, the relationships and choices that mattered.
3. **Conduct interviews.** Aim for 30 to 100 interviews depending on community size. Each interview is 30 to 60 minutes. Record or take detailed notes.
4. **Analyze the stories.** Identify themes, repeated conditions, unique factors (leadership patterns, relationships, cultural practices) that made the peak moments possible.

### Phase 2: Dream (a session or two)

5. **Gather the broader community.** A summit format works well. People share the stories they heard.
6. **Invite the room to imagine.** "If our community amplified what was happening in these stories, what would it look like in five years?" Visual, narrative, sometimes embodied.

### Phase 3: Design (a session or two)

7. **Create provocative propositions.** Statements describing the community as if the dream were already true. Bold, specific, written in present tense. Example: *"In our neighborhood, every newcomer is greeted within their first week and has at least three named connections by the end of their first month."*
8. **Identify the structures that make each proposition real.** Practices, programs, agreements, infrastructure, decision-making processes.

### Phase 4: Destiny (ongoing)

9. **Commit to specific actions.** Who is doing what, by when. Tied to the propositions.
10. **Implement and reflect.** What's working? What needs adjustment? AI sees implementation as another cycle of inquiry, not an end point.

## Variations

**Mini-AI for a specific question.** A weekend version focused on one specific community challenge. Interview phase compressed; summit lasts a day.

**AI inside an organization.** Used widely in nonprofits, schools, and faith communities for strategic planning. Often produces longer-lasting change than traditional SWOT-style strategy work.

**AI as orientation.** A new group or coalition uses the appreciative interview as the first conversation. Sets a culture from the start.

## Stories from neighborhoods

The methodology emerged from David Cooperrider and Diana Whitney at Case Western Reserve University. The Center for Appreciative Inquiry has documented applications across community development organizations, municipal governments, schools, faith communities, and rural development initiatives.

In neighborhood-scale work, AI has been used by communities recovering from disasters, neighborhoods undergoing gentrification, schools rebuilding trust with families, and faith communities renewing their sense of purpose.

## Where to learn more

- The home: [Center for Appreciative Inquiry](https://centerforappreciativeinquiry.net/)
- Community application: [centerforappreciativeinquiry.net/appreciative-inquiry-community-development](https://centerforappreciativeinquiry.net/appreciative-inquiry-offering/appreciative-inquiry-community-development/)
- Foundational text: David Cooperrider and Diana Whitney, *Appreciative Inquiry: A Positive Revolution in Change*
- Adjacent recipes: [World Cafe](./world-cafe.md), [Art of Hosting](./art-of-hosting.md), [Map Your Neighborhood](../07-resilience/map-your-neighborhood.md)

items.body:
## What it is

Not a single method but a framework that integrates several. Art of Hosting (AoH) practitioners treat themselves as "hosts" of conversations rather than "facilitators" running an agenda. They prepare a clear purpose, invite the right mix of people, arrange the space, and then move fluidly between different gathering forms depending on what the work needs.

The community of practice emerged in the late 1990s through facilitators including Chris Corrigan, Toke Møller, Monica Nissén, and others.

## Why it works

A complex social challenge rarely fits one format. Some conversations need a circle. Some need rotating tables. Some need self-organized sessions. Some need a strengths-focused inquiry. Art of Hosting is a way of holding a multi-day or multi-session gathering that moves between forms as the work requires, rather than forcing every conversation into one method.

The framing of "host" rather than "facilitator" also does work. A facilitator stands in front of a process. A host welcomes a guest. The relational frame changes what the room feels like.

## What you need

- **Time:** 2 to 8 hours for a single session. Multi-day for intensive work.
- **People:** 8 to 1,000+ participants. Diverse perspectives are essential.
- **Space:** Physical space with movable furniture, multiple breakout areas, welcoming atmosphere.
- **Materials:** Flip charts, markers, name tags, optional recording equipment.
- **Skills:** Facilitation training. Comfort with emergence and uncertainty. Ability to listen deeply. Capacity to hold space.
- **Energy level:** Moderate to high.

## How to host it

1. **Get clear on purpose first.** AoH starts with the "calling question": *Why are we gathering? What is the work we're being called to do?* Spend real time here. A clear calling question is the spine of the whole gathering.
2. **Invite the right mix.** Diversity of perspective, lived experience, role, and power. Not "the usual suspects." A small core team can map who needs to be in the room.
3. **Prepare the space.** Movable furniture. Multiple corners for breakouts. Welcoming sound and light. Food. The room is one of your co-hosts.
4. **Open with circle.** Begin most AoH gatherings with a circle check-in (see [Talking Circle](./talking-circle.md)). It establishes presence and accountability before any task begins.
5. **Move between methods.** Over the course of a session or multi-day, draw on:
   - [World Cafe](./world-cafe.md) for cross-pollinating ideas across small groups.
   - [Open Space Technology](./open-space.md) for participant-driven sessions on emerging topics.
   - [Appreciative Inquiry](./appreciative-inquiry.md) for strengths-based exploration.
   - Talking circles for the deeper or harder conversations.
   - Pro-action cafe for moving from conversation to commitment.
6. **Build harvesting in.** AoH treats "harvesting" as as important as hosting. What does the group take away in writing, in commitments, in images, in body memory? Use graphic recording, summary writers, photo documentation, group action lists.
7. **Close with circle.** End the way you began. Each voice. Each presence acknowledged.
8. **Plan the follow-through before you leave.** Who is doing what, by when? What is the next gathering? How will the harvest be shared?

## Variations

**Single-method use.** Most communities don't host days-long AoH gatherings; they pick one method (cafe, circle, Open Space) for a specific need. That's fine. AoH is also a way of thinking, not just a multi-day format.

**Cohort training.** AoH practitioners run multi-day trainings that introduce the methodology. These are deep introductions and worth attending if you do this work regularly. See [artofhosting.org](https://artofhosting.org/) for upcoming offerings.

**Online AoH.** Adapts to virtual contexts. The methods scale to video.

## Stories from neighborhoods

The AoH community of practice has been used by nonprofits addressing social change, city planning initiatives, healthcare reform, climate adaptation, and organizational transformation. Practitioners work in Toronto, Vancouver, the Nordic countries, the U.S., the U.K., across Africa, and globally.

The strongest single reference is **Chris Corrigan's blog** at [chriscorrigan.com](https://chriscorrigan.com/), which has been published since 2002 and includes a deep archive of practice writing.

## Where to learn more

- The home community: [Art of Hosting](https://artofhosting.org/)
- Practitioner blog: [Chris Corrigan](https://chriscorrigan.com/)
- Adjacent recipes: [World Cafe](./world-cafe.md), [Open Space Technology](./open-space.md), [Talking Circle](./talking-circle.md), [Appreciative Inquiry](./appreciative-inquiry.md)

## What it is

A small group of families who watch each other's children on a points-or-tokens system. Each family earns points by sitting and spends them when they need care. The math is simple. The relationships are the real product.

Babysitting co-ops have been quietly running for decades in some neighborhoods. They save families hundreds to thousands of dollars a year. More importantly, kids grow up with multiple trusted adults nearby. That changes everything.

## Why it works

A regular sitter costs a lot and is one relationship. A co-op costs nothing and embeds your kids in a network of caring adults who know them, their schedules, their allergies, and their bedtime rituals. The relationships flow both ways: the co-op becomes the social spine of the families involved.

The points system removes awkwardness. Nobody owes anyone a favor. Everyone is participating in a balanced exchange.

## What you need

- **Time:** 1 to 2 hours of initial planning. 10 to 15 minutes per exchange. Quarterly meetings.
- **People:** 4 to 12 families with kids, geographically close enough to walk or drive easily.
- **Space:** Members' homes.
- **Materials:** A tracking system. A shared spreadsheet, poker chips, or printed "babysitting bucks." All work.
- **Skills:** Light facilitation, communication, flexibility.
- **Energy level:** Low to moderate, distributed across the group.

## How to host it

1. **Find 4 to 8 interested families.** Pitch it at a [block party](../01-knowing-your-neighbors/block-party.md), a parent group, a school pickup. Look for families whose kids are similar ages or who get along.
2. **Hold a setup meeting.** Decide your points system together. A common version: each family starts with 20 points. One hour of sitting = 1 point (per family, not per child). Night hours after 9pm count double. Multiple kids count 1.5x. Holidays optional.
3. **Pick a tracking method.** A shared Google Sheet is easiest. Poker chips are charming. Printed "babysitting bucks" feel like real money. Use what your group likes.
4. **Write a one-page guidelines doc.** Cancellation policy (24 hours notice), what happens if someone falls into significant point debt, food/snacks expectations, bedtime norms, emergency contacts.
5. **Run your first exchange.** Pick a family who needs a date night first. The cycle begins.
6. **Hold quarterly meetings.** Address frictions, balance issues, invite new families if you want to. Use the meeting to deepen relationships, not just to do logistics.
7. **Welcome new families slowly.** Each new family needs to be vouched for. Two existing families is a good rule. Trust scales with shared experience.

## Variations

**Sleep version.** Extends to overnight care for older kids. Higher trust threshold, much higher value when it works.

**Day-care swap.** Two families with similar schedules trade days. Lower-key, doesn't need a points system, works for two families that click.

**Cross-block version.** A co-op that spans a few blocks rather than one. More families, slightly more driving.

**Inter-co-op gatherings.** Larger gatherings where multiple co-ops bring kids together. Builds the network of networks.

## Stories from neighborhoods

**Montana State University student housing.** Families formed a co-op with nothing but poker chips and monthly meetings. Chips exchanged at each sitting. Worked beautifully for a population that had little money and a lot of need.

**East Coast co-ops.** Some have run for decades with 20 to 30 families. Sophisticated systems. Printed bucks. Annual potlucks. Long histories of kids who grew up across each other's houses and now organize co-ops of their own with their kids.

The average family in an active co-op saves an estimated $500 or more a year. The harder thing to measure is what it means for a kid to grow up knowing four other families well enough to feel at home in them.

## Where to learn more

- Setup guide: [Nolo's How to Form a Community Babysitting Co-op](https://www.nolo.com/legal-encyclopedia/how-form-community-babysitting-co-op.html)
- Adjacent recipes: [Mutual Aid Pod](./mutual-aid-pod.md), [Time Banking](../03-mutual-aid/timebanking.md), [Block Party](../01-knowing-your-neighbors/block-party.md)
