items.body:
## What it is

A loose family of practices for building relationships across religious and spiritual difference. Interfaith dialogue circles, joint service projects, study groups across traditions, shared meals, and structured curricula like Interfaith America's BRIDGE program for campus interfaith engagement.

The work is older than the term. Religious communities have practiced cross-tradition dialogue and shared service for centuries. Contemporary movements have built more visible infrastructure and curricula.

## Why it works

Religious difference is one of the deepest fault lines in many communities. It's also one where people often share more than they realize: a commitment to care for the stranger, to honor the dead, to mark sacred time, to feed each other. Practices that put people from different traditions into shared room and shared work surface those overlaps without erasing the real differences.

The work is not "we're all really the same." It's closer to "we are different in ways that matter, and we can still do this together."

## What you need

- **Time:** Varies dramatically. A single dialogue: 90 minutes. A semester-long curriculum: months. A long-running interfaith partnership: years.
- **People:** Faith leaders or lay leaders willing to organize. Participants from multiple traditions.
- **Space:** Often rotates across the participating communities' spaces (mosque, church, synagogue, temple). Neutral spaces also work.
- **Materials:** A discussion guide or curriculum. [Interfaith America](https://www.interfaithamerica.org/) and others provide many. Food that honors dietary practices across traditions.
- **Skills:** Facilitation across difference. Willingness to handle awkward moments. Respect for what each tradition considers sacred.
- **Energy level:** Moderate.

## How to host it

1. **Start with leaders, not events.** Before any public event, spend time with the leaders of the participating communities. One-on-one conversations. Build the relationships that will hold the work together when something goes wrong.
2. **Decide the form.** Common forms:
   - **Dialogue circles.** Small group conversations on shared themes (hospitality, grief, justice, holy time).
   - **Joint service.** A shared project (a community garden, a winter coat drive, a hot meal program).
   - **Study group.** Reading sacred texts from each other's traditions together, often led by clergy or scholars from each.
   - **Visits.** Attending each other's services as observers.
   - **Curricula.** Programs like [Interfaith America's BRIDGE](https://www.interfaithamerica.org/curricula/bridge/) for campus contexts.
3. **Set respectful agreements.** Confidentiality. No proselytizing. Permission to ask questions, including hard ones, with humility. Permission to say "I don't want to answer that yet."
4. **Honor practices and constraints.** Dietary laws. Prayer times. Holy days. Gender-segregation traditions in some communities. Schedule and food planning needs to reflect these from the start.
5. **Let the form go deeper over time.** A first dialogue is introductory. By the fifth or tenth, real depth becomes possible. Be patient with the arc.
6. **Move toward shared work.** Dialogue alone has a ceiling. Shared service builds different kinds of trust. Most strong interfaith partnerships have both.
7. **Acknowledge difference.** Don't paper over genuine theological or political disagreement. Sit with it. Surface what you can, and live with what you can't.
8. **Pass it on.** Stronger interfaith work involves the next generation. Bring in young people. Train new facilitators.

## Variations

**Refugee resettlement.** Interfaith partnerships often grow out of joint refugee resettlement work. Sponsoring a family together is a long-term shared project that builds relationship through shared responsibility.

**Civic interfaith.** Faith communities organizing together on issues like housing, immigration, climate, or racial justice. The shared work is the bridge.

**Spiritual but not religious.** Many contemporary "interfaith" spaces include people who are spiritual but not affiliated with a tradition. Communities like [Nuns & Nones](https://www.nunsandnones.org/) bridge religious and post-religious spiritual seekers.

**Campus interfaith.** Structured programs for universities and colleges. [Interfaith America's BRIDGE Curriculum](https://www.interfaithamerica.org/curricula/bridge/) is the most-used resource.

## Stories from neighborhoods

**Interfaith America** (founded by Eboo Patel as Interfaith Youth Core) has built one of the largest interfaith networks in the U.S., training thousands of young leaders and producing extensive curricula.

**Parish Collective** has supported neighborhood-rooted Christian communities in interfaith partnerships across the U.S. and internationally.

**Nuns & Nones** has built relationships between Catholic women religious and unaffiliated millennial spiritual seekers around shared commitments to justice and contemplative life.

Many of the most durable interfaith partnerships started locally and quietly: a rabbi and an imam meeting for coffee for ten years, a church and a mosque sharing a building, a Sikh community and a Methodist church running a food pantry together.

## Where to learn more

- The largest network: [Interfaith America](https://www.interfaithamerica.org/)
- Campus curriculum: [BRIDGE Curriculum](https://www.interfaithamerica.org/curricula/bridge/)
- Christian neighborhood network: [Parish Collective](https://parishcollective.org/)
- Catholic-secular bridge: [Nuns & Nones](https://www.nunsandnones.org/)
- Adjacent recipes: [Story-Sharing Potluck](../01-knowing-your-neighbors/story-sharing-potluck.md), [Civic Saturday](./civic-saturday.md), [Talking Circle](../04-gathering-design/talking-circle.md)

## What it is

A community-led transformation of a residential street intersection into a small public square. A large painted design covers the asphalt. Around the edges, neighbors build seating, message boards, a tiny library, sometimes a community tea station or tool exchange. The intersection becomes a place where neighbors stop instead of pass through.

The practice was pioneered by the [City Repair Project](https://cityrepair.org) in Portland, Oregon, starting in 1996. Their flagship project, **Share-It Square** at SE 9th and SE Sherrett, is the model that hundreds of others have followed.

## Why it works

Most residential streets are over-engineered for cars and under-imagined for everything else. An intersection is the most public point on a block. Paint and a few simple structures turn it from a hazard into an invitation. The act of building it together is at least as important as the result.

Intersection repair is also tactical urbanism that often becomes permanent infrastructure. Cities that initially resisted have learned that these spaces reduce traffic speed, build social cohesion, and improve neighborhood safety more than enforcement does.

## What you need

- **Time:** 2 to 4 weeks of planning. 1 to 3 days of construction and painting.
- **People:** 5 to 50+ volunteers. A core team of 3 to 5 organizers and designers.
- **Space:** A residential intersection. Adjacent space for materials and tool storage.
- **Materials:** Paint and brushes (lots), wood for structures, basic tools, plants, mulch. Optional: bricks, pavers, signage materials.
- **Skills:** Artistic design, community organizing, basic construction, painting, negotiation with the city.
- **Energy level:** High. Sustained physical labor and creative energy.

## How to host it

1. **Get the neighbors together first.** Knock on every door on the four corners (and the adjacent block) at least twice. The project will only work if there is genuine consent. A few resistant neighbors can kill it; bringing them in early often turns them.
2. **Form a design team.** 5 to 10 neighbors who'll meet a few times to shape the design. Include kids. Include longtime residents. Include the building owners of every corner.
3. **Get city permission.** This varies enormously. Some cities have intersection repair permitting (Portland does). Most don't. A few options:
   - Apply for a "block party" permit and do it under that umbrella for one day. Some communities have kept the result and the city has accepted it.
   - Apply for a temporary art installation permit. Some cities have these.
   - Build relationships with city staff and councilmembers. Many cities will work with you if you start the conversation early.
   - Do it without permission and accept the risk. Some communities have done this; outcomes vary. Not generally recommended unless you've thought it through.
4. **Design.** The painted mural is the centerpiece. Bold geometric shapes work; so do figurative designs, mandalas, neighborhood maps, native plants, ancestral imagery. The design should reflect the specific block, not be downloaded from somewhere else.
5. **Plan the build.** Identify the side structures: a sitting bench, a tiny library, a community board, a tea or coffee station, a tool exchange. Distribute the build tasks.
6. **Hold the build day(s).** A "barn raising" weekend. Food, music, all ages. Different tasks for different skills. End each day with celebration.
7. **Identify stewards.** Who is going to maintain this? Repaint when it fades? Keep the tiny library stocked? A pair or trio of nearby neighbors usually steps up.
8. **Throw a dedication.** A block party at the new intersection. Invite the city. Invite the press.

## Variations

**Mini repair.** A single corner rather than a whole intersection. Lower bar, smaller impact, easier first attempt.

**Parking lot repair.** Some churches, schools, and community centers have under-used parking lots that become great candidates for the same treatment.

**Alley activation.** Some cities have used the same logic on alleys.

**Annual repaint.** The most successful intersections have an annual repainting tradition. The repainting is itself a [block party](../01-knowing-your-neighbors/block-party.md) that keeps the work alive.

## Stories from neighborhoods

**City Repair Project**, founded in 1996 in Portland, Oregon, pioneered the methodology. Their flagship project, **Share-It Square** at SE 9th and SE Sherrett, transformed a dangerous intersection into a beloved community gathering space.

Their annual **Village Building Convergence** brings together thousands of volunteers across 50+ sites for natural building, permaculture design, and intersection repairs simultaneously. Hundreds of intersection repairs have happened in Portland and in cities across North America.

The model has spread to many neighborhoods. The City Repair website maintains stories and materials.

## Where to learn more

- The original practice: [City Repair Project](https://cityrepair.org)
- Annual gathering: [Village Building Convergence](https://cityrepair.org/vbc)
- A foundational resource: Mark Lakeman and others, multiple writings at cityrepair.org
- Adjacent recipes: [Placemaking (PPS)](./placemaking.md), [Community-Built Playspace](./community-built-playspace.md), [Block Party](../01-knowing-your-neighbors/block-party.md)

## What it is

A citizen-led walking conversation through a neighborhood. The walker who leads it isn't a tour guide or an urban planner. They're someone who lives there and has stories to tell. Walks are free, open to anyone, and typically last an hour or two.

Jane's Walks are named for Jane Jacobs, the urbanist who insisted that cities are best understood at walking pace. Since 2006 they've happened in over 500 cities globally, especially in early May around her birthday.

## Why it works

Walking shifts something. You meet your neighbors at a different angle. The street that you pass at 30 miles an hour every day reveals itself differently at 3 miles an hour. Walking together also dissolves the speaker-audience hierarchy that other formats build in. Everyone is on the same pavement.

A neighborhood that gets walked is a neighborhood that gets known. A neighborhood that gets known is one where people start to feel ownership.

## What you need

- **Time:** 6 weeks of light planning. 1 to 2 hours for the walk itself.
- **People:** A walk leader. A handful of curious neighbors. No upper limit; large groups can split.
- **Space:** Whatever you want to show. Streets, parks, alleys, plazas. Pick a route you can lead confidently.
- **Materials:** A simple map (drawn or printed). Optional: printouts of photos, historical documents, or stories. A clipboard or notebook for notes.
- **Skills:** Local knowledge. Storytelling. Comfortable speaking outdoors. Basic route planning.
- **Energy level:** Moderate. The walking itself is light. The hosting is real but not heavy.

## How to host it

1. **Pick your route.** Two to three miles is plenty for two hours. Fewer if you have a lot to show. Pick somewhere with stories. Avoid heavy traffic and steep grades unless you're prepared to handle accessibility.
2. **Pick your stops.** Five to ten places where you'll pause and tell a story. Each story is two to five minutes. Examples: where the old grocery store used to be, the corner where someone organized a protest in 1972, the tree planted when a kid was born, the contested intersection.
3. **Walk the route yourself first.** Time it. Note hazards. Note seating for breaks.
4. **Invite people.** A simple flyer, a [Front Porch Forum](./front-porch-forum.md) post, a few words at a neighborhood meeting. Tell people it's free, no signup, all ages, all paces. List start time, start location, expected length.
5. **Start on time.** Welcome people. Set expectations: walking pace, ask questions whenever, stick together at intersections. Two minutes of orientation is enough.
6. **At each stop, tell the story.** Be specific. Name people, dates, what happened. Invite anyone who has their own story about that place to add it. Some of the best Jane's Walk moments come from a neighbor in the group adding a detail the leader didn't know.
7. **End at a place people can linger.** A cafe, a park bench, an ice cream shop. Walks that end at "thanks, bye" lose the relationships they could have made.
8. **Tell people about the next one.** If you only run one, that's fine. If you might run another, mention it.

## Variations

**Themed walk.** History walk. Trees and gardens walk. Public art walk. Civil rights walk. Hidden architecture walk. Disability access walk. Food walk.

**Children's walk.** Shorter route. More physical things to point at. Snacks. Best when led by older neighbors who can speak to kids about the neighborhood's past.

**Bike version.** Same recipe, longer route, slower pace than you'd think. Tour goes farther but stops feel different. Drop the "walk" in the name if you ride.

**Cross-neighborhood swap.** Two neighborhoods exchange walks. You lead one in their neighborhood, they lead one in yours. The contrast is the point.

**Recurring walk.** Some neighborhoods run a Jane's Walk monthly. Different leaders, different routes, same rhythm. Especially good in summer.

## Stories from neighborhoods

**Toronto, Canada.** The first Jane's Walks happened in 2007, a year after Jane Jacobs died. Her former neighbors organized walks through the places she'd walked. The format spread quickly through the urbanist and placemaking communities.

**Globally.** Since 2007 walks have happened in over 500 cities across North America, Europe, Asia, Africa, and South America. The annual Jane's Walk Festival is the first weekend in May. The official organizing nonprofit is at [janeswalk.org](https://janeswalk.org/).

Walks have been organized by neighborhood residents, community organizations, libraries, cultural institutions, schools, and individual urbanists. Themes include public space, displacement, transit, climate, hidden histories, and dozens more.

## Where to learn more

- The organization: [janeswalk.org](https://janeswalk.org/)
- The book that started it: Jane Jacobs, *The Death and Life of Great American Cities* (1961)
- Adjacent recipes: [Placemaking](../06-placemaking/placemaking.md), [Map Your Neighborhood](../07-resilience/map-your-neighborhood.md)

items.body:
*The need:* 'Everyone helps with everything' feels friendly and quietly kills groups.

Teams matter in organizing because relationships deepen commitment — and because a team can hold more than the sum of its members. Effective teams share three elements:

**Shared purpose.** A team must be able to say what it exists to do and with whom — clear, challenging, and significant to the members themselves. A compelling organizing purpose is a response to a real injustice, and it should be measurable so the team can see progress. (Your story of now is a good first draft of purpose.)

**Interdependent roles.** Every member holds a real piece of work that the others depend on — canvass captain, welcome lead, data keeper — matched to their skills and stretching them slightly. No silos, and no ghosts: a role nobody depends on is a role nobody keeps.

**Explicit norms.** Decide out loud: how often we meet, how we decide, how we communicate, what happens when someone drops a commitment — and how we correct norm violations so the norms stay real. Teams with explicit ground rules outperform teams running on vibes, because norms make it possible to talk about how things are going.

In the snowflake model, teams interconnect: a core team keeps the whole coherent while local teams adapt strategy to their ground and feed back what they learn. Accountability points both ways. Leadership is distributed — and every member shares the deepest norm of all: developing new leaders, so the team can grow without burning out its founders.

ingredients: 3-8 people who've had 1:1s with each other
a purpose worth saying out loud
norms written where everyone can see them
metadata.source_note: From 'Organizing: People, Power, Change' (2014), Structuring Teams. The shared purpose / interdependent roles / explicit norms triad follows team-effectiveness research by Wageman & Hackman cited in the Ganz tradition.
how_it_works: Draft shared purpose together — who we are, what we're here to do, how we'll know.
Name interdependent roles; every member holds work others depend on.
Set explicit norms: meetings, decisions, communication, and how we repair dropped commitments.
Connect to the wider snowflake: what does this team adapt locally, and what does it feed back?
Revisit norms openly as the team grows — updating them is a sign of health, not failure.
success_signals: members can recite the purpose
work continues when any one person is sick
norm violations get named and repaired without drama

items.summary: Effective teams share three things: a purpose members can recite, interdependent roles so nobody works alone, and explicit norms the team actually enforces on itself.

items.body:
## What it is

A small structure stocked by neighbors and accessible to anyone, any hour, with no paperwork or eligibility check. People leave cans, pasta, rice, hygiene products, diapers, school supplies. People take what they need. The model is direct, dignified, and runs on a gift economy.

The first Little Free Pantry was built in 2016 by Jessica McClard in Fayetteville, Arkansas, who saw Little Free Libraries and thought: what if we did this with food. There are now thousands of them across North America.

## Why it works

The barriers to food access in most cities are not just about money. They're about hours, paperwork, transportation, and the stigma of asking. A pantry on a sidewalk with no door, no staff, and no question of who deserves it removes all of those barriers at once.

The pantry also gives neighbors a near-zero-friction way to give. You drop off a bag of cans on your way to work. The whole loop closes in a way that food drives and 501(c)(3) intake forms cannot match.

## What you need

- **Time:** 2 to 3 weeks of setup. 1 to 2 hours a week to maintain.
- **People:** 1 to 2 stewards. 5 to 10 neighbors willing to stock regularly.
- **Space:** A high-traffic, accessible spot. Sidewalks, church grounds, library lawns, school edges. Permission from the property owner.
- **Materials:** A small weatherproof cabinet. Repurposed bookcase, custom build, or a kit. Sturdy enough to last a year. Plus initial stock: canned goods, pasta, peanut butter, soap, menstrual products, baby supplies.
- **Skills:** Light carpentry or repurposing. Basic communication. Willingness to be the contact person.
- **Energy level:** Low to moderate. Mostly the stocking and weekly check.

## How to host it

1. **Find the right spot.** Visible from the street. Reachable on foot. Safe to access at night. Talk to the property owner: a church, school, library, business, or a neighbor with a corner lot. Get written permission.
2. **Check zoning.** Most cities allow these as accessory structures, but a quick call to your city or a permit search avoids surprises.
3. **Build the structure.** Three options. Buy a kit ($150 to $400, search "little free pantry kit"). Repurpose a bookcase, old cabinet, or newspaper box, weatherproofed. Build from scratch. Whatever it is, it should have a roof, a door, a shelf or two, and weatherproofing.
4. **Stock it.** First fill: canned vegetables, fruit, soup, beans, peanut butter, pasta, rice, granola bars, hygiene products (soap, toothpaste, toothbrushes, menstrual products), basic kitchen items (Ziploc bags, plastic utensils). Skip anything that needs refrigeration (for that, see [Community Fridge](./community-fridge.md)) or anything that can melt or expire fast.
5. **Add signage.** "Take what you need. Leave what you can." Plus your contact info as the steward. Optionally a printed list of common items needed.
6. **Promote.** Post in neighborhood forums, Buy Nothing groups, church bulletins, library boards. Both for users and for donors.
7. **Maintain weekly.** Once a week, walk over. Remove damaged items, expired food, and anything that looks unsafe. Restock the gaps. Note what runs out fastest. Some pantries become very busy; others stay quiet. Both are fine.
8. **Build a stocking team.** 5 to 10 neighbors who commit to dropping off items regularly. A simple group text or shared sheet helps coordinate.

## Variations

**With fridge.** A community fridge can be co-located with a pantry for perishables. See [Community Fridge](./community-fridge.md).

**Apartment building version.** Inside a lobby or laundry room. Lower visibility but reliable supply chain.

**School version.** Schools that host pantries report high uptake by families who would never apply for food assistance.

**Themed pantry.** Hygiene products only (menstrual products are particularly hard to access). Pet food. School supplies in August. Holiday-themed stocks.

**Bilingual version.** Signage in the languages spoken in your neighborhood.

## Stories from neighborhoods

**Jessica McClard** in Fayetteville, Arkansas. May 2016. A $250 microloan. The first Little Free Pantry on her church grounds. The idea spread without a platform, without a franchise, without a fee. Today there are thousands across North America.

The movement proved especially vital during COVID-19. Cities that had a few pantries in 2019 had dozens by 2021. Many have stayed.

## Where to learn more

- The original: [Little Free Pantry](https://www.littlefreepantry.org)
- Setup guide: [littlefreepantry.org/start-a-pantry](https://www.littlefreepantry.org/build-a-pantry)
- Adjacent recipes: [Community Fridge](./community-fridge.md), [Free Store](./free-store.md), [Buy Nothing](./buy-nothing.md)

items.body:
*The need:* Some communities are absent from public narratives, spaces, and decisions.

Some communities are invisible in public narratives, public spaces, and public decisions. This recipe makes their presence undeniable: communities that have been erased or marginalized coordinate to make themselves visible through art, stories, data, and persistent presence until they cannot be ignored. The community must control its own narrative entirely, include joy and not only struggle, prepare for backlash with support ready, and ensure economic benefit flows to the people doing the work.

**How it works**
1. Map where the community is invisible: media, public art, decision tables.
2. Collect stories, photos, and contributions that usually get overlooked.
3. Design a visibility campaign such as murals, posters, or a social media takeover.
4. Launch all at once for undeniable impact.
5. Keep it sustained through multiple channels.
6. Document how the narrative shifts.
7. Celebrate the newly visible community.

**Ingredients**
- a core team from the community itself
- ways to collect stories and images
- artists from the community
- walls/windows/platforms
- a launch moment

**Minimum resources:** $100-500 for materials and printing.

**You'll know it's working when**
- 'I didn't know they were here' becomes 'I notice them now'
- invited to decision tables
- pride instead of shame
- resources flow to unmet needs

**Field tips**
- community controls its own narrative entirely
- include joy not only struggle
- prepare for backlash
- economic benefit flows to the community

**Building from (real projects)**
- Inclusive Local Ancestry Posters
- PublicSource Points of Pride
- Asset-Framing Post-It Notes
- Invisible Cities

items.body:
## What it is

A structured 2- to 3-hour neighborhood meeting that produces a simple map of skills, resources, and vulnerabilities on your block. Originally developed for earthquake preparedness in the Pacific Northwest, the practice has spread to fire-prone, flood-prone, hurricane-prone, and heat-prone neighborhoods.

The map is what produces value during a disaster. The relationships built while making the map are what produce value for everything else.

## Why it works

In the first hours and days after a major disaster, official responders are not coming. Neighbors are the first responders. The neighborhoods that recover fastest are the ones where neighbors already know who has medical training, who has water, who has a generator, who needs help, and where everyone is.

You cannot build that knowledge under crisis. You can only build it before.

## What you need

- **Time:** 2 to 3 hours per session. Optional follow-up sessions.
- **People:** 15 to 20 households per project. 1 to 3 core organizers.
- **Space:** Community center, library, church, park, or someone's living room.
- **Materials:** Simple forms or maps, contact list templates, flip charts.
- **Skills:** Basic facilitation. Comfort with people talking about their vulnerabilities.
- **Energy level:** Moderate.

## How to host it

1. **Contact your local fire department or emergency management agency.** Most cities have a neighborhood mapping program with materials, forms, and sometimes a facilitator. Use it. The forms are well-designed and free.
2. **Invite 15 to 20 households on your block.** Personal invitations work best. A flyer drop alone usually gets a thin response. Combine with a [block party](../01-knowing-your-neighbors/block-party.md) or [porch conversations](../01-knowing-your-neighbors/porch-conversations.md) for warmth.
3. **Hold the meeting.** Walk through:
   - What emergencies could affect your area (geographic and seasonal: earthquake, fire, flood, ice storm, heat wave).
   - What each household can provide: medical skills, tools, generator, water, food storage, emergency radio, transportation.
   - What each household might need: mobility help, language support, medical equipment, child or pet care.
   - Where vulnerable neighbors live: elders alone, people with disabilities, families with young children.
4. **Make the map.** A physical drawing or printed map of the block. Mark each household. Note skills and needs (with consent). The map is not for sharing publicly; it's for the participants.
5. **Identify a meeting place.** Where to gather if phones don't work and homes are damaged. A specific corner, a park, a school yard.
6. **Identify a comms plan.** Who has a battery radio. Who has a backup generator. What's the plan if cell networks are down (often: walk to the meeting place and check in).
7. **Identify a basic supply pool.** Some neighborhoods designate one household that stores extra water, first aid, and tools for the group. Others have each household maintain their own.
8. **Hold a follow-up.** Three to six months later. What's changed? Who's moved in? Who's moved out? Refresh the map.

## Variations

**Apartment building version.** A single building or complex rather than a block. Often run by a tenant association.

**Faith community version.** A congregation maps its members across geography, especially for elders.

**Block-level version.** A more thorough version with first-aid training, supply drills, and an annual neighborhood emergency exercise. See [CERT (Community Emergency Response Team)](https://www.ready.gov/cert) training for a deeper structure.

**Mutual aid pod overlap.** The map produced here often becomes the seed of a [Mutual Aid Pod](../02-small-groups-for-support/mutual-aid-pod.md). The two recipes pair naturally.

## Stories from neighborhoods

**San Francisco NERT (Neighborhood Emergency Response Team)** has trained thousands of neighbors since the 1990s. A Marina District neighborhood did the mapping work in summer 2018. When an earthquake hit in 2022, neighbors responded immediately: they knew Mr. Chen used a walker and needed assistance, the Garcia family had medical training, and two homes had generators and stored water. The group quickly coordinated, treated minor injuries, and shared supplies while waiting for responders.

Afterward, the neighbors said something common to communities that have done this work: the preparation had also created lasting friendship and cohesion, separate from the emergency.

## Where to learn more

- A model program: [San Francisco NERT: Map Your Neighborhood](https://sf-fire.org/nert/map-your-neighborhood)
- For deeper training: [CERT (Community Emergency Response Teams)](https://www.ready.gov/cert)
- Adjacent recipes: [Mutual Aid Pod](../02-small-groups-for-support/mutual-aid-pod.md), [Block Stewards](../01-knowing-your-neighbors/block-stewards.md), [Resilience Hub](./resilience-hub.md)

items.body:
## What it is

A coordinated rotation of meal deliveries for a household going through a major life event: a new baby, surgery, the death of a family member, a serious illness, or a long recovery. A few weeks of dinners delivered by friends and neighbors so the person at the center can rest, heal, and not have to think about food.

The Meal Train is one of the oldest mutual aid practices in human community. It also happens to be the easiest one to start.

## Why it works

When someone is in crisis or transition, decision fatigue is real. Even ordering food is a decision. A meal train removes that decision for weeks. It also gives the people who love them a structured way to show up. Friends who don't know what to do almost always know how to cook one meal.

The cumulative effect is more than the food. A meal train is the visible care of a community wrapping around someone. People remember it for the rest of their lives.

## What you need

- **Time:** 1 to 2 hours to set up. 20 to 40 minutes per delivery. Typically runs 2 to 8 weeks.
- **People:** 1 organizer. 5 to 20 meal contributors.
- **Space:** Recipient's home for delivery.
- **Materials:** A shared calendar (paper or digital). A platform like [Meal Train](https://www.mealtrain.com/), [Give InKind](https://www.giveinkind.com/), or [Take Them A Meal](https://www.takethemameal.com/) can help. Containers (reusable if possible).
- **Skills:** Coordination, communication, basic cooking (or willingness to order).
- **Energy level:** Low to moderate. Most contributors give one meal.

## How to host it

1. **Ask the recipient first.** Not everyone wants a meal train. Some find it overwhelming. Confirm they're up for it before starting.
2. **Gather the basics.** Dietary restrictions, allergies, food preferences, family size, drop-off instructions (porch? Doorbell? Cooler outside?), best times of day.
3. **Set up the calendar.** [Meal Train](https://www.mealtrain.com/) is free and well-designed. A shared Google Sheet works too. Add the recipient's preferences at the top.
4. **Pick the duration.** New baby: 2 to 4 weeks. Surgery recovery: depends on the surgery. Grief: 2 to 6 weeks is typical, but some communities run light meal trains for months.
5. **Pick the frequency.** Two or three deliveries a week usually works. Daily can feel overwhelming for the recipient. Weekly leaves too much gap.
6. **Send the invite.** Email, text, group thread. Include the calendar link. Make it easy to sign up.
7. **Coordinate the protocol.** Drop-off without staying, unless the recipient has explicitly said they want company. Use disposable or reusable containers (label them with names if reusable). Drop notes if you want; long visits are usually too much.
8. **Check in midway.** Are dishes adequate? Is timing working? Adjust.
9. **Close gracefully.** End on a planned date. Send a thank-you note from the recipient if appropriate.

## Variations

**Extended version.** A "low-key" meal train that delivers one meal a week for several months. Useful for long-term illness or extended recovery.

**Care train.** Beyond meals: childcare, pet care, errands, lawn mowing, snow shoveling, gift cards. Same calendar format, broader help. [Lotsa Helping Hands](https://www.lotsahelpinghands.com/) supports this format.

**Workplace version.** A meal train coordinated through a workplace for a colleague's life event. Different network, same form.

**Faith community version.** Many congregations have built-in meal train infrastructure. If you're in one, learn it. The patterns are deep.

## Stories from neighborhoods

The Meal Train predates the platform. Churches, mosques, synagogues, and informal neighborhood networks have run meal trains for generations. The platforms ([Meal Train](https://www.mealtrain.com/), [Give InKind](https://www.giveinkind.com/), [Take Them A Meal](https://www.takethemameal.com/), [Lotsa Helping Hands](https://www.lotsahelpinghands.com/)) made it easier to organize across groups that don't share a congregation, but the practice itself is older than the internet.

After a major illness, surgery, birth, or death, people who run meal trains often hear later that the meal train was what made the difference. Not because the food was extraordinary. Because someone showed up, and then someone else did, and then someone else.

- Broader care coordination: [Lotsa Helping Hands](https://www.lotsahelpinghands.com/), [Give InKind](https://www.giveinkind.com/)
- Adjacent recipes: [Mutual Aid Pod](./mutual-aid-pod.md), [Babysitting Co-op](./babysitting-coop.md)

items.body:
## What it is

A facilitated listening circle where men gather regularly to speak and listen with vulnerability and integrity. The format is borrowed from older circle traditions, including Indigenous council practices. The work of the council is mutual recognition: men hearing each other without trying to solve, perform, or compete.

Council is one of the most reliable forms of emotional infrastructure for men, who in most modern contexts lack a structured place to be honest with each other about their lives.

## Why it works

Men in many cultures are trained to relate through doing, performing, and problem-solving. Council interrupts that pattern. The talking piece, the turn-taking, the deep listening protocol create a space where the usual moves are unavailable. What emerges is what doesn't usually get said out loud: about marriage, fathering, work, grief, purpose, fear, masculinity itself.

Over months of regular meetings, the trust deepens until council becomes the place where the harder, slower personal work can actually happen.

## What you need

- **Time:** 90 minutes to 2 hours per session, monthly or biweekly, recurring indefinitely.
- **People:** 8 to 12 men per circle. A trained facilitator is essential.
- **Space:** A comfortable room with privacy and chairs in a circle. No tables in the middle.
- **Materials:** A talking piece (optional). Posted ground rules. Refreshments. Comfortable seating.
- **Skills:** Deep listening, non-judgment, comfort with silence, basic facilitation.
- **Energy level:** Moderate. Emotionally engaged but not physically demanding.

## How to host it

1. **Get trained.** This is the one recipe in this book where outside training matters. [Journeymen](https://www.journeymen.us/mens-council) trains facilitators in council practice. There are other paths (ManKind Project, Sacred Sons, local circle traditions). Find one. Apprentice with an experienced facilitator before opening your own circle.
2. **Recruit 8 to 12 men.** Personal invitations. People you trust to follow through on a multi-month commitment.
3. **Hold an orientation meeting.** Explain the format. Set expectations. Establish confidentiality. Have everyone speak briefly about what brought them.
4. **Set a regular meeting time.** Same day each month or every two weeks. Predictability builds the container.
5. **Run the format.** A typical session:
   - Opening grounding (breath, silence, intention).
   - Check-in round: each man speaks briefly about how he arrives.
   - Theme or open council: men speak as called, using the talking piece. No interruption, no fixing, no advice.
   - Listening pauses between speakers.
   - Closing round.
6. **Protect the rules.** Confidentiality is absolute. No advice unless requested. No interrupting. No therapizing. The facilitator gently brings people back to the form.
7. **Allow the circle to deepen.** First few months are introductions. Months 3 to 12 are where the real work begins. Years are where the relationships become foundational.

## Variations

**Boys' Council.** Adapted for adolescent boys. [Journeymen](https://www.journeymen.us/) and others run formal programs. Schools have adopted the model.

**Women's Council.** Same form, different ground.

**Mixed council.** Some traditions run mixed-gender or non-gendered councils. Different dynamic, same protocol.

**Theme council.** A council formed around a shared identity or experience: fathers, recovery, queer men, men of color, men leaving organized religion.

## Stories from neighborhoods

**Journeymen** is a 501(c)(3) based on Vashon Island, Washington, founded on principles of mentorship and social-emotional learning. Their Men's Council program has facilitated groups across the Pacific Northwest and beyond. They also run Boys' Council and the CIRCLES program for schools.

Participants in long-running councils report deeper emotional expression, stronger connection to themselves and others, and healthier ways of relating to other men in their lives. Many councils stay together for years, becoming a primary friendship structure for their members.

## Where to learn more

- Practitioner organization: [Journeymen](https://www.journeymen.us/mens-council)
- Related: [ManKind Project](https://mankindproject.org/), [Sacred Sons](https://www.sacredsons.com/)
- Adjacent recipes: [Microsolidarity Crew](./microsolidarity-crew.md), [Talking Circle](../04-gathering-design/talking-circle.md)

items.body:
## What it is

A funding mechanism that distributes small grants ($50 to $100) to neighbors who want to host community gatherings: block parties, potlucks, porch sits, seasonal celebrations, community conversations. The application is short (3 to 5 minutes). The approval is fast (often within a day). The reporting is light (a photo and brief note about what happened). The program trusts that neighbors know what their communities need.

The model has been developed and refined by [Connective Tissue](https://connectivetissue.substack.com/), Trust for Civic Life, and other organizations exploring how to lower the barrier to civic participation.

## Why it works

The barrier to hosting a community gathering is rarely desire or idea. It is the psychological lift of *can I do this* combined with the practical lift of *who pays for the snacks*. A small grant resolves both. The money signals permission. Someone external believed enough to fund it. The neighbor can show up to their own gathering with confidence.

The light reporting and high trust matter. Every layer of bureaucracy reduces who can apply. Three minutes and a photo is a real recipe. Two hours of paperwork and receipt tracking is a different program with worse outcomes.

## What you need

- **Time:** 3 to 5 minutes to apply. 2 to 4 hours to host. 10 minutes to document.
- **People:** A host plus 8 to 15 attendees. A coordinating team to review applications and distribute funds.
- **Space:** Any welcoming neighborhood space. Porch, backyard, park, community room, library.
- **Materials:** $50 to $100 in funds. Basic supplies for whatever the gathering type is.
- **Skills:** Basic facilitation. Ability to reach neighbors.
- **Energy level:** Moderate.

## How to host it

### If you're a neighbor applying for one

1. **Find a program.** Some neighborhood foundations, libraries, or organizations offer this. The [Connective Tissue](https://connectivetissue.substack.com/) site documents several models. Trust for Civic Life pilots have run in multiple cities.
2. **Apply.** Most applications ask: what's the gathering, when, where, roughly who will come, why it matters to your block. Aim for clarity, not length. Three sentences each.
3. **Host the gathering.** Use the funds for supplies, food, simple decorations, accessibility (translation, childcare, transportation if relevant).
4. **Document lightly.** A photo. A few sentences about what happened. Any commitments or next steps that emerged.

### If you're running a microgrant program

1. **Decide on the budget.** Even $3,000 distributes 30 grants of $100 each. That's 30 neighborhood gatherings.
2. **Define the criteria.** Common ones: open to anyone in a defined geography, must be a community gathering (not a private party), must invite people beyond the host's immediate circle, alcohol policy if relevant.
3. **Build the application form.** 5 questions max. Make it accessible online and on paper. Multilingual if your neighborhood is.
4. **Set up fast review.** A small committee that turns applications around in 1 to 3 business days. Speed is part of the design.
5. **Distribute funds simply.** Some programs use Venmo or PayPal for speed. Some send a check. Some give a Visa gift card. Choose what fits your community.
6. **Set the documentation requirement.** A photo and a paragraph. No receipts. No itemized accounting. Trust.
7. **Capture stories.** The program's outcomes are stories, not just numbers. Compile what neighbors say about their gatherings. Share back.
8. **Reiterate annually or seasonally.** A program that runs once is a pilot. A program that runs each year becomes infrastructure.

## Variations

**Recurring gathering microgrant.** A slightly larger grant ($200 to $500) for a host who'll run a monthly gathering for a season. Higher commitment, deeper relationships.

**Themed microgrants.** Grants specifically for block parties (see [Block Party](../01-knowing-your-neighbors/block-party.md)) or [story-sharing suppers](../01-knowing-your-neighbors/story-sharing-potluck.md) or holiday gatherings.

**Microgrant + coaching.** Some programs pair the money with light coaching from an experienced host. Useful for new conveners.

**Tiered grants.** $50 for a porch hang. $200 for a block party. $500 for a longer project. The bigger ones require slightly more application.

## Stories from neighborhoods

**Connective Tissue's Charlottesville pilot** in spring 2023 received 70 applications and distributed $100 microgrants to 30 hosts. Within a few weeks, the program reached nearly 500 neighbors across 25 different neighborhoods. Almost every attendee committed to concrete next steps afterward. Some hosts started recurring monthly gatherings. Others organized neighborhood improvements. Many simply deepened relationships with people they had never met.

One host's reflection captured the program's logic: *the barrier wasn't desire or ideas. It was the psychological lift of "Can I do this?" The $100 answered that question.*

**Trust for Civic Life** and other funders have piloted similar programs in multiple cities, with consistent outcomes: dramatically expanded participation, ideas surfaced from neighbors who would never have applied to a traditional grant process, and a flowering of small gatherings that bigger funding mechanisms can't catalyze.

## Where to learn more

- A practitioner write-up: [Connective Tissue: A Simple Act to Strengthen Civic Life](https://connectivetissue.substack.com/p/a-simple-act-to-strengthen-civic)
- Related funder: [Trust for Civic Life](https://trustforciviclife.org/)
- Adjacent recipes: [Block Party](../01-knowing-your-neighbors/block-party.md), [Story-Sharing Potluck](../01-knowing-your-neighbors/story-sharing-potluck.md), [Reinvent the Potluck](../04-gathering-design/reinvent-the-potluck.md)

items.body:
## What it is

A microsolidarity crew is a small, committed group that meets often enough to actually know each other and stays together long enough to weather things. It is consciously built where extended family and tight neighborhoods used to do this work by default. It is not therapy, not a book club, not a board, not a friendship. It is closer to what older traditions called a circle, a cell, or a chosen family.

The work of the crew is mutual support: peer listening, practical help, accountability. The structure is light. The commitment is real.

## Why it works

Modern life atomizes people. You may have a hundred acquaintances and no one who knows what's actually going on for you this month. A crew that meets every few weeks with structure, even simple structure, builds the kind of knowing that turns into real support over time.

The size matters. Three to six is small enough that everyone gets time and is missed when absent. Larger groups dilute the intimacy that makes it work.

## What you need

- **Time:** 1 to 2 hours per meeting, monthly or biweekly. Plus light check-ins in between.
- **People:** 3 to 6 people with baseline trust and willingness to be vulnerable.
- **Space:** A quiet room, in-person or video, where people can speak freely.
- **Materials:** Minimal. A timer is useful. A shared note for action items if you want.
- **Skills:** Listening, asking good questions, comfort with vulnerability, ability to not fix.
- **Energy level:** Moderate. Emotionally demanding but not logistically heavy.

## How to host it

1. **Pick 3 or 4 people to invite.** People you already trust at some level and want to know better. Don't try to assemble strangers. Don't invite anyone you'd be performing for.
2. **Propose a time-bounded experiment.** Four to six meetings over three to four months. This lowers the stakes. People say yes to experiments who would say no to commitments.
3. **Set the rhythm.** Pick a day and time you can repeat. Same place if possible. Predictability does a lot of the work.
4. **Use the Case Clinic format for meetings.** Each meeting, one person takes the focused time:
   - 10 minutes: they describe a real situation, challenge, or decision they're sitting with.
   - 10 minutes: the group asks clarifying questions (no advice yet).
   - 15 minutes: the group offers perspectives or what they're noticing while the person listens silently.
   - 10 minutes: the person reflects on what was useful and what wasn't.
   - 5 minutes: simple closing round.
5. **Rotate who takes the focus.** Over your first six meetings, everyone should get a turn. Track it.
6. **After the experiment, hold a retrospective.** Did this work? Is it worth continuing? If yes, decide what changes: frequency, format, whether to add anyone.
7. **Slowly add other rhythms.** Co-working sessions. Quarterly longer meetings. A weekend retreat once a year. Skill-shares. Practical mutual aid (meals when someone's sick, brainstorming during a crisis).
8. **Stay small.** A crew of 6 has more depth than a crew of 12. If you want to grow, grow by spawning a second crew, not by inflating the first.

## Variations

**Online crew.** Video meetings only. Works across distance. Tighter time discipline is needed.

**Theme crew.** A crew formed around shared identity or situation: new parents, queer elders, people leaving a religious community, people in recovery, people starting businesses. Shared context deepens trust faster.

**Multi-crew.** A "congregation" of 3 to 10 crews that share occasional events while each crew maintains its own meetings. See Richard Bartlett's *[Congregation: 8 Design Patterns for Gathering](https://medium.com/microsolidarity/congregation-how-to-ffe35c65d70)* if you want to think at this scale.

## Stories from neighborhoods

**Richard Bartlett** developed microsolidarity after years in cooperative and decentralized organizations. His writings at [microsolidarity.cc](https://www.microsolidarity.cc/) are the most thorough open-source guide to this practice.

**A documented crew of four.** Two teachers, a nurse, a freelancer. They started meeting after one experienced burnout and isolation. Began with case clinics, quickly moved to practical mutual aid: meals when someone's parent got sick, brainstorming sessions for a work crisis, accountability for starting a business. By year two they were co-working monthly and had become each other's primary support system. Several said it was as meaningful as therapy but more tailored to their actual lives.

## Where to learn more

- The practitioner: [Richard Bartlett at Microsolidarity.cc](https://www.microsolidarity.cc/practices/how-you-can-get-started)
- Deeper companion practice: [The Reciprocity Game](./reciprocity-game.md)
- Adjacent recipes: [Mutual Aid Pod](./mutual-aid-pod.md), [Men's Council](./mens-council.md)

**Richard Bartlett** developed microsolidarity after years in cooperative and decentralized organizations. His writings at [microsolidarity.cc](https://www.microsolidarity.cc/) are the most thorough open-source guide to this practice.

**A documented crew of four.** Two teachers, a nurse, a freelancer. They started meeting after one experienced burnout and isolation. Began with case clinics, quickly moved to practical mutual aid: meals when someone's parent got sick, brainstorming sessions for a work crisis, accountability for starting a business. By year two they were co-working monthly and had become each other's primary support system. Several said it was as meaningful as therapy but more tailored to their actual lives.

items.body:
## What it is

A mutual aid pod is a small, committed network that meets practical needs through direct, reciprocal support. It is distinct from charity in a specific way: everyone gives and everyone receives. There are no helpers and helped, just people who, in different seasons, need different things.

Mutual aid has deep roots in working-class, immigrant, and Black radical organizing. Dean Spade's 2020 book *Mutual Aid* is the modern foundational text. The practice is older than the term.

## Why it works

Most needs in a neighborhood are small enough that one person can solve them and large enough that no one is going to navigate a bureaucracy to ask. A working pod removes the bureaucracy. Someone needs a ride to a medical appointment. Someone needs groceries this week. Someone needs help carrying a piece of furniture upstairs. Pods make these solvable in a text thread.

The deeper effect is that the pod becomes a place where you can ask for help without shame. That is rare and worth a lot.

## What you need

- **Time:** 2 to 4 hours monthly for coordination, plus the actual help.
- **People:** Start with 3 to 5. Grow to 5 to 20 organically.
- **Space:** Mostly digital communication. Occasional in-person.
- **Materials:** A group chat, a simple shared spreadsheet or document, optionally a shared calendar.
- **Skills:** Coordination. Comfort with vulnerability. Willingness to ask.
- **Energy level:** Moderate, scales with the scope of needs.

## How to host it

1. **Start with 3 to 5 trusted people.** Don't try to launch a 30-person pod from day one. Build relationships first.
2. **Map your existing pod.** Write down everyone you'd already feel okay asking for help: rides, meals, childcare, emotional support, money in a pinch. This is your starting network, even before the pod is named.
3. **Pick a name and a channel.** A group text or Signal group is usually enough. Larger pods sometimes use a dedicated Discord or a shared sheet.
4. **Identify one shared commitment to start.** Examples: meals during anyone's hardship, a tool-share, rides to medical appointments, a babysitting trade, monthly mutual budget check-ins. One thing, done well.
5. **Use a simple request rhythm.** Someone has a need, they post it. Someone who can, replies. Confirm in DM. Follow through. Report back to the group.
6. **Hold monthly check-ins.** 30 to 60 minutes. What's working, what isn't, who needs what, who has capacity. This is when small frictions get named and unstuck.
7. **Grow slowly.** Each new member should be vouched for by at least one existing member. Trust scales slower than logistics.
8. **Decide together what scope you can hold.** Pods that try to do everything burn out. Pods that pick a few things and do them well last.

## Variations

**Building pod.** A pod within a single apartment building or condo complex.

**Mom pod / parent pod.** A pod of caregivers trading childcare, sick days, meals. Often the gateway form for people who haven't been in mutual aid before.

**Crisis pod.** Activated during emergencies (illness, eviction, disaster), then either disperses or evolves into ongoing support.

**Larger network.** Multiple pods that coordinate occasionally on bigger projects. See [Mutual Aid Networks](https://www.mutualaidnetwork.org/) and the [Mutual Aid Hub](https://www.mutualaidhub.org/).

## Stories from neighborhoods

**A Brooklyn mutual aid pod during 2020** started with 10 people organized through Instagram. They identified that seniors needed grocery shopping and medication pick-up. They created a simple system: people texted needs, volunteers confirmed pickup, payment ran on an honor system. Within months the pod grew to 40 people, added a cooking team, coordinated rent support, provided tech help, and connected people to benefits. By 2023 it had formalized while maintaining mutual aid principles. Members emphasize that the magic is that everyone gives and receives.

The U.S. saw an explosion of mutual aid pods in 2020, documented at the [Mutual Aid Hub](https://www.mutualaidhub.org/), which lists thousands of active pods. Many of the strongest pods have continued and deepened in the years since.

## Where to learn more

- Foundational book: Dean Spade, *Mutual Aid: Building Solidarity During This Crisis (And the Next)* (Verso, 2020)
- Practical toolkit: [Big Door Brigade Mutual Aid Toolbox](https://bigdoorbrigade.com/mutual-aid-toolbox/)
- Hub: [Mutual Aid Hub](https://www.mutualaidhub.org/)
- Adjacent recipes: [Microsolidarity Crew](./microsolidarity-crew.md), [Meal Train](./meal-train.md), [Babysitting Co-op](./babysitting-coop.md)

items.body:
## What it is

A community practice and social movement founded in 2016 by **Tricia Hersey** that frames rest as a radical act against white supremacy, capitalism, and overwork culture. The Nap Ministry facilitates immersive nap sessions, performance art installations, and community gatherings where people rest together in sacred, protected space.

The work is rooted in Black liberation, womanism, somatics, and Afrofuturism. It is explicitly political: rest is named as a tool for dismantling systems of oppression, especially those that have demanded constant labor from Black communities.

## Why it works

Grind culture treats rest as deviance. The Nap Ministry treats rest as ancestral, sacred, and essential. The practice creates "portals," in Hersey's language: spaces where people can temporarily escape the demands of capitalism and find themselves in a different relationship to their bodies and to each other.

For Black participants especially, the work names a specific inheritance: ancestors whose rest was stolen by enslavement, sharecropping, and labor exploitation. Communal rest becomes a form of repair and an act of generational care.

## What you need

- **Time:** Nap sessions: 30 minutes to 2 hours. Immersive events: 4 to 8 hours. Trainings: 2 to 4 hours.
- **People:** Facilitators trained in somatic and healing practices, ideally from Black communities for Black-centered events. Community participants. Optional: musicians, artists, healers.
- **Space:** Sacred, comfortable spaces. Community centers, parks, galleries, churches. Soft surfaces (rugs, mats, blankets). Dim lighting. Sound management.
- **Materials:** Blankets, pillows, mats. Optional: music, visual art, sacred objects. The **REST DECK** (a deck of 50 cards with practices for resisting grind culture) is one of the practice's primary tools.
- **Skills:** Facilitation, somatic awareness, spiritual grounding, cultural competency, creating psychological safety.
- **Energy level:** Low physically. High spiritually. Restorative.

## How to host it

This is a practice with a specific founder and tradition. Honor that lineage when you engage with it.

1. **Engage with the source.** Read **Tricia Hersey's** book *Rest Is Resistance: A Manifesto*. Follow [The Nap Ministry](https://thenapministry.com/). Don't treat the practice as generic mindfulness; it has specific roots.
2. **Be honest about who you are.** If you are not Black and you want to bring this practice to your community, do so with explicit acknowledgment of the lineage and without claiming the parts of the practice that are specifically about Black ancestral healing. There are broader practices around communal rest that draw on this work and that other communities can practice in good faith.
3. **For a Black-centered event.** Find a Black facilitator with somatic, spiritual, or healing background. Hold the event in a culturally aligned space. Center Black participants. Use music and art rooted in Black cultural tradition.
4. **Set up the space.** Dim lighting. Soft surfaces. Quiet enough for actual rest. Comfortable temperature. Optionally: ambient music or guided audio (Tricia Hersey has produced many).
5. **Open with framing.** A few minutes naming what this is, why we are gathered, the lineage that holds it. Permission to rest fully.
6. **Hold the rest.** People settle in. Some sleep. Some drift. Some meditate. The facilitator holds space without interrupting.
7. **Close gently.** A return to sound, a brief reflection, an option to share a word or a feeling. No pressure to perform an experience.
8. **Consider what continues.** A single nap session is meaningful. A practice of rest sustained over time changes lives. Bring the practice home.

## Variations

**Workplace rest space.** Some workplaces have created rest rooms or quiet rooms inspired by the practice. Adapt with care.

**Family rest.** A version for families, often with kids. Quiet time together, embracing rest as togetherness.

**REST DECK practice.** The deck of 50 practices is designed to be used solo or with a group. Pulling a card a day and committing to its practice is a way of building rest into daily life.

**Communal sleep events.** Some practitioners run all-night communal sleep gatherings. Higher commitment, deeper practice.

## Stories from neighborhoods

**Tricia Hersey** founded The Nap Ministry in 2016 after experiencing exhaustion in graduate school and reconnecting with the rest her ancestors were denied. The work began as performance art and community gatherings; it has grown into a movement with hundreds of thousands of followers, a bestselling book, and adopted practices in churches, universities, organizations, and homes globally.

**Communities and organizations** have integrated Nap Ministry frameworks into wellness programming, racial justice work, and creative spaces. The work has been particularly impactful in organizing communities where burnout is endemic.

## Where to learn more

- The source: [The Nap Ministry](https://thenapministry.com/)
- The book: Tricia Hersey, *Rest Is Resistance: A Manifesto* (Little Brown, 2022)
- Newsletter: [tricia.substack.com](https://tricia.substack.com/)
- Adjacent recipes: [Trauma-Informed Community Building](./trauma-informed.md), [Community Acupuncture](./community-acupuncture.md), [Death Cafe](../02-small-groups-for-support/death-cafe.md)

items.body:
*The need:* Resources exist but systems are too complex to access.

Resources exist (food assistance, healthcare, housing help) but people cannot access them because the systems are too complex and the barriers too high. This recipe creates human bridges: instead of handing out phone numbers or websites, it builds networks of neighbors who have successfully navigated these systems and will literally walk others through the process, documenting every barrier and workaround and organizing to remove the systemic ones. Lived experience matters more than professional credentials, and the work is made celebratory rather than clinical.

**How it works**
1. Find people who have successfully navigated systems; they are your experts.
2. Pay them as navigators.
3. When someone needs help, a navigator physically goes with them.
4. Document every barrier and every workaround.
5. Share what works across the network.
6. When you find systemic barriers, organize to remove them, including publishing better guidance than currently exists.

**Ingredients**
- 5-10 people who've navigated systems
- a way to reach out (text/WhatsApp/office hours)
- transport money or drivers
- sympathetic insiders
- a shared tracking doc

**Minimum resources:** Navigator stipends unless volunteer.

**You'll know it's working when**
- unused resources get used
- agencies ask navigators how to simplify
- helped people become navigators

**Field tips**
- lived experience over credentials
- build insider relationships
- make it celebratory

**Building from (real projects)**
- Community Help Desk
- FYLPRO COVID-19 Task Force
- Up the Block
- Zinester's Guide

items.body:
*The need:* Neighborhoods described only by their deficits start believing the description.

John Kretzmann and John McKnight's 'Building Communities from the Inside Out' (1993) opens with two maps of the same place. The **needs map** — poverty rates, crime stats, dropout numbers — is 'part of the truth' mistaken for the whole truth; taken as the map, it teaches residents 'to see themselves as people with special needs that can only be met by outsiders,' routes money to service providers instead of residents, and forces leaders to win funding by denigrating their neighbors. The **assets map** starts from what is present: it is asset-based, internally focused, and relationship-driven.

What goes on the assets map (the tradition's six categories): the **gifts of residents** (skills, knowledge, passions); **associations** (block clubs, choirs, leagues, the domino table — 'an association is the collective word for citizen'); **institutions** (schools, libraries, parks, churches, businesses); **physical places**; **exchange** (barter, timebanks, buying clubs, money); and **stories** — 'treasure maps that help us discover the hidden bounty.'

How a neighborhood actually does it, per McKnight and Russell's sequence: **discover** the neighborhood's natural connectors → **welcome** everyone, especially people at the margins, through learning conversations and listening campaigns → **portray** what you've heard (this is the map — a byproduct of conversations, never a data-scrape) → **share** through skill swaps, repair cafés, seed exchanges → **celebrate** → **vision** together.

Two cautions from the source itself: an asset map does not mean the neighborhood needs nothing from outside — internal assets are 'absolutely necessary but usually not sufficient'; and ABCD is meant to complement and often precede organizing, not substitute for it. The map hands the organizing arc its answer to question three — and a gift list waiting for question four.

field_tips: inventory associations, not just individuals — McKnight's checklist runs from block clubs to stamp collectors
the most powerful communities identify the gifts of people at the margins
never let the map substitute for the conversations
ingredients: somewhere shared to portray it all

how_it_works: Discover the natural connectors and convene them.
Welcome: run gift conversations door by door, margins first.
Portray: compile a shared, evolving picture — the map is the byproduct, the relationships are the product.
Share: skill swaps, repair cafés, seed exchanges — on-ramps where gifts meet.
Celebrate, then vision together — and only then bridge to outside resources.

an association does something beyond its founding purpose
outside agencies respond to a community agenda instead of setting one

items.summary: Asset-based community development's core practice: before listing what your neighborhood lacks, inventory what it has — residents' gifts, associations, institutions, places, exchange, and stories — and connect them.
items.title: The Asset Map (Not the Needs Map)

items.body:
## What it is

A neighborhood-level civic structure where residents organize collectively to advocate for the neighborhood, improve local conditions, and participate in city governance. Forms vary widely: some are loose volunteer-led nonprofits, some are city-recognized governance bodies with specific advisory roles. Most major U.S. cities have neighborhood association systems.

The structure does the slow, ongoing work that one-off events can't: a continuing entity that shows up to city hearings, maintains a contact list, organizes neighbors, and outlasts any single leader.

## Why it works

A neighborhood without a representative structure has no continuing voice. Each issue (a new development, a budget cut, a traffic change) is litigated by whoever happens to show up that month. With a neighborhood association, the neighborhood has a known address, a meeting schedule, a recognized voice, and institutional memory across years.

The association is also the connective tissue between specific recipes in this book. Block parties, mutual aid pods, [block stewards](../01-knowing-your-neighbors/block-stewards.md), placemaking projects: all benefit from a shared neighborhood organization that holds them together.

## What you need

- **Time:** Monthly meetings minimum. Officer roles take 5 to 20 hours per month depending on the role and the association's scope.
- **People:** Resident members, elected officers, committee members, community partners, city liaisons.
- **Space:** A regular meeting location (library, school, community center). Defined neighborhood boundaries.
- **Materials:** Bylaws, meeting agendas, communication channels (newsletter, email list, website), planning documents.
- **Skills:** Meeting facilitation, advocacy, community organizing, relationship building.
- **Energy level:** Moderate to high. Ongoing meetings, occasional advocacy intensity.

## How to host it

### If you're starting a new neighborhood association

1. **Check what already exists.** Many neighborhoods already have an association, even if it's been dormant for years. Reviving an existing structure is often easier than starting fresh.
2. **Define the boundaries.** A few blocks, a defined district, a recognized neighborhood. Many cities have official neighborhood boundaries that can be used.
3. **Hold an organizing meeting.** Promote widely. Goal of the meeting: confirm interest, draft initial purpose and structure, identify a steering committee.
4. **Write bylaws.** Most cities have templates. Cover: who can be a member, how officers are elected, meeting frequency, decision-making, dues if any, dissolution.
5. **Decide on formal recognition.** Some cities formally recognize neighborhood associations and provide them with specific advisory roles, funding, or insurance. Look into your city's process. Portland, Los Angeles, and many other cities have well-developed systems.
6. **Hold regular meetings.** Monthly is standard. Same time, same place. Agendas distributed in advance. Minutes kept.
7. **Pick a few initial projects.** Don't try to do everything in year one. A clean-up day, a block party, advocacy on one local issue, a welcome practice for new neighbors. Building competence and trust before scope.
8. **Communicate.** A monthly newsletter, an email list, a [Front Porch Forum](../01-knowing-your-neighbors/front-porch-forum.md), bulletin boards. Multiple channels reach more neighbors.

### If you're joining or reviving an existing association

1. **Attend a meeting.** See who's there, what's discussed, where the energy is.
2. **Volunteer for something specific.** A committee, a project, an event. Build credibility before standing for office.
3. **Bring fresh energy carefully.** Long-time members often have deep knowledge; new members often have new ideas. Both matter. Tension between them is part of the work.
4. **Refresh communication.** Many neighborhood associations have stale newsletters or websites. Often a single volunteer with current tech skills can transform reach.

## Variations

**Neighborhood council.** A formally recognized governmental structure. Los Angeles has 99 neighborhood councils with elected boards and specific advisory roles. Portland has chartered neighborhood associations with budget allocations.

**Block club.** A smaller informal version, often just one block. Less formal structure, more relational depth. Many cities have block clubs alongside neighborhood associations.

**Issue-based group.** A neighborhood organization focused on a specific issue (traffic safety, schools, housing). Sometimes precedes a broader neighborhood association.

**Coalition of block clubs.** A neighborhood association built from a federation of block-level clubs. Bottom-up rather than top-down.

**Equity-centered association.** Some neighborhood associations have deliberately restructured to address the history of exclusion in many U.S. neighborhood organizations (which have sometimes been organized by homeowners against renters, against unhoused people, or against people of color). The work involves rewriting bylaws, broadening membership, and changing meeting times and locations.

## Stories from neighborhoods

**Portland, Oregon** has one of the most formalized neighborhood systems in the U.S. Its neighborhood associations are chartered by city code (Chapter 3.96), organized into seven district coalitions, and have specific advisory roles in city government.

**Los Angeles** has 99 elected neighborhood councils that advise the city on land use, budget, and other decisions. Members are elected; budgets are allocated to each council.

**Chicago's block clubs**, especially in Black neighborhoods, have a deep history of building local civic culture, neighborhood safety, and intergenerational connection across decades.

In smaller towns and cities, neighborhood associations often function more like extended block clubs: a smaller scale, more relational, less institutional. Both forms can produce strong outcomes.

## Where to learn more

- A model city: [Portland Neighborhood System](https://www.portland.gov/civic/myneighborhood/about-neighborhood-system)
- Los Angeles model: [Empower LA](https://empowerla.org/)
- Adjacent recipes: [Block Stewards](../01-knowing-your-neighbors/block-stewards.md), [Microgrant Gathering](./microgrant-gathering.md), [Participatory Budgeting](./participatory-budgeting.md), [Good Neighbor Agreement](../01-knowing-your-neighbors/good-neighbor-agreement.md)

**Block club.** A smaller informal version, often just one block. Less formal structure, more relational depth. Many cities have block clubs alongside neighborhood associations.

**Issue-based group.** A neighborhood organization focused on a specific issue (traffic safety, schools, housing). Sometimes precedes a broader neighborhood association.

**Coalition of block clubs.** A neighborhood association built from a federation of block-level clubs. Bottom-up rather than top-down.

**Equity-centered association.** Some neighborhood associations have deliberately restructured to address the history of exclusion in many U.S. neighborhood organizations (which have sometimes been organized by homeowners against renters, against unhoused people, or against people of color). The work involves rewriting bylaws, broadening membership, and changing meeting times and locations.

ingredients.time: Monthly meetings minimum. Officer roles take 5 to 20 hours per month depending on the role and the association's scope.
ingredients.space: A regular meeting location (library, school, community center). Defined neighborhood boundaries.
ingredients.people: Resident members, elected officers, committee members, community partners, city liaisons.
ingredients.skills: Meeting facilitation, advocacy, community organizing, relationship building.
ingredients.materials: Bylaws, meeting agendas, communication channels (newsletter, email list, website), planning documents.
ingredients.energy_level: Moderate to high. Ongoing meetings, occasional advocacy intensity.

**Portland, Oregon** has one of the most formalized neighborhood systems in the U.S. Its neighborhood associations are chartered by city code (Chapter 3.96), organized into seven district coalitions, and have specific advisory roles in city government.

**Los Angeles** has 99 elected neighborhood councils that advise the city on land use, budget, and other decisions. Members are elected; budgets are allocated to each council.

**Chicago's block clubs**, especially in Black neighborhoods, have a deep history of building local civic culture, neighborhood safety, and intergenerational connection across decades.

In smaller towns and cities, neighborhood associations often function more like extended block clubs: a smaller scale, more relational, less institutional. Both forms can produce strong outcomes.

items.body:
*The need:* You can't organize people you don't know, and you don't know people until you know why they care.

The one-to-one meeting is the foundational tool of relational organizing: a deliberate, scheduled conversation — usually 30 to 60 minutes, often over coffee — whose purpose is to build a public relationship, not to chat. Every 1:1 has four movements:

1. **Purpose** — Be up front about why you're meeting. If you plan to ask for a commitment at the end, say so when you set it up.
2. **Exploration** — Most of the meeting. Ask probing questions to learn the other person's story, values, and resources: "Why is this important enough for you to act?" "Can you remember the first time you stood up for something you believed in?"
3. **Exchange** — Share your own story where it connects. A relationship forms when both people commit their most valuable resource — time — and leave with something: insight, support, a connection.
4. **Commitment** — End with a specific next step together. Never leave without one.

The don'ts matter as much as the dos: don't try to persuade instead of listen; don't skip stories to "get to the point"; don't end without a plan; split the bill (paying makes it feel transactional).

Organizers use three types of 1:1s: **recruitment** (start a relationship), **maintenance** (every two weeks with the people you organize alongside — don't wait for a problem), and **escalation** (invite someone into more responsibility). And because relationships take real attention, each part-time organizer can genuinely maintain about five; a full-timer, about ten. In a neighborhood, the 1:1 is simpler and older than any of this: it's how neighbors become people to each other.

field_tips: Maintenance 1:1s every two weeks, before problems, not after
ingredients: a public-ish place (coffee shop, park, porch)
a real question and a real ask
metadata.source_note: Structure (purpose / exploration / exchange / commitment), the three types of 1:1s, and sustainable relationship ratios from 'Organizing: People, Power, Change' (2014). The relational meeting as a named discipline descends from the Industrial Areas Foundation.
how_it_works: Schedule it and name the purpose up front.
Spend most of the time exploring: their story, their values, what they'd bring.
Exchange — connect their story to yours; offer something back.
End with a specific commitment and a next date.
Log who you met and what you learned; follow up within 48 hours.
success_signals: you can say what they care about and why
they made a commitment
a second meeting exists on a calendar

items.summary: A scheduled 30–60 minute conversation between two people, built on stories rather than small talk, that ends with a commitment. The basic unit of organizing.
