items.body:
## What it is

A self-organizing format developed by Harrison Owen, who noticed that the most valuable parts of conferences happened during coffee breaks. Open Space gives an entire day or longer the texture of a coffee break. The organizers set one big compelling question. The participants then propose their own sessions on whatever they care about within that question. Sessions self-fill. People move between them freely.

Open Space has been used with groups from 5 to 2,000 people across 140+ countries.

## Why it works

Open Space trusts the room. Most agendas are guesses about what the people in the room care about; Open Space asks them directly and lets them choose. The result is sessions of unusual intensity because everyone in the session chose to be there.

Four principles and one law do the work:
- *Whoever comes is the right people.*
- *Whatever happens is the only thing that could have.*
- *Whenever it starts is the right time.*
- *When it's over, it's over.*
- *The Law of Two Feet: if you're not learning or contributing, move.*

## What you need

- **Time:** 2 hours minimum. Typically 4 hours to 3 days.
- **People:** 5 to 2,000+. Diversity matters more than count.
- **Space:** A large gathering room plus multiple breakout rooms or corners. A bulletin board or wall big enough for the marketplace.
- **Materials:** Index cards, markers, a large wall board for posting sessions, name tags, note-taking materials. Optional: a small bell to signal time.
- **Skills:** Understanding of self-organization. Comfort letting go of control.
- **Energy level:** Moderate to high. Participants move.

## How to host it

1. **Set the question.** This is the heart. The question should matter to everyone in the room, be open-ended, and welcome multiple paths. Examples: *"What does our neighborhood need next?" "How do we hold this work together?" "What can we build before the next election?"*
2. **Gather everyone in a circle.** Welcome. Introduce the theme. Explain the principles and the Law of Two Feet plainly. The principles will sound strange the first time. Read them anyway.
3. **Open the marketplace.** Invite anyone who has a session they want to host to come to the center, write the topic on an index card, and post it to the wall with a time slot and location.
4. **Let people propose.** The first 5 or 10 minutes is uncertain. Hold the silence. Eventually someone steps up. Then another. By 20 minutes, you usually have 10 to 30 sessions posted.
5. **People sign up loosely.** Participants scan the wall, talk briefly with each other, and head to the session they want.
6. **Sessions happen.** Each session is led by whoever proposed it. The Law of Two Feet means anyone can leave at any time. Most sessions take notes (a one-page summary goes back on the wall).
7. **Multiple rounds.** Typically 3 to 5 sessions over the day, with breaks between.
8. **Closing circle.** Bring everyone back. Open mic for what people learned and what they want to commit to next. The closing carries the energy of the day forward.

## Variations

**Mini Open Space.** A half-day version with one or two rounds. Lower bar to facilitate, almost as much value.

**Hybrid agenda.** Some structured sessions in the morning, Open Space in the afternoon. Useful when leadership wants to set context first.

**Themed Open Space.** A more specific question (rather than fully open). Trades some emergence for more focused output.

**Action-oriented Open Space.** A "convergence" session at the end where participants commit to projects and assemble teams.

## Stories from neighborhoods

Harrison Owen developed Open Space Technology in the mid-1980s. The method has been used by the United Nations, the World Health Organization, corporate strategy sessions, climate adaptation gatherings, education reform conferences, and many neighborhood-scale events.

A common pattern: organizers fear that no one will propose sessions or that "the wrong things" will get prioritized. Almost always, the room produces a richer agenda than the organizers would have designed.

## Where to learn more

- Brief user's guide: [Harrison Owen on Open Space](https://openspaceworld.org/wp2/hho/papers/brief-users-guide-open-space-technology/)
- The community: [Open Space World](https://openspaceworld.org/)
- Adjacent recipes: [World Cafe](./world-cafe.md), [Art of Hosting](./art-of-hosting.md)

items.body:
## What it is

Not one recipe, but a toolkit. Specific facilitation moves that shift gatherings toward distributed participation. Things like opening with a warm-up that requires everyone to talk and laugh in the first ten minutes. Using "1-2-4-All" so people think privately, then share with a partner, then a small group, then the whole room. Rotating who makes announcements. Embedding "raise your hand if..." moments throughout a presentation.

The underlying frame is moving from "Hub" structures (power centered on a presenter) toward "Web" structures (everyone connecting to each other).

## Why it works

Most meetings default to a single speaker model that consolidates power in whoever holds the mic. The default model also lets quieter people stay invisible. Tactics that explicitly distribute speaking, listening, and decision-making produce more participation without anyone needing to be braver than they already are.

The key principle: structure quiet warm-ups before high-stakes participation. By the time the whole-group conversation happens, everyone has already spoken to one other person and a small group. The big share is the third or fourth time they've used their voice in the session.

## What you need

- **Time:** Variable. Tactics range from 5-minute warm-ups to full-session designs.
- **People:** Works at any group size from 5 to 200+.
- **Space:** Flexible. Works in-person and online.
- **Materials:** Depends on the tactic. Timers, notecards, flip charts, shared documents.
- **Skills:** Comfort with facilitation, awareness of power dynamics, willingness to experiment.
- **Energy level:** Moderate to high. Active facilitation is required.

## A starter set of tactics

### Openings

1. **Everyone talks and laughs in the first 10 minutes.** A short warm-up question. People at tables of 4 take turns. By 10 minutes in, every voice has been heard at small scale.
2. **Collaborative agenda check.** Show the agenda. Ask: anything missing, anything you'd cut, anything that needs more time? Adjust on the fly.
3. **Rotate the welcome.** Different people open each meeting. Different person makes announcements.
4. **Pulse check.** Quick reading of the room: "Show me on your fingers how present you are right now, one to five." Useful temperature read.

### Discussions and shares

5. **1-2-4-All.** Pose a question. Each person thinks for 2 minutes (silent, written). Pair-share for 4 minutes. Groups of 4 for 6 minutes. Whole group for 10 minutes. Builds confidence before anyone has to risk speaking publicly.
6. **Raise your hand if...** Embed throughout a talk. Forces engagement without requiring speech.
7. **Rotating speakers.** Multiple voices presenting in turn instead of one long presentation.
8. **Unconference style.** See [Open Space Technology](./open-space.md).

### Decision-making

9. **Warm up with low-stakes practice.** Don't try a new decision method on a high-stakes decision. Use it on something easy first.
10. **Multiple modes.** Some people decide better in conversation, some after time alone with the materials. Build in both.
11. **Dot voting.** Each participant gets a few stickers; place them on the options they support. Quick, visual, distributed.
12. **Polls plus discussion.** Take a quick poll. Show the room the distribution. Then discuss. Surfacing the spread changes the conversation.

### Throughout

13. **Stack the speakers list.** Track who has spoken. Invite voices that haven't. Don't shame the quiet ones; just open space.
14. **Move bodies.** People standing, walking, moving to corners by their position. Movement shifts attention.
15. **Build in silence.** Two or three minutes of genuine silence after a hard question. Real thought takes longer than the social pressure to fill space.

(There are many more. The full list and the philosophy behind them is at [grouphug.substack.com/p/pluralize-the-power](https://grouphug.substack.com/p/pluralize-the-power-group-participation-ideas).)

## Variations

The tactics combine. Most well-facilitated gatherings use 4 to 8 of them across the day. The trick is to use them deliberately, not as gimmicks. Each tactic is solving a specific problem (quiet voices, unequal access to the mic, decision-making without enough preparation). Match the tactic to the problem.

## Stories from neighborhoods

**Oakland's participatory budgeting process** shifted from public hearings (where mostly the already-powerful spoke) to participatory design using many of these tactics: group warm-ups, small-group conversations, 1-2-4-All for brainstorming, rotating facilitators. Participation more than tripled.

A quieter community member said it directly: *"I never would have spoken up, but starting with a pair conversation made it feel safe. By the time we talked as a whole group, I had things to say."*

## Where to learn more

- The source: [Pluralize the Power: Group Participation Ideas](https://grouphug.substack.com/p/pluralize-the-power-group-participation-ideas)
- A related deep toolkit: [Liberating Structures](https://www.liberatingstructures.com/) (33 microstructures with similar logic)
- Adjacent recipes: [World Cafe](./world-cafe.md), [Open Space Technology](./open-space.md), [Community Agreements](./community-agreements.md)

items.body:
## What it is

A democratic process where community members directly decide how to spend a public budget. Residents propose projects. Volunteers and staff develop the strongest proposals into concrete projects with budgets. The community votes on which projects to fund. Selected projects are implemented and reported back.

The practice was developed in **Porto Alegre, Brazil** in 1989 and has spread to over 11,500 processes globally. In the U.S., participatory budgeting has been used by city councils, mayors, public housing authorities, schools, and youth-led initiatives.

## Why it works

The conventional way public budgets get spent: elected officials and bureaucrats make decisions, residents react. The result is that most residents have no direct relationship to public spending and most public spending bears little resemblance to what residents would have prioritized.

Participatory budgeting changes that. Residents identify their own priorities. The process surfaces what neighborhoods actually need (often: traffic calming, lighting, parks, programs for elders, programs for youth, very rarely the things bureaucracies tend to prioritize). Civic engagement grows because the choices are real.

## What you need

- **Time:** 6 to 12 months for a full annual cycle.
- **People:** Community facilitators, project managers, agency or government staff, volunteer voter guides, diverse residents across the community.
- **Space:** Multiple accessible venues for brainstorming and voting. Libraries, schools, community centers. Online options as well.
- **Materials:** Proposal templates, budget worksheets, voting ballots, community education materials. Multilingual everything.
- **Skills:** Facilitation, budget literacy, project management, accessibility coordination.
- **Energy level:** High during the active months. Requires sustained outreach.

## How to host it

This is a recipe that typically requires institutional partnership (city, county, school, or housing authority) because the budget being spent is public money. The community-organizing version is bringing this to your jurisdiction. The implementation version requires partnership.

### If you're advocating for participatory budgeting

1. **Find allies.** Often other community organizations have already been exploring this. [Participatory Budgeting Project](https://www.participatorybudgeting.org/) maintains a national network.
2. **Build a case.** Document successful pilots elsewhere. New York City has run PB through city council districts; Chicago, Cambridge, Boston, Seattle, and many others have produced strong evidence.
3. **Pitch a pilot.** A defined budget ($500K to $5M), a defined area, a defined timeline. Most cities will start with one council district or one program.
4. **Demand community design.** The strongest PB processes are designed with substantial community input on the rules, the eligibility, and the voting mechanism. Watch for "PB-lite" versions where the city retains too much control.

### If you're running participatory budgeting

The cycle:

1. **Idea collection (4 to 8 weeks).** Residents submit project ideas through forms, neighborhood meetings, schools, online platforms, intercept events. Aim for many ideas; quality emerges from quantity.
2. **Proposal development (6 to 12 weeks).** Volunteer "budget delegates" work with agency staff to translate the most popular ideas into concrete projects with realistic budgets and implementation plans. This phase is where most of the labor happens.
3. **Community voting (1 to 4 weeks).** Residents vote on the proposals. Voting age is often lowered (16, sometimes 14). Multiple voting locations and online options. Multilingual materials. Aim for genuine accessibility, not just compliance.
4. **Implementation and reporting (the rest of the year).** The winning projects are implemented by the city or its partners. Updates back to the community at quarterly intervals.

## Variations

**Youth PB.** Significant portion or all of a budget allocated by young people. Boston's Youth Lead the Change is a leading example.

**School PB.** Students decide how to spend a school budget. Some districts now do this in every school.

**Public housing PB.** Residents of housing authorities decide on improvements to common spaces, programming, and capital projects.

**Climate PB.** A budget specifically directed at climate or sustainability projects. Used in several European cities and emerging in U.S. contexts.

**Universal participation models.** Some jurisdictions allow undocumented residents to vote in PB. The process is about civic life, not citizenship status.

## Stories from neighborhoods

Over 11,500 participatory budgeting processes have been implemented globally since the model's start in **Porto Alegre** in 1989. In the U.S.:

- **Boston's Youth Lead the Change** invested $1M in projects identified by young people.
- **Cambridge, MA** has allocated $1M+ annually via PB since 2014.
- **King County, Washington** distributed $11.75M across 42 community-chosen projects in 2024.
- **New York City** has run PB through city council districts since 2011.

Outcomes consistently include: increased civic participation (often 5x to 10x voting on PB compared to local elections), better-targeted spending, and stronger community-government relationships.

## Where to learn more

- The national hub: [Participatory Budgeting Project](https://www.participatorybudgeting.org/)
- Global network: [International Observatory on Participatory Democracy](https://www.oidp.net/)
- Foundational text: Josh Lerner, *Making Democracy Fun*
- Adjacent recipes: [Microgrant Gathering](./microgrant-gathering.md), [Neighborhood Association](./neighborhood-associations.md), [Appreciative Inquiry](../04-gathering-design/appreciative-inquiry.md)

items.body:
## What it is

A restorative practice with deep roots in Indigenous traditions, adapted into contemporary use in criminal justice, schools, families, and community contexts. Peacemaking circles bring together those affected by harm in a structured circle format with trained facilitators. Over multiple sessions, the group works toward shared understanding, accountability, repair, and reintegration.

The form has been carefully developed by First Nations practitioners and Indigenous knowledge keepers. Many contemporary practitioners (Kay Pranis, the late Howard Zehr, and others) have written extensively about it, always crediting the Indigenous lineage.

## Why it works

The conventional justice system asks: *who did what, and what's the punishment*. Restorative practice asks different questions: *who was harmed, what do they need, who has obligations, and how do we move forward*.

Circles answer those questions through structure. The circle puts everyone in equal physical space. The talking piece ensures equal voice and deep listening. The multiple sessions allow time and trust to develop. The presence of community members alongside victim and person who caused harm distributes the work.

The outcomes consistently show lower recidivism and higher victim satisfaction than conventional punitive responses.

## What you need

- **Time:** Multiple sessions. Pre-circles over 2 to 4 weeks. Main circle 2 to 4 hours. Follow-up circles ongoing.
- **People:** Trained facilitators (essential). 8 to 50+ participants depending on the case.
- **Space:** A quiet, safe space allowing a true circle. Often community centers, schools, faith spaces, or council chambers.
- **Materials:** A talking piece. Optionally candles, plants, opening and closing readings.
- **Skills:** Circle facilitation, trauma-informed practice, conflict resolution, community organizing.
- **Energy level:** Medium to high. Sustained commitment and emotional presence.

## How to host it

This is a recipe that requires training to do well. The steps below describe the structure, not a substitute for facilitator training.

1. **Get trained.** Practitioner programs exist through restorative justice networks. **Living Justice Press**, **Restorative Justice Council**, **Howard Zehr's** work at Eastern Mennonite University, and Indigenous-led training programs are starting points.
2. **Determine fit.** Not every situation belongs in a circle. Cases involving ongoing power imbalance, current safety risk, or coercion need different responses. Skilled facilitators assess fit carefully.
3. **Conduct pre-circles.** Meet separately with each participant beforehand. Build trust. Prepare them for what the main circle will look like. Address fears. Ensure consent.
4. **Set the container.** Arrange chairs in a circle with a centerpiece (talking piece, often a feather, stone, or shell). Open with grounding: a moment of silence, a reading, an acknowledgment of the land if appropriate.
5. **Establish agreements.** Each circle starts with shared agreements: respect, confidentiality, speaking from the heart, listening with intention, non-interruption.
6. **Open the conversation.** The facilitator names what brought everyone together. The talking piece begins to move.
7. **Each round serves a purpose.** Common rounds:
   - Introductions and intentions.
   - The harm: what happened, who was affected.
   - Impact: how each person was affected.
   - Needs: what does each person need now.
   - Accountability and repair: what the person who caused harm commits to.
   - Community support: how the community will support both victim and person who caused harm.
   - Closing.
8. **Plan the follow-through.** A circle alone does not produce repair. The plan that emerges from it does. Follow-up circles, check-ins, and continued support are part of the practice.

## Variations

**School circle.** Used in schools for discipline, conflict resolution, and community building. Increasingly common as schools move away from suspension-based discipline.

**Family circle.** A family-level restorative process, often in cases of intergenerational conflict, divorce, or harm within a family.

**Community-level circle.** A circle convened by a community to address harm that affected the whole neighborhood. Often public-safety related.

**Healing circle.** A circle focused on collective healing rather than a specific harm. Used after community trauma (police violence, mass shootings, disasters).

**Reintegration circle.** A circle to support someone returning from incarceration, hospitalization, or another difficult separation.

## Stories from neighborhoods

Peacemaking circles have been used by Indigenous communities for generations. Contemporary applications have spread widely:

**Criminal justice.** Many jurisdictions in the U.S. and Canada now have restorative justice diversion programs that include circles. Outcomes show reduced recidivism and higher victim satisfaction.

**Schools.** Hundreds of schools across the U.S. have implemented circle-based restorative practices. Schools that have done this carefully report reduced suspensions and improved climate.

**Communities.** Circles have been used to address racial harm, community-police tensions, gang conflict, and large-scale community grief. Each adaptation respects the form while shaping content to context.

## Where to learn more

- Foundational text: Kay Pranis, *The Little Book of Circle Processes*
- Foundational text: Howard Zehr, *The Little Book of Restorative Justice*
- Publisher: [Living Justice Press](https://livingjusticepress.org/)
- A resource hub: [Transform Harm](https://transformharm.org/)
- Adjacent recipes: [Talking Circle](../04-gathering-design/talking-circle.md), [Creative Interventions](./creative-interventions.md), [Community Mediation](./community-mediation.md)

*The need:* Communities losing connection to place lose part of themselves.

Places hold memory, identity, and possibility, and when communities lose connection to place through displacement, development, or erasure, they lose part of themselves. This recipe turns one specific place into a canvas for collective memory: pick a single street, corner, or building and document it so intensively that it becomes a mirror for the whole community to see its history and its future. Specificity creates universality, displays change regularly to build anticipation, all histories are included (especially the ignored ones), and the space itself is allowed to determine the format.

**How it works**
1. Choose a place that is under threat or undervalued.
2. Document everything: who was here, what happened, what it means.
3. Layer past onto present, such as old photos in current windows and elder stories on young walls.
4. Make the invisible history visible in the actual place.
5. Change the display regularly to pull people back.
6. Let the place tell its own story through accumulated details.

**Ingredients**
- one specific place that matters
- 10-15 people with stories about it
- ways to make documentation visible
- someone who loves details
- permission to claim space

**Minimum resources:** Free with phones; $ for printing if physical.

**You'll know it's working when**
- people return to see what's new
- 'I never knew this happened here' becomes common
- the place becomes protected through community love

**Field tips**
- specificity creates universality
- change displays regularly
- include all histories
- let the space determine the format

**Building from (real projects)**
- Westminster Stories
- Greene Street
- The Wall of Wrigley Field
- Oakland Lowdown
- Memories of the Market

## What it is

A method for designing public space that puts the people who use the space at the center of the design process. Developed and codified by the [Project for Public Spaces (PPS)](https://www.pps.org/), founded in 1975. Placemaking can be applied to plazas, parks, streets, waterfronts, libraries, transit stops, and almost any public space that isn't quite working.

The signature move is "lighter, quicker, cheaper": test ideas with temporary, low-cost interventions before committing to expensive permanent changes. A cardboard chair will tell you something a rendering can't.

## Why it works

Most public space design is done by experts, presented to communities for "input," then built. The result is often a space that nobody uses despite being technically well-designed. Placemaking inverts the order. The community observes, dreams, and tests first. The experts come in to support what the community has discovered.

The "lighter, quicker, cheaper" principle is the practical engine. A movable chair, a temporary parklet, a pop-up cafe, a painted crosswalk: each one teaches the community what they actually want, faster than any planning process can.

## What you need

- **Time:** 3 to 12 months for an initial transformation. Ongoing stewardship indefinite.
- **People:** Community members. Local organizations. City partners. 30+ engaged in the core work.
- **Space:** The public space being transformed. Meeting venues for design sessions.
- **Materials:** Camera or notes for observation. Flip charts for visioning. Paint and basic materials for experiments. Photography documentation.
- **Skills:** Community engagement, observation, facilitation, design thinking, project management.
- **Energy level:** Moderate to high. Includes both physical activity and strategic thinking.

## How to host it

The PPS framework moves through five steps:

1. **Meet the community and identify stakeholders.** Who uses this space? Who lives near it? Who doesn't use it that you'd want to? Map the stakeholders. Hold initial conversations. Listen.
2. **Assess the site and its assets.** Spend time there. PPS recommends visiting at different times of day, days of the week, weather conditions. Notice: where do people stop? Where do they pass through? What's broken? What's working but not enough? What does the space want to be?
3. **Create a vision.** Convene the community to articulate what the space could become. Use a [World Cafe](../04-gathering-design/world-cafe.md), [Appreciative Inquiry](../04-gathering-design/appreciative-inquiry.md), or charrette format. The vision is the destination; the path will be iterative.
4. **Develop an implementation plan with "lighter, quicker, cheaper" experiments.** Don't try to build the final state immediately. Pilot pieces:
   - Movable chairs in a plaza.
   - A pop-up cafe or food truck.
   - A temporary parklet (a parking space turned into seating and planting).
   - Painted crosswalks or sidewalk extensions.
   - A community garden bed.
   - Music or programming during certain hours.
   Each experiment is a learning opportunity. Document what works.
5. **Manage ongoing activation.** A space that's been transformed needs continued care. Programming, events, maintenance, evolution. Build the community of stewards.

## Variations

**Tactical urbanism.** A faster, sometimes guerrilla version of placemaking. Smaller-scale interventions, sometimes done without permission, that demonstrate what's possible. [Tactical Urbanists' Guide](http://tacticalurbanismguide.com/) is a strong resource.

**Permanent placemaking.** When experiments have proven a direction, more permanent capital investment follows: better seating, lighting, plantings, programming staff.

**Internal placemaking.** Some institutions (libraries, schools, hospitals) apply placemaking principles to their own spaces. Same methodology, smaller scope.

**Equitable placemaking.** Placemaking that specifically addresses displacement, gentrification, and the history of who has been excluded from public space. PPS and others have produced significant materials on this.

## Stories from neighborhoods

**Project for Public Spaces** has worked on hundreds of public space transformations since 1975. Some of the better-known: **Bryant Park** in New York City, **Detroit's Campus Martius Park**, the **Times Square** redesign, public market revivals in Pike Place (Seattle), Reading Terminal (Philadelphia), and others.

At smaller scale, the methodology has been used by neighborhood associations, business improvement districts, libraries, and grassroots groups across the country.

The **Great Places** index that PPS has maintained for decades is a useful reference for what well-functioning public space looks like.

## Where to learn more

- The home organization: [Project for Public Spaces](https://www.pps.org/)
- Method overview: [What is Placemaking?](https://www.pps.org/article/what-is-placemaking)
- Tactical urbanism: [Tactical Urbanists' Guide](http://tacticalurbanismguide.com/)
- Foundational text: [Eric Klinenberg, *Palaces for the People*](https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/Palaces-for-the-People/Eric-Klinenberg/9781524761172) (2018)
- Adjacent recipes: [Intersection Repair](./intersection-repair.md), [Community-Built Playspace](./community-built-playspace.md), [Community Garden](./community-garden.md)

## What it is

A national program that partners with schools to embed play-based strategies into school culture. Playworks places on-site coaches, trains school staff, and provides curricula that turn recess from chaotic free-for-all into an intentional space for play, cooperation, peer leadership, and conflict resolution.

The program has operated for nearly 30 years and reaches tens of thousands of students annually. Research consistently shows improved peer relationships, increased physical activity, better classroom focus, and reduced behavioral issues.

## Why it works

Recess is often the most chaotic part of a school day. For some kids, especially those targeted in social hierarchies, it's the worst part. Intentional facilitation changes the dynamics: more kids included in games, fewer fights, more peer leadership, more physical movement. The shift in recess culture often shifts the school's broader culture as well.

The model doesn't prescribe specific games. It trains adults to facilitate play that naturally builds cooperation, fairness, and communication. The same games most kids already know, played with light facilitation, work.

## What you need

This is primarily a school-level recipe, not a neighborhood-level one. It's included here because neighborhoods often include schools, and the schools' culture shapes the neighborhood's children significantly.

- **Time:** Ongoing. Typically 1 to 2 hours of recess time daily, plus staff training time.
- **People:** 1 to 2 on-site coaches per school in the full Playworks model. Whole-school staff participation in the lighter implementation models.
- **Space:** School playgrounds, gymnasiums, multipurpose spaces.
- **Materials:** Games, sports equipment, conflict-resolution tools, digital platform access, training curricula.
- **Skills:** Play facilitation, coaching, conflict resolution, leadership development.
- **Energy level:** Medium to high. Sustained staff engagement.

## How to host it

### If you're a school

1. **Engage with [Playworks](https://www.playworks.org/).** Multiple service levels exist, from on-site coaches (most intensive) to staff training only (lighter, lower cost).
2. **Pick the right model for your school.** Budget and capacity vary widely. Even the lightest version (staff training) produces meaningful change.
3. **Onboard staff.** Recess monitors, PE teachers, classroom teachers, and administrators learn play facilitation, conflict resolution, and youth leadership development.
4. **Implement.** Coaches or trained staff facilitate recess: introducing games, inviting all kids into play, modeling de-escalation, building peer leaders.
5. **Develop student leaders.** Older students learn to lead games and resolve disputes. The peer leadership is one of the deepest impacts.
6. **Measure and adjust.** Schools track: incident reports, physical activity, peer reports of belonging, classroom focus, attendance.

### If you're a parent or neighborhood organizer

1. **Advocate.** Bring Playworks materials to your school principal or PTA. Most schools have heard of it; many haven't found the resources to implement.
2. **Fundraise.** Some neighborhood organizations and businesses partner with schools to fund a Playworks coach. The annual cost is real but smaller than many school programs.
3. **Look for adjacent programs.** Some communities have less formal versions (volunteer-led recess facilitation, university student partnerships, AmeriCorps placements) that achieve similar outcomes at lower cost.
4. **Apply the lessons to community programs.** The principles (intentional facilitation, peer leadership, conflict resolution, inclusion) transfer to youth programs, sports leagues, summer camps, and library programs in neighborhoods.

## Variations

**Junior Coaches.** Older students trained as peer play leaders. Reduces adult labor and builds youth leadership.

**Recess at Home / Recess Reset.** Modified versions launched during and after the pandemic for households and schools dealing with extended remote learning.

**Community recess.** Some neighborhood parks have adopted variants for after-school programs and weekend gatherings.

**Sport-specific play.** Some neighborhood youth sports leagues have integrated Playworks principles into practices and games, reducing the often-toxic adult dynamics of youth sports.

## Stories from neighborhoods

**Playworks** has operated since 1996 and has reached tens of thousands of students. Research at Playworks schools shows:

- 95% of educators agree the program creates engaging learning environments.
- 94% report increased physical activity.
- 96% note improved peer relationships.
- Schools see better classroom participation, improved attendance, and higher grades.

The model has expanded from individual school partnerships to district-wide implementations in several cities. The cumulative effect across years and grades is significant.

## Where to learn more

- The organization: [Playworks](https://www.playworks.org/)
- Free resources and games: [playworks.org/resources](https://www.playworks.org/resource/)
- Broader play research: [Lego Foundation](https://www.legofoundation.com/) on the value of play
- Adjacent recipes: [Community-Built Playspace](../06-placemaking/community-built-playspace.md), [Come Out & Play](./come-out-and-play.md)

## What it is

The practice of being visibly present in the front of your home, ready to talk to anyone who walks by. Porch sitting is the smallest, lowest-energy practice in this book. It requires nothing. It produces, over time, more neighbor relationships than almost anything else.

Front porches existed because pre-air-conditioned homes were too hot to sit in during summer evenings. People sat outside because they had to. Out of that necessity grew the social infrastructure of pre-television neighborhoods. The porch was where you found out what was happening, who was sick, who needed help, who'd had a baby.

You can rebuild that infrastructure. It just takes sitting down.

## Why it works

Most of why people don't know their neighbors is structural. Cars carry us into garages. Phones absorb the time we used to spend outside. The result is that we live in the same place as twenty other households and never see any of them.

Porch sitting reverses the structural default. If you are visibly outside, neighbors who pass will eventually say hi. If they say hi enough times, they will start to slow down. If they slow down enough times, you will know their names. The whole thing takes weeks. It does not require any plan.

## What you need

- **Time:** Anywhere from 20 minutes to a few hours. Best when it becomes routine.
- **People:** You. One chair is enough.
- **Space:** A front porch, stoop, or street-facing yard. Anywhere visible to people walking by.
- **Materials:** A chair. Coffee or tea or a beer. Optionally a book or a project. Optionally a sign that says "come say hi."
- **Skills:** Hospitality. Comfort with small talk. Willingness to be interrupted.
- **Energy level:** Low. This is the practice you can do when you have no energy for anything else.

## How to host it

1. **Put a chair where people can see you.** This is the entire setup. If you have a porch, use it. If you have a stoop, sit on it. If you have a driveway, drag a chair to the end of it.
2. **Set a time you'll do this regularly.** Friday afternoons. Sunday mornings. Weekday evenings before dinner. Routine matters more than duration. Neighbors will start to know you'll be there.
3. **Bring something to do with your hands.** A book, a beverage, a small project. The point is you're available but not staring at every passerby. People who feel watched walk faster.
4. **Smile and say hi to people who pass.** Don't push. A nod, a wave, a hi. That's enough. They'll stop when they're ready.
5. **When someone stops, ask one real question.** Not "how are you" but "have you lived here long" or "do you know what's blooming in that yard." A real question gets a real answer.
6. **Don't keep them.** Two minutes the first time is fine. Five minutes the third time is great. Friendship moves at the speed of slow.
7. **Notice patterns.** Same dog walker every morning. Same family with the stroller. Same kid on the skateboard. Over weeks, you'll start to know who lives where.
8. **Invite someone in eventually.** When a porch acquaintance becomes a porch friend, the next move is a real conversation inside or in the backyard. That's how it deepens.

## Variations

**Coordinated porch hour.** Several neighbors on the same block agree to be on their porches Friday afternoons from 5 to 7. Suddenly the block is alive at the same time. Conversations start to flow between porches.

**Porch sign.** A small sign that says "porch is open" or "come say hi" or "free coffee" lowers the social cost of stopping. Some neighbors put out a thermos and cups.

**Porch project.** Knit, whittle, sketch, garden. Visible activity invites curiosity. People will ask what you're doing.

**Apartment version.** No porch? Sit in the lobby. Sit in the courtyard. Sit on the building's front steps. Same idea, different infrastructure.

## Stories from neighborhoods

**Front Porch Republic** is both a publication and a loose movement of communities reclaiming porch culture. Their core insight: physical design shapes social possibility. Porches close to the street invite neighboring; suburbs designed around garages prevent it.

Across the country, individual blocks and faith communities have organized intentional porch hours where neighbors agree to be visible at the same time. The simplest version of this practice has been catalogued at [the Front Porch Republic's writings](https://www.frontporchrepublic.com/2017/07/sitting-on-the-porch/).

## Where to learn more

- Front Porch Republic: [frontporchrepublic.com](https://www.frontporchrepublic.com/)
- Adjacent recipes: [Block Party](./block-party.md), [Welcome Wagon](./welcome-wagon.md), [Block Stewards](./block-stewards.md)

steps: **Put a chair where people can see you.** This is the entire setup. If you have a porch, use it. If you have a stoop, sit on it. If you have a driveway, drag a chair to the end of it.
**Set a time you'll do this regularly.** Friday afternoons. Sunday mornings. Weekday evenings before dinner. Routine matters more than duration. Neighbors will start to know you'll be there.
**Bring something to do with your hands.** A book, a beverage, a small project. The point is you're available but not staring at every passerby. People who feel watched walk faster.
**Smile and say hi to people who pass.** Don't push. A nod, a wave, a hi. That's enough. They'll stop when they're ready.
**When someone stops, ask one real question.** Not "how are you" but "have you lived here long" or "do you know what's blooming in that yard." A real question gets a real answer.
**Don't keep them.** Two minutes the first time is fine. Five minutes the third time is great. Friendship moves at the speed of slow.
**Notice patterns.** Same dog walker every morning. Same family with the stroller. Same kid on the skateboard. Over weeks, you'll start to know who lives where.
**Invite someone in eventually.** When a porch acquaintance becomes a porch friend, the next move is a real conversation inside or in the backyard. That's how it deepens.

**Coordinated porch hour.** Several neighbors on the same block agree to be on their porches Friday afternoons from 5 to 7. Suddenly the block is alive at the same time. Conversations start to flow between porches.

**Porch sign.** A small sign that says "porch is open" or "come say hi" or "free coffee" lowers the social cost of stopping. Some neighbors put out a thermos and cups.

**Porch project.** Knit, whittle, sketch, garden. Visible activity invites curiosity. People will ask what you're doing.

**Apartment version.** No porch? Sit in the lobby. Sit in the courtyard. Sit on the building's front steps. Same idea, different infrastructure.

ingredients.skills: Hospitality. Comfort with small talk. Willingness to be interrupted.

**Front Porch Republic** is both a publication and a loose movement of communities reclaiming porch culture. Their core insight: physical design shapes social possibility. Porches close to the street invite neighboring; suburbs designed around garages prevent it.

items.body:
*The need:* Communities set priorities constantly but nothing happens.

Communities set priorities all the time through surveys, listening sessions, and civic engagement, and then nothing happens. This recipe ensures a community's priorities actually influence real decisions, budgets, and action. The basic idea: start with small, real decisions someone has genuine authority over, have the community set priorities, implement them exactly as decided with no reinterpretation, show the result, and build toward bigger decisions from there. It can run with institutions (willing partners), around them (organize directly with people), or despite them (build alternatives). Starting small is what builds the trust that makes bigger decisions possible later.

**How it works**
1. Start small, like how to spend $500 in programming money or which library hours to change.
2. Be transparent about what is actually possible and what is not.
3. Let the group research, discuss, and decide using whatever process works for them.
4. Implement exactly what they decided, with no interpretation or adjustment.
5. Show what happened because of their decision.
6. Ask the group what to decide next.

**Ingredients**
- someone with real budget/program authority
- 15-25 affected people
- a way to convene
- clear explanation of constraints
- a trusted facilitator

**Minimum resources:** Free; meeting space and time.

**You'll know it's working when**
- people show up because it's real
- authority expands what communities decide
- other departments ask how

**Field tips**
- start small to build trust
- pay people for their time
- document so it survives staff turnover

**Building from (real projects)**
- My Oakland Agenda
- Promise Tracker
- Give Us Your Two Cents
- What's On Your Ballot
- Complaints Choir

items.body:
## What it is

A facilitation game developed within the microsolidarity practice tradition. Crew members each name a current need and a current gift. The group then plays rounds of making and accepting offers based on those needs and gifts. By the end, the group has produced real commitments and also surfaced patterns: who finds it hard to ask, who can't stop giving, where the flow is stuck.

It is part party game, part group therapy, part agreement-renegotiation. It is one of the best tools for unsticking a crew that has plateaued.

## Why it works

Many crews drift into imbalance over time. One person becomes the helper. One becomes the helped. Resentments build that no one names. The game makes the underlying pattern visible because it asks everyone, in the same moment, the same questions. Patterns that were invisible become impossible to miss.

## What you need

- **Time:** 2 to 3 hours per session. Done monthly or quarterly works well.
- **People:** 3 to 8 people in an established crew. Strangers can play but the depth comes from existing trust.
- **Space:** A comfortable gathering space with privacy. Around a table works.
- **Materials:** Written cards for offers and needs (index cards). A facilitator guide. Reflection prompts.
- **Skills:** Active listening, vulnerability, creative problem-solving, willingness to commit.
- **Energy level:** Moderate to high. Emotionally engaging but generative.

## How to host it

1. **Choose a facilitator.** Someone in the crew or an outsider. The facilitator participates lightly but holds the form.
2. **Open with a check-in.** Each person, briefly: how are you arriving, what's been heavy or light lately.
3. **Write your need.** Each person, silently, on a card: a current need. Material (a place to stay next month, money for X), emotional (a witness for something hard), skill (help writing a hard email, learning a software), social (an introduction, a partner for a trip).
4. **Write your gift.** Same, on another card: something you can offer. A skill, time, a resource, attention, an introduction, a space.
5. **Share.** Round-robin, each person reads their need and their gift. Listen without commenting.
6. **Play rounds.** Anyone can make an offer: "I can do X for your need." The receiver can accept, decline, or modify. If accepted, the pair writes down the commitment with a specific follow-through date.
7. **Notice patterns.** Halfway through, the facilitator asks: who has made many offers? Who has accepted few? Who has asked? Who hasn't? Don't judge; just notice.
8. **Reflect together.** Last 30 minutes. What did you learn about your own asking and giving? What did you learn about the crew? What needs to shift?
9. **Confirm commitments.** Each accepted offer becomes a real follow-through with a real date. Track them. Check in on them next meeting.

## Variations

**Two-person version.** Done as a one-on-one exercise. Useful for romantic partners, business partners, or any two-person relationship.

**Larger group version.** Up to 12 with strong facilitation. Past that, breaks into smaller groups.

**Theme version.** All needs and gifts within a particular domain: money, time, creative work, emotional support. Useful for crews focused on one shared project.

**Quarterly cadence.** Played 3 or 4 times a year as a regular practice. Each cycle catches what changed.

## Stories from neighborhoods

**A Toronto crew of social workers** used the Reciprocity Game to address unspoken resentment about labor imbalance. Playing it revealed that one member felt unable to receive help and another felt obligated to give constantly. After the game, they renegotiated their agreements and established explicit time-banking. The crew survived. Without the game, it probably wouldn't have.

The game has been adopted by crews across Europe and North America as part of regular microsolidarity practice. The most thorough write-up is in [Richard Bartlett's third Microsolidarity essay](https://medium.com/microsolidarity/microsolidarity-part-3-the-reciprocity-game-4109e702a07d).

## Where to learn more

- Original write-up: [Richard Bartlett, "The Reciprocity Game"](https://medium.com/microsolidarity/microsolidarity-part-3-the-reciprocity-game-4109e702a07d)
- Adjacent recipes: [Microsolidarity Crew](./microsolidarity-crew.md), [Time Banking](../03-mutual-aid/timebanking.md)

## What it is

A potluck that adds light facilitation. People still bring dishes. People still eat together. But the gathering is shaped around a question, a decision, a skill-share, or a relationship-building practice. The meal anchors the social warmth. The facilitation moves the room from socializing to actually doing something together.

The term comes from a [Shareable](https://www.shareable.net/how-to/how-to-reinvent-the-potluck/) framing of an older practice. Communities have done this forever; the recipe just names it.

## Why it works

A meeting is intimidating. A potluck is not. Most neighbors will come to a potluck who wouldn't come to a "community meeting." When you add a clear, light frame to the potluck, you get the participation of the potluck and the productivity of the meeting in the same room.

The eating-together is doing real work. People relax. They tell stories. They notice each other. By the time the structured part starts, the room is warmer than any meeting agenda could engineer.

## What you need

- **Time:** 2 to 3 hours for the event. 2 to 3 weeks of light planning.
- **People:** A host or small organizing crew. 8 to 30 attendees works best.
- **Space:** A home, community room, backyard, or park.
- **Materials:** Whatever the dish-sharing logistics require. Optional: a printed prompt, a flip chart, a talking piece.
- **Skills:** Light facilitation. Comfort framing a question and bringing the room to it.
- **Energy level:** Moderate.

## How to host it

1. **Decide the purpose.** A potluck without a purpose is just a potluck. (That's fine too; see [Block Party](../01-knowing-your-neighbors/block-party.md) and [Story-Sharing Potluck](../01-knowing-your-neighbors/story-sharing-potluck.md).) But "reinventing" means you have a specific intention. Examples:
   - Decide on a project the group will take on together.
   - Share skills around a theme (canning, mending, civic engagement).
   - Welcome new neighbors and make introductions across the group.
   - Plan for an upcoming neighborhood event.
   - Process something that happened in the neighborhood (a loss, a conflict, a change).
2. **Invite with the purpose named.** Don't surprise people with structure. The invitation should say: *We'll eat from 6 to 7. From 7 to 8 we'll have a short structured conversation about [purpose]. Bring a dish and your thoughts.*
3. **Coordinate dishes.** A simple shared sheet to prevent four pasta dishes. Or just trust your neighbors.
4. **Welcome and eat first.** Don't rush the meal. The food has to do its work before the structure does.
5. **Open the structured time.** A clear transition: "Let's gather around. I want to take 30 to 60 minutes to do the thing we came together for."
6. **Use a method that fits.** For decisions: dot voting, [community agreements](./community-agreements.md). For relationship: a story round, a [reciprocity game](../02-small-groups-for-support/reciprocity-game.md). For skill share: rotating short demos. For shared problem-solving: a small [World Cafe](./world-cafe.md).
7. **Close with commitments or appreciations.** Each person, briefly: what they're taking, what they're committing to, or what they appreciate from the night.
8. **Linger.** The structured time should not consume the whole evening. Leave space for dessert, more conversation, the relationships that the structured time made possible.

## Variations

**Repeating potluck.** A monthly version with a different purpose each time. Builds rhythm and trust over months.

**Single-issue potluck.** Organized around one specific local issue: traffic on the street, a school decision, a budget proposal. The food creates room for the issue to be discussed without performance.

**Skill potluck.** Each person brings a dish and a skill. The skill share happens between the meal and dessert. Lighter form of a [skillshare](../03-mutual-aid/skillshare.md).

**Outdoor potluck.** A park, a public plaza. Less control over weather, more visibility to passersby. Strong for [placemaking](../06-placemaking/placemaking.md) work.

## Stories from neighborhoods

Community organizers have used potlucks as organizing tools for decades. Faith communities, labor organizers, civil rights movements, mutual aid pods, neighborhood associations. The reframing as a "reinvented" practice in the Shareable toolkit names a discipline that has run quietly for a long time.

Online coordination platforms like [Meal Train](https://www.mealtrain.com/), [Perfect Potluck](https://www.perfectpotluck.com/), and shared spreadsheets reduce the friction of coordinating dishes across larger groups.

## Where to learn more

- The framing: [Shareable's How to Reinvent the Potluck](https://www.shareable.net/how-to/how-to-reinvent-the-potluck/)
- Adjacent recipes: [Block Party](../01-knowing-your-neighbors/block-party.md), [Story-Sharing Potluck](../01-knowing-your-neighbors/story-sharing-potluck.md), [Microgrant Gathering](../11-civic-rhythms/microgrant-gathering.md)

items.body:
## What it is

A community organizing approach where the unit of work is the one-on-one conversation, and the unit of growth is the relationship that already exists. Organizers identify people in a community who have natural credibility and strong ties. Those connectors reach into their networks. The invitation to participate, vote, donate, or act arrives through someone the receiver already trusts.

The method draws from many traditions: labor organizing, faith-based organizing (Industrial Areas Foundation, PICO/Faith in Action), community organizing in the Saul Alinsky lineage, civil rights movement organizing. It has been re-popularized recently by [Southerners on New Ground](https://southernersonnewground.org/) and other contemporary movements.

## Why it works

Cold outreach treats people as numbers. Relational organizing treats people as relationships. The first approach scales by volume. The second scales by trust. When someone you already know and respect asks you to do something, the request crosses the gap that a stranger's call never could.

The one-on-one conversation is the basic unit. Done well, it is a 30- to 60-minute mutual inquiry about what each person cares about, what they're working on, and what they might do together. The relationship itself is the product. The action that comes out of it is the second-order effect.

## What you need

- **Time:** Ongoing. Relationship-building runs in months and years. Each one-on-one is 30 to 60 minutes.
- **People:** Key connectors with strong existing relationships. Trained organizers or coordinators. The wider community network.
- **Space:** Informal spaces: coffee shops, homes, workplaces, parks, community centers.
- **Materials:** A contact tracking system (a simple spreadsheet or a CRM). Conversation guides if useful. Background materials on issues.
- **Skills:** Active listening, relationship-building, one-on-one facilitation, knowledge of the local context.
- **Energy level:** Medium. Sustained over a long time.

## How to host it

1. **Identify the connectors.** Who in your community already has trust capital? Pastors, hairdressers, bartenders, teachers, longtime residents, faith leaders, restaurant owners, recovery group leaders. Not necessarily the people with the loudest voices; the people other people listen to.
2. **Have one-on-ones with each of them.** Not a pitch. A real conversation. *What are you working on? What matters to you about this neighborhood? Who else should I be talking to?* Listen for hours, not minutes. Don't rush.
3. **The good one-on-one has a structure.** 30 to 60 minutes. About half listening to them, about half about the work or the cause. Always ends with: *Who else should I be talking to? Can you make that introduction?*
4. **Map the network.** As one-on-ones produce names, draw the network. Who knows whom. Who has influence in which subgroup. Where the gaps are.
5. **Invite connectors into shared work.** This is where it tips from "I'm getting to know people" to "we're doing something together." A small initial commitment: come to a meeting, bring two neighbors, contribute one thing.
6. **Use the network for asks, not just contacts.** When the campaign or project needs people to show up, vote, write, or give, the ask moves through the network. Not a mass email. A real ask from one trusted person to another.
7. **Hold meetings of connectors.** The connectors themselves benefit from knowing each other. Quarterly gatherings, retreats, dinners. Their relationships with each other strengthen the network as a whole.
8. **Sustain it over years.** This is the part that organizations under-invest in. Relational organizing is not a quarterly tactic. It is a way of working that compounds over decades.

## Variations

**Listening campaigns.** A focused round of one-on-ones (often 100 to 1,000) to surface what a community actually cares about, before deciding what to organize around. Industrial Areas Foundation does this well.

**Relational voter contact.** Voter turnout work done through the network: friends texting friends, neighbors knocking on neighbors. Higher conversion than cold contact.

**Faith-based organizing.** Relational organizing rooted in congregations. PICO/Faith in Action, IAF, and Gamaliel are the main networks.

**Healthcare community organizing.** Hospitals and health systems increasingly use relational organizing to build community partnerships. The model adapts.

## Stories from neighborhoods

The lineage is deep. **Ella Baker's** organizing work in the civil rights movement was profoundly relational, focused on building local leaders rather than charismatic figureheads. **Saul Alinsky's** Industrial Areas Foundation institutionalized the one-on-one as a core organizing practice. **PICO (now Faith in Action)** built faith-based federations that run on the one-on-one. **Southerners on New Ground** organize across race, class, gender, and sexuality through deep relational practice.

Contemporary campaigns on labor, immigration, climate, housing, and electoral work have all used relational organizing. The pattern is consistent: campaigns built on real relationships outlast campaigns built on lists.

## Where to learn more

- A practical guide: [Commons Library: How to Do Relational Organizing](https://commonslibrary.org/how-to-do-relational-organizing-video-tip-sheet-and-work-sheet/)
- The IAF tradition: [Industrial Areas Foundation](https://www.industrialareasfoundation.org/)
- Faith-based organizing network: [Faith in Action](https://faithinaction.org/)
- Adjacent recipes: [Deep Canvassing](./deep-canvassing.md), [Block Stewards](../01-knowing-your-neighbors/block-stewards.md), [Neighborhood Associations](../11-civic-rhythms/neighborhood-associations.md)

metadata.stories_from_neighborhoods:
The lineage is deep. **Ella Baker's** organizing work in the civil rights movement was profoundly relational, focused on building local leaders rather than charismatic figureheads. **Saul Alinsky's** Industrial Areas Foundation institutionalized the one-on-one as a core organizing practice. **PICO (now Faith in Action)** built faith-based federations that run on the one-on-one. **Southerners on New Ground** organize across race, class, gender, and sexuality through deep relational practice.

Contemporary campaigns on labor, immigration, climate, housing, and electoral work have all used relational organizing. The pattern is consistent: campaigns built on real relationships outlast campaigns built on lists.

items.summary: Organizing through existing relationships instead of cold outreach. The work moves through trusted networks, person by person.

items.body:
## What it is

A few-hour event where neighbors bring broken items and work alongside volunteer "fixers" to repair them rather than throw them out. Clothes, electronics, bicycles, furniture, ceramics, small appliances. People come in expecting to learn something. They leave with a working thing and a few new neighbors.

Repair Cafes are a quiet movement. More than 2,000 of them run regularly in 37 countries.

## Why it works

Three things at once: less waste, less money spent, more relationships. The act of fixing something with another person is intimate in a low-key way. There's a problem in front of you both. You solve it together. By the end you know each other's names and you have a working lamp. That dynamic, repeated across a room of twenty pairs, produces a particular kind of community feeling that's hard to manufacture any other way.

## What you need

- **Time:** 4 to 6 weeks of planning. A full day for the event.
- **People:** 5 to 10 volunteer fixers. 2 to 3 organizers. 20 to 50 participants per event.
- **Space:** A community venue with tables, chairs, good lighting, and electrical outlets. A church hall, library, school cafeteria, or community center.
- **Materials:** Basic shared tools, solder, sewing supplies, glue. Fixers bring specialized tools. Tablecloths to protect surfaces. Refreshments.
- **Skills:** Repair knowledge across categories. Light coordination. Outreach.
- **Energy level:** Moderate. Hands-on but social.

## How to host it

1. **Request the starter kit from [repaircafe.org](https://www.repaircafe.org/en/).** It includes templates, intake forms, liability language, and signage. Use it. The Foundation makes this freely available.
2. **Recruit fixers.** Reach out to local makers, hobbyists, retired engineers, seamstresses, bike mechanics, electronics tinkerers. Most communities have more skilled fixers than people realize. Three to five categories of repair is plenty: electrical, textiles, bikes, small appliances, ceramics.
3. **Find a venue.** Library meeting rooms, faith spaces, community centers, school cafeterias. Free or low-cost. Make sure there's enough power, light, and table space.
4. **Set up intake.** Each participant fills out a short intake card describing the item and the problem. This helps fixers triage and protects both parties around liability.
5. **Promote 3 to 4 weeks out.** Flyers, neighborhood mailing lists, Nextdoor, [Front Porch Forum](../01-knowing-your-neighbors/front-porch-forum.md). List the categories of repair you'll have available. People won't bring things if they don't know it's possible.
6. **Day of: set up zones.** One area per repair category. Refreshments away from electronics. A welcome table for intake. A "next steps" sign for items that can't be fixed today.
7. **Pace the event.** 3 to 4 hours is right. Longer drains fixers. Encourage participants to stay for the whole repair, not just drop off.
8. **Close warmly.** Group photo of what got fixed. Thanks to fixers. Date for the next one.

## Variations

**Monthly Cafe.** Smaller, more regular. Lower bar to attend. Higher relationship density over time.

**Themed Cafe.** Bike repair only. Mending only. E-waste only. Sometimes the focused version draws people who'd be intimidated by the general one.

**Library partnership.** Many libraries now host monthly Repair Cafes. They have the space, the audience, and the institutional staying power. Pitch this to your local library if you don't have a venue.

**Pop-up at events.** A Repair Cafe table at a [block party](../01-knowing-your-neighbors/block-party.md), farmers market, or festival.

## Stories from neighborhoods

**Martine Postma**, a Dutch journalist, launched the first Repair Cafe in Amsterdam on October 18, 2009, at Fijnhout Theater. She'd noticed how many usable items neighbors threw away because they couldn't fix them. The Repair Cafe Foundation was established in March 2010.

Today over 2,000 Repair Cafes operate in 37 countries. The Foundation provides starter kits, ongoing support, and a network of organizers in the open. The model is a near-perfect example of what this book is about: a real practice, kept open by its founders, spread by neighbors, with no platform extraction in between.

## Where to learn more

- The Foundation: [repaircafe.org](https://www.repaircafe.org/en/)
- Starter kit and toolkit: [repaircafe.org/en/visit](https://www.repaircafe.org/en/visit/)
- Adjacent recipes: [Tool Library](./tool-library.md), [Skillshare](./skillshare.md), [Free Store](./free-store.md)

items.body:
## What it is

A community facility that serves neighbors year-round as a gathering space and resource center, and shifts into a coordination and support center during disasters. Rather than building separate emergency infrastructure that sits unused 95% of the time, Resilience Hubs enhance existing trusted institutions with backup power, supplies, and partnership networks.

The model has been formalized by the [Urban Sustainability Directors Network](https://www.usdn.org/resilience-hubs.html) and is being deployed in cities including Baltimore, Seattle, Los Angeles, Portland, and many others.

## Why it works

In a crisis, people go where they already feel safe. They don't suddenly learn to trust an emergency-only government facility. They go to their church, their community center, their library, their neighborhood cultural center. The Resilience Hub model accepts this reality and resources the places people already trust.

The "year-round + emergency" framing is the structural insight. A hub that only existed in emergencies would atrophy. A hub that runs programming all year, with backup capacity, is exercised infrastructure when it matters.

## What you need

- **Time:** 6 to 12 months to establish. Ongoing coordination.
- **People:** 5 to 10 community leaders. Volunteers. A staffed facility partner.
- **Space:** An existing community facility, 1,500+ square feet, with accessibility.
- **Materials:** Backup power (solar plus battery is ideal). Emergency supplies. Communication equipment. Programming infrastructure.
- **Skills:** Community organizing, project management, emergency response knowledge.
- **Energy level:** High to set up. Moderate to sustain.

## How to host it

1. **Identify the right facility.** Look for a place that is already community-trusted and community-led. Churches, cultural centers, community centers, libraries, food banks, and neighborhood nonprofits all work. Avoid converting a building that isn't already woven into the neighborhood.
2. **Assess what exists.** What programming runs there now? Who shows up? What hours? What's the relationship to the neighborhood?
3. **Identify the gaps.** What would be needed to function during a crisis?
   - Backup power. Solar plus battery is increasingly standard.
   - Communication. Satellite, ham radio, charged backup phones, WiFi backup.
   - Stockpiled supplies. Water, first aid, food, medication storage, blankets.
   - Climate control. Cooling and heating capacity that can run on backup power.
   - Sanitation. Bathroom function during power outages.
4. **Build the partnerships.** A hub works because it's networked. Local food bank for emergency food. Public health for medical coordination. Mutual aid pods for community response. City emergency management for official coordination. Faith communities for volunteer mobilization. Build these relationships in calm times.
5. **Run year-round programming.** Classes, meetings, celebrations, food distribution, social services drop-ins. The programming is what keeps the hub alive and trusted.
6. **Train.** Hub staff and volunteers should be prepared: first aid, mental health first aid, basic emergency response, communication protocols.
7. **Practice.** Annual drills are common. A planned outage to test the backup power. A scenario walkthrough of a heat wave or earthquake.
8. **Activate during emergencies.** When a crisis hits, the hub shifts: extended hours, expanded supplies distribution, coordination with mutual aid, shelter capacity if needed, information distribution.

## Variations

**Climate Resilience Hub.** Specifically focused on heat, cold, wildfire smoke, and storm response. Includes air filtration, HVAC capacity, and climate-specific supplies. See the [CREW (Climate Resilience Education and Work)](https://climateresolve.org/resilience-hubs/) network.

**Multi-hub network.** Multiple hubs across a city or county that coordinate. Some cities are building toward "no neighbor more than a mile from a hub."

**Cultural anchor hub.** A hub explicitly built around a cultural community (Black church, Korean community center, Latine cultural space). The cultural specificity is part of what makes it a hub for the people it serves.

**Hub-lite.** A smaller version with limited backup capacity but strong programming and community trust. Some grocery stores, libraries, and small businesses serve this role informally.

## Stories from neighborhoods

**Seattle.** Lake City Collective opened the **qwiʔqwuʔ center** (meaning "little water" in Lushootseed) in 2020. It hosts cultural celebrations, community gardens, tutoring, and serves as an emergency hub.

**Los Angeles.** The Boyle Heights Arts Conservatory operates as a resilience hub seven days a week. Their manager noted that they "were a resilience hub before we were designated one because we're grassroots, community engagement." That captures the pattern: the strongest hubs grow organically from authentic community work rather than top-down planning.

**Baltimore, Portland, Oakland, Miami, and others** have built city-supported networks of community-led hubs in recent years.

## Where to learn more

- The framework: [Urban Sustainability Directors Network: Resilience Hubs](https://www.usdn.org/resilience-hubs.html)
- Climate-specific: [Climate Resolve: Resilience Hubs](https://climateresolve.org/resilience-hubs/)
- Adjacent recipes: [Map Your Neighborhood](./map-your-neighborhood.md), [Warming/Cooling Center](./warming-cooling-center.md), [Community Fridge](../03-mutual-aid/community-fridge.md)

items.body:
## What it is

A multi-track, free, neighbor-taught event. Bike repair in one room. Sourdough in another. Improv comedy in a third. Mending. Tax basics. Storytelling. Capoeira. Solar panels. Composting. The classes are short (60 to 90 minutes each). The instructors aren't professionals. They are neighbors who know something and want to share it.

Skillshares have happened in dozens of communities. Somerville, Massachusetts ran an early model in 2014 that drew 800 attendees to 40 free classes.

## Why it works

A neighborhood has more expertise in it than any educational institution can offer, and most of it goes unused because there's no infrastructure to surface it. A skillshare temporarily builds that infrastructure for a day. The result is people meeting their neighbors as teachers and learners, which produces a different kind of relationship than meeting as residents passing on a sidewalk.

The free, no-credentials nature of it also signals something about who gets to teach. Anyone with a thing they know well can offer a class. That redistribution of teaching authority does real work.

## What you need

- **Time:** 150 to 200 hours of planning over 5 to 6 months. 8 to 10 hours on the day.
- **People:** 3 to 5 organizing team. 30 to 50 instructors. 20 to 40 day-of volunteers. 300 to 1,000 attendees.
- **Space:** A venue with 4 to 8 rooms or workshop spaces. Schools, community centers, large churches, libraries with annexes.
- **Materials:** Signage, printed program, instructor supplies (varies by class), name tags, refreshments.
- **Skills:** Event coordination, outreach, instructor recruitment, volunteer management, day-of facilitation.
- **Energy level:** High for organizers. Moderate for instructors. Low for attendees.

## How to host it

1. **Start 5 to 6 months out.** Lock down the venue first. Schools, libraries, and community centers often donate space for a community event.
2. **Form the organizing team.** 3 to 5 people. Split the work: instructor outreach, logistics and venue, communications and promotion, day-of operations.
3. **Begin instructor recruitment 4 months out.** Reach out personally to local artists, crafters, hobbyists, small business owners, retired professionals, makers. A simple one-page submission form. Make it easy to say yes.
4. **Curate the class list.** Aim for 30 to 50 classes across a range. Practical (bike repair, mending, simple plumbing). Creative (drawing, songwriting, improv). Civic (organizing, public meeting navigation). Wellness (basic yoga, breathwork). Food (sourdough, pickling, knife skills).
5. **Confirm instructors 8 to 10 weeks out.** Assign rooms based on equipment needs. Send each instructor a one-page logistics sheet (what time, what room, what supplies provided, what to bring).
6. **Build partnerships.** A local library, school, neighborhood association, or business will often help promote in exchange for being a co-sponsor.
7. **Open registration.** Many skillshares are first-come-first-served on the day. Some pre-register popular classes. Hybrid models work. Free is essential.
8. **Print the program.** A simple booklet or fold-out map. Lists every class, location, time, instructor, materials needed.
9. **Day-of: clear signage, greeters, breaks.** Three or four sessions through the day with 30-minute breaks between. Refreshments and gathering space in between. Volunteers at every junction.
10. **Close with a debrief and a thank-you.** Group photo. Names of all the instructors read aloud. Decide whether to do it again next year. Most skillshares that happen once happen at least three times.

## Variations

**Mini-skillshare.** Six to eight classes in one afternoon at a community center. Same energy, much lower planning bar.

**Themed skillshare.** Repair-focused (overlaps with [Repair Cafe](./repair-cafe.md)). Food-focused. Arts-focused. Civic-focused.

**Apartment building skillshare.** Several neighbors in a single building teaching short classes in the lobby on a Saturday.

**School-paired skillshare.** A skillshare held at a school where students are also instructors. Strong intergenerational draw.

**Recurring weekly classes.** Once a year's skillshare proves the demand, some communities run a weekly or monthly "Skill Night" with one or two classes per evening.

## Stories from neighborhoods

**Somerville, Massachusetts.** The first annual Somerville Skillshare in March 2014 attracted nearly 800 residents to 40 free classes: urban beekeeping, storytelling, jewelry making, community organizing, printmaking, yoga, tai chi. The event was organized by neighbors with no institutional sponsor. It became annual.

Similar events have launched in dozens of communities since. The consistent finding from organizers: their neighborhoods are hungry for this kind of learning and connection.

## Where to learn more

- A practical how-to: [Shareable's Skillshare Guide](https://www.shareable.net/how-to/how-to-organize-a-successful-skillshare/)
- Adjacent recipes: [Tool Library](./tool-library.md), [Repair Cafe](./repair-cafe.md), [Block Party](../01-knowing-your-neighbors/block-party.md)

attribution.name: Marshall Ganz & the New Organizing Institute tradition

items.body:
*The need:* Movements that depend on one heroic coordinator die when that person burns out — and most do.

The snowflake model is the organizational shape of the Ganz tradition: interconnected teams, with leadership distributed and mutual accountability instead of top-down management.

Its working parts:
- **Core and local teams.** A core leadership team keeps the whole coherent and holds long-term strategy; local teams deliver short-term goals, adapt strategy to their turf, and feed lessons back. Decision-making is decentralized whenever possible.
- **Sustainable relationship ratios.** Nobody maintains more relationships than they truly can: about five if you're organizing part-time (most neighbors), about ten if full-time. The snowflake grows by adding *teams*, not by overloading *people*.
- **Mutual accountability.** The arrows point both ways: a local team can task the core team just as the core team tasks locals. Commitments are agreed, not assigned.
- **Clear roles.** Every task belongs to a named person; every person knows what others count on them for.
- **Exponential growth through leadership development.** Everyone is responsible for identifying, recruiting, and developing new leaders. Leaders develop leaders who develop leaders — which is how five people become 25, then 125, without anyone holding 125 relationships.

People step up the **ladder of engagement** — supporter, volunteer, team member, leadership prospect, organizer — through real tests: run the phone bank once before you're asked to captain it. Follow up within 48 hours at every rung; invest in the people who show up rather than chasing the ones who don't.

ingredients: patience for the math of small numbers
metadata.source_note: From 'Organizing: People, Power, Change' (2014): the snowflake model, sustainable relationship ratios, ladder of engagement, and team stages.
how_it_works: Start with one team: purpose, roles, norms.
Cap everyone's active relationships at what they can truly maintain (about five, part-time).
Test and escalate: give growing members real responsibility, then real leadership.
When the team is strong (4+ core organizers), split or seed a new team on new turf.
Keep core and local teams accountable to each other in both directions.
success_signals: no single point of failure
new leaders run things founders used to run
growth comes in teams, not in one person's overloaded contact list

items.summary: A structure where leadership is distributed into interconnected small teams, everyone maintains a sustainable number of relationships, and every leader's first job is developing more leaders.
items.title: The Snowflake: Distributed Leadership

attribution.name: Marshall Ganz
attribution.source: Organizing: People, Power, Change (2014); Ganz, 'Why Stories Matter', Sojourners (2009)

items.body:
*The need:* Facts don't move neighbors to act together. Shared values do — and values are carried in stories.

Public narrative is the leadership practice of telling a story that communicates why you care (Story of Self), what "we" share (Story of Us), and why we must act now (Story of Now). Ganz built it on Rabbi Hillel's three questions: "If I am not for myself, who will be for me? If I am only for myself, what am I? And if not now, when?"

Each story runs on the same engine: a character faces a **challenge**, makes a **choice**, and experiences an **outcome**. That structure is what makes a story a story instead of a list of events — and what lets a listener feel the lesson rather than just understand it.

**Story of Self** — Find your choice points: When did I first care about being heard? When did I first experience injustice? What did I do? Pick one moment, and tell it with enough detail that listeners can see it.

**Story of Us** — The character becomes the community. What have we faced together? What did we choose? Don't only tell challenge stories; lift up successes. "Hope is one of the most precious gifts we can give each other."

**Story of Now** — The urgent challenge to our shared values, the nightmare if we don't act, the dream if we do — ending with a specific, concrete ask someone can say yes to tonight.

Emotion is the mechanism, not decoration: stories work when hope outweighs fear, urgency outweighs inertia, solidarity outweighs isolation, and people feel *you can make a difference*. And it's not speech-making — you practice public narrative in a kitchen, at a house meeting, in a 1:1, wherever someone asks "so why do you do this?"
