items.body:
## What it is

A communal meal where everyone brings a dish and also brings a two-to-three-minute story shaped by a prompt. The prompt is the difference. It's what moves the table from "nice to meet you" to "I will remember you."

A good story supper makes 15 strangers feel like 15 people who know something real about each other within three hours.

## Why it works

Most adult conversation defaults to surface. A prompt that is personal but not partisan gives people permission to go one layer down. The food gives them something to do with their hands while they listen. The structure makes it safe to actually speak.

This isn't therapy. It's the opposite of therapy. It's everyday narrative skill, practiced in the company of neighbors.

## What you need

- **Time:** 4 to 6 weeks planning. About 3 hours for the event.
- **People:** 2 to 3 organizers. 15 to 30 attendees works best. Smaller is more intimate, larger needs more structure.
- **Space:** A warm room. A community center, a church basement, a backyard, a large dining room. Tables that can be arranged so everyone can see everyone.
- **Materials:** Tables, chairs, tablecloths, place settings. Notebooks if you want to compile recipes or stories afterward. Flowers if you want them.
- **Skills:** Light facilitation. Enough comfort to hold the room when one story runs long or another stays quiet.
- **Energy level:** Moderate. The emotional work of creating safety is the most demanding part.

## How to host it

1. **Pick the prompt first.** This is the most important decision. Make it personal but not partisan. Examples that work: *Share a food from your childhood and what it meant to you. Tell us about a meal that brought someone unexpected into your life. Share a place you've left and what you carry from it.* Avoid prompts that ask about politics, religion, or "what's wrong with the world."
2. **Set a date and invite.** Send the invitation 3 to 4 weeks out. Tell people up front that they will share a 2-to-3 minute story responding to the prompt. This is the most important sentence in your invitation. It is also the one that scares people. Reassure them: it's a story, not a speech.
3. **Plan the meal.** Potluck works. Or pick a theme that fits the prompt (childhood foods, foods from where people are from). Don't over-engineer. People will bring more than enough.
4. **Arrange the room.** One long table if possible. If you have to do multiple tables, build in a moment when stories are shared across them.
5. **Open warmly.** Welcome people. Explain the rhythm. Read the prompt aloud. Set expectations: 2 to 3 minutes each, no questions interrupting, applause is welcome.
6. **Do a first round with volunteers.** Two or three people who agreed in advance to go first. They warm up the room.
7. **Eat.** Stories continue informally as people serve themselves. Encourage table conversation about what they've heard.
8. **Do a closing round before dessert.** Anyone who hasn't spoken yet who wants to. A practiced storyteller can perform something prepared.
9. **Collect.** Pass around a notebook for recipes, lines, or favorite moments. If you want, compile a small cookbook afterward and send it to everyone who came. This is the artifact that keeps the supper alive in people's homes.

## Variations

**Smaller version.** 6 to 10 people, dining room, one shared meal cooked together. Closer to a dinner party. Less ceremony, deeper conversation.

**Public version.** 50 to 100 people, library or community center. Needs more structure and stronger facilitation. See [The Longest Table](./longest-table.md) for the much larger format.

**Theme variations.** Migration stories. Place stories. Hands stories (something your hands have learned to do). Loss stories (in a healing-focused setting, see [Dinner Party Grief](../02-small-groups-for-support/dinner-party-grief.md)). Letter-to-younger-self stories.

**Cross-generational version.** Pair an elder with a teenager at each seat. Prompt is shaped to invite mentorship and curiosity.

## Stories from neighborhoods

**Community Plate**, based in Maine, has facilitated story-sharing suppers across the state, from Lewiston to Lubec. NPR featured their work in a 2025 story about fighting loneliness through community suppers.

At one coastal Maine supper, an elderly immigrant shared how her mother's recipe was her anchor when arriving in America. A teenager heard this and realized her grandmother made the same dish. After the supper, the grandmother began teaching the teenager her family cooking tradition, something that hadn't happened in years. The supper didn't "solve" isolation. It made one new intergenerational relationship possible.

If you've hosted a story supper, your story belongs in this list. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](../../CONTRIBUTING.md).

## Where to learn more

- Original practitioner: [Community Plate](https://www.communityplate.me/suppers)
- Adjacent recipes: [Block Party](./block-party.md), [The Longest Table](./longest-table.md), [Dinner Party Grief](../02-small-groups-for-support/dinner-party-grief.md)

items.body:
## What it is

A community-based organization that runs a global network of over 90 chapters. Members gather regularly (often monthly) for events featuring curated speakers, live music, opportunities to volunteer, and time to actually meet each other. The three core values are *Live Better, Help Often, Wonder More*. The form is borrowed from religious services. The content is secular and life-oriented.

The model started in London in 2013 and spread internationally. It is volunteer-run, free to attend, and locally autonomous within a shared framework.

## Why it works

Secular life lacks rhythmic gathering. Many people who don't identify with a religious tradition still want what religion provides: a regular reason to be in a room with other people, a curated experience, a sense of shared values, a place where they're known. Sunday Assembly is one of the more developed answers to that hunger.

The weekly or monthly cadence matters. A one-off event creates a one-off relationship. A recurring assembly builds friendships across months. Regulars know each other. New attendees can become regulars within a few visits.

## What you need

- **Time:** Weekly to monthly gatherings, 1 to 2 hours per meeting.
- **People:** 10 to 20 core organizers. 50 to 300+ attendees per chapter.
- **Space:** A public venue with seating capacity. Community centers, theaters, halls, sometimes churches that rent.
- **Materials:** Speaker invitations, music playlists or live performers, signage, refreshments.
- **Skills:** Event facilitation, volunteer management, public speaking, community outreach.
- **Energy level:** Medium to high for organizers. Low for attendees.

## How to host it

1. **Engage with [Sunday Assembly](https://www.sundayassembly.org/).** They support startup chapters with model agendas, recommended speakers, music guidance, volunteer structure, and a network of other chapters to learn from.
2. **Build a small organizing team.** 5 to 10 people initially. Distribute work: programming, venue, communications, hospitality, volunteer coordination.
3. **Find a venue.** Community centers, theaters, libraries with auditoriums, schools, sometimes generously priced rentals from faith communities. Affordable and accessible.
4. **Design the gathering.** A typical hour-and-a-half:
   - Welcome and opening song (often communal singing).
   - Reading or short story.
   - Featured speaker on a life theme (15 to 30 minutes).
   - More music, sometimes performed by a local artist.
   - Community-building moment (small group discussion, sharing, volunteer opportunity).
   - Closing song.
   - Refreshments and conversation afterward.
5. **Curate speakers thoughtfully.** Local thinkers, doers, artists. Themes that matter: belonging, work, change, grief, joy, ethics, civic life. Avoid speakers selling something.
6. **Build music into the experience.** A house band, a local musician, or thoughtful playlists. Live music outperforms recorded for energy.
7. **Promote.** Local cultural networks, neighborhood lists, secular and humanist circles. Word of mouth carries the most weight after the first few gatherings.
8. **Sustain it.** The first year is the hardest. Once a chapter is established and has a core of regulars, the rhythm carries itself.

## Variations

**Smaller version.** 20 to 40 attendees in a living room or small cafe. Lower stakes, deeper conversations.

**Themed assembly.** Around current events, seasonal transitions, or specific life moments (graduation season, election week, holiday season).

**Civic-leaning variant.** See [Civic Saturday](../05-bridging-difference/civic-saturday.md), which is similar in form but more explicitly oriented around civic life.

**Spiritual-but-not-religious variant.** Some chapters have woven in more contemplative practice (silence, meditation, ritual) without becoming religious.

## Stories from neighborhoods

**Sunday Assembly** launched in London in 2013, founded by **Sanderson Jones** and **Pippa Evans**. Within a few years, chapters had launched in North America, Europe, and Australia.

**Sunday Assembly London** regularly hosts 200+ attendees. Chapters in San Francisco, Seattle, Atlanta, and many other cities have built durable communities. Members describe the experience as providing meaningful connection and purpose, often filling a gap they didn't know they had until they encountered it.

The organization has navigated the challenges of any growing volunteer-led network: some chapters thrive, some pause, some adapt the model significantly. The open structure has helped the model survive in many forms.

## Where to learn more

- The home: [Sunday Assembly](https://www.sundayassembly.org/)
- Starting a chapter: [sundayassembly.org/start-your-own](https://www.sundayassembly.org/start-your-own)
- Adjacent recipes: [Civic Saturday](../05-bridging-difference/civic-saturday.md), [Microgrant Gathering](./microgrant-gathering.md), [Story-Sharing Potluck](../01-knowing-your-neighbors/story-sharing-potluck.md)

items.body:
*The need:* Busy groups mistake activity for progress and burn through volunteers doing tactics that build nothing.

Before committing to any action — a canvass, a petition, a community dinner, an app — run it through the sweet spot test. A tactic is worth doing when it is:

1. **Strategic** — it produces concrete, measurable progress toward the campaign goal;
2. **Organization-strengthening** — it attracts and engages new people and increases the community's capacity to work together;
3. **Individual-developing** — the people who carry it out grow in skill, leadership, and confidence.

The sweet spot is where all three overlap. A tactic that hits the goal but chews people up costs you the next campaign. A tactic that's fun but strategically pointless spends trust. 

The companion practice is **motivational engagement** — designing the work so people want to do it again. Motivational actions are *meaningful* (the person can see the difference it makes), grant *autonomy* (responsibility matched to skill, with room to make real choices), and build in *feedback and learning* (progress is visible; coaching is available). Five design checks: Does the person do a whole thing start to finish? Do they see its impact? Does it use varied skills — head, heart, hands? Do they own decisions? Can they see results as they work?

Nearly any task can be redesigned to meet these criteria — turning data entry into scoreboard-keeping, or a lone flyer route into a paired story-collecting walk. People don't leave because work is hard. They leave because it's meaningless, invisible, or lonely.

how_it_works: Score the tactic: strategic? strengthens the organization? develops individuals?
Redesign until it hits all three, or cut it.
Design for motivation: meaningful, autonomous, feedback-rich.
Check: whole task, visible impact, varied skills, real choices, visible results.
After the action, ask participants: would you do this again? Why?

items.body:
## What it is

A practice from Indigenous First Nations traditions for communication, decision-making, healing, and conflict resolution. People sit in a circle with no head position. A talking piece (feather, stick, shell, stone) moves around the circle. Only the holder speaks. Everyone else listens without interrupting, fixing, or planning a reply.

This is an Indigenous practice. It has been generously shared by First Nations elders into many contemporary contexts. When you use it, acknowledge that lineage explicitly.

## Why it works

Most group conversations are won by the loudest voice, the highest status, the most articulate. The talking circle removes all of that. The piece holds the floor. The quiet person speaks at the same volume of authority as the loud person. The listener is freed from preparing a counter-argument because they aren't going to speak next; they're going to listen now.

Over the arc of a circle, things get said that would never come out in any other format.

## What you need

- **Time:** 1 to 2 hours for a circle.
- **People:** 4 to 20 participants. A facilitator. Optionally an Indigenous knowledge keeper if appropriate.
- **Space:** Any space where people can sit in a circle without a table or barrier in the middle. Quiet. No clocks dominating.
- **Materials:** A talking piece. Often a feather, stick, shell, stone, or another object with meaning. Optionally sacred medicines if smudging is appropriate and welcome.
- **Skills:** Facilitation, deep listening, emotional presence, willingness to acknowledge origins.
- **Energy level:** Low to moderate.

## How to host it

1. **Acknowledge the lineage.** Open by naming that this is an Indigenous practice. If you are on Indigenous land, acknowledge whose land. If a knowledge keeper from a local nation is willing to lead, defer to them. Don't claim authorship of a practice that isn't yours.
2. **Arrange the space.** Chairs in a true circle with no head. The talking piece in the center or held by the facilitator initially. No table in the middle.
3. **Open with a centering moment.** Silence, a breath, a brief reading, or smudging if appropriate and welcome. The opening sets the container.
4. **Explain the practice.** Whoever holds the piece speaks. Everyone else listens. You may pass when the piece comes to you. There is no fixing, advice, or interruption. The circle is sacred space.
5. **The facilitator speaks first.** Holds the piece. Speaks from the heart. Sets the depth. Then passes the piece to the next person (typically to the left, but follow local tradition).
6. **The circle moves.** Each person speaks or passes. If someone passes, they can request the piece back later. Some circles do multiple rounds: introductions, then the heart of the matter, then a closing round.
7. **Listen without preparing.** The discipline is to actually listen, not to plan a response. The piece will come to you eventually.
8. **Close.** A closing round (one word, one sentence, gratitude), a moment of silence, or a closing reading. The closing matters as much as the opening.

## Variations

**Healing circle.** Used to address harm or grief. Smaller, slower, often with a survivor's request driving the topic. See [Peacemaking Circles](../08-healing-and-conflict/peacemaking-circles.md) for the restorative-justice extension.

**Classroom circle.** Used in schools for community-building or discipline. The kids learn the form quickly and often regulate each other.

**Decision-making circle.** A circle structured around a decision the group needs to make. Multiple rounds: information, feelings, options, decision.

**Online circle.** A video call with a clear "talking piece" convention (the speaker is muted-by-default; only they unmute). Works, with care.

## Stories from neighborhoods

Talking circles have been used since time immemorial by Indigenous peoples across the Americas. First Nations elders in Canada and the U.S. have generously shared this practice with non-Indigenous communities, knowing its potential to transform listening.

In contemporary use, circles run in classrooms, healing groups, restorative justice processes, conflict mediation, men's councils, and organizational meetings. Educators report that circles shift dynamics: quiet students find voice, dominant voices regulate themselves, listening deepens. In communities working across cultural difference, circles build bridges that other formats can't reach.

[First Nations Pedagogy Online](https://firstnationspedagogy.ca/circletalks.html) maintains a generous reference on circles as a teaching and community-building practice.

## Where to learn more

- Indigenous reference: [First Nations Pedagogy Online](https://firstnationspedagogy.ca/circletalks.html)
- The book: Kay Pranis, *The Little Book of Circle Processes*
- Adjacent recipes: [Men's Council](../02-small-groups-for-support/mens-council.md), [Peacemaking Circles](../08-healing-and-conflict/peacemaking-circles.md), [Community Agreements](./community-agreements.md)

items.body:
*The need:* Groups that skip the debrief repeat their mistakes; groups that skip the celebration repeat their burnout.

Every action and every campaign closes with a debrief — and the debrief asks two distinct questions, because a group can win a fight and come out weaker, or lose one and come out stronger.

**Question one: did it work?** Compare outcomes to the measurable goal you set. Be honest in both directions: never claim a victory that isn't yours, and never pretend a loss is a win — either lie robs the effort of its value. If you lost, contextualize the loss, interpret what happened, accept responsibility, and prepare for next time.

**Question two: are we stronger now?** Count what capacity-building actually looks like: How many new people took action for the first time? Who took on a bigger role than last time? Which relationships deepened? What can the team now do that it couldn't before? What did we learn about our opposition and our own leverage? This is the sweet-spot test applied in the rear-view mirror — and it's the question that separates organizing from mere mobilizing.

**Then celebrate.** Recognize specific contributions by name. When we win, we sometimes party without learning; when we lose, we sometimes analyze without honoring the courage and work people gave. Do both, every time.

Write down the three biggest lessons where the next campaign will find them. There is always a next time, and the debrief is where the next campaign quietly begins.

items.body:
*The need:* Most people never join because nobody actually asked them.

A hard ask is a request that results in a commitment to a specific action. "Would you maybe be interested in getting involved sometime?" is a soft ask; it protects the asker and loses the person. A hard ask sounds like: *"Can you come to our team meeting Wednesday at 6pm at Alisha's?"*

The practices:
- **Be concise, plain, and specific.** If it's an event, include date, time, and place. If it's a role, name the role.
- **Never apologize for asking.** You are not imposing a burden; you are offering someone a way to act on what they already care about. Organizing is an opportunity, not a favour.
- **Convey urgency, and make them the solution:** "We need one more canvass lead to hit our goal. Will you take it on?"
- **Then stop talking and let them answer.**

When the answer is no, listen for which no it is. **"Not now"** — offer another time ("we also meet Sunday at 1, can you make that?"). **"Not that"** — offer another way in ("no door-knocking? come help plan the welcome night instead"). **"Not ever"** — thank them warmly and move on; no guilt, theirs or yours.

And secure what you win: follow up within 48 hours, never let anyone leave without knowing the next time you'll see them, confirm commitments so people know you're counting on them — and plan for half your yeses to no-show (need four people? schedule eight). The deepest reason people don't return isn't overwork — it's that no one explained why their work mattered, or no one asked.

ingredients: a specific action with a date, time, and place
a person whose story you know
metadata.source_note: From 'Organizing: People, Power, Change' (2014), Building Relationships: hard asks, three types of no, and recruitment & retention best practices.
how_it_works: Name the urgent need in one sentence.
Make the specific ask: this role, this day, this time, this place.
Don't apologize; don't pad it; let them answer.
Sort the no: not now → new time; not that → new task; not ever → warm thanks.
Follow up within 48 hours and calendar the next touch.

half your asks get a yes of some kind
no-shows stop surprising you because you planned for them

items.body:
*The need:* Rallies reach the already-convinced. Living rooms reach networks.

The house meeting, refined by Fred Ross Sr. organizing with the Community Service Organization in the 1940s–50s, is a small gathering — a living room's worth of people — convened by a **host who invites their own network**: family, coworkers, church friends, the neighbors they actually talk to. The organizer doesn't supply the guest list; the host's relationships are the meeting.

The shape: the host welcomes people they trust into a comfortable setting (food matters — it marks the gathering as hospitality, not procedure). The organizer or a developing leader shares story and purpose, listens hard to what these particular people care about, and closes with asks — including the ask that makes the method compound: *who here will host the next meeting, with their own people?* Ross ran roughly three-week cycles of house meetings building toward one large organizing meeting, then further cycles toward a founding convention of a real organization.

The house meeting does three jobs at once. It **recruits through trust** — people come because someone they know asked. It **surfaces what the community actually cares about**, in a setting where people speak freely. And above all it **reveals leaders**: watch who convenes people, who speaks with authority in their own kitchen, who follows through. That's how Ross found Cesar Chavez — at a house meeting in Chavez's own living room (the story is on this shelf) — and it's how the UFW and the 2008 neighborhood teams built bases that lists never could.

A chain of house meetings is the six questions running on hospitality: who are my people, what do we care about, and who will commit to convening next.

ingredients: a story, an ear, and an ask
metadata.source_note: Method and three-week cycle structure per the Zinn Education Project and Beyond Chron's history of the Ross house-meeting tradition; leader-spotting function per Thompson's biography.
how_it_works: Find a host; the host invites their own people — the organizer never supplies the list.
Gather small: a living room's worth, with food.
Share story and purpose briefly; spend most of the time listening.
Close with commitments — including who will host the next meeting.
Run cycles of meetings toward one big founding gathering; watch for who convenes and follows through — those are your leaders.
metadata.min_resources: Free. Someone's couch and a pot of coffee.
success_signals: each meeting produces its next host
the organizer hears concerns they didn't arrive with
leaders emerge whom no sign-up sheet would have found

items.body:
## What it is

A free public meal at one continuous outdoor table. Neighbors arrive with potluck dishes (or just themselves) and sit down with people they've never met to eat together. The visual is the point: a 500-foot table down the middle of a street says something about a place that no flyer can.

The Longest Table is what happens when a [block party](./block-party.md) grows up and decides to invite the whole neighborhood.

## Why it works

Scale changes what's possible. A 20-person dinner is intimate. A 500-person dinner is civic. People who would never sit at a small table with strangers will sit at a long one, because the table itself is the invitation.

The long table also signals welcome in a way that a fenced event cannot. No registration. No ticket. No dress code. If you are walking past, you can sit down.

## What you need

- **Time:** 2 to 4 weeks of organizing. 2 to 3 hours for the event. 2 to 3 hours of setup and cleanup.
- **People:** 2 to 3 core organizers. A dozen volunteers for setup, food coordination, and cleanup. 50 to 1,000+ participants.
- **Space:** A public outdoor space. A closed street works best. A park or plaza works if the table can be built end-to-end.
- **Materials:** Many tables (folding works), many chairs, plates, utensils, cups, napkins, tablecloths, potluck dishes. Sound for opening remarks. Waste and recycling stations.
- **Skills:** Event coordination at scale. Volunteer wrangling. Calm in the face of weather.
- **Energy level:** Moderate to high. The day-of logistics are real. The planning is lighter than the event suggests.

## How to host it

1. **Find your space.** A street works best for the visual but requires a permit. A plaza or park can work and is easier. Look for somewhere with foot traffic, parking access, and shade or shelter if your climate needs it.
2. **Get the permits.** Street closure, public gathering, and possibly food service depending on jurisdiction. Start this conversation 6 to 8 weeks out.
3. **Build the organizing team.** 2 to 3 people who will own different pieces: logistics, communications, food coordination. Avoid one person trying to do all of it.
4. **Recruit volunteers.** Reach out 4 weeks out. You need helpers for setup, food intake, water station, cleanup. A volunteer per 25 attendees is a reasonable ratio.
5. **Publicize.** Local Nextdoor or [Front Porch Forum](./front-porch-forum.md). Posters in cafes, libraries, schools. Local newsletter. Word of mouth on each block. Emphasize: free, open to anyone, bring food if you can, just show up if you can't.
6. **Set up the table.** Folding tables end to end. Place settings every two feet. A few feet of space between table sections for movement. Decorate simply if you decorate at all (flowers in jars).
7. **Run a simple rhythm.** Brief welcome and thanks. People serve themselves potluck. Mingling and eating for 90 minutes. A short closing word before things break up. Don't over-program.
8. **Document something.** A photographer or a few volunteers with phones. The image of the long table is what travels and brings people back next year.
9. **Clean up together.** Volunteers stay. Many attendees will help if you ask. The street should be cleaner than you found it within 90 minutes of the meal ending.

## Variations

**Indoor version.** Long table down the center of a community center, school gymnasium, or church hall. Works in cold climates.

**Sectioned version.** If you can't fit one continuous table, build it in 30-to-50-foot segments with walkways between. Maintain the visual.

**Themed version.** Build the meal around a theme that fits your neighborhood (harvest, lunar new year, founding anniversary). Don't over-theme.

**Smaller version.** 50 to 100 people, one long table in a park. Lower stakes, easier to start.

## Stories from neighborhoods

**Chelsea, New York City.** During the isolated early months of 2020, Maryam Banikarim envisioned a communal gathering inspired by shared meals in Egypt. She posted the concept on Nextdoor and received an overwhelming response. Co-founder Andy Lerner joined. The first Longest Table on West 21st Street drew 500 neighbors to a 544-foot table made of 68 connected smaller tables.

By recent events, more than 1,000 neighbors gather. 90% of attendees report feeling more positive about their neighborhood afterward. The model has been replicated in Harlem, Kansas City, California, and Paris.

## Where to learn more

- Original toolkit: [longesttablecommunity.org](https://www.longesttablecommunity.org)
- Adjacent recipes: [Block Party](./block-party.md), [Story-Sharing Potluck](./story-sharing-potluck.md), [Reinvent the Potluck](../04-gathering-design/reinvent-the-potluck.md)

*The need:* Teams drift when the plan lives in a document nobody rereads.

The organizing sentence is the smallest complete container for a campaign plan:

> **We are organizing** (our people) **to** (strategic goal) **through** (tactics) **by** (timeline).

Every team in an effort — the core team and each local team — writes its own. A neighborhood example: *We are organizing renters on the six blocks around Hart Park to win weekly repairs office hours with the property manager, through door-knocking all 214 units and a joint letter, by March 1.*

The sentence forces the four honest answers: who exactly are our people (not "the community" — which people?); what outcome, with a number where possible; which tactics we're actually committing to; and by when. It also makes nested strategy legible — a citywide effort's sentence and a single block's sentence should visibly add up.

Write it at the team launch, put it at the top of every agenda, and rewrite it when strategy changes. When someone new joins, the sentence is the fastest true answer to "so what is this?"

Make WHO specific people, WHAT a measurable outcome, HOW real tactics, WHEN a date.
Each team writes its own; check that local sentences add up to the shared one.
Put it at the top of every agenda; rewrite when strategy changes.
success_signals: new members can repeat it after one meeting
agenda items visibly serve the sentence

items.body:
*The need:* Plans fail quietly when nobody can say how the work leads to the win.

Strategy is turning what you *have* (your people's resources) into what you *need* (power) to get what you *want* (a clear goal). Strategizing starts with three questions in order: Who are our **people**? What is their **problem** — and why hasn't it been solved? What is our **goal**?

Then compress your whole strategy into a theory of change statement:

> **If we do** (tactics), **then** (strategic goal), **because** (reason).

The Montgomery bus boycott, stated this way: *If Black residents of Montgomery boycott the buses, then the bus company will desegregate them, because the lost fares will make segregation cost more than it pays.*

A goal is strategic when it is measurable (a number with units — people, signatures, dollars, votes); focuses your limited resources on one outcome; builds your constituency's capacity; uses a real point of leverage (your strength or your opposition's weakness); is visible and motivating to your people; and can be repeated by others.

Big goals nest: the "mountaintop" goal is reached through smaller goals that each build capacity for the next — a living-wage bylaw might start with electing two supportive councillors; a safer-streets campaign might start with one crosswalk. And remember strategy is a verb: you act your way into new thinking, adjusting the sentence as reality answers back. If the *because* clause is hand-waving, the sentence has already told you what you need to know.

ingredients: their problem, analyzed (why hasn't it been solved?)
metadata.source_note: Strategy framework and theory-of-change format from 'Organizing: People, Power, Change' (2014); Montgomery example follows the guide's own treatment (see Taylor Branch, 'Parting the Waters').
how_it_works: Answer in order: who are our people? what is the problem? what is our goal?
Draft: if we do X, then Y, because Z.
Test the goal: measurable, focused, capacity-building, leveraged, motivating, repeatable.
Nest it: what smaller goal builds the capacity to reach the mountaintop?
Say it out loud to someone outside the team. If the 'because' wobbles, rework it.
success_signals: every team member can recite the sentence
the goal has a number and a date
tactics that don't serve the sentence get cut

items.summary: If we do TACTICS, then CHANGE, because REASON. If your neighborhood campaign's theory of change doesn't fit in one honest sentence, it probably won't work.
items.title: A Strategy You Can Say Out Loud

items.body:
## What it is

A formal exchange system where everyone's time is valued equally, regardless of what they do with it. Members offer skills and services. Members request what they need. Hours are tracked. Credits earned by giving can be spent by asking.

Time banking has its modern roots in the work of Edgar Cahn in the 1980s, who built it as a tool for community development and an alternative to charity. Today there are thousands of time banks worldwide.

## Why it works

A time bank fixes one of the most stubborn problems in mutual aid: the imbalance between people who give a lot and people who are afraid to ask. The shared currency (hours) makes asking neutral. You aren't owing anyone a favor; you're spending what you earned.

The flat-hour value (everyone's hour counts the same) is the radical move. It refuses the market's hierarchy. The doctor who needs help moving and the mover who needs help reading a medical form trade hours one for one.

## What you need

- **Time:** 1 to 3 months to establish. Ongoing indefinitely.
- **People:** 10 to 30 founding members. Grows organically.
- **Space:** Minimal. Members' homes. Occasional community gathering space.
- **Materials:** A tracking system. [TimeBanks.org](https://www.timebanks.org/) offers software (hOurworld is the main open platform). A spreadsheet works for small banks.
- **Skills:** Relationship building. Light coordination. Conflict resolution when exchanges go sideways.
- **Energy level:** Low to moderate. The administrative work is real but distributed.

## How to host it

1. **Recruit 10 to 20 founding members.** People who share enough trust to make the first exchanges feel safe. Mix of life stages, skills, and needs.
2. **Hold a launch meeting.** Explain the model. Each member writes a short list of what they can offer and what they might want. Examples: home cooking, dog walking, basic plumbing, tutoring, computer help, listening, garden work, transportation, hair cuts.
3. **Pick a tracking system.** [hOurworld](https://www.hourworld.org/) is the most-used open platform. Some banks use Time and Talents or in-house spreadsheets. Whatever you pick, it should let people see offers and needs and log hours.
4. **Set the agreements.** One hour = one credit. Each member gets a starting balance (often 5 to 10 hours) so people can begin asking immediately. Cancellation norms. Confidentiality. What happens if someone goes into significant negative balance.
5. **Run the first exchanges.** A member posts a need. Another member responds. They arrange the help. Afterward, the hours are logged.
6. **Hold monthly gatherings.** Potlucks, skill-shares, celebrations. The bank is more than logged hours. The relationships are the substance.
7. **Build a steward team.** 2 to 4 people who manage onboarding, troubleshoot stuck exchanges, and run the gatherings.
8. **Welcome new members slowly.** Each new member should be introduced. Trust scales with shared experience.

## Variations

**Senior-focused.** Many of the most successful time banks center older adults. They have time. They have skills. The bank reduces isolation. See the Member Connect models that AARP and others have run.

**Cross-organization.** A bank that includes both individuals and small organizations (a community garden, a school, a youth program). Hours flow both ways.

**Domain-specific.** A skill-share-only bank. A childcare-only bank (similar to a [Babysitting Co-op](../02-small-groups-for-support/babysitting-coop.md), but more formalized).

**Hybrid.** A time bank that also accepts traditional volunteer hours, donations, or in-kind contributions. More complex; works when the founding team has experience.

## Stories from neighborhoods

**Edgar Cahn**, a legal scholar, founded the modern time banking movement in the 1980s as a tool for community development, especially in places where traditional volunteer programs missed the people they meant to serve. [TimeBanks USA](https://www.timebanks.org/) (now succeeded by the [TimeBanks Network](https://www.hourworld.org/)) has supported thousands of banks since.

Reports from active time banks consistently show two things: members save $300 to $1,200 a year through service exchanges, and (more importantly) older adults in time banks report 90% more new friendships through participation. The hours are real but they aren't the point.

## Where to learn more

- Open platform: [hOurworld](https://www.hourworld.org/)
- The history and theory: Edgar Cahn, *No More Throw-Away People* (Essential Books, 2000)
- Adjacent recipes: [Reciprocity Game](../02-small-groups-for-support/reciprocity-game.md), [Skillshare](./skillshare.md), [Mutual Aid Pod](../02-small-groups-for-support/mutual-aid-pod.md)

items.body:
## What it is

A community-owned collection of tools and equipment that members can borrow. Memberships typically run $20 to $100 a year. The library tracks loans the way a book library does. Some libraries also include a workshop space, classes, and a maker community around the inventory.

There were around 40 tool libraries in 2013. Now there are hundreds across North America, with active expansion still happening.

## Why it works

Most households own a drill that they use 12 minutes a year. A neighborhood of 200 households owns 200 drills, almost all of them idle almost all of the time. A tool library replaces the 200 drills with one good drill that gets used hundreds of times. The math is so obvious that the only real question is why it isn't standard infrastructure in every neighborhood.

The relational effect is real too. Tool libraries become hubs where neighbors meet other people working on similar projects. Beginners borrow with confidence because more experienced members are usually around to offer help.

## What you need

- **Time:** 6 to 12 months to launch a real library. Ongoing 5 to 15 hours per week per active steward.
- **People:** A founding team of 3 to 6. A volunteer board over time. Eventually 1 part-time staff person if the library reaches 100+ members.
- **Space:** A dedicated room or unit with shelving, secure storage, and workspace. Often donated or rented cheaply.
- **Materials:** Initial tool inventory (donations + seed purchases). Library management software (Lendr, MyTurn, or open-source alternatives). Member tracking. Tool safety signage.
- **Skills:** Tool knowledge, library management basics, teaching, safety training, ongoing community facilitation.
- **Energy level:** Moderate to high. Real organizational work.

## How to host it

1. **Form a founding team.** 3 to 6 people who will carry the launch. Mix of tool-skilled folks and organization-skilled folks.
2. **Pick a structure.** Most tool libraries are 501(c)(3) nonprofits. Some are fiscally sponsored. Some operate as informal collectives. Talk to existing libraries before picking. [The Tool Library Network](https://localtools.org/) is the field hub.
3. **Find space.** Libraries (the book kind) sometimes host tool libraries inside. Community centers, churches, and donated retail space all work. You need 400 to 1,500 square feet to start.
4. **Acquire the first tool inventory.** Three sources: donations from the community (run a one-day collection drive at a [Block Party](../01-knowing-your-neighbors/block-party.md)), retired tools from contractors, seed purchases for the most-needed categories. 100 to 300 tools is a credible launch inventory.
5. **Set up tracking.** Lendr ([lendingtools.org](https://lendingtools.org/)), MyTurn, or a simple spreadsheet to start. Track who has what, when it's due, condition history.
6. **Set the membership model.** Sliding scale is common: $0 to $100. Most libraries offer free memberships for households below an income threshold. Some are entirely free.
7. **Write a clear safety and use policy.** What requires a quick training before borrowing. What can be loaned to anyone. Liability waivers (talk to a lawyer who's done this work; templates exist).
8. **Open with a launch event.** A "show off the tools" day before formal lending starts. People come, see the inventory, sign up.
9. **Run regularly.** Open hours 2 to 4 days a week is typical for new libraries. Slowly add classes, workshops, repair clinics ([Repair Cafe](./repair-cafe.md) format).
10. **Connect to the network.** [Local Tools](https://localtools.org/) and the Tool Library Network share software, policy templates, fundraising help, and operational wisdom.

## Variations

**Apartment building tool library.** A closet or storage room with shared tools for one building or complex. Smaller, simpler, more intimate.

**Tool share without a building.** A spreadsheet of "who has what" and direct neighbor-to-neighbor loans. Easier to start. Less inventory. No central space.

**Maker space.** A tool library that includes workspace, classes, and a maker community. More complex to run; more capability when running well.

**Specialty libraries.** Sewing machines (a "stitch library"). Cooking equipment. Outdoor gear. Children's toys. The model adapts.

## Stories from neighborhoods

**Berkeley Tool Library** has run since 1979, one of the longest-operating in the U.S. It's based in a public library branch, free for any Berkeley resident with a library card. The model proves tool lending can sit inside public infrastructure.

**Portland Tool Library**, **Halifax Tool Library**, and dozens of others have demonstrated the model at neighborhood scale, with 1,000+ members and tool inventories in the thousands.

The [Tool Library Network](https://localtools.org/) tracks libraries, shares software, and supports new launches. The growth from 40 libraries in 2013 to several hundred in 2025 is steady and mostly volunteer-driven.

## Where to learn more

- The field hub: [Local Tools](https://localtools.org/)
- Open-source library software: [Lendr](https://lendingtools.org/)
- Adjacent recipes: [Repair Cafe](./repair-cafe.md), [Skillshare](./skillshare.md), [Buy Nothing](./buy-nothing.md)

steps: **Form a founding team.** 3 to 6 people who will carry the launch. Mix of tool-skilled folks and organization-skilled folks.

**Pick a structure.** Most tool libraries are 501(c)(3) nonprofits. Some are fiscally sponsored. Some operate as informal collectives. Talk to existing libraries before picking. [The Tool Library Network](https://localtools.org/) is the field hub.
**Find space.** Libraries (the book kind) sometimes host tool libraries inside. Community centers, churches, and donated retail space all work. You need 400 to 1,500 square feet to start.

**Acquire the first tool inventory.** Three sources: donations from the community (run a one-day collection drive at a [Block Party](../01-knowing-your-neighbors/block-party.md)), retired tools from contractors, seed purchases for the most-needed categories. 100 to 300 tools is a credible launch inventory.
**Set up tracking.** Lendr ([lendingtools.org](https://lendingtools.org/)), MyTurn, or a simple spreadsheet to start. Track who has what, when it's due, condition history.
**Set the membership model.** Sliding scale is common: $0 to $100. Most libraries offer free memberships for households below an income threshold. Some are entirely free.
**Write a clear safety and use policy.** What requires a quick training before borrowing. What can be loaned to anyone. Liability waivers (talk to a lawyer who's done this work; templates exist).
**Open with a launch event.** A "show off the tools" day before formal lending starts. People come, see the inventory, sign up.
**Run regularly.** Open hours 2 to 4 days a week is typical for new libraries. Slowly add classes, workshops, repair clinics ([Repair Cafe](./repair-cafe.md) format).
**Connect to the network.** [Local Tools](https://localtools.org/) and the Tool Library Network share software, policy templates, fundraising help, and operational wisdom.

items.body:
*The need:* Groups burn out trying to persuade everyone, when the work is usually to move a few specific actors.

Power is the relationship between interests and resources — so before acting, a team maps who holds what. This is a leadership-team exercise with markers, post-its, and two big sheets:

**Step 1: Map the actors.** Write every individual and group with influence (actual or potential) over your effort on post-its. Sort them into five zones: your **constituency** (the people with the problem, standing together), your **leadership** (drawn from within that constituency, accountable to it), **supporters** (share your values, hold resources, aren't directly affected), **competitors** (share some interests, compete for the same people or money — can often be turned into allies), and **opposition** (their interests conflict with yours).

**Step 2: The field of play.** Draw a spectrum from "greatest interest in change" to "greatest interest in the status quo," with sidelines. Place every actor. Mark who is actively in play and who is watching from the sidelines.

**Step 3: Debrief.** Are there key supporters on the sidelines — and what would pull them in? Which competitors could become allies? Which opposition efforts need to be neutralized, and which can be safely ignored? Don't try to address every actor; pick the few that matter most.

For each key actor, ask the power questions: what do they want, and what do we have that they need? A neighborhood group that runs this exercise usually discovers it has more leverage than it thought — votes, stories, relationships, attention, legitimacy — and a much shorter list of people to actually move.

ingredients: two flipchart sheets or a whiteboard
metadata.source_note: The 'Map the Actors' and 'Field of Play' exercise from the appendix of 'Organizing: People, Power, Change' (2014). Kin to the Midwest Academy strategy chart tradition of power mapping.
how_it_works: Map the actors: constituency, leadership, supporters, competitors, opposition.
Place every actor on the field of play, from 'wants change' to 'wants status quo', noting who's on the sidelines.
Debrief: who could we pull off the sidelines? Who could we convert? Who must we neutralize?
For the few actors who matter most, answer: what do they want, and what do we hold that they need?
Revisit the map at every campaign peak — power shifts as you build it.
success_signals: the team can name its three most important actors
at least one 'competitor' becomes a supporter
effort stops going to actors who don't matter

items.body:
## What it is

A global movement of communities building resilience and reducing dependence on fossil fuels. Transition groups form locally, identify their community's specific priorities, and organize around them: community gardens, repair cafes, renewable energy cooperatives, local currencies, skill-shares, food coops.

The movement started in 2006 in **Totnes, UK**, with the work of **Rob Hopkins** and others, and now spans 67+ countries. It is intentionally distributed: each Transition group is autonomous, working from a shared framework but adapted to local conditions.

## Why it works

Climate change, energy uncertainty, supply chain fragility, and economic precarity all argue for stronger local capacity. Transition Towns is one of the longer-running models for community organizing around that argument. It is not survivalist; it is built on relationships and shared work, with the understanding that resilience and connection grow together.

The framework is intentionally light. There is no central authority. Local groups pick from a menu of "ingredients" (originally 12, now 43) and apply what fits.

## What you need

- **Time:** Long arc. Most successful Transition groups operate over years and decades.
- **People:** A founding group of 5 to 20 committed neighbors. Working groups for specific projects.
- **Space:** Meeting space (homes, community centers, libraries). Specific project sites (gardens, workshops, distribution points).
- **Materials:** Whatever each project requires. Shared documents, communication channels, project-specific equipment.
- **Skills:** Community organizing, project management, technical skills relevant to specific projects (gardening, building, electrical, etc.).
- **Energy level:** Moderate. Distributed across many people and projects.

## How to host it

1. **Connect with the [Transition Network](https://transitionnetwork.org/).** They support new initiatives with materials, training, and a global network of practitioners.
2. **Form a founding group.** 5 to 10 neighbors committed to the work. Mix of perspectives and skills.
3. **Pick your initial focus.** The movement's 43 ingredients are a menu, not a checklist. Common starting points:
   - Community gardens or food forests.
   - A repair cafe or skill-share series.
   - Local food initiatives (CSAs, farmers markets, community kitchens).
   - Energy descent or efficiency projects.
   - A local currency or time bank.
   - Community-supported agriculture or producer coops.
4. **Run "awareness raising" alongside action.** Film screenings, talks, walks, workshops. The events that bring more neighbors into the conversation.
5. **Build working groups.** Each project gets its own working group of 3 to 10 people. The main initiative coordinates, supports, and connects them.
6. **Partner widely.** Local government, schools, businesses, faith communities, neighborhood associations. Transition Towns is meant to be a connector, not a competitor.
7. **Document and celebrate.** Each project completed, each garden bed dug, each repair night, each meal cooked together. The visibility carries the next group of participants in.
8. **Sustain over time.** Many Transition Towns experience cycles of high energy and lower energy. The strongest groups have learned to operate at multiple paces and to welcome people back after long absences.

## Variations

**Sector-specific.** Some communities run only the food piece (a Transition Food Hub) or only the energy piece (a Transition Energy Coop) without taking on the full framework.

**Neighborhood scale within a city.** Larger cities sometimes have multiple Transition groups by neighborhood, plus a citywide coordinating body.

**Local economy focus.** Some groups have led with local currency, time banks, or producer cooperatives as the unifying project.

**Cohousing connection.** Some Transition Towns have spawned [cohousing](../12-shared-land-and-home/cohousing.md) projects as the next step in committing to shared local life.

**Faith-based variant.** Some congregations have organized around Transition principles. The faith framing provides additional moral language and member commitment.

## Stories from neighborhoods

**Totnes, UK**, the founding Transition Town (2006), has built community gardens, a renewable energy cooperative, a local currency (the Totnes Pound), a community brewery, and many other projects across two decades.

**Transition US**, the U.S. hub, supports hundreds of Transition initiatives across the country. Notable examples include Transition Sebastopol (California), Transition Pittsburgh, and many smaller-town initiatives.

**Globally**, the movement has spread to 67+ countries with thousands of local initiatives. Each looks different. The underlying commitment to community-led local resilience is the constant.

The model has also informed adjacent movements: solidarity economy networks, eco-villages, climate adaptation organizing, food sovereignty movements. The boundaries between these are porous.

## Where to learn more

- The global hub: [Transition Network](https://transitionnetwork.org/)
- The U.S. hub: [Transition US](https://transitionus.org/)
- Foundational book: Rob Hopkins, *The Transition Handbook*
- Adjacent recipes: [Community Garden](../06-placemaking/community-garden.md), [Tool Library](../03-mutual-aid/tool-library.md), [Time Banking](../03-mutual-aid/timebanking.md), [Resilience Hub](../07-resilience/resilience-hub.md)

items.body:
## What it is

An approach to community development that recognizes the impact of trauma (individual, collective, historical) and designs practices, programs, and physical environments to avoid re-traumatization. It operates on four principles: **Do No Harm**, **Acceptance**, **Community Empowerment**, and **Reflective Process**.

The framework has been developed especially in communities that have lived with concentrated violence, displacement, racial trauma, and economic disinvestment. Practitioners include community development organizations in cities like San Francisco, Baltimore, Memphis, and elsewhere.

## Why it works

Most community development assumes a baseline of safety, agency, and well-being that many neighborhoods do not have. Practices that work in stable middle-class settings can re-injure communities that are already carrying significant collective trauma. Asking residents to "share their stories" in a public meeting, for example, can be empowering in one context and re-traumatizing in another.

Trauma-informed community building doesn't slow the work down. It adjusts the methods so the work doesn't compound the harm.

## What you need

- **Time:** Ongoing. Planning: 3 to 6 months for serious integration. Implementation: 1 to 3 years or longer.
- **People:** Community members with lived experience of trauma. Trained facilitators and organizers. Mental health practitioners (ideally from the community). Diverse leadership reflecting community demographics.
- **Space:** Community centers, parks, cultural spaces, homes. Multiple accessible gathering spaces. Welcoming and safe.
- **Materials:** Art supplies, gardening materials, music and sound equipment, comfortable seating, culturally relevant resources. Training curricula and peer support guides.
- **Skills:** Trauma awareness, facilitation, cultural competency, listening, flexibility, systems thinking, community knowledge.
- **Energy level:** Medium to high. Emotionally and physically demanding but nourishing.

## How to host it

The four core principles guide practice:

### Do No Harm

1. **Recognize trauma in your community.** Police violence, gun violence, immigration enforcement, eviction, racial violence, sexual violence, generational poverty, historical displacement. Different communities carry different wounds. Name what's here.
2. **Audit existing practices.** What are you asking of people? Are public testimony requirements safe for everyone? Do meeting times work for people with caregiving responsibilities? Are physical spaces accessible? Is the language clinical or accessible?
3. **Avoid re-traumatization.** Stop asking "share your story" of harm without consent. Avoid surveillance practices (heavy ID checks, sign-ins, photo-taking) that mirror systems of harm. Be mindful of authority figures (police, immigration officials, child welfare workers) in spaces meant to be community-safe.

### Acceptance

4. **Meet people where they are.** Don't require people to be "ready" before participating. Don't gatekeep based on language, education, housing status, employment, sobriety, or behavior.
5. **Multiple ways to participate.** Some people will speak in meetings. Some will write. Some will draw. Some will listen. Some will help by cooking. All count.

### Community Empowerment

6. **Center those most affected in leadership.** Not as advisors. As decision-makers. Pay them. Give them real authority.
7. **Build healing into the work.** Art, movement, music, gardening, food sharing, ritual. These are not extras. They are infrastructure for processing collective experience.
8. **Train local leaders.** Mental health first aid, peer support, facilitation. Build the local capacity to hold the community's healing work.

### Reflective Process

9. **Build in regular reflection.** What's working? What isn't? Who isn't here who should be? Who is struggling? Adjust.
10. **Listen for signals.** Disengagement, conflict, burnout, and tension are often signals that something in the approach needs to shift.

## Variations

**Healing justice.** A related and broader frame, especially as developed by the **Kindred Southern Healing Justice Collective** and others. Healing justice connects individual healing to collective liberation and is rooted in Black, queer, and disabled traditions.

**Sanctuary model.** A trauma-informed organizational framework used in residential treatment, schools, and human services. Specific tools and language for whole-organization implementation.

**Cultural healing practices.** Indigenous, Black, Latine, Asian, and other cultural traditions have specific healing practices that should be centered when working in those communities. Outsiders should follow rather than lead.

**Disaster-recovery context.** Trauma-informed community building is especially relevant after major disasters or violent events. Different from baseline conditions; same principles apply.

## Stories from neighborhoods

The framework has been articulated and refined in many places. **Organizing Engagement** maintains a useful synthesis [at organizingengagement.org](https://organizingengagement.org/models/trauma-informed-community-building-model/).

Practitioners in **San Francisco** (BMAGIC, the Bayview-Hunters Point), **Memphis** (Memphis Allies), **Baltimore** (numerous community health worker programs), and elsewhere have integrated trauma-informed practice into their community organizing. Outcomes are difficult to measure on conventional metrics; the lived experience of community members consistently affirms the approach.

The **Kindred Southern Healing Justice Collective** has produced foundational resources for healing justice as a practice, distinct from clinical mental health and connected to liberation work.

## Where to learn more

- A framework reference: [Organizing Engagement: Trauma-Informed Community Building](https://organizingengagement.org/models/trauma-informed-community-building-model/)
- Healing justice: [Kindred Southern Healing Justice Collective](http://kindredsouthernhjcollective.org/)
- Foundational reading: Resmaa Menakem, *My Grandmother's Hands*
- Foundational reading: Bessel van der Kolk, *The Body Keeps the Score* (clinical lens)
- Adjacent recipes: [Peacemaking Circles](./peacemaking-circles.md), [Nap Ministry](./nap-ministry.md), [Community Acupuncture](./community-acupuncture.md)

items.body:
## What it is

A consumer-driven model for aging in community. Elders pay annual dues (often $300 to $800) and receive coordinated access to volunteer help, social and educational programming, transportation, technology coaching, and referrals to vetted professionals. Members are also volunteers for each other: the reciprocity is structural.

The movement began in Boston's Beacon Hill in 2001 (Beacon Hill Village) and has grown to over 300 active Villages with many more in development.

## Why it works

The conventional choices for U.S. elders are: stay in the home you've lived in for forty years and slowly lose the supports that made it sustainable, or move to senior housing and lose the neighborhood you've spent a lifetime in. Both options are common; neither is good. The Village Movement creates a third option that keeps the home, builds the supports, and adds community.

The membership model produces an unusual feature: elders are not "served" but participate. Most members give and receive in roughly equal measure. The reciprocity is part of what keeps the model alive across decades.

## What you need

- **Time:** 1 to 2 years to establish a Village. 1 to 2 hours per week of typical member engagement.
- **People:** Member elders (typically 55+). Volunteer supporters. A coordinator or part-time staff. A board.
- **Space:** Members' homes primarily. Gathering spaces for events and programs.
- **Materials:** A volunteer coordination system. Programming materials. Transportation coordination tools.
- **Skills:** Community organizing, program coordination, volunteer management, relationship facilitation.
- **Energy level:** Low to moderate for members. Higher for organizers in the launch phase.

## How to host it

1. **Connect with [the Village to Village Network](https://www.vtvnetwork.org/).** This national network supports new Villages with model documents, training, governance frameworks, and a community of established Villages willing to share what they've learned. Don't start from scratch.
2. **Form a founding committee.** 5 to 15 people, often a mix of current elders, family members of elders, professionals (social workers, geriatricians), and community organizers.
3. **Conduct community assessment.** What do older neighbors want and need? Surveys, focus groups, one-on-one conversations. The Village should fit the specific community.
4. **Choose governance.** Most Villages are 501(c)(3) nonprofits. Some are fiscally sponsored. Some have municipal partnerships.
5. **Set the membership model.** Annual dues. Sliding scale or reduced-fee membership for income-qualified members. Define services included.
6. **Build the volunteer pool.** Vetted neighbors and family members who can help with rides, light home help, technology, social calls. Background checks and basic training are standard.
7. **Launch programming.** Educational events. Social gatherings. Wellness activities. Trips. Programming builds the community that makes the help feel mutual rather than transactional.
8. **Operate and adjust.** Most Villages take 2 to 5 years to find their groove. Member feedback is the primary tool for adjustment.

## Variations

**Virtual Village.** A Village with a strong online component, useful in rural areas or for elders with mobility limitations.

**NORC (Naturally Occurring Retirement Community) Village.** A Village inside a single building or housing complex with a high concentration of elders.

**Faith-community Village.** A Village anchored in a congregation. Stronger initial trust. Sometimes narrower demographic reach.

**Multi-generational Village.** Some Villages explicitly include younger members and family caregivers. Adds capacity and complexity.

## Stories from neighborhoods

**Beacon Hill Village** (Boston) launched in 2001 and is the founding model. **Capitol Hill Village** (DC), **Avenidas Village** (Palo Alto), and dozens of others have followed in major cities. **Smaller-town Villages** have grown in places like Vermont, Maine, and rural Oregon, often with stronger volunteer participation than urban versions.

The model has demonstrated outcomes in member health, social connection, and ability to age in place. Members consistently report that the value is more than the services: it's the experience of being part of something where they are seen.

## Where to learn more

- The national network: [Village to Village Network](https://www.vtvnetwork.org/)
- Foundational model: [Beacon Hill Village](https://www.beaconhillvillage.org/)
- Adjacent recipes: [Bridge Meadows](./bridge-meadows.md), [Block Stewards](../01-knowing-your-neighbors/block-stewards.md), [Mutual Aid Pod](../02-small-groups-for-support/mutual-aid-pod.md)

**Form a founding committee.** 5 to 15 people, often a mix of current elders, family members of elders, professionals (social workers, geriatricians), and community organizers.
**Conduct community assessment.** What do older neighbors want and need? Surveys, focus groups, one-on-one conversations. The Village should fit the specific community.
**Choose governance.** Most Villages are 501(c)(3) nonprofits. Some are fiscally sponsored. Some have municipal partnerships.
**Set the membership model.** Annual dues. Sliding scale or reduced-fee membership for income-qualified members. Define services included.
**Build the volunteer pool.** Vetted neighbors and family members who can help with rides, light home help, technology, social calls. Background checks and basic training are standard.
**Launch programming.** Educational events. Social gatherings. Wellness activities. Trips. Programming builds the community that makes the help feel mutual rather than transactional.
**Operate and adjust.** Most Villages take 2 to 5 years to find their groove. Member feedback is the primary tool for adjustment.

**Beacon Hill Village** (Boston) launched in 2001 and is the founding model. **Capitol Hill Village** (DC), **Avenidas Village** (Palo Alto), and dozens of others have followed in major cities. **Smaller-town Villages** have grown in places like Vermont, Maine, and rural Oregon, often with stronger volunteer participation than urban versions.

The model has demonstrated outcomes in member health, social connection, and ability to age in place. Members consistently report that the value is more than the services: it's the experience of being part of something where they are seen.

## What it is

A community space that opens during extreme cold or heat to provide refuge for neighbors who need it. Traditional centers are basic: a room with HVAC, water, maybe cots. Modern Climate Resilience Hubs (see the [Resilience Hub](./resilience-hub.md) recipe) extend the model significantly: year-round programming, social services, emergency preparedness, community connection.

This recipe covers the simpler version. The fuller version is in the Resilience Hub recipe.

## Why it works

Extreme heat is the deadliest weather hazard in the U.S. Extreme cold kills as well. People die in extreme weather not because the weather is unbearable in the abstract, but because they cannot escape it. A neighborhood with reliable, accessible cooling and warming infrastructure is a neighborhood with fewer preventable deaths.

The "trusted local space" framing matters. A cooling center in a building people already use is reachable. A cooling center in an emergency-only government building most people have never entered is a poster, not a service.

## What you need

- **Time:** 3 to 6 months of planning. Seasonal operation with full daily activation during extreme weather.
- **People:** A facility coordinator, volunteer or paid staff, outreach team.
- **Space:** Existing trusted community space with HVAC capacity. Library, church, school, community center, mutual aid hub.
- **Materials:** Reliable HVAC. Backup power if possible. Water, snacks, basic first aid. Comfortable seating. Charging stations for phones. Multilingual signage.
- **Skills:** Coordination, hospitality, light triage and welfare-check skills.
- **Energy level:** Moderate during normal times. High during active extreme weather.

## How to host it

1. **Identify the space.** A community-trusted institution that has the HVAC to function during extreme weather. Libraries are often willing partners. Churches and faith communities sometimes have unused weekday capacity. Schools out of session.
2. **Talk to your city or county.** Many jurisdictions have a heat or cold response plan. Get your space listed officially. Some cities pay community centers for operating during heat or cold events. Get on those lists.
3. **Set the trigger conditions.** When does the center open? Common triggers:
   - Heat advisories or excessive heat warnings (90F+ depending on region).
   - Cold below freezing, especially with wind chill warnings.
   - Wildfire smoke at AQI thresholds.
   - Power outages affecting the neighborhood.
4. **Stock supplies.** Water (lots). Basic snacks. First aid. Charging stations and a couple of power strips. Comfortable seating that can handle multi-hour visits. Books, magazines, board games. Wifi. Cool/warm refreshments.
5. **Set hours.** Cooling centers typically run during peak heat hours (10am to 8pm). Warming centers run extended hours and often need overnight capacity, which is different and requires more planning.
6. **Train staff and volunteers.** Mental health first aid. Heat stroke recognition. Hypothermia recognition. De-escalation. Knowing when to call medical services.
7. **Outreach.** Don't just open the doors. Reach people who need to know:
   - Multilingual flyers in places people already go (laundromats, bus stops, food pantries, senior buildings).
   - Door-knocking on streets with elderly or isolated residents.
   - Welfare-check partnerships with health and social services.
   - Coordination with mutual aid networks (see [Mutual Aid Pod](../02-small-groups-for-support/mutual-aid-pod.md)).
8. **Operate with dignity.** People coming in are often vulnerable. The space should feel like a community living room, not a triage tent. No paperwork. No proof of address. No ID checks.

## Variations

**Climate Resilience Hub.** The expanded model. See [Resilience Hub](./resilience-hub.md).

**Mobile center.** A van or bus that travels to neighborhoods. Useful in rural or sprawling areas where one fixed location can't serve everyone.

**Library-based.** Many libraries are unofficial cooling centers already. A formal partnership and resources turn an informal practice into reliable infrastructure.

**Wildfire smoke center.** A clean-air refuge during smoke events. Requires air filtration capacity beyond standard HVAC.

**24-hour winter shelter.** A more substantial commitment with overnight capacity. Often run in partnership with homeless service organizations.

## Stories from neighborhoods

**Maricopa County, Arizona** runs one of the most extensive cooling center networks in the country. The county coordinates with churches, community centers, libraries, and faith groups across the Phoenix metro area. During the deadly summers of recent years, the network has been a primary intervention.

**Climate Resilience Hubs**, an evolution of the model, have been deployed in Los Angeles, Baltimore, and elsewhere. These hubs operate year-round and shift into expanded mode during extreme weather.

The pattern across all of these: the strongest centers are run by community-trusted institutions with strong neighborhood relationships, not by emergency management departments alone.

## Where to learn more

- The fuller model: [Resilience Hub](./resilience-hub.md)
- Climate Resilience Hubs: [Climate Resolve](https://climateresolve.org/resilience-hubs/)
- For research: [CDC Heat and Health](https://www.cdc.gov/extremeheat/index.html)
- Adjacent recipes: [Resilience Hub](./resilience-hub.md), [Map Your Neighborhood](./map-your-neighborhood.md)

items.body:
## What it is

The practice of welcoming new neighbors with a small gesture and useful local information. Welcome wagon practices have existed for a century in various forms, from formal chamber-of-commerce welcome baskets to a neighbor showing up with bread.

The recipe is simple. The effect is disproportionate. A neighbor who is greeted in their first week is a neighbor who knows at least one face, has one phone number, and feels like the block has noticed them.

## Why it works

Moving is hard. The first few weeks in a new place are when belonging is most fragile and most influenceable. A small welcoming gesture in that window says "you're not invisible here." That message is hard to deliver any other time.

This also creates a low-pressure reason to meet a neighbor. You're not knocking to start a relationship. You're knocking to drop something off. The relationship is the side effect.

## What you need

- **Time:** 30 to 60 minutes total. About 10 minutes at the door.
- **People:** You. Optionally a partner or a kid to come along.
- **Space:** Their doorstep.
- **Materials:** Something useful or hospitable. Baked goods, a bouquet from your garden, a gift card to a nearby restaurant or coffee shop. A one-page local info sheet (more on this below).
- **Skills:** Friendly. Brief.
- **Energy level:** Low.

## How to host it

1. **Notice the move.** Moving truck, new car in the driveway, "for sale" sign coming down. Give them a few days to land. Two to seven days after they move in is the sweet spot. Sooner feels rushed. Later feels late.
2. **Bring something simple.** A loaf of banana bread. Cookies. Fresh flowers from your yard. A small gift card (5 to 15 dollars) to a nearby spot. Not expensive. The gesture is what matters.
3. **Bring a one-page local info sheet.** This is the part that does the most work. Include: trash and recycling day, nearest grocery, nearest pharmacy, your name and number, names of a few other neighbors with their permission, a couple of favorite local restaurants, the name of the local park, the WiFi password for the porch network if there is one.
4. **Knock once. Step back.** Stand back from the door so they don't feel crowded when they open it.
5. **Introduce yourself in one sentence.** "Hi, I'm [name] from [number] across the street. I just wanted to welcome you to the block." Hand them what you brought. Smile.
6. **Don't push to come in.** If they invite you, great. If not, that's fine. Say "I'm at [number] if you need anything. There's my number on the sheet." Wave. Go home.
7. **Follow up casually.** Wave when you see them. Stop to chat for a minute when paths cross. Invite them to the next block thing that comes up.

## Variations

**Coordinated welcome.** If your block has a few connected neighbors, do a coordinated welcome. Different neighbors drop different things over the first week or two. New family meets four neighbors instead of one.

**Kid version.** If you have kids, bring them. New neighbors with kids especially appreciate this. The kids do the talking.

**Renter inclusive version.** Welcome renters as warmly as homeowners. People often skip the rental units. Don't.

**Apartment building version.** Knock on the door above and below yours. Bring something simple. Same recipe, different walls.

**Welcome basket version.** Some neighborhoods coordinate a more formal welcome basket: 5 to 10 small items contributed by different neighbors, delivered together. Beautiful when sustained but heavier to coordinate.

## Stories from neighborhoods

**The original Welcome Wagon** was a commercial organization founded in 1928 that delivered welcome baskets door to door for decades. It is largely gone in its original form, but the practice has scattered into thousands of informal versions across the country.

Many neighborhoods now run informal welcome rotations through their neighborhood association, faith community, or block-level Nextdoor or [Front Porch Forum](./front-porch-forum.md) threads. Churches and faith communities often lead formal welcoming practices.

The shift from corporate welcome wagon to neighbor-led welcome is, in itself, on-thesis for this book. The practice belongs in neighbors' hands.

## Where to learn more

- A reference: [Welcome Wagon's tips for welcoming new neighbors](https://welcomewagon.com/blog/tips-for-making-new-neighbors-feel-like-part-of-the-community/)
- Adjacent recipes: [Porch Conversations](./porch-conversations.md), [Block Stewards](./block-stewards.md), [Block Party](./block-party.md)
