## What It Is

A participatory, strengths-based process where community members together identify, document, and map the human, social, organizational, cultural, and physical resources already present in their neighborhood. Asset mapping shifts focus from problems and deficits to capacities, relationships, and existing strengths.

## How It Works

Community members gather to identify assets in their neighborhood—which might include individual skills and knowledge, community organizations and associations, institutions like schools and libraries, businesses, public spaces and infrastructure, and cultural traditions. Using paper maps, digital mapping tools, or online platforms, participants visually chart these assets geographically. The process involves walking the neighborhood, interviewing residents and leaders, and recording both obvious assets (parks, schools) and hidden assets (neighborhood elders' expertise, informal networks, community culture). The resulting map becomes a planning tool that helps communities see their own capacity, build on existing strengths, and identify where connections can be made between assets. Asset mapping is fundamentally about connection—linking neighbors to each other and to the resources and networks already present in their community.

## Who 'S Done It

Used by community development organizations, urban planners, public health departments, and grassroots neighborhood groups across North America. Philadelphia, Evanston, and many cities have integrated asset mapping into neighborhood planning. Community science organizations and participatory research initiatives use this practice.

## Connections

Rooted in Asset-Based Community Development (ABCD) framework developed by John Kretzmann and John McKnight. Connected to participatory planning, community research, and strengths-based approaches. Related to community visioning, participatory budgeting, and neighborhood planning processes.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: 6-12 weeks for comprehensive mapping; individual sessions: 2-3 hours
- *People*: 10-50+ community members; 1-2 facilitators/coordinators; optional: professional mappers or technicians
- *Space*: Community center, library, neighborhood meeting space; public spaces for walking tours
- *Materials*: Large paper maps or digital mapping platform (ArcGIS, Maptionnaire, or open-source tools); markers, photos, sticky notes; notebooks; optional: camera, GPS units, video
- *Skills*: Community facilitation, mapping (digital or paper), listening, data recording, relationship-building
- *Energy Level*: Medium—involves both gathering and collaborative analysis

## What It Is

Community Plate facilitates free, public, intergenerational story-sharing potluck suppers designed to build connections, address loneliness, and preserve community histories through shared meals and storytelling. Events are non-partisan and focused on increasing social connection and civil discourse.

## How It Works

To host a Story Sharing Supper, organizers download the Community Partner Guide from Community Plate's website and contact them at community@communityplate.me for support. Before the event, community members are invited to bring a dish to share along with a story related to that dish. Organizers provide story prompts that are personal, nonpartisan, and food-centered to guide conversation. During the meal, participants share stories across tables based on these prompts, creating informal cross-generational and cross-cultural dialogue. As dessert is served, prepared storytellers perform or read stories they've crafted on the evening's theme. After the supper, Community Plate compiles all recipes, stories, and photos into a community cookbook distributed to attendees, creating a lasting artifact of the event and the connections made.

## Who 'S Done It

Community Plate, based in Maine, has hosted Story Sharing Suppers in communities across Maine and beyond. Events have taken place in Westbrook, Norway, Orono, and multiple other locations. The model has attracted diverse participants including families, seniors, and cross-cultural groups. Press coverage documents how suppers have strengthened community ties, particularly in smaller towns and communities experiencing social fragmentation.

## Connections

The Story Sharing Supper builds on potluck traditions while adding intentional storytelling and documentation. It reflects contemporary interest in narrative justice, food sovereignty, and community-based placemaking. The model connects to broader food-based community building and oral history preservation practices.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: 2-3 hours for the supper event; advance planning of 4-6 weeks
- *People*: Organizers/hosts; 20-50+ community members; prepared storytellers; Community Plate support
- *Space*: Community gathering space (library, church, community center, school)
- *Materials*: Dishes/food; story prompts; cookbook creation materials (photos, text compilation)
- *Skills*: Community outreach, facilitation, basic storytelling/writing for documenting
- *Energy Level*: High during event; moderate for planning and follow-up documentation

## What It Is

A direct relationship between farmers and consumers where community members buy shares of a farm's harvest in advance, sharing both risks and benefits of food production. Rather than purchasing food from distant industrial supply chains, CSA members make a season-long commitment to support local farmers, receiving regular boxes of freshly harvested food.

## How It Works

Community members purchase shares or subscriptions at the beginning of the growing season (typically $400-700 for a season), paid upfront or in installments. In exchange, they receive weekly or bi-weekly boxes of seasonal produce throughout the harvest (roughly May-November in northern climates). Some CSAs offer additional items like eggs, dairy, meat, dried goods, or flowers. Members sometimes participate in farm work, making decisions about what's planted, or volunteering at harvest. The model eliminates shipping and processing costs, reducing environmental impact and price.

## Who 'S Done It

As of 2020, 7,244 farms in the US operated CSA programs. CSAs are widespread across North America and Europe with growing adoption globally. Urban and rural CSAs exist, including innovative models serving low-income communities with subsidized shares and delivering to multiple neighborhoods.

## Connections

Originated in Japan in the 1960s among women concerned with pesticides and food system sustainability; formalized in Europe in the 1970s. Connected to slow food movement, local food systems, buy nothing groups, and food sovereignty movements. Represents a shift from consumer passivity to producer-consumer interdependence and mutual aid economics.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: One growing season minimum commitment; typically May-November
- *People*: Farmers/growers, CSA coordinator, participating members, volunteer crew members
- *Space*: Farm land, distribution point (farm, community center, markets), storage/packing area
- *Materials*: Farm equipment, seedlings, packaging/boxes, communication about seasonal offerings
- *Skills*: Farming/growing, logistics coordination, communication, customer relationship management
- *Energy Level*: Moderate—receiving weekly deliveries, optional farm participation

## What It Is

Peter Block's 2008 book that reframes community building around 'belonging'—the experience of being part of something, having voice and agency. Block argues authentic community emerges not from problem-solving but from conversations that build relationships, possibility, and shared ownership.

## How It Works

Block proposes five types of conversations that create the conditions for belonging: (1) conversations of possibility—what could be, what we want to build together; (2) conversations of ownership—how do we take responsibility, what's ours to do; (3) conversations of dissent—creating space for real disagreement and diverse views; (4) conversations of commitment—how will we show up, what are we promising; (5) conversations of gifts—recognizing and building on each other's capacities. The book emphasizes that transformation is linguistic and relational—real change happens when communities shift how they speak and listen together.

## Who 'S Done It

Block's frameworks have influenced community development practitioners across North America. Documented example: A neighborhood struggling with disinvestment applied Block's conversation model, moving from meetings focused on 'what's wrong' to structured dialogues about assets, possibility, and shared commitment. Within two years, residents had initiated a community garden, started a tool library, and strengthened existing informal networks.

## Connections

Builds on traditions of participatory community development, appreciative inquiry, and relational sociology; directly influences microsolidarity frameworks and Living Room Conversations design.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: Months to years for deep community shift; individual conversations 1-2 hours
- *People*: Start with 5-10 core people, build to 50-100+ in community
- *Space*: Multiple gathering spaces in neighborhood (homes, cafes, parks, community centers)
- *Materials*: Conversation guides, facilitation training resources, documentation tools
- *Skills*: Facilitation, systems thinking, appreciative listening, group convening
- *Energy Level*: Sustained moderate—ongoing patience and relationship-tending

## What It Is

An economic development model that transforms local economies through democratic ownership and control of assets. Rather than wealth flowing out of communities to distant shareholders, community wealth building systematically connects and scales institution-building practices (cooperatives, land trusts, public banking, ethical procurement) to create broadly-shared prosperity, racial equity, and ecological sustainability.

## Who 'S Done It

Scotland has adopted a national community wealth building approach with all 32 local governments developing CWB action plans and a government Minister for Community Wealth. In the US, cities and regions are adopting CWB frameworks. The model is being adapted internationally and has influenced economic policy discussions globally.

## Connections

Articulated by The Democracy Collaborative in 2005, drawing on cooperative economics, community land trust movements, public banking theory, and critiques of extractive capitalism. Connected to mutual aid economics, cooperatives, community ownership models, and Indigenous economic practices. Part of broader movement toward economic democracy.

## What It Is

A public health approach to palliative care empowering community members to support those experiencing serious illness, dying, and grief. Emerging from Dr. Allan Kellehear's 1999 concept of health-promoting palliative care, the movement normalizes these life experiences as part of everyone's journey while building community-wide capacity to care.

## How It Works

The Compassionate Communities model operates through several mechanisms: (1) Recognizing that serious illness, dying, and grief are normal life experiences affecting everyone, not individual crises. (2) Creating community support networks—including neighbors, faith groups, workplaces, schools—that provide practical and emotional support. (3) Distributing responsibility for grief care across communities rather than confining it to professional domains. (4) Emphasizing early detection and support during loss, not just crisis response. (5) Organizing projects and initiatives implementing these principles across specific regions. Ontario's compassionate communities strategy currently operates 17+ projects across 12 regions.

## Who 'S Done It

The Compassionate Communities model has been implemented across Canada and internationally. Community initiatives demonstrate increased support for grieving individuals, normalized conversations about death and dying, and distributed caring capacity. Participants report feeling less isolated in grief and experiencing meaningful community support.

## Connections

Emerges from palliative care and public health frameworks. Relates to broader movements around death positivity, grief justice, and community resilience. Connects to practices addressing end-of-life care, collective grief, and community accountability.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: Ongoing community initiatives; varies by program structure
- *People*: Community members, trained volunteers, faith leaders, healthcare providers, community organizations
- *Space*: Communities, organizations, neighborhoods; integrates across existing community structures
- *Materials*: Educational resources, training guides, grief support frameworks
- *Skills*: Grief accompaniment, community facilitation, organizational coordination
- *Energy Level*: Medium; distributed across many community members

## What It Is

Richard Bartlett's guide to designing large gatherings (congregations of 30-200+ people) that maintain relational depth, shared decision-making, and meaningful participation. This resource provides eight reusable design patterns that have proven effective in diverse contexts.

## How It Works

The eight patterns address: (1) arrival and welcome; (2) creating psychological safety and establishing group norms; (3) structuring participation so everyone can contribute (not just dominant voices); (4) decision-making processes that are clear and inclusive; (5) managing conflict or dissent within large groups; (6) distributing power and facilitating peer-to-peer connection; (7) maintaining continuity and collective memory; (8) closing and next steps. Each pattern includes multiple design variations, examples from different contexts, and troubleshooting for common challenges. The patterns work together to create conditions where large groups can maintain the relational quality of small groups.

## Who 'S Done It

These patterns have been applied in convergence networks, activist conferences, cooperative business gatherings, and community organizing spaces. One example: a 150-person housing rights gathering in Chicago used the patterns to structure both plenary sessions and breakout work, enabling meaningful contribution from members with varying experience levels while reaching concrete decisions about campaign strategy.

## Connections

Draws from facilitation traditions, participatory democracy practices, and relational organizing; connects to Peter Block's conversations framework and Living Room Conversations structure.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: 1-3 days for congregation gathering, 20+ hours facilitation prep
- *People*: 30-200+ people plus 3-5 facilitation team members
- *Space*: Large flexible space (community center, outdoor venue) with breakout rooms
- *Materials*: Detailed facilitation guide, visual graphics, recording/documentation tools
- *Skills*: Large group facilitation, design thinking, conflict resolution, systems mapping
- *Energy Level*: High—requires careful choreography and sustained focus from facilitators

## What It Is

Richard Bartlett's proposal for building communities of 30-200 people organized into small crews of 3-8, where emotional intimacy and economic cooperation develop together. This essay articulates the theory and vision behind microsolidarity as a response to isolated individualism and unsustainable activism.

## How It Works

The model works in nested layers: (1) Crews form as the basic unit—small groups that create conditions for genuine belonging through practices of enthusiastic listening, praising, challenging, and acknowledging each other; (2) crews develop emotional intimacy first, which creates the foundation for economic cooperation (shared resources, time-banking, collective purchasing, income-sharing); (3) multiple crews coordinate into larger structures (congregations of 30-200) that allow for movement-building while maintaining relational depth; (4) courage is cultivated collectively—people encourage each other to persist toward meaningful work without guarantees of success. The process emphasizes that courage and meaning-making are social capacities, developed through regular practiced intimacy with people who share values.

## Who 'S Done It

Microsolidarity crews have been piloted in community building spaces, activist networks, and cooperative housing projects. In one documented case, a London-based crew organized around social change work met bi-weekly for emotional check-ins alongside quarterly economic discussions about shared resources. After 18 months, the group had collectively funded three members' sabbaticals, started a community garden, and maintained connection through two members' major life crises that might have caused group fracture.

## Connections

Builds on commoning traditions, cooperative economics, queer kinship structures, and Buddhist sangha models; related to intentional communities, co-housing movements, and solidarity economy frameworks.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: 2 hours bi-weekly for crew meetings, 4-8 hours monthly for coordination across crews
- *People*: 3-8 per crew, 30-200 in a congregation, with a core facilitation team
- *Space*: Intimate gathering spaces (homes, cafes), larger spaces for congregation events
- *Materials*: Facilitation guides, shared economic tracking (spreadsheets or software), communication platforms
- *Skills*: Emotional facilitation, economic literacy, systems thinking, conflict transformation
- *Energy Level*: High—requires sustained emotional presence and regular practice

items.body:
## What It Is

A framework and toolkit for communities to respond to interpersonal violence — abuse, assault, harassment — without relying on police or the criminal justice system. It centers survivors, mobilizes friends and family, and sometimes includes the person who caused harm in a process of accountability and transformation.

## How It Works

The toolkit provides step-by-step guides for different roles. For survivors: think through what you need, who you trust, what safety looks like. For friends/family: concrete ways to support — believing them, offering practical help, not pushing toward any particular choice. For someone who caused harm: accountability practices — understanding impact, taking responsibility, changing behavior. For the broader community: creating conditions where violence is less likely. The process: 1) name what happened clearly, 2) identify who should be involved (survivor decides), 3) direct conversations, 4) accountability plan, 5) monitoring and support, 6) evaluation. It's slow, hard, relational work — not a quick fix, but a genuine alternative.

## Who 'S Done It

Creative Interventions started in 2004 in Oakland, California, from activist communities and survivor-led movements. Since then, thousands worldwide have used the toolkit — activists, survivors, advocates, faith communities. The toolkit has been translated into Spanish and French, with German and Japanese in progress. Communities report that this approach honors survivors more fully, holds people accountable more meaningfully, and sometimes transforms harm rather than containing it.

## Connections

Draws on survivor activism, particularly from communities of color and LGBTQ+ communities who recognized that calling police often meant further harm. Connects to abolition, transformative justice, Indigenous restorative practices, and relational ethics. Strengthens when embedded in strong community relationships — block parties, co-ops, and neighborhood gatherings create trust that makes accountability possible. It's the deepening of community that's only possible when people already know each other.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: Weeks to months for accountability processes; survivor support is ongoing
- *People*: Survivor, 2-8 trusted people, sometimes the person who caused harm, possibly a trained facilitator
- *Space*: Safe, private space for conversations
- *Materials*: Creative Interventions Toolkit (free online), facilitator guides
- *Skills*: Deep listening, conflict facilitation, understanding of trauma and power
- *Energy Level*: High — emotional intensity; shared among multiple people

## What It Is

Informal community gatherings where people of all ages, beliefs, and backgrounds meet to discuss death, dying, and mortality over tea, coffee, and cake. Death Cafés are agenda-free, non-religious, and focus on increasing awareness of death to help people make the most of their finite lives.

## How It Works

A facilitator gathers a small group (typically 5-20 people) in a comfortable setting with refreshments. The facilitator creates a safe, non-judgmental space for open conversation about death, dying, end-of-life wishes, grief, funeral planning, and what gives life meaning. Discussions are guided by the facilitator but follow the group's natural curiosity and concerns. There is no agenda, advertising, set conclusions, therapy, or counseling—just honest conversation. The environment emphasizes relaxation, community, and shared reflection on a topic most people avoid discussing.

## Who 'S Done It

Over 23,000 Death Cafés held in 97 countries. Started in Switzerland by Bernard Crettaz (2004) and brought to the UK by Jon Underwood (2011). Now held regularly in communities across North America, Europe, Asia, and beyond. Hospitals, hospices, libraries, churches, and community centers host them.

## Connections

Rooted in Swiss and European traditions of death discussion (café mortel). Aligned with death positivity and end-of-life care movements; connected to grief work, narrative medicine, and community healing practices. Related to storytelling circles and talking circles.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: 2-3 hours for a session; minimum 1 month for planning and outreach
- *People*: 1 trained facilitator; 5-20 participants
- *Space*: Comfortable, quiet setting: coffee shop, library, church, community center, or private home
- *Materials*: Tea, coffee, cake or light refreshments; comfortable seating; optional: printed discussion prompts or reflection materials
- *Skills*: Facilitation, active listening, creating psychological safety, comfort with silence and emotion
- *Energy Level*: Low to medium—contemplative but emotionally engaged

## What It Is

A structured conversation practice designed to shift people's beliefs through long, empathic one-on-one conversations. Developed by LGBTQ+ organizers to win ballot campaigns, Deep Canvassing uses storytelling, active listening, and compassionate curiosity to help people reconsider their positions on social issues.

## How It Works

A canvasser initiates a conversation by introducing themselves and asking the person being canvassed to rate their support for an issue on a scale of 1-10. Rather than delivering a pitch, the canvasser practices open-ended questioning and active listening, inviting the other person to share their perspective, experiences, and concerns. The canvasser shares their own relevant personal story and listens deeply to understand the other person's values and motivations. The conversation is unhurried and genuine, focusing on building human connection rather than winning an argument. The canvasser leaves space for the person to reach their own conclusions, following up later to reinforce any shifts in thinking. Deep Canvassing emphasizes assertiveness balanced with empathy and is specifically designed to move people across ideological divides.

## Who 'S Done It

Developed by LGBTQ+ rights organizers (LGSM—Lesbians and Gays Support the Miners); scaled and researched by People's Action; used by progressive campaigns on immigration, animal rights, racial justice, and housing. David Broockman and Josh Kalla have conducted rigorous research documenting its effectiveness.

## Connections

Emerged from grassroots LGBTQ+ and labor movements; connected to relational organizing, listening practices, and narrative work. Related to street-level persuasion, one-on-one organizing, and public narrative frameworks. Part of broader tradition of movement-based voter and community engagement.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: 8-15 minutes per conversation; 20-40 conversations per canvasser per week; training: 2-4 hours
- *People*: Trained canvassers (ideally from or close to affected communities); target audience (voters, community members, or decision-makers)
- *Space*: Doorstep conversations, phone calls, video calls, or public spaces; no dedicated space needed
- *Materials*: Conversation script (flexible framework, not rigid); personal stories/narratives; tracking sheet for noting support shifts; optional: follow-up contact information
- *Skills*: Active listening, storytelling, emotional intelligence, comfort with discomfort, assertive communication, patience
- *Energy Level*: High—emotionally and intellectually demanding

## What It Is

A foundational framework articulating 10 core principles of disability justice as developed by the disability justice movement, exemplified through the work of Sins Invalid (a disability justice performance project). The principles guide collective organizing, community care, and justice work centered on disabled people's leadership and self-determination.

items.body:
City Bureau, founded on Chicago's South Side in 2015, built the Documenters program around a simple exchange: train residents in note-taking and public-meeting procedure, then **pay them** to attend and document the school board, the zoning committee, the park district — the meetings where neighborhood decisions actually happen and no reporter sits anymore. The notes are published; the meetings enter the public record in practice, not just in law.

The model spread into a national Documenters Network across dozens of cities, and its technical substrate is open source: the City Scrapers project standardizes public-meeting schedules from dozens of fragmented government sites into one usable feed.

For this shelf it's the strongest working answer to a question every neighborhood has: who is watching the decisions that shape our block? The answer that works is not an app — it's paid, trained neighbors with a shared standard, plus scrapers so finding the meeting isn't the hard part. (It also models the 'pay local stewards' survivor pattern from the graveyard framework.)

**Neighborhood remix:** one block's documenter — a rotating, honoraria-paid neighbor who attends the community board meeting and posts plain-language notes where the block actually reads.

## What It Is

A digital platform and community hub empowering young people (ages 13-25) to become civic leaders and activists. With over 1 million active members globally, DoSomething.org provides youth with tools, campaigns, and peer community to take action on issues they care about.

## How It Works

Young people engage through multiple pathways: (1) Browse and select causes—climate action, mental health, book banning, food insecurity, and many others. (2) Participate in specific campaigns with concrete action steps—organizing street cleanups, collecting period products for unhoused individuals, creating educational PSAs. (3) Earn volunteer credits toward scholarships and recognition. (4) Connect with other changemakers across the U.S. and 189 countries. The platform emphasizes accessibility and achievable action, breaking down large issues into doable campaigns. Youth develop leadership skills through participation, build peer networks around shared causes, and experience tangible impact from collective action.

## Who 'S Done It

DoSomething.org has mobilized over 8 million young people across U.S. area codes and internationally. Campaigns demonstrate diverse youth leadership—from environmental activism to social justice organizing. Young people report building confidence, developing skills, and finding 'their people' around shared values. The platform has created measurable social impact through coordinated youth campaigns addressing systemic issues.

## What It Is

Community spaces and networks where people give and receive goods for free, operating on gift economy principles to combat waste, build community connections, and meet material needs without payment. Free Stores provide physical gathering spaces while Freecycling networks coordinate exchanges online and locally.

## How It Works

Free Stores operate as permanent or pop-up physical locations (storefronts, market stalls, warehouses, or street corners) where community members drop off unwanted items and pick up new-to-them goods at no cost. Freecycle networks function through online forums or apps where members post items they want to give away or request, then arrange local pickup. Both models prioritize reuse and keeping goods out of landfills. Free Stores often become informal community hubs where neighbors meet and build relationships while accessing needed items. No purchase, trade, or bartering required—the fundamental ethic is generosity and collective care.

## Who 'S Done It

Freecycle Network (global, 5+ million members); Free Store Project (New York City, founded by Myles Smutney, 2020); Really Really Free Markets (distributed across North America); Buy Nothing groups; numerous independent Free Stores in cities across the U.S. and Canada.

## Connections

Part of broader gift economy and sharing economy movements; connected to Buy Nothing groups, mutual aid networks, and community sharing practices. Rooted in anti-consumerism and environmental sustainability activism. Related to repair cafés and tool libraries as alternative resource access models.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: Ongoing (daily for Free Stores; weekly to monthly for Freecycling groups)
- *People*: 4-10 core organizers/volunteers; 20+ regular participants; wider community for drop-offs/pickups
- *Space*: Physical storefront, warehouse, shipping container, market booth, or street-level space for Free Stores; digital platform (email, Facebook, Freecycle app) for Freecycling networks
- *Materials*: Shelving, display tables, storage system; internet connection and digital platform for online networks; optional: signage, maps, logistics tracking
- *Skills*: Community coordination, basic logistics, marketing/outreach, conflict resolution, systems thinking
- *Energy Level*: Medium—requires consistent volunteer coordination and light physical work

## What It Is

A civility-focused digital neighborhood forum where neighbors post about local news, recommendations, concerns, and connections. Unlike algorithmically-driven platforms, Front Porch Forum uses real address verification, real names, human moderation, and daily email digests instead of infinite scrolls. It's designed to get people offline and into real relationships.

## How It Works

Enter your actual address — the platform verifies you live there. Create a real-name account. Post about anything neighbors discuss: lost pets, recommendations, street concerns, block parties, safety issues, buy/sell/give items. Posts arrive in daily or weekly digests rather than a notification stream. This is a radical design choice: you read once a day in a purposeful way. Moderators ensure posts stay respectful and on-topic. Conversations that start online often move offline: neighbors meet for coffee, help each other, organize collectively. The platform exists to strengthen actual community, not substitute for it.

## Who 'S Done It

Front Porch Forum began in Vermont and now serves 235,000 active members among Vermont's 270,000 households. Members post about everything from mechanic recommendations to wildlife sightings to organizing around local issues. The platform's success shows what's possible when digital tools are designed for place and relationship rather than engagement metrics. It creates something increasingly rare: a trusted, civil, genuinely local online space.

## Connections

Grows from the insight that the internet went wrong when it became global and algorithmic instead of local and human-moderated. Part of a growing 'local first' internet movement. Connects to resilience hubs and microgrant gatherings by providing digital infrastructure for local organizing. Pairs well with Public Narrative and block steward work.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: 5-10 minutes daily to check posts
- *People*: Neighborhood with 100+ households, volunteer moderators
- *Space*: Digital
- *Materials*: Internet access, email account
- *Skills*: Basic digital literacy, moderation skills
- *Energy Level*: Low for users; moderate for moderators

## What It Is

A non-binding written agreement developed collaboratively between a neighborhood and a business or institution, designed to address specific concerns through mutual understanding and compromise. Good Neighbor Agreements formalize what neighbors and businesses want from each other and create ongoing channels for communication.

## How It Works

Start with a neighborhood organization with legitimacy in the area. Organize listening sessions to understand what residents care about — not vague complaints but specifics (noise hours, parking, waste, local employment). Document everything. Then convene a negotiation meeting with neighborhood reps and business leadership. Each side explains perspective, constraints, and goals. The agreement addresses specifics: operating hours, noise management, local hiring, waste disposal, process for problems, regular check-in meetings. It's explicitly non-binding — not a legal contract but a good-faith understanding. Both parties sign. Schedule regular check-ins (quarterly or annual) to discuss how it's working and adjust. Examples from CHUN Denver include agreements with restaurants, dispensaries, and shelters.

## Who 'S Done It

CHUN (Capitol Hill United Neighborhoods) in Denver has facilitated Good Neighbor Agreements since 2010. Park Tavern, a bar in a residential neighborhood, was generating late-night noise concerns. Instead of hostility, they proposed a Good Neighbor Agreement. The negotiation resulted in: 11pm noise cutoff on weeknights, designated parking areas, a resident contact person, quarterly check-ins. The bar also hired from the neighborhood and created a community advisory group. Several years later, when a new building added residents nearby, the bar proactively suggested updating the agreement.

## Connections

Rooted in community organizing and environmental justice traditions, particularly around managing conflicts between different land uses. They connect to community benefit agreements, participatory planning, and conflict resolution. They're a formalization of the principle that neighbors have stake in how businesses operate in their community. They complement neighborhood mapping and mutual aid by institutionalizing ongoing relationship.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: 3-6 months of negotiation, ongoing annual check-ins
- *People*: 3-5 community organizers, neighborhood residents, business leadership
- *Space*: Neutral meeting space
- *Materials*: Template agreement, notes from listening sessions, written documentation
- *Skills*: Negotiation, listening to multiple perspectives, willingness to compromise
- *Energy Level*: Moderate — emotionally demanding to hold both perspectives

## What It Is

A political strategy and framework for building community-led, survivor-centered responses to collective trauma and systemic oppression. Healing Justice centers healing as a tool for liberation and social transformation, integrating traditional healing practices with social justice organizing to address generational trauma and build collective resilience.

## How It Works

Healing Justice operates on the principle that healing is political and collective, not just individual. The framework brings together healers (spiritual practitioners, wellness workers, artists, therapists), organizers, and community members to: map existing healing resources and traditions in communities; create healing spaces in movement work and at times of collective crisis; facilitate spaces for people to process trauma together; develop healing practices rooted in southern (and other) traditions of resilience; and integrate healing into organizing strategy and decision-making. Kindred Southern Healing Justice Collective, for example, has organized healing justice spaces at movement-building events and in response to collective crises, mapping healers and practitioners throughout the Southeast and creating networks of healing support. The work honors the fact that organizers and activists experience trauma, burnout, and secondary trauma, and that sustainable movements must center healing alongside organizing. Healing Justice rejects the idea of healing as consumer commodity and centers community accountability, cultural wisdom, and collective transformation.

## Who 'S Done It

Kindred Southern Healing Justice Collective (founded 2005-2006, based in Atlanta); Black Rose Anarchist Federation; healing circles in racial justice movements; various local organizations adopting healing justice frameworks; practitioners throughout the Southeast and beyond building healing justice networks.

## Connections

Rooted in Black radical traditions, healing practices from African diaspora, and southern resilience traditions. Connected to disability justice, transformative justice, and community healing practices. Part of broader convergence of healing and justice work. Related to somatic practices, community therapy, and collective care.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: Ongoing; healing circles: 2-4 hours; immersive trainings: 1-3 days; integration into organizing: ongoing
- *People*: Healers (spiritual/alternative practitioners, bodyworkers, artists, therapists from communities); organizers; community members and people with lived experience of trauma
- *Space*: Community gathering spaces, healing centers, outdoor spaces; creates intentional, sacred containers
- *Materials*: Art supplies, music/sound, plants/herbs, healing ritual materials, documentation/mapping tools
- *Skills*: Healing facilitation, somatic awareness, cultural competency, trauma awareness, organizing, community knowledge
- *Energy Level*: Medium to high—emotionally and spiritually engaged, requires care and rest

## What It Is

A secular gathering modeled on faith-based services, designed to strengthen civic participation and community connection through shared ritual, meaningful texts, and collective reflection on what it means to be a citizen together.

## How It Works

Plan a gathering for 50-200 people in a welcoming venue. Create a flowing agenda: opening poems or quotes to set intention, communal singing (protest songs or hymns reimagined for civic purpose), a 'civic sermon' — a 20-30 minute keynote on a civic theme like citizenship, democracy, or community. Include readings of meaningful civic texts: passages from the Constitution, civil rights speeches, poetry about community, or statements from local community members. Build in moments of silence for reflection. Close with a recommitment ritual where people share what they're committing to civically. Create an atmosphere that feels celebratory and sacred: good sound, thoughtful lighting, flowers, refreshments afterward. The ritual structure intentionally creates space to ask: 'What are your civic values? How do we form a cohesive fabric together?'

## Who 'S Done It

Citizen University, founded by Eric Liu, has hosted Civic Saturdays across multiple cities. In one southern city, the event focused on 'what it means to be a neighbor' and drew 120 people. A young Black woman from a housing advocacy nonprofit gave the civic sermon. Attendees reported not having had space like that in their adult lives — a place that treated civic participation as sacred. Several participants formed study groups afterward. Another city used Civic Saturday as a platform for emerging leaders, breaking down isolation by creating space to think about politics as shared work, not partisan disagreement.

## Connections

Civic Saturday is rooted in congregational traditions, public ritual, and the civic renewal movement. It assumes secular community needs ritual spaces just like faith communities do. It connects to World Café and story suppers as practices for collective thinking, and to the work of Sunday Assembly (secular congregation). The Civic Saturday Fellowship trains people across the country to host their own.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: 2-3 months planning, 2-3 hours for the event
- *People*: 2-4 core organizers, 30-200+ attendees
- *Space*: Community center, church, auditorium, outdoor venue with good acoustics
- *Materials*: Microphone/sound system, flowers, printed programs, refreshments
- *Skills*: Facilitation, curating meaningful speakers and texts, comfort with ritual design
- *Energy Level*: Moderate — logistics are straightforward but emotional curation takes thought

## What It Is

Shareable's comprehensive guide to organizing successful skillshare events where community members teach and learn practical skills from each other. Skillshares are non-commercial, skill-centered gatherings that democratize knowledge and build community.

## How It Works

Begin by creating a shared spreadsheet to coordinate logistics, budget, contacts, and publicity with other organizers. Select a venue with adequate classroom spaces, capacity, water access, and available furniture. Consider space constraints to determine how many classes you can offer. Build an online presence through a simple website, Facebook page, or social media using free tools like WordPress. Create an event identity through a logo and consistent branding. Develop fundraising strategies including benefit concerts, business donations, Kickstarter campaigns, or grant applications to cover overhead, food, and supplies. Promote widely through Eventbrite, local papers, blogs, listservs, Meetup.com, and all social media platforms. Recruit teachers and volunteers from your network and publicly advertise skill areas being sought.

## Who 'S Done It

Skillshares have been organized in communities worldwide as low-cost alternatives to formal education and skill-building. The model has been adapted for diverse communities, from urban neighborhoods to rural areas, demonstrating flexibility and accessibility.

## Connections

Skillshares build on traditions of collective learning, apprenticeship, and knowledge-sharing in communities. They align with the sharing economy, alternative education movements, and commons-based organizing.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: 8-12 weeks planning; 1-2 days execution
- *People*: Core organizing team; community teachers/volunteers; participants
- *Space*: Community center, school, library, or flexible venue with multiple classroom areas

## What It Is

Shareable's guide transforming potlucks from casual social meals into intentional community organizing tools. By adding structure, facilitation, and shared purpose, potlucks become vehicles for collective decision-making, relationship-building, and community action.

## How It Works

Reimagine the potluck as a structured gathering rather than an informal meal. Add facilitation elements such as opening circles for relationship-building, structured conversation prompts or discussion topics relevant to community concerns, group decision-making processes around a shared issue or project, or skill-sharing components. Use the shared meal as a foundation for deeper engagement, moving beyond casual socializing to intentional community-building work. Consider online coordination tools like Potluck, Perfect Potluck, or Meal Train to manage RSVPs, assign dishes, track dietary needs, and share photos/stories from the gathering. Build community through the act of collective contribution and the ritual of breaking bread together.

## Who 'S Done It

Community organizers have used potlucks as organizing tools for decades. Contemporary examples include using potlucks to launch neighborhood organizing campaigns, coordinate mutual aid efforts, build cross-cultural understanding, and strengthen community bonds around shared challenges or values.

## Connections

Potlucks connect to long traditions of communal meals across cultures. This guide reimagines the potluck through an organizing lens, building on traditions while adding intentionality and structure. It relates to community organizing, collective decision-making, and food-based placemaking.

## Key Ingredients

## What It Is

Structured improv activities designed around spontaneous, scriptless role-playing and collaborative scene-building. Used in community settings to break down social barriers, build psychological safety, strengthen trust, and deepen interpersonal connections through shared laughter and creative collaboration.

## How It Works

Improv games operate under specific principles that create safety and connection: (1) 'There are no mistakes' removes fear of failure and judgment. (2) 'Yes, and...' principle teaches collaborative idea-building where participants build on each other's contributions. (3) Emphasis on play over performance creates space for risk-taking. Games typically involve small groups acting out scenarios spontaneously, responding to prompts, and building narratives together. Facilitators emphasize that the goal is engagement and joy rather than entertainment quality. Participants practice creative thinking, quick responses, and mutual support of ideas. The shared laughter and vulnerability generated during games creates positive emotional memories that strengthen group bonds and build psychological safety.

## Who 'S Done It

Improv games have been widely adopted in team-building, classroom settings, organizational culture change, and community organizing. Participants report experiencing breakthrough moments of connection and reduced initial awkwardness. Organizations use improv to combat workplace burnout, build team happiness, and humanize professional settings. Community groups use improv games to help new members feel welcome and to strengthen group cohesion across diverse participants.

## Connections

Originates from acting and comedy training traditions. Relates to New Games Movement philosophy emphasizing cooperation and joy. Connects to broader practices using play for team-building, conflict resolution, and community bonding. Used in education, organizational development, and social justice organizing.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: Sessions: 30-90 minutes; can be ongoing activity
- *People*: 5-50+ participants; works across various group sizes
- *Space*: Open space allowing movement; could be classroom, meeting room, outdoor space
- *Materials*: Minimal—optional: music, prompt cards, simple props
- *Skills*: Facilitation, comfort with spontaneity and vulnerability, ability to create psychological safety
- *Energy Level*: Medium-to-high; requires active participation and creative engagement

## What It Is

A community-led placemaking practice that transforms urban street intersections into vibrant public squares through collaborative design, artistic expression, and infrastructure building. Intersection repairs combine public art (murals), seating and gathering spaces, tool libraries, little free libraries, and community message boards to reclaim streets as community spaces.

## How It Works

Identify an intersection in need of community activation and gather interested neighbors. Form a design team to envision the transformation, creating sketches and proposals that reflect community input. Seek city permits if required, or work with City Repair's legal toolkit if pursuing permitted community art. Organize a work party or 'barn raising' where volunteers contribute labor. Tasks include designing and painting a large central mural, building a kiosk or tea station, installing a tiny library box, creating seating areas, and developing community message boards. The design should reflect the neighborhood's character and values while serving practical community functions. After completion, identify stewards for ongoing maintenance. City Repair's Village Building Convergence provides annual opportunities for intensive intersection repairs, training, and connection with other practitioners.

## Who 'S Done It

City Repair Project, a Portland-based 501(c)(3) founded in 1996, pioneered intersection repair methodology. Their flagship project, Share-It Square at SE 9th and SE Sherrett in Portland, transformed a dangerous intersection into a beloved community gathering space. Since then, hundreds of community-led intersections repairs have occurred in Portland and other cities. The annual Village Building Convergence brings together thousands of volunteers across 50+ sites to conduct natural building, permaculture design, and intersection repairs simultaneously.

## Connections

Intersection repair draws from radical urban planning, participatory design, street art traditions, and indigenous place-making. It connects to broader placemaking movement, DIY urbanism, and right-to-the-city activism. It shares DNA with community art projects, tactical urbanism, and movements reclaiming public space for community use.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: 2-4 weeks for planning; 1-3 days for construction/painting
- *People*: 5-50+ volunteers; core team of 3-5 organizers and designers
- *Space*: Street intersection; adjacent space for materials and tool storage
- *Materials*: Paint and brushes, wood for structures, tools, plants, mulch, optional bricks/pavers, signage materials
- *Skills*: Artistic design, community organizing, basic construction, painting, negotiation with city
- *Energy Level*: High; requires sustained physical labor and creative energy

## What It Is

A global grassroots movement of free, citizen-led walking conversations that celebrate public spaces and neighborhood stories inspired by urbanist Jane Jacobs. Walking groups gather annually (especially around May 4th, Jacobs' birthday) to explore neighborhoods, uncover hidden histories, and build civic dialogue through movement and conversation.

## How It Works

Anyone can organize a Jane's Walk—no formal training required. Organizers plan a walking route through their neighborhood and invite others to join. Walks are not led by experts but by passionate residents who share stories about their communities: local history, culture, challenges, and visions. Walks typically last 1-2 hours, are completely free, and welcome all ages and mobility levels (with options for different paces). No pre-registration required.

## Who 'S Done It

Since 2006 in Toronto, Jane's Walks now occur in over 500 cities globally across North America, Europe, Asia, Africa, and beyond. Walks happen in major cities (New York, London, Vancouver) and small towns, organized by neighborhood residents, community organizations, and cultural institutions.

## Connections

Inspired by Jane Jacobs' 1961 book 'The Death and Life of Great American Cities' which championed community-based city building and the importance of street-level public life. Connects to placemaking, community storytelling, public narrative, and neighborhood-based civic engagement. Related to porch conversations and walking groups as neighboring practices.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: 2-3 hours per walk; 6+ weeks planning for organizers
- *People*: Walk organizer/leader, diverse neighbors, volunteers to help promote
- *Space*: Neighborhood streets, public spaces, parks—any walkable community area
- *Materials*: Maps, walking route cards, signage, optional printed histories or stories
- *Skills*: Community knowledge, storytelling ability, basic route planning, enthusiasm

## What It Is

A small accessible structure stocked by community members and placed in a public location where anyone can take or leave food and supplies without paperwork, judgment, or eligibility requirements. It runs on a gift economy: people give what they can and take what they need.

## How It Works

Secure permission from the property owner and research local zoning. Choose a high-traffic, visible location with safe access at all hours. Build or repurpose your structure — wood cabinet, old bookcase, or purchased kit — weatherproof it. Stock regularly with nonperishable foods (cans, pasta, rice, beans), hygiene products (menstrual products, soap, toothpaste), and household items. If using a fridge, include perishables. Build community awareness through door-to-door conversations and social media. Maintain weekly by removing damaged items. The pantry runs on a gift economy: people give what they can and take what they need.

## Who 'S Done It

Jessica McClard of Fayetteville, Arkansas noticed Little Free Libraries popping up and had an idea: what if we did the same for food? In May 2016, with a $250 microloan, she installed the first Little Free Pantry on her church grounds. Today, thousands exist across North America. The movement proved especially vital during COVID-19 and demonstrated that neighbors are eager to care for one another when given simple, dignified structures to do so.

## Connections

Builds on the Little Free Library movement and emerges from gift economy principles, mutual aid traditions, and food security work. Connects to food justice, food sovereignty, and direct mutual aid as alternative to institutional charity. Reflects participatory economics, commons stewardship, and the understanding that dignity matters — people access food without applications or shame.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: 2-3 weeks setup, 1-2 hours weekly maintenance
- *People*: 1-2 organizers, 5-10 community volunteers for stocking
- *Space*: Public or semi-public location with high foot traffic
- *Materials*: Pantry/fridge structure, weatherproofing, shelving, food and supplies
- *Skills*: Basic construction or repurposing, community organizing
- *Energy Level*: Low-to-medium

## What It Is

A collection of 150+ carefully designed conversation guides covering topics from healthcare to belonging to money to family to criminal justice. Each guide is structured for 4-7 people to have a 90-minute dialogue that fosters genuine listening and understanding across differences, specifically designed so anyone can facilitate without expert training.

## How It Works

Participants gather in person or online and follow the guide structure: (1) conversation agreements (confidentiality, respectful listening, staying curious); (2) round 1: personal questions that reveal values and lived experience; (3) round 2: exploration of the specific topic with questions designed to go deeper than surface debate; (4) round 3: finding common ground and exploring possibilities; (5) closing reflection. The pacing is intentionally slow—people listen significantly more than they speak. Guides are designed so facilitators don't need expertise, just willingness to follow the structure and hold space.

## Who 'S Done It

Living Room Conversations have been held in thousands of homes, libraries, and community spaces across the US and internationally. One example: faith communities in rural/urban divides have used the 'Faith' guide to have genuine conversations about religious practice and politics, discovering shared values about community care that transcend surface differences.

## Connections

## What It Is

A disaster preparedness program that strengthens community resilience by having neighbors systematically get to know each other and plan together for emergencies. Mapping reveals who has critical skills (medical, first aid), resources (tools, generator), and vulnerabilities (elderly living alone, disabled neighbor needing assistance).

## How It Works

Contact your local fire department or emergency management agency about their neighborhood mapping program. Organize a 2.5-hour community meeting with 15-20 neighbors on your block. Walk through: what emergencies could affect your area, what each household can provide (food, water, medical skills, tools), and what each household needs. Create a simple map. Identify where your water main is. Learn basic first aid together. Designate meeting places if phones don't work. Coordinate who has emergency supplies. Create a simple contact list and share it. The philosophy: learning to quickly and safely take actions that minimize damage means knowing your neighbors now, before crisis hits.

## Who 'S Done It

San Francisco's NERT program has trained thousands of neighbors since the 1990s. A Marina District neighborhood did the mapping work in summer 2018. When an earthquake hit in 2022, neighbors responded immediately: they knew Mr. Chen used a walker and needed assistance, the Garcia family had medical training, and two homes had generators and water. The group quickly coordinated to check on vulnerable neighbors, treat injuries, and share supplies while waiting for responders. Afterward, they said the disaster-preparedness work had also created lasting friendship and cohesion separate from the emergency.

## Connections

Neighborhood mapping connects to broader disaster preparedness and community resilience work. It's rooted in community organizing traditions that recognize neighbors as a resource. It complements mutual aid networks, block parties, and good neighbor agreements — all practices that make neighborhood-level collective action normal. In California, the Neighbor-to-Neighbor program invested $10M statewide in this approach, finding that knowing six neighbors dramatically increases disaster readiness.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: 2-3 hours per session, plus informal mapping over months
- *People*: 15-20 households per project, 1-3 core organizers
- *Space*: Community center, library, church, park
- *Materials*: Simple forms or maps, contact list template, flip charts
- *Skills*: Basic facilitation, comfort talking about vulnerability
- *Energy Level*: Moderate — mostly listening and organizing information

## What It Is

A coordinated system where community members take turns delivering home-cooked or purchased meals to someone experiencing a major life event or crisis. Meal Trains reduce stress for people going through challenging periods (new baby, surgery, loss, illness) by ensuring they have nutritious food without having to cook or shop.

## How It Works

One person organizes the Meal Train by setting up a calendar or online platform (Meal Train, Give InKind, Take Them A Meal, or MealRally) with available time slots and any dietary preferences. Community members sign up for specific dates and meal times. Participants prepare a meal at home or purchase prepared food and deliver it to the recipient's home on their assigned date. The calendar prevents duplicate meals and ensures consistent coverage over the planned period (typically 2-8 weeks). Modern platforms allow people to coordinate not just meals but also childcare, pet care, errands, and financial support through gift cards. The practice operates on the principle of collective mutual aid—the community surrounds the person in need with practical care.

## Who 'S Done It

Widely used in churches, religious communities, neighborhoods, and workplaces across North America. Popularized by platforms like Meal Train, Give InKind, Lotsa Helping Hands, Take Them A Meal, and MealRally. Common after births, deaths, hospitalizations, and major illnesses.

## Connections

Rooted in religious and faith-based traditions of community care and congregational support. Connected to broader mutual aid practices, meal-sharing, and collective care systems. Related to community meals, potlucks, and care webs. Part of informal neighborhood interdependence.

## Key Ingredients

## What It Is

A structured deep listening circle program where men gather regularly to speak and listen truthfully with vulnerability and integrity. Guided by trained facilitators, these councils create safe space for men to share challenges, build mutual understanding, and support one another without judgment or attempts to fix.

## How It Works

Men's Council typically meets monthly or bi-weekly in groups of 8-12. Facilitators open with grounding practices—often breathing exercises or centering moments. The council uses council protocols: participants sit in circle; a talking piece or clear turn-taking ensures everyone speaks without interruption; listeners practice deep listening without planning responses, fixing problems, or offering unsolicited advice. Topics emerge naturally from participants' lives—relationships, fatherhood, grief, purpose, masculinity, challenges—rather than following agendas. Facilitators establish ground rules emphasizing confidentiality, respect, and non-judgment. Sessions typically last 90 minutes to 2 hours. The consistency of regular meeting creates trust that deepens over months. Journeymen provides training for facilitators in the council process, shadow practices for new leaders, and support for establishing groups.

## Who 'S Done It

Journeymen is a 501(c)(3) based on Vashon Island, Washington, founded on principles of mentorship and social-emotional learning. Their Men's Council program has facilitated groups across the Pacific Northwest and beyond. Participants report experiencing safer emotional expression, deeper connection with themselves and others, and healthier ways of expressing emotions. The organization has adapted council work for boys (Boys Council) and school settings (CIRCLES program).

## Connections

Men's Council draws from Indigenous circle traditions, contemporary peacebuilding practices, and men's movement work. It connects to Circle practices used in Art of Hosting and restorative justice circles. The deep listening protocol reflects dialogue traditions and therapeutic group work. It represents a application of ancient council practices to contemporary men's social-emotional development.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: 90 minutes to 2 hours per session; monthly or bi-weekly recurring
- *People*: 8-12 men per circle; trained facilitator essential
- *Space*: Comfortable room where people can sit in circle; adequate privacy and minimal distractions
- *Materials*: Talking piece (optional), ground rules poster, refreshments, comfortable seating

## What It Is

A simple funding mechanism that gives neighbors $50-100 to host their own community gatherings, removing the barrier of cost and democratizing who can convene people. Paired with organizing support — checklists, facilitation guides — it trusts that neighbors know what their communities need.

## How It Works

The process is intentionally frictionless. Interested hosts complete a 3-5 minute application describing their gathering and its connection to neighborhood life. Applications are reviewed and approved within one business day. The host receives their $50-100 grant plus an organizing toolkit with facilitation checklists, sample agendas, communication templates. They host their gathering — block party, potluck, seasonal celebration, community conversation. After the event, the only requirement is a photo and brief notes on what happened and any commitments that emerged. No receipts needed, no complex reporting. The whole cycle emphasizes simplicity and trust.

## Who 'S Done It

In Connective Tissue's Charlottesville pilot in spring 2023, they received 70 applications and distributed $100 microgrants to 30 hosts, reaching nearly 500 neighbors across 25 neighborhoods in a few weeks. Almost every attendee committed to concrete next steps afterward — some started recurring monthly gatherings, others organized neighborhood improvements, many deepened relationships with people they'd never met. One host noted the barrier wasn't desire or ideas — it was the psychological lift of asking 'Can I do this?' The $100 answered that question.

## Connections

Builds on ABCD wisdom that people closest to a problem are closest to the solution. Connected to participatory budgeting and subsidiarity — decisions and resources flowing to the most local level. Connective Tissue is part of a movement recognizing that civic infrastructure has eroded and small, repeatable gestures rebuild it. Pairs with Front Porch Forum for amplification and Public Narrative for articulation.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: 3-5 min to apply, 2-4 hours to host, 10 min to document
- *People*: 1 host + 8-15 neighbors; coordinating team for applications
- *Space*: Any welcoming neighborhood space (porch, backyard, park, community room)
- *Materials*: Basic supplies for the gathering type
- *Skills*: Basic facilitation, ability to reach neighbors
- *Energy Level*: Moderate

## What It Is

A networked cooperative model that combines timebanking, cooperative lending, and community currencies to create location-specific solidarity economies. Originally developed in Madison, Wisconsin, MANs pool community capacity and reward socially and environmentally useful work through democratic participation and exchange systems.

## How It Works

Members earn and spend 'MAN hours' by helping one another—every hour of help provides one hour of credit usable throughout the network. The system integrates timebanking as the primary exchange mechanism while also facilitating cooperative lending, community savings pools, and shared manufacturing or community spaces. Participants access leadership training and participate in democratic decision-making about resource allocation and community priorities. The Madison MAN Cooperative serves as the home base and founding member of HUMANs (Humans United in Mutual Aid Networks), a global cooperative network designed for mutual learning and support.

## Who 'S Done It

Madison Mutual Aid Network in Madison, Wisconsin (founded by Stephanie Rearick); Dane County Time Bank (2,800 members); HUMANs global network; communities adopting the model across North America and internationally.

## Connections

Evolved from 20 years of local economic development work in Wisconsin, building on Madison HOURS currency (1990s) and expanding from the Dane County Time Bank model. Connected to broader timebanking movement, cooperative economics, and community currency initiatives. Part of emerging networked cooperativism and solidarity economy frameworks.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: Ongoing weekly/monthly participation; initial training 2-4 hours
- *People*: 15-50+ active participants per fledgling network; diverse skill sets and backgrounds
- *Space*: Community hub for coordination, meetings, and resource sharing (cooperative workspace, community center, or rotating locations)
- *Materials*: Digital or paper-based time ledger system; currency or credit tracking system; communication platform (email, app, or forum)
- *Skills*: Facilitation, cooperative governance, conflict resolution, basic accounting, communication
- *Energy Level*: Medium to high—requires consistent participation and democratic engagement

## What It Is

A small network of neighbors or friends (typically 5-20 people) who pool resources, skills, and time to meet each other's basic needs directly, without relying on nonprofit or government systems. Mutual aid flips the script: instead of charity given to needy people, it's reciprocal support among equals.

## How It Works

Start with 3-5 trustworthy people committed to showing up for each other. Build relationships first. Create a 'pod map' — visualize existing connections by writing down people you trust who you can support in basic needs: food, transportation, emotional support, childcare. This reveals your actual network before you expand. Then brainstorm what your specific community actually needs. Begin locally and small — within your building, block, or friend group. Start with one commitment: a meal chain during hardship, a tool library, a babysitting exchange, a ride-sharing arrangement. Prioritize shared decision-making over top-down authority. Keep it reciprocal — everyone gives and receives. The goal isn't to solve poverty but to be honest that everyone needs help sometimes.

## Who 'S Done It

A Brooklyn mutual aid pod during 2020 started with 10 people organized through Instagram. They identified that seniors needed grocery shopping and medication pick-up. They created a simple system: people texted needs, volunteers confirmed pickup, payment was through an honor system. Within months, the pod expanded to 40 people, added a cooking team, coordinated rent support, provided tech help, and connected people to benefits. By 2023, they'd formalized but maintained mutual aid principles. Members emphasized that the magic was that people gave and received — not separated into helpers and helped.

## Connections

Mutual aid has deep roots in working-class, immigrant, and Black radical organizing traditions. It's distinct from charity. Dean Spade's book 'Mutual Aid' is the modern foundational text. The practice connects to cooperative economics, popular education, and community resistance traditions. It complements microsolidarity crews, neighborhood mapping, block parties, and story suppers — all practices that build relationships as foundation for collective action.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: 2-4 hours monthly for coordination, plus volunteer time
- *People*: 5-20 core members, growing organically
- *Space*: Minimal — mostly digital communication, occasional in-person meetings
- *Materials*: Simple communication system (group chat, spreadsheet, shared calendar)
- *Skills*: Coordination, comfort with vulnerability and asking for help
- *Energy Level*: Moderate to high — depends on scope of needs

## What It Is

Formal civic structures where residents organize to advocate for neighborhood interests, improve local conditions, and participate in municipal governance. Neighborhood associations range from grassroots nonprofit organizations to formally-recognized governmental bodies, providing structured infrastructure for collective voice and neighborhood-level decision-making.

## How It Works

Residents within defined geographic boundaries organize into neighborhood associations, often with elected officers, regular meetings, and stated mission addressing neighborhood concerns. Associations may engage in advocacy, community beautification, crime prevention, planning participation, or service provision. Some neighborhoods also have formal neighborhood councils—governmental structures recognized by city code that give neighborhoods official voice in municipal decisions. Both models enable residents to collectively address shared concerns, represent neighborhood interests to city government, and build community.

## Who 'S Done It

Most major US cities have neighborhood association systems. Portland, Oregon has formalized neighborhood associations through city code (Chapter 3.96), with recognized districts and officer structures. Los Angeles has neighborhood councils with formal governmental status. Smaller cities and towns have neighborhood associations that function as advocacy groups and community organizers.

## Connections

Emerged in earnest in late 1980s-early 1990s as cities formalized neighborhood governance structures. Connected to participatory democracy, civic participation, decentralized governance, and neighborhood-level organizing. Related to block associations, civic councils, and community organizing traditions.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: Monthly meetings minimum; variable ongoing engagement based on role
- *People*: Resident members, elected officers, committee members, community partners, city liaisons
- *Space*: Regular meeting location (library, school, community center), neighborhood boundaries
- *Materials*: Bylaws, meeting agendas, communication channels, planning documents
- *Skills*: Meeting facilitation, advocacy, community organizing, relationship building
- *Energy Level*: Moderate to high—ongoing meetings, advocacy work, volunteer leadership

items.body:
The News Futures Charter holds that news is an act of care; that civic information should serve the public interest rather than commercial incentives; that the approach must be participatory and reparative; that people excluded from media must shape its future; and that news exists to strengthen civic life.

Ten working principles follow:

1. **News as Care** — information as a public good and a service; design with care and empathy as primary values.
2. **Hierarchy of Information Needs** — survival info first (housing, food, transport, economic opportunity), then connection, then abstract/luxury info.
3. **Information Equity** — fair creation and distribution so a person's identity does not determine their outcomes; design for multilingual, low-income, low-tech access.
4. **Do-ocracy** — decisions made by those doing the work; power to those who show up.
5. **Reparative Journalism** — those excluded from media shape its future; address historical harms of exclusion.
6. **News as Public Infrastructure** — civic information as shared infrastructure like parks or libraries, with community ownership.
7. **Listening First** — start with community listening before producing anything; let residents drive what gets covered.
8. **Collaborative Over Competitive** — share resources and coordinate across outlets rather than compete.
9. **Care for the Caregivers** — sustainability requires caring for the people doing the work; build in rest and anti-burnout practice.
10. **Community Accountability** — media accountable to the communities it serves, with real community power in governance.

## What It Is

A self-organizing conference methodology created by Harrison Owen that replaces pre-planned agendas with participant-driven topics. Groups gather around a compelling central question, and attendees themselves propose and facilitate the sessions they want to participate in, guided by four principles and one law of movement.

## How It Works

To run Open Space, first identify a clear, compelling theme—a question, challenge, or purpose that matters to participants. Gather the group in a large circle and introduce the theme and the four principles: Whoever comes is the right people; Whatever happens is the only thing that could have been; Whenever it starts is the right time; When it's over it's over. Present the Law of Two Feet: if you find yourself not learning or contributing, move to somewhere more productive. Next, open a marketplace where participants post session topics on a board with time and location. Participants then attend sessions of their choosing, free to move between sessions using their two feet. Facilitators are typically responsible for creating a marketplace wall, managing logistics, and ensuring note-taking. Sessions unfold organically with minimal structure. Open Space works particularly well when no single entity has all answers and diverse perspectives are essential to solving the challenge.

## Who 'S Done It

Harrison Owen developed Open Space Technology in response to his observation that the most valuable moments in conferences occurred during coffee breaks. The method has been used globally by organizations ranging from corporate strategy sessions to international development projects. In the UN, the World Health Organization, and across nonprofits and municipalities, groups have applied Open Space to address climate change, education reform, and community resilience. It has been deployed with groups from 5 to 2000+ participants in over 140 countries.

## Connections

Open Space Technology emerged from Owen's reflection on systems theory, dialogue practices, and community organizing traditions. It connects to self-organization principles found in complex adaptive systems theory and to participatory democracy movements. It's frequently used as one component within larger Art of Hosting frameworks.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: 2 hours minimum; typically 4 hours to 3 days
- *People*: 5-2000+ participants; diversity of perspectives crucial
- *Space*: Large gathering space plus multiple breakout rooms; bulletin board for marketplace
- *Materials*: Index cards, markers, large wall/bulletin board, name tags, note-taking materials
- *Skills*: Understanding of self-organization, comfort with uncertainty, ability to let go of control
- *Energy Level*: High; requires active movement and decision-making

items.body:
The core reference behind this shelf: a 50-page guide to community organizing in the Marshall Ganz tradition, originally adapted from the work of Dr. Marshall Ganz of Harvard University and resources from the Leading Change Network and the New Organizing Institute, revised collaboratively by organizers at the Dogwood Initiative, Leadnow, One Cowichan, the David Suzuki Foundation, Stonehouse Institute, and genius (Shea Sinnott and Peter Gibbs, eds., 2014).

It covers the whole arc in teachable form: what organizing is (people, power, change); public narrative (self / us / now, with full worksheets); building relationships (the 1:1, hard asks, the three nos, recruitment and retention); coaching (the five-step process, head/heart/hands); structuring teams (shared purpose, interdependent roles, explicit norms; the snowflake model; the ladder of engagement; team stages); strategizing (people/problem/goal, power-with and power-over, nested goals, theory of change); and acting (the tactics sweet spot, motivational engagement, campaign timelines, the organizing sentence). The appendix worksheets — developing your public narrative, coaching stories, and tracking down the power — are ready to run with any group.

The guide is free to reproduce, distribute, and adapt for your own training (attribution must stay; it may not be sold), which is why its practices could be carried onto this shelf in full. Most recipes on this shelf cite it as their source.
