## What It Is

An approach to community development and engagement that recognizes the impact of trauma on individuals and communities, and intentionally designs practices, policies, and environments to mitigate re-traumatization and support healing. It acknowledges that many communities have experienced systemic and historical trauma and builds resilience and collective power in response.

## How It Works

Trauma-informed community building operates on four foundational principles: Do No Harm (being aware of trauma and avoiding re-traumatization), Acceptance (meeting people where they are), Community Empowerment (centering self-determination and resident leadership), and Reflective Process (continuously learning and adjusting). Practically, this means: building trust and transparency in all community interactions; creating physical and psychological safety; elevating community voices throughout planning and implementation; offering varied ways to participate (accommodating different comfort levels); providing cultural outlets for collective processing (art, movement, music); organizing community-building activities (gardening, exercise, art projects); training local leaders in trauma-informed practices; and building support networks where people can process recurring trauma. The work is collaborative, recognizes the full humanity of people affected by trauma, and understands healing as collective rather than just individual.

## Who 'S Done It

Community development organizations in traumatized neighborhoods (areas affected by violence, poverty, disinvestment); public health departments; housing authorities; grassroots organizations led by people with lived experience of trauma. Practiced particularly in communities recovering from police violence, community violence, historical displacement, and systemic oppression.

## Connections

Rooted in trauma psychology research and adapted for community work by grassroots organizers. Connected to healing justice, restorative justice, transformative justice, and community healing practices. Related to peer support models, mutual aid, and collective care. Influenced by Indigenous healing traditions and African diaspora healing practices.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: Ongoing; planning: 3-6 months; implementation: 1-3+ years or longer
- *People*: Community members with lived experience of trauma; trained facilitators/organizers; mental health practitioners (ideally from the community); diverse leadership that reflects community demographics
- *Space*: Community centers, parks, cultural spaces, homes; multiple accessible gathering spaces; creates welcoming, safe environments
- *Materials*: Art supplies, plants/gardening materials, music/sound equipment, comfortable seating, culturally relevant materials; optional: training curricula, peer support guides
- *Skills*: Trauma awareness, facilitation, cultural competency, listening, flexibility, systems thinking, community knowledge
- *Energy Level*: Medium to high—emotionally and physically demanding but nourishing

## What It Is

A consumer-driven membership model where older adults aging in place create formal or virtual villages—geographically-based communities where neighbors commit to mutual support for aging. Rather than entering senior housing, elders remain in their own homes while accessing a coordinated network of volunteers, services, and social programming.

## How It Works

Members pay annual membership dues ($300-800+) and in exchange receive access to services including volunteer support for light home maintenance and transportation, coordination of social and educational programs, wellness activities, technology coaching, and referrals to professional services. Villages are member-governed with a coordinator managing operations. Members volunteer to support each other, creating reciprocal relationships and mutual aid. Regular social events build community.

## Who 'S Done It

The movement began in Boston's Beacon Hill in 2001 and has grown to over 300 active Villages with many in development across the US. The Village to Village Network founded in 2010 supports village development and shares best practices. Examples include villages in urban neighborhoods, suburbs, and increasingly in rural areas.

## Connections

Emerged as response to aging population and desire to age in community rather than in institutions. Connected to successful aging frameworks, aging in place movements, intergenerational communities, and mutual support models. Related to Circles of Support and broader community care approaches.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: Ongoing annual membership; 1-2 hours per week typical engagement
- *People*: Member elders (typically 55+), volunteer supporters, coordinator/staff, board members
- *Space*: Members' homes primarily; gathering spaces for events and programs
- *Materials*: Volunteer coordination system, program materials, transportation coordination tools
- *Skills*: Community organizing, program coordination, volunteer management, relationship facilitation
- *Energy Level*: Low to moderate—flexible based on individual participation level

## What It Is

Public facilities that provide refuge during extreme weather (warming centers in winter, cooling centers in summer) that are increasingly being reimagined as 'Climate Resilience Hubs'—multifunctional community gathering spaces offering emergency services, social services, education, and community connection alongside climate protection.

## How It Works

Traditional cooling/warming centers provide basic emergency relief—air conditioning or heating for people without adequate climate control. Modern Climate Resilience Hubs expand this model significantly. They operate out of trusted community institutions like libraries, churches, schools, community centers, or nonprofits that are already well-used in the neighborhood. Beyond climate control, hubs offer: emergency supplies and resources; phone charging; welfare checks on vulnerable neighbors; emergency preparedness education; social services (housing, food assistance, mental health support); community connection and programming; and they're retrofitted with solar panels and battery backup so they can operate independently during power outages. Hubs function year-round, with expanded services during extreme weather. They are rooted in community relationships and trust, led by community members, and address the interconnected challenges of climate change, economic vulnerability, and social isolation.

## Who 'S Done It

CREW (Climate Resilience Education and Work) network; Community Resilience Projects in Los Angeles and other cities; cooling centers in Maricopa County, Arizona; numerous city and county heat action initiatives; Community Resilience projects across the U.S.; programs increasingly adopted as climate adaptation strategy by cities and counties.

## Connections

Related to emergency preparedness, public health, climate adaptation, and mutual aid. Connected to community gathering spaces and neighborhood resilience. Part of broader climate justice and environmental health movements. Related to emergency response networks and disaster-preparedness practices.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: Planning: 3-6 months; year-round operation with seasonal intensity; staffing: 1-5 people
- *People*: Community organizers, hub coordinators, trained staff, volunteers, community members
- *Space*: Existing trusted community institution (library, church, school, nonprofits, community center) with HVAC flexibility and accessibility
- *Materials*: Climate control equipment (A/C, heating); solar panels and batteries (for resilience); emergency supplies; communication equipment; resource materials; comfortable seating
- *Skills*: Community coordination, emergency response, systems thinking, care-work, climate literacy
- *Energy Level*: Medium—ongoing operation with varying intensity by season

## What It Is

Together Project's volunteer matching initiative that connects groups of local volunteers with refugee newcomer families. The program facilitates social integration and settlement support through sustained community relationships over 3-6 months.

## Who 'S Done It

Together Project has matched hundreds of volunteer groups with refugee families across five Canadian cities since 2016. The initiative gained momentum with Syrian refugee sponsorships in Canada and has since supported newcomers from over 25 countries. Impact studies document that Welcome Group participants report increased social capital, better employment outcomes, and stronger community belonging. Volunteers report personal transformation through the relationships formed.

## Connections

This approach reflects best practices in volunteer-led settlement support and builds on the sponsorship model developed for refugee resettlement in Canada. It aligns with peer support and social capital literature demonstrating that informal community networks significantly enhance integration outcomes.

items.body:
## What It Is

A comprehensive volunteer training resource from Together Project for refugee integration. The manual equips volunteer groups with knowledge and skills to support newly arrived refugee families in Canadian communities.

## How It Works

The training manual guides volunteer groups of 3-5 people through a structured process of matching with refugee families over 3-6 months. Volunteers learn to assess family needs, provide conversational English practice, help navigate healthcare and employment services, support youth school transitions, and facilitate community orientation and social activities. The program recommends approximately 1 hour of weekly interaction (online or in-person) shared among group members, totaling 3-4 hours monthly per volunteer. Together Project provides ongoing support and resources, and can connect volunteers who speak Arabic, Farsi, French, Dari, Kurdish, Pashto, Somali, Spanish, Swahili, or Tigrinya as cultural ambassadors to bridge language and cultural gaps. Matching considers location, family size, shared interests, volunteer skills, family composition, and volunteer availability.

## Who 'S Done It

Together Project has operated since 2016, initially responding to the arrival of Syrian refugee families in Toronto. The program now operates in Toronto, Mississauga, Vancouver, Winnipeg, and Moncton, and has recently expanded across Canada to Atlantic Canada, the Prairies, and the West Coast. Volunteer groups have successfully supported refugee families from over 25 different countries, with documented positive outcomes in terms of social integration, employment pathways, and community belonging. The program demonstrates that structured volunteer-community partnerships create meaningful, long-term support networks for newcomers.

## Connections

Together Project's model builds on social integration theory and volunteer-based community support models. It connects to broader refugee welcome movements across North America while adapting to the Canadian context. The approach complements formal settlement services by providing informal social capital and community belonging—elements research shows are crucial for successful long-term integration.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: 3-6 months per match; 1 hour weekly per volunteer (3-4 hours monthly)
- *People*: Groups of 3-5 volunteers; refugee families; cultural ambassadors for language support
- *Space*: Flexible (in-person or online interactions based on preference)
- *Materials*: Training manual; resources on settlement topics; communication tools
- *Skills*: Patience, cultural humility, active listening, basic problem-solving; no prior experience required
- *Energy Level*: Moderate; sustained, consistent engagement over months rather than intensive

## What It Is

Traditional and contemporary practices of welcoming newcomers to neighborhoods through intentional gestures, information-sharing, and relationship-building. From historic door-to-door welcome wagon visits bearing gifts and community information to modern neighboring practices, welcoming practices lower barriers to community belonging and integration for new residents.

## How It Works

Traditional practice: community members or Chamber of Commerce representatives visit new households with welcome baskets containing local business coupons, service information, church listings, and community resources. Modern practice: neighbors leave welcome notes, deliver baked goods or flower bouquets, offer helpful information (garbage pickup schedules, restaurant recommendations, community maps), provide gifts cards to local businesses, and assist with moving. Some neighborhoods coordinate group welcomes when moving trucks arrive. The goal is immediate connection and belonging.

## Who 'S Done It

Welcome Wagon was widespread in mid-20th century America. Many communities continue welcome traditions through neighborhood associations, chambers of commerce, welcome committees, and individual neighbors. Churches and faith communities often lead formal welcoming practices.

## Connections

Historical practice rooted in small-town neighboring traditions before car-dependent suburbs and isolation. Connected to hospitality practices, block stewards, neighbor-to-neighbor initiatives, and front porch culture. Represents intentional reciprocal neighboring and community integration.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: 30 minutes to 1 hour per visit or gesture; minimal ongoing commitment
- *People*: Welcoming neighbor(s), new residents, optional welcome committee coordinator
- *Space*: New resident's home/doorstep, community information gathering place
- *Materials*: Welcome baskets/cards, local restaurant menus, community information sheets, gift items
- *Skills*: Hospitality, community knowledge, clear communication, relationship building
- *Energy Level*: Low—brief, warm, welcoming gestures

## What It Is

A global framework developed by the World Health Organization defining eight interconnected domains for making cities inclusive and health-promoting for people of all ages. Built on UN Principles of Independence, Participation, Care, Self-fulfillment, and Dignity.

## Connections

Informs Building Resilient Neighbourhoods and Neighbor-to-Neighbor programs. Complements Encore.org and Generations United's intergenerational vision.

items.body:
The most-shared single piece of writing on public narrative: Marshall Ganz's 2009 Sojourners essay 'Why Stories Matter: The Art and Craft of Social Change.' In a few pages it lays out the case that social movements move on narrative — that stories communicate values through emotion where facts cannot, that leaders have a responsibility to author a public account of themselves ('if we don't author our own story, others will'), and that the story of self, the story of us, and the story of now together turn values into agency.

A good first send to a neighbor who asks what this storytelling business has to do with getting the crosswalk fixed. Pairs with the Public Narrative recipe on this shelf and the worksheets in the Organizer's Handbook.
items.summary: Ganz's short, canonical essay on the craft of public narrative — why social change runs on stories of self, us, and now, written for Sojourners in 2009.
items.title: Why Stories Matter (Marshall Ganz)

items.body:
## What It Is

A cyclical research methodology where young people investigate problems affecting their communities, analyze findings collaboratively, and use results to advocate for concrete solutions. YPAR positions youth as legitimate researchers and change agents, transforming who gets to produce knowledge about community issues.

## How It Works

YPAR operates through a connected cycle: (1) Youth collaboratively identify and investigate problems they experience directly—conducting surveys, interviews, focus groups, and collecting data. (2) Participants analyze evidence together, examining patterns and root causes. (3) Youth use research findings to advocate for concrete change through presentations, reports, policy recommendations, or direct action. Facilitators support youth in developing research skills, critical thinking, and evidence-gathering capacity while building what researchers call 'sociopolitical development'—deeper understanding of systemic roots of problems. The process emphasizes that youth are experts in their own experiences and that their knowledge production is valuable for community change.

## Who 'S Done It

YPAR has been successfully implemented in schools, community organizations, and youth-serving agencies, particularly with marginalized young people. Youth researchers have investigated homelessness, school discipline policies, housing discrimination, environmental justice, and other community issues. Projects have resulted in policy changes, institutional reform, and increased youth leadership. Participants report increased confidence, critical consciousness, and motivation for ongoing activism.

## Connections

Emerges from participatory action research traditions and critical pedagogy movements. Relates to youth organizing, popular education, and social justice frameworks. Connects to broader movements positioning young people as change agents rather than passive recipients of services.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: 8-16 weeks typically; can be ongoing program
- *People*: 10-30 youth; 2-4 adult facilitators
- *Space*: Community organization, school, or trusted community space
- *Materials*: Research tools, data collection instruments, analysis guides, presentation materials
- *Skills*: Research design, data collection, critical analysis, facilitation, advocacy communication
- *Energy Level*: Medium-to-high; requires sustained engagement and opportunity for authentic voice

items.body:
## What It Is

A global organization serving 'opportunity youth' (ages 16-24, or 15-29 in some countries) who are out of school and unemployed. YouthBuild combines education, job training, construction skills, and community leadership development, with young people building actual housing projects while earning credentials.

## How It Works

YouthBuild operates through an integrated model connecting education and construction: (1) Youth enroll in comprehensive programs addressing education and employment simultaneously. (2) Students work on real construction projects that build affordable housing, community facilities, or renovations—gaining hands-on trades training (construction, electrical, plumbing, etc.). (3) Parallel classroom instruction supports high school diploma or GED completion plus additional skill training (healthcare, IT, retail as alternatives). (4) Leadership development emphasizes community service, civic participation, and personal development. (5) Job placement and continued support help transition youth into employment. The dual focus ensures youth develop both practical construction skills and educational credentials while building something tangible for their communities. Leadership development connects housing work to broader community benefit.

## Who 'S Done It

YouthBuild operates 340+ programs across seven countries, serving tens of thousands of young people. In the U.S., 84% of enrollees earn high school diplomas or equivalent credentials. Alumni demonstrate increased economic mobility, stable employment, and community leadership. Participants describe experiencing 'a place to grow, a place to achieve things you never thought you could achieve.' The model has successfully positioned opportunity youth as solutions—building both physical infrastructure and human potential.

## Connections

Emerges from youth development, workforce development, and housing movements. Relates to affordable housing initiatives, trades training programs, and youth leadership development. Part of broader movements recognizing young people's capacity as assets rather than problems.

## Key Ingredients

- *Time*: 6-24 months typically; ongoing program participation
- *People*: 15-30 young people per cohort; trained instructors and mentors; construction supervisors
- *Space*: Training facility, classroom space, construction sites
- *Materials*: Construction materials, educational curriculum, tools, safety equipment, job placement resources
- *Skills*: Construction trades, classroom instruction, mentoring, job placement support
- *Energy Level*: High; requires full engagement in both classroom and hands-on construction work

items.body:
Paula Z. Segal obtained a New York City spreadsheet listing all publicly owned vacant land in Brooklyn — 596 acres of it — and did two things with it. The expected one: put it online as a map (which grew into Living Lots NYC). And the brilliant one: **zip-tied laminated signs to the chain-link fences of the lots themselves**, telling whoever walked past exactly who owned this land, that it was public, and how to organize with neighbors to get access.

The map found the data; the signs found the people. The online tool added a crucial social feature — strangers who cared about the *same lot* could find each other — and 596 Acres supported 143 neighbor-led campaigns that turned NYC vacant lots into community gardens, farms, and play spaces before the organization sunset. The model spread: Grounded in Philly mapped 32,000+ vacant Philadelphia lots with the Public Interest Law Center; Chicago's Large Lots program (a sibling story on this shelf) turned the same insight into $1 city lot sales.

What it teaches: public data becomes neighborhood power through three moves — map it, **post it physically at the exact place it describes**, and wire it so people organizing the same place meet each other. The fence sign is the most underrated interface in civic tech.

metadata.source_note: 143 campaigns per 596acres.org's own record; organizational sunset ~2018 with Living Lots continuing — Living Lots platform code: django-livinglots core is BSD-3-Clause, the NYC deployment AGPL-3.0.

items.summary: A lawyer turned a city spreadsheet of vacant public land into maps — and zip-tied physical signs to lot fences saying who owned the land and how to organize for it. 143 lots became gardens, farms, and plazas.
items.title: 596 Acres: Signs on Fences

attribution.name: Erik Michaels-Ober (Code for America); Forest Frizzell (Honolulu); SFPUC Adopt-a-Drain

items.body:
In 2011, Code for America fellow Erik Michaels-Ober built Adopt-a-Hydrant for Boston: a map of the city's fire hydrants where a resident could claim one and pledge to shovel it out after snowstorms. That's the whole app. It encoded exactly one civic relationship — *this piece of shared infrastructure is mine to care for* — and Code for America open-sourced it.

The remixes came fast. Honolulu's IT deputy director Forest Frizzell re-skinned it in 2012 as **Adopt-a-Siren** for tsunami sirens, with residents reporting failures during monthly tests. Chicago did sidewalks; multiple cities did storm drains. San Francisco's utility launched **Adopt-a-Drain** in 2016 with the crucial upgrade of *naming rights*: 25,000 drains with stewards and names like Drainy McDrainface and Drainmond Green — and the program nearly doubled in 2023, because whimsy is a retention mechanic, not decoration.

One honest caveat traveled with every remix: the code alone never spread it. Each city needed a champion — a fellow, an IT deputy, a utility program manager — proving again that the deployment is a relationship even when the app is twenty files.

What it teaches: the adopt-a-thing pattern is the most reliably remixable shape in civic tech, and it's block-sized by nature: tree wells, benches, little libraries, community fridges — anything that needs a person gets one, by name.

metadata.source_note: Lineage per Boston.gov, Honolulu's 2012 press materials, and KQED's Adopt-a-Drain coverage; repo is BSD-3-Clause (Code for America, 2011).

items.summary: A tiny Rails app let Bostonians claim a hydrant to shovel out — and got re-skinned within months for Honolulu's tsunami sirens and, later, San Francisco's named storm drains. Small apps encoding one relationship remix best.
items.title: Adopt-a-Hydrant and Its Descendants

attribution.name: Saumya Gupta and Colton Heward-Mills, Build IRL

items.body:
Colton Heward-Mills grew up in New Jersey among Ghanaian immigrants — he had, as he puts it, an abundance of aunties. People in his life who knew him and cared about him, beyond just his parents. Saumya Gupta grew up in India, moved nine times as a kid, and figured out survival early: the best way to go from new girl to your best friend in a week is to help others make friends.

Neither of them realized they were "community builders" until they started Build IRL in San Francisco. Before launching anything, they spent weeks listening — meeting dozens of people who run in-person community groups focused on everything from science to swing dance to grief processing. They kept hearing the same thing: building in-person community is incredibly hard, and — ironically — it's lonely. Organizers hold space for others to find belonging, but they don't get to enjoy it themselves. The work feels underappreciated and unseen.

At the end of these interviews, organizers would ask who else Saumya and Colton had talked to, then want to be connected. That was the aha moment: what if they created a community of practice where builders could learn from each other and feel supported?

Build IRL became a five-week accelerator for in-real-life community groups. They released an application, dozens of groups applied, and they selected 25 clubs for the first cohort: Children of Diaspora (celebrating cultural commonalities), Noisebridge (a beloved makerspace), The Plenary (art and science engagement), Sommanat (processing grief into joy), The Dog House (swing dance with beginner nights), Run Your Life (running and reflection), and more.

Over five weeks, they ran workshops, expert talks, and social gatherings. It culminated in a showcase and club bazaar where 200+ people came to discover and join these communities. After the cohort ended, builders didn't stop — they hosted five or six events on their own within weeks. Members started joining each other's communities. The Dog House's beginner night became a gathering point for builders across the cohort.

One of Saumya's key moves was reframing the money conversation. Most community builders were deeply uncomfortable talking about funding. But when she shifted from "How do you make money?" to "How do you create resources for resilience?" people engaged seriously. By the end, builders were saying things like, "I would feel better if I was paid for this work. It would make me feel like I'm valued." The mindset change — that community-building is valuable enough to invest in — was as important as any tactical learning.

Build IRL already has 40 clubs on the waitlist for the next cohort. Their advice for the "community curious": start with your eyes and ears open. Go to local events. Find people already doing the work. Then do something yourself. The worst case scenario is two people show up to your dinner and you make two new friends.
items.summary: Build IRL is a five-week accelerator for in-real-life community groups in San Francisco. After interviewing dozens of organizers, they discovered that building in-person community is incredibly hard — and ironically lonely. Their first cohort of 25 clubs culminated in a bazaar where 200+ people discovered new communit…
items.title: An Accelerator for Community Builders

items.body:
Looking across the street in January, I wanted to know my neighbors. I wanted them to know me. I wanted them to know I cared about them, and I wanted to know they cared about my kids. It felt like a clear call to action. I had experienced the disconnectedness that so many of us feel in American culture, and at some level I knew it didn't need to stay this way. This story is an account of relational tech happenings in my neighborhood this year. Of course, it's an incomplete picture.

Our first piece of relational tech was a small paper flyer that I co-created and co-distributed with my five-year-old daughter. We invited neighbors to a coffee and donuts hangout, just to say hello and consider forming a group.

The next tool was a sign-up sheet sitting beside the donuts. It gathered contact info, ideas, and votes on our block nickname ("Cozy Corner"). Neighbors also left little notes of gratitude (unprompted, very sweet) that became visible to all.

From there, we set up a WhatsApp group and I built a simple neighbor hub at cozycorner.place. The stated point of the group was "support each other and plan our next party." When I asked what kind of party, people suggested closing the street so kids could play and everyone would know something social was happening. Soon we were planning our first block party.

My favorite early use of the hub was a simple sign-up for block party jobs and supplies. I could see coverage and gaps at a glance, then draft a day-of plan that went to 20+ volunteers. It was surreal to watch someone wave hello on the sidewalk, then minutes later sign up to help out.

As I paid attention to other block parties and third spaces, I noticed plenty of activity but no digital bulletin board. That inspired Outer Sunset Today, a neighborhood calendar that pulls from dozens of sites and menus into one place. It lets anyone upload a flyer, which AI scans and formats for review. People were really excited to see this! Building this also led me to sketch out a Neighborhood API: a shared format for how neighbors, stewards, and organizations might publish events and updates and other things relevant to neighborhood life, with the Outer Sunset as a reference implementation.

Mid-spring, a friend mentioned buying party supplies they wanted other families to use, too. He had this intention but no system to offer them up. That night I built the first version of Community Supplies and texted him the link! Our local mutual aid group picked it up weeks later, asking me if they could spread it into parents' groups.

Other pieces fell into place as needed: a custom linktree-like site at byfor.us to help me do neighborhood demos, a human-readable privacy and terms page, and a reusable footer that invited remixing each tool.

For the September block party, we spread the word through email, chats, posters, and chalk signs. I printed handouts to orient folks, introduce the hub and WhatsApp, and share ideas for neighbor coupons and resilience frameworks (the wind kept us from using them all that day, rocks kept the critical ones in sight). The joyful party itself seeded the next round of ideas: digital coupons, a disaster prep page, and a system to extend microgrants for gatherings across SF. (Perhaps other blocks could get support for mini gatherings in the Spring and larger gatherings in the Fall.)

It's worth noting that some experiments are on pause. A local organizer imagined using the same tools to care for Sunset Dunes Park, starting with community-led sand abatement. The organizing tool is ready, but because the park is so politically charged, we've held off for now.

Meanwhile, my curiosity about neighbors' stories grew! Inspired by the Human Library project, I created Neighbor Stories as a way to organize small circles in local third spaces. My first attempt asked neighbors to propose stories – but the initial group was unsure of what to propose. Recently, I flipped the design to shared prompts that anyone could answer. My next step is to print flyers with QR codes for little free libraries.

Through all this, the most powerful shift has been relational. Each experiment produced not just a tool but a thread – something to share, talk about, respond to, or evolve with care. The more we create together, the more ideas flow back, and the stronger our ties become. What started with a flyer and some donuts now feels like the beginnings of an ecosystem.

items.title: An Outer Sunset Story

attribution.name: Septima Clark, Bernice Robinson, Esau Jenkins & Highlander Folk School
attribution.source: King Institute (Stanford); SNCC Digital Gateway; Southern Cultures on Septima Clark

items.body:
Myles Horton founded Highlander Folk School in Monteagle, Tennessee in 1932 — by the 1950s one of the only places in the segregated South where Black and white activists lived, ate, and planned together. Rosa Parks attended a two-week Highlander workshop in the summer of 1955, four months before her arrest in Montgomery.

Highlander's deepest invention was the **citizenship school**. Septima Clark — a Charleston teacher fired for her NAACP membership — built adult literacy-plus-civics classes so Black Southerners could pass the voter-registration tests designed to exclude them. Esau Jenkins, a bus driver on Johns Island, South Carolina, had been teaching neighbors to read the constitution on his bus route; the first school was built for his island. And to teach it, Clark chose her cousin **Bernice Robinson — a beautician, deliberately selected because she wasn't a credentialed teacher**. The point was the pedagogy: 'the answers come from the people.' Teachers who looked like school would teach like school; a neighbor taught like a neighbor.

The program spread through the South — by 1961, when the Southern Christian Leadership Conference took it over, it had helped tens of thousands register — and its teachers became the movement's local backbone.

What it teaches the shelf: leadership development is not a credential pipeline. The people best positioned to teach a neighborhood are often the ones no institution would think to hire — and a movement that trains beauticians and bus drivers as teachers is answering 'are we stronger now?' every single week. Clark said it plainly: 'I train the people to do their own talking.'

attribution.name: Bed-Stuy Strong (Sarah Mathews & thousands of neighbors)
attribution.source: Vice; Rights CoLab case study; bedstuystrong.com

items.body:
In March 2020, Sarah Mathews posted a handmade sign in Bedford-Stuyvesant inviting neighbors into a Slack workspace. Within a week it held a thousand people; at its height, Bed-Stuy Strong moved about $1.2 million in grassroots donations into a week's groceries for roughly 28,000 neighbors, prioritizing elderly, disabled, and immunocompromised people in a historically Black neighborhood hit early and hard.

The stack was deliberately humble: Slack for coordination, Airtable for intake tickets split across the neighborhood's four quadrants, a Google Voice hotline for neighbors without internet, and a thin layer of volunteer-written bots (Alyssa Dizon and George Farcasiu among the engineers) routing tickets into channels where nearby volunteers claimed them. Farcasiu's design principle deserves engraving: 'We're looking at the social system we have and augmenting and enabling that.' The hotline wasn't a fallback — it was an equity decision.

When the crisis ebbed, the network didn't: working groups turned to vaccine access, free public Wi-Fi, letters to incarcerated neighbors, and small-business preservation.

What it teaches: off-the-shelf tools plus a little glue code can run a several-thousand-person neighborhood logistics operation — and a mutual aid moment, handled relationally, leaves behind exactly what the organizing shelf calls power: relationships, lists, practiced people, and infrastructure looking for its next job.

metadata.source_note: Figures per Rights CoLab and Vice's April 2020 reporting; founder-story details vary across accounts (single founder vs. co-founders) — Mathews credited per Rights CoLab.

items.summary: A handmade sign invited Bedford-Stuyvesant neighbors into a Slack group as COVID hit. With Airtable, volunteer-written bots, and a deliberately phone-first hotline, ~28,000 neighbors got groceries — and the network stayed.
items.title: Bed-Stuy Strong: Slack, Airtable, and a Phone Number

attribution.name: Howard Lawrence & the block connectors of Highlands, Edmonton
attribution.source: Abundant Community Edmonton; Highlands Community League; Edify Edmonton

items.body:
In January 2013, Howard Lawrence launched an experiment on his own street in Edmonton's Highlands neighbourhood, explicitly inspired by McKnight and Block's 'The Abundant Community.' The architecture is small enough to memorize: one **neighbourhood connector** recruits roughly fifty **block connectors**; each block connector visits every household on their own block — not with a survey, but with a conversation guide of six friendly topics: what makes a great neighbourhood, what would make ours better, what activities you'd join with neighbours, what interests you'd pursue together, what skills and gifts you'd share, and what life experience you'd offer.

The results get compiled into what the block actually wants: interest groups, a skills exchange, shared priorities — and, mostly, neighbors who know each other's names. Carmen Lawrence served as the Highlands' neighbourhood connector; the city's community services department picked the model up and spread it across Edmonton as **Abundant Community Edmonton**, and other Alberta municipalities followed.

What it teaches: this is the gift conversation practice running at municipal scale with zero technology beyond a conversation guide — proof that the unit of neighborhood organizing is one person per block who agrees to knock on their own neighbors' doors. For builders, it's also the cleanest spec for what a tool should and shouldn't do: the conversations are irreplaceably human; what a tool can hold is the guide, the compiled interests, and the follow-through.

metadata.source_note: Model architecture and six-topic guide per the Highlands Community League's Abundant Community pages and abundantcommunity.com.

items.summary: One neighbor in Edmonton's Highlands recruited fifty 'block connectors,' each visiting every household on their own block with six friendly questions. The model spread across the city as Abundant Community Edmonton.
items.title: The Block Connectors of Edmonton

items.body:
Before the Boston Ujima Project officially launched in 2017, its creators spent years hosting study circles and discussion groups in Roxbury, Dorchester, Jamaica Plain, and Mattapan — predominantly working-class communities of color — hashing out how an economy that actually worked for them might operate. The name Ujima is Swahili for collective work and responsibility. What they built is a democratic, member-run organization with a radical proposition: that investment decisions should be made by the people most affected by them.

In December 2018, Ujima launched the nation's first democratically governed investment fund, pooling $5 million in capital from more than 300 investors. The minimum investment was just $50. The fund is structured so that lower-income investors take on the least risk and receive equivalent or better returns than wealthier investors — the inverse of how finance typically works. Investment decisions flow through a participatory budgeting process. Ujima hosts neighborhood and citywide planning assemblies where hundreds of residents, local businesses, and employees set investment priorities and vote on where money goes. Local finance professionals conduct due diligence, but the final vote belongs to the members.

Their first fund vote, in December 2019, invested $100,000 in CERO Co-op, a commercial composting company in Dorchester. Since then, members have invested $2.2 million and counting in Black- and Indigenous-owned small businesses and cooperatives. Ujima is now raising a second fund focused on real estate and has launched a Translocal Membership to support peers outside Boston in building similar economic democracy ecosystems. The relational technology is the democratic process itself — the assemblies, the votes, the study circles. Ujima didn't just create a fund; it created a practice of collective economic discernment rooted in neighborhood relationships.
items.summary: Before launching in 2017, Ujima's creators spent years in study circles across Boston — building a democratic, member-run organization for collective investment.
items.title: Boston Ujima Project

items.body:
The Bradley Street Bicycle Co-op started with a serendipitous encounter. In 2015, John Martin — an architect by training — was refurbishing a brick building at 138 Bradley Street in New Haven's East Rock neighborhood. The building had been his father's — Martin Electric. Joel LaChance, who had owned bicycle shops for years, and Paul Hammer, who ran a pedicab service, were both nearby, rehabbing bikes. They got to talking. What emerged was a cooperative bicycle workshop that welcomes anyone and everyone.

The Co-op's mission is twofold. First, it provides space for cyclists to repair their own bikes, or learn how — with volunteers on hand, access to tools, and periodic classes in basic maintenance. Second, it refurbishes donated bikes for resale at reasonable prices, while others go to the Connecticut Mental Health Center and to new arrivals through Integrated Refugee and Immigrant Services. A major source of bikes is the New Haven Police Department, which turns over unclaimed bikes after a year. What makes Bradley Street a story about relational technology is how the bicycle becomes a connector across difference. In a city that is diverse but often divided, the Co-op creates a space where Yale students, longtime residents, recent immigrants, and people navigating mental health challenges all find themselves working side by side, hands greasy, figuring out a derailleur together. The shared activity — tangible, physical, useful — creates the conditions for relationships that New Haven's social geography might not otherwise produce.
items.summary: A serendipitous encounter in 2015 led to a cooperative bicycle workshop in New Haven where cyclists repair bikes and build relationships across difference.
items.title: Bradley Street Bicycle Co-op, New Haven

items.body:
Maff Potts had spent years as CEO of various charities in the UK, working on homelessness, domestic abuse, and social isolation. What he kept noticing was that traditional approaches addressed symptoms but missed root causes. The two things every person needs, he concluded, are friends and purpose. In 2015, he founded Camerados — a "gentle tea drinking revolution" — from his bedroom. The concept was the Public Living Room: a space furnished like a comfortable living room — sofas, bean bags, soft furnishings, usually a piano — placed in a public setting where anyone could walk in, sit down, have a cup of tea, and simply be alongside other people. No agenda, no intake forms, no case management. Just presence.

A "Camerado" is somewhere between a stranger and a friend — liberated from the compulsion to fix someone's problems, free to simply be with them. Maff received nearly three quarters of a million pounds from the National Lottery to roll out Public Living Rooms across the UK. Within a decade, the movement had established over 170 Public Living Rooms across five countries — in libraries, marketplaces, community centers, a cafe in Australia, a university in Scotland, and even a prison. In Blackpool, the Living Room became a space where people experiencing loneliness could find informal support and company without the stigma of seeking services.

The insight driving Camerados is that loneliness is not a condition to be treated but a signal that the built environment has failed to provide what humans need: comfortable places to simply be together. The Public Living Room is relational technology at its most elemental — a sofa, a kettle, and the permission to belong.

items.body:
The idea that a randomly selected group of ordinary citizens can make better decisions than elected officials sounds radical until you realize it's one of the oldest ideas in democracy. Athenian democracy ran on sortition — selection by lottery — for most public offices. The concept resurfaced in the 1970s when Ned Crosby in Minnesota and Peter Dienel in Germany independently invented the citizens' jury: a small group of randomly selected people, given time and information, deliberating on a public question. For decades, the practice remained niche. Then, starting around 2010, something shifted. Ireland used citizen deliberation — first a constitutional convention, then a citizens' assembly — to break decades-long deadlocks on marriage equality and abortion, questions that had paralyzed elected politicians. France convened 150 randomly selected citizens to deliberate on climate policy. And across dozens of cities and regions, from Australia to Belgium to Oregon, variations of the model began appearing with increasing frequency.

By the mid-2020s, citizens' assemblies had been used over 600 times at local, regional, national, and international scales. In 2024, DemocracyNext — a research and advocacy organization — published a comprehensive Assembly Guide distilling the practical wisdom of this growing movement into a step-by-step manual. The guide covers everything from how to recruit participants by democratic lottery (send invitations to thousands of random addresses, then stratify for demographics), to how to structure deliberation days (learning phases, small-group discussion, plenary sessions, drafting recommendations), to what happens after the assembly ends (follow-up, member aftercare, institutionalization). The guide is honest about what makes assemblies work: participants need at least forty hours together to move past surface positions and find genuine common ground. Anything less, and you get a focus group dressed up as democracy.

What the citizens' assembly movement reveals is that the bottleneck in democratic life is rarely a lack of good ideas — it's a lack of good process. When you give a representative cross-section of people the time, information, and facilitation to deliberate seriously, they consistently produce thoughtful, nuanced recommendations that reflect the complexity of real tradeoffs. The assembly model is not a replacement for representative democracy but a complement to it — a way of bringing the lived experience and common sense of ordinary people into decisions that are too important or too contentious for politicians alone. The relational technology here is the process itself: the lottery that ensures no one is excluded, the facilitation that ensures everyone is heard, and the time that ensures depth over speed.
items.summary: The citizens' assembly model — randomly selected people, given time and information to deliberate on public questions — has been used over 600 times worldwide. items.body:
In the mid-1990s, architect Mark Lakeman returned from villages in Central America where residents gathered in common spaces at the center of their communities. He looked at his own neighborhood in Portland, Oregon — the Sellwood neighborhood — and saw something different: intersections dominated by cars, where no one lingered. In 1996, neighbors at the intersection of 8th and Sherrett created a tea stand, a children's playhouse, and a community library on the corner. They renamed it Share-It Square. Then they decided to paint the intersection itself — a giant, colorful mural on the asphalt.

The Portland Department of Transportation was not amused. One city official told Lakeman: "That's public space. Nobody can use it." The neighbors went guerrilla. They painted without permission. The resulting confrontation eventually led, in January 2000, to Portland City Council passing an Intersection Repair ordinance — allowing neighborhoods to develop public gathering places in certain street intersections. The movement Lakeman founded, City Repair, has since been responsible for over 1,200 placemaking projects in Portland and beyond.

The Village Building Convergence — an annual ten-day event — brings together workshops on natural building, permaculture, and intersection repair, producing painted intersections, cob benches, information kiosks, and community gardens. Research has confirmed what neighbors already knew: people living near Intersection Repairs report being healthier, happier, and more content with their neighborhoods. Police calls decrease. The intersection — the most mundane piece of civic infrastructure — becomes a commons. The relational technology is the act of painting together. Neighbors of different ages and backgrounds gather with brushes and paint, co-creating something visible and permanent on the ground they share. The mural marks the place. But the painting builds the community.
items.summary: In the 1990s, architect Mark Lakeman returned from Central America and led neighbors in painting a Portland intersection — sparking a movement of over 1,200 placemaking projects.
items.title: City Repair and Intersection Painting, Portland

items.body:
David Gershon had spent decades studying how to change behavior at scale when he arrived at a deceptively simple insight: the block — the eight or so households that share a stretch of sidewalk — might be the most powerful unit of social change. He created Cool Block, a program that brings neighbors together over nine meetings across four and a half months to take action on carbon reduction, water stewardship, disaster resilience, and neighborhood livability. Participants work through a handbook with 112 action items, choosing which ones fit their households and which ones to tackle as a block.

The program was piloted on 125 blocks across five California cities — Los Angeles, San Francisco, Palo Alto, Mountain View, and Isla Vista. The results were striking: participating households achieved an average carbon reduction of 25 to 32 percent and took 25 actions, including seven to build resilience. When all neighbors on a block were invited, 55 percent of those who chose to learn more joined a team. Cool Block won a NASA competition as the most outstanding solution for addressing humanity's impact on planetary sustainability. In Los Angeles, Cool Blocks became a project of the Neighborhood Council Sustainability Alliance in partnership with the city's Climate Emergency Mobilization Office, working toward the city's goal of carbon neutrality.

But what Gershon found was that the climate outcomes, while real, were almost secondary to what happened between neighbors. The nine meetings created relationships where there had been none. People who had lived on the same block for years and never spoken were suddenly coordinating, planning, looking out for each other. The block — mundane, overlooked, the smallest unit of civic geography — turned out to be the right scale for both environmental action and human connection.
items.summary: David Gershon created Cool Block — a program bringing neighbors together over nine meetings to take action on carbon reduction, resilience, and livability.
items.title: Cool Block

attribution.name: Ernesto Cortés Jr., Andy Sarabia, Beatrice Gallego & COPS (Industrial Areas Foundation)
attribution.source: COPS/Metro's own accomplishments record; Texas Monthly; San Antonio Report

items.body:
Communities Organized for Public Service was not founded at its founding convention. It was founded in more than a thousand one-on-one relational meetings that Ernesto Cortés Jr., freshly trained by the Industrial Areas Foundation, ran through the Catholic parishes of San Antonio's Mexican-American west and south sides in 1974. The IAF's Ed Chambers — who systematized Saul Alinsky's craft into teachable practice — called the relational meeting 'the most radical thing we teach': thirty to forty-five minutes, face to face, probing another person's interests, stories, anger, and talent.

What the conversations surfaced wasn't an issue an organizer imported — it was flooding. West-side residents documented that drainage bonds had been approved for their neighborhoods for decades and never spent there. They built a 'counter-budget' of capital projects, and in August 1974 packed roughly five hundred members into City Council chambers, where leader Beatrice Gallego held the microphone until the council heard them out. First president Andy Sarabia — a civilian Air Force employee and parish leader — embodied the model: leadership from within the constituency, accountable to it.

Over fifty years COPS/Metro has won drainage, paved streets, sidewalks, parks, libraries, a west-side natatorium, the shift to single-member council districts that ended minority-rule politics in a majority-Mexican-American city, the Project QUEST job-training program, and by its own accounting helped direct some two billion dollars in infrastructure bonds to neighborhoods that had been promised them for generations.

What it teaches: the founding meeting is the last step of founding. Institutions people already trust — parishes, congregations, schools — are organizing infrastructure. And the IAF's iron rule rides through every practice on this shelf: never do for people what they can do for themselves.

metadata.place: West and south sides, San Antonio, Texas
metadata.source_note: Founding-year relational meetings, counter-budget, and council action per Texas Monthly and the Museo del Westside; fifty-year totals per COPS/Metro's own accounting (copsmetro.com). Chambers's 'most radical thing' from 'Roots for Radicals' (2003).

items.summary: Ernesto Cortés Jr. came home to San Antonio in 1974 and did over a thousand relational meetings before founding COPS — which then packed city hall, held the microphone, and won the west side its drainage, sidewalks, and two billion dollars of infrastructure.
items.title: COPS: A Thousand Conversations Before the First Meeting

attribution.name: newDemocracy Foundation / Participedia / City of Darebin

items.body:
Darebin is a municipality in Melbourne's northern suburbs — diverse, working-class, and not the kind of place that usually makes headlines for democratic innovation. In 2014, the city council had two million dollars in infrastructure funding and a question: who should decide how to spend it? Rather than the usual process — council staff drafting proposals, a few residents showing up to public comment — they convened a citizens' jury. Forty-four residents were randomly selected from a pool of 3,000 invitation letters sent to households across the municipality, then stratified to ensure the jury reflected Darebin's actual demographics. The jurors were asked a single question: how should we best spend two million dollars to improve our community?

The jury met four times over four months. They heard from community organizations, reviewed project proposals, debated priorities, and voted. Their eight recommendations included $865,000 for a new neighbourhood house in Preston East — an area that had long lacked a dedicated community gathering space — along with funding for exercise equipment in public parks and multipurpose sports courts. Every single recommendation was adopted unanimously by the council. Not as suggestions to consider. Not as input to weigh alongside other factors. As decisions. The council treated the jury's recommendations as binding, a level of commitment that remains rare in participatory budgeting anywhere in the world.

The newDemocracy Foundation and the City of Darebin both commissioned independent research on what the process did to participants. The findings pointed to something beyond the budget outcomes: jurors reported increased trust in local government and a deeper sense of civic agency. People who had never attended a council meeting — who had assumed government happened elsewhere, to other people — discovered that they were capable of making consequential decisions about their own community. The two million dollars mattered. But the shift in who got to decide may have mattered more. Darebin's experiment suggests that participatory budgeting works best not when it asks citizens for their opinions, but when it gives them actual power.
items.summary: A working-class Melbourne suburb gave 44 randomly selected residents actual power over two million dollars in infrastructure spending. Every recommendation was adopted unanimously — and the deeper outcome was a shift in who gets to decide.
items.title: Darebin Participatory Budgeting

attribution.name: Philip Neustrom, Mike Ivanov, Paul Ivanov & the residents of Davis, California
attribution.source: DavisWiki's own Wiki History; Nieman Lab

items.body:
In June 2004, housemates Philip Neustrom, Mike Ivanov, and Paul Ivanov sketched an idea over burritos: an openly editable encyclopedia of Davis, California — everything local, from bike-route lore and burrito rankings to city council politics and neighborhood history. Within three weeks of launch it had a hundred users and six hundred pages; within months it was core infrastructure. Surveys found roughly one in seven residents had *contributed*, and nearly three-quarters of residents used it as their primary housing resource; the community famously crowd-exposed a serial con artist through it.

A Knight News Challenge grant generalized the software into LocalWiki, and hundreds of communities started their own. Few reached Davis's density. The software was never the scarce ingredient — the habit was: a decade of residents reflexively writing down what they knew, tending pages the way other towns tend gardens.

What it teaches: a town-scale knowledge commons is achievable by residents when editing is radically easy and the scope is *everything local*. And the honest corollary from the replication record: launch is nothing, habit is everything. A neighborhood remixing this should start with twenty pages neighbors actually need weekly — not an empty wiki and an announcement.

metadata.source_note: Founding story, usage figures, and LocalWiki arc per DavisWiki's Wiki History page and Nieman Lab's Encyclo entry.

items.summary: Three housemates sketched a wiki for their college town over burritos in 2004. It became Davis's most-used local resource — one in seven residents contributed — and the scarce ingredient turned out to be habit, not software.
items.title: DavisWiki: The Town That Wrote Itself Down

attribution.name: Barcelona City Council & the Decidim community

items.body:
Barcelona's 2020–2023 participatory budget dedicated €30 million to fund the most-voted neighborhood proposals in each of the city's districts, run on Decidim — the open-source platform the city itself birthed. Residents drafted geolocated proposals with budgets attached; 64,571 people participated digitally and 11,970 in person, through a pandemic.

The number worth studying is the second one. The process was hybrid *by design*: neighborhood meetings and street-level 'support points' — staffed tables where residents could learn, propose, and vote with help — fed in exactly the people a digital-only process filters out. The platform held the ledger; the folding tables held the democracy.

What it teaches: a city can run neighborhood-grained democracy on commons-licensed software it governs with its citizens — and the transferable practice isn't the platform config, it's the support point. Any block remixing a digital decision process should budget for its equivalent: a card table, a laptop, and a patient neighbor at the farmers market.

metadata.source_note: Participation figures per Decidim's published case study.

items.summary: Barcelona put €30M to the most-voted neighborhood proposals in every district on its own open-source platform — with street-corner support points feeding in the neighbors who would never participate online.
items.title: Barcelona's Neighborhood Budget: Hybrid by Design

attribution.name: Citizen of the Earth, Taiwan & g0v contributors

items.body:
Taiwan was losing roughly 1,500 hectares of farmland a year to illegal factory construction, and the official reporting process required citizens to attach their personal identification — which meant reporting the factory often meant reporting your neighbor, with your name on it. Reports didn't come.

A staff member of Citizen of the Earth, Taiwan — a small crowdfunded environmental group with no developers — brought the problem to a **g0v hackathon** in 2019. Volunteer civic hackers built Disfactory: drop a pin and a photo of a suspect factory, anonymously; the organization files the official paperwork with its own name on it. MIT-licensed code, reports released as open data.

In ten months: 1,500+ reports, 200+ official filings, seven factories demolished, and a reporting pipeline that finally matched how villages actually work.

What it teaches: anonymity here isn't anti-social — it's *relational* design, protecting the reporter's standing with neighbors while still protecting the farmland. (Contrast the design-for-care framework: anonymity aimed at land and buildings, never at people.) And the collaboration model is the cleanest on this shelf: the community group brings the problem and the legitimacy; the civic hackers bring the build; the institution files the paperwork.

metadata.source_note: Figures per CommonWealth Magazine's English coverage and the project's TICTeC presentation.

items.summary: A small Taiwanese environmental group brought a problem to a g0v hackathon; civic hackers built a map where villagers could report illegal factories on farmland without rupturing village relationships. Seven factories down.
items.title: Disfactory: Anonymity as a Relational Design Choice

attribution.name: Ché Madyun & the residents of the Dudley Street neighborhood
attribution.source: National Park Service; DSNI's historic timeline; Medoff & Sklar, 'Streets of Hope' (1994)

items.body:
By the early 1980s, arson-for-insurance and disinvestment had left about 1,300 vacant parcels — a fifth of the land — in Boston's Dudley Street neighborhood, which outsiders used as an illegal dump. Foundations and agencies arrived with a revitalization plan. At an early meeting in 1985, resident Ché Madyun stood up and asked the planners: **'How many of you live in this neighborhood?'**

The question restructured the whole initiative. The Dudley Street Neighborhood Initiative rebuilt itself around a resident-majority board — 35 seats, elected every two years, with mandated parity across the neighborhood's four communities: African American, Cape Verdean, Latino, and white. Madyun became its president the next year. The first campaign was 'Don't Dump On Us' (1986): residents forced the city to close the illegal trash-transfer stations, tow the abandoned cars, and clean and fence the lots — a winnable first fight that proved the muscle.

Then the structural move: DSNI formed its land-holding arm, Dudley Neighbors Inc., in August 1988, and on November 10, 1988 the Boston Redevelopment Authority approved its application — making DSNI the first community group in the United States to win the **power of eminent domain** over vacant private land in the 62-acre Dudley Triangle. The land trust today holds about 30 acres: 225 permanently affordable homes, a community greenhouse, an urban farm, parks — the neighborhood's own phrase is 'development without displacement.'

What it teaches: governance design is a power question, not a formality. A resident-majority board with ethnic parity wasn't process decoration — it was the difference between a plan for the neighborhood and a plan by it. And the sequence matters: dumpsters before land trusts; a visible win before a structural one.

metadata.source_note: Madyun's question and board structure per the National Park Service and DSNI's own timeline; eminent-domain approval dated by the BRA's Report and Decision of Nov. 10, 1988 (cited in Medoff & Sklar, 'Streets of Hope', 1994; DSNI's timeline agrees — some later retellings misdate the vote to 1989).

items.summary: One resident's question at a 1985 planning meeting forced a foundation-led initiative to hand its board to the neighborhood — which went on to win eminent domain over vacant land and build a community land trust with 225 permanently affordable homes.
items.title: Dudley Street: 'How Many of You Live in This Neighborhood?'

attribution.name: E-Democracy.org (Steven Clift) & its Twin Cities outreach organizers
attribution.source: Knight Foundation; Twin Cities Daily Planet

items.body:
Steven Clift's E-Democracy.org — a pioneer of online civic space since 1994 — launched neighborhood Issues Forums across Minneapolis–St. Paul starting in 2007, including in Cedar-Riverside, a neighborhood of about 7,500 residents where thousands of Somali and Oromo neighbors lived alongside Latino, Korean, and Vietnamese communities.

The forums' real innovation wasn't software — it was the admission that inclusive online space is built offline. With Ford and Knight Foundation support, organizers ran **129 in-person outreach events**, door-knocked over two summers with a St. Paul team speaking **ten languages**, and gathered **three thousand sign-ups on paper**. The rules-based forums (real names, civility nudges, careful moderation) then had a membership that actually looked like the neighborhood.

The organization eventually wound down — founder-dependence and funding drought, the classic nonprofit causes — and its forums are archived. But its inclusion playbook is the permanent artifact, and the graveyard lesson is generous rather than grim: two decades of civility-by-design knowledge, free for the taking.

What it teaches: this is the bridge between this shelf and the organizing one. The tool is the 10%; the door-knocking in ten languages is the 90%. Any neighborhood platform that launches without an offline recruitment plan has chosen its demographics already.

metadata.source_note: Outreach figures per the Knight Foundation's own account; forums now archived — the inclusion method is the durable artifact.

items.summary: Minneapolis–St. Paul's neighborhood forums became genuinely inclusive the only way it happens: 129 in-person outreach events, organizers speaking ten languages, and three thousand paper sign-ups gathered on doorsteps.
items.title: E-Democracy: The Forums Built by Door-Knocking

items.body:
In 2017, residents of an Oakland apartment complex learned their landlord had put their building on the open market. Facing displacement in one of America's most expensive housing markets, they approached a new organization: the East Bay Permanent Real Estate Cooperative. EB PREC, founded that same year and incubated out of a partnership between the People of Color Sustainable Housing Network and the Sustainable Economies Law Center, had a radical proposition — what if housing could be permanently removed from the speculative market? The building purchase closed in 2018 as a partnership between EB PREC and the Northern California Land Trust. The residents — a group of queer, indigenous, and people of color who organized together — became co-stewards of their own home. That project, known as Coop 789, was the first of several.

EB PREC is a Black women-led cooperative organizing its community to finance, acquire, and co-steward land and make it permanently affordable. The model is called a Permanent Real Estate Cooperative — a hybrid that combines features of community land trusts, limited equity housing cooperatives, and real estate investment cooperatives. Unlike traditional land trusts (which are nonprofits), the cooperative structure allows EB PREC to take capital in multiple forms and isn't restricted to serving only low-income residents. The idea is that everyone — high- and low-income alike — should stop profiting from property and live in price-stabilized housing.

Director Noni Session puts it simply: "Our protection of properties lasts into perpetuity, not 99 years like a typical land trust. Communities need permanence to be able to build their vision." To date, EB PREC has raised $5 million through a direct public offering, with shares at $1,000 and target dividends of 1.5 percent. They've liberated several properties and grown to nearly 600 members. One property, donated by its owner, now houses three Black women artists and educators. Another, Esther's Orbit Room, is being transformed into affordable housing for artists above and a launchpad for Black-led cooperative businesses below. The relational technology here is the cooperative structure itself — a legal and financial form that turns housing from a commodity into a covenant, and neighbors from tenants into co-stewards.
items.summary: Facing displacement in Oakland, residents partnered with EB PREC to permanently remove housing from the speculative market through a cooperative model.
items.title: East Bay Permanent Real Estate Cooperative, Oakland

attribution.name: Edmonton Federation of Community Leagues / ABCD Institute

items.body:
In 1917, residents of a neighborhood in Edmonton, Alberta, formed the city's first community league. By 1921, nine leagues existed, and the Edmonton Federation of Community Leagues was established to support them. Today, virtually every residential community in Edmonton has a corresponding community league — 157 in all. Each league is an independent nonprofit volunteer organization with its own bylaws, policies, and governing structure. They advocate to the municipal government on behalf of their community, publish newsletters, and — critically — provide shared amenities: community halls, tool libraries, sports facilities, community gardens.

Edmonton's community leagues represent one of the most complete examples of neighborhood-level civic infrastructure in North America. What makes the system remarkable is its combination of universality and independence — the leagues cover the entire city, but each one is distinct, self-governed, and responsive to the particular character of its place. In recent years, Edmonton has layered an explicit Asset-Based Community Development practice onto this infrastructure through the Abundant Community Edmonton initiative. Neighborhood Connectors and Block Connectors help residents identify strengths — skills, passions, local knowledge — and build from them rather than from deficits. The city has shifted its own role, too: Community Resource Coordinators serve as touchpoints for neighborhoods, supporting community-led work rather than directing it.

Edmonton's lesson for relational technologists is about the long arc. A community league system that began over a century ago is still functioning, still evolving, and still providing the civic soil in which neighbor-to-neighbor connection can take root. The technology is governance structure — bylaws, elected boards, community halls. The innovation is that it has been sustained, generation after generation, by volunteers who believe their neighborhood matters.
items.summary: Since 1917, Edmonton has built a system of 157 community leagues — independent neighborhood nonprofits covering the entire city with halls, gardens, and civic infrastructure.
items.title: Edmonton's Community League System

attribution.name: Michael & Valerie Wood-Lewis, Front Porch Forum
attribution.source: Center for Media Engagement study; Seven Days; frontporchforum.com

items.body:
In 2000, Michael and Valerie Wood-Lewis — new to Burlington, Vermont's Five Sisters neighborhood and wanting to meet neighbors — started an email list advertised with paper flyers slipped door to door. For six years Michael hand-compiled each day's five or six messages into one nightly digest. In 2006 the practice became Front Porch Forum, now covering every Vermont town.

The constitution barely changed: members verified to a real address; one forum per place; **one digest email a day**; a dozen paid human moderators; no algorithm, no comments, no infinite scroll. It's a Vermont public benefit corporation funded by local ads — and it deliberately refused to scale beyond one state, the exact trade the graveyard's dead hyperlocal networks refused to make.

The evidence is the strongest in neighborhood tech: with 250,000 active members among Vermont's roughly 270,000 households — a majority of the state — a 13,000-user study by New_ Public and UT-Austin's Center for Media Engagement found 81% felt FPF made them more informed citizens (versus 26% for Facebook users and 32% for Nextdoor), and FPF members were significantly more likely to attend local events, talk with neighbors, and volunteer. When Tropical Storm Irene hit in 2011, arriving federal workers found towns already self-organized through their forums.

What it teaches: the code was never the product — the *pace* was. You can't fork the software (it's proprietary), but any block can fork the constitution: real names, one geography, one send a day, a human moderator. That's buildable in an afternoon.

metadata.source_note: Membership 250,000 per FPF's own 2025 Annual Benefit Corporation Report (linked from frontporchforum.com/about-us); study findings per the Center for Media Engagement report. CTFG notes a pivot toward employee ownership.

items.summary: Front Porch Forum began as one Burlington neighborhood's hand-compiled nightly email digest. Twenty-five years on, half of Vermont's adults are members — and the studied effects are offline: more volunteering, more neighbors talking.
items.title: The Five Sisters Forum: Slow by Design

items.body:
The legend — which happens to be true — is that it started in a pub. A group of locals in Frome, a small town in Somerset, England, had been meeting as regulars over the course of many evenings, united primarily by their dissatisfaction with the local town council. The council, they felt, lacked ambition. One of those regulars was Peter Macfadyen — a mild-mannered Englishman with strong views about why Frome deserved better governance, particularly on climate. The pub conversations coalesced into something concrete: a slate of independent candidates, unbeholden to any party, running as Independents for Frome. In 2011, they won every seat on the Town Council. Macfadyen became mayor.

What followed was a quiet revolution in local governance. Freed from party discipline and centralized messaging, the council could actually respond to what Frome needed. Macfadyen wrote a booklet about the experience — Flatpack Democracy: A DIY Guide to Independent Politics — which spread rapidly. Since 2014, the movement has grown from one disgruntled pub table into a nationwide phenomenon. Around fifty towns and parishes across England are now run by groups of independents working together for the benefit of their communities. In Frome, Independents for Frome won every available seat again in 2019, and again in 2022.

The story of Frome is a story about relational technology in the oldest sense — a group of people who see each other regularly, in a place they share, who decide to translate their shared frustration into shared governance. The pub is the infrastructure. The regular meetings are the practice. The ballot is the tool. Flatpack Democracy suggests that the most radical act in local politics may simply be showing up — repeatedly, as neighbors, without a party telling you what to think.
items.summary: In a pub in Frome, England, frustrated locals formed a slate of independents — won every council seat in 2011, and sparked a nationwide movement in local governance.
items.title: Flatpack Democracy, Frome, England

attribution.name: Convention Citoyenne pour le Climat / Involve Foundation

items.body:
In the autumn of 2018, the Gilets Jaunes — Yellow Vests — erupted across France. Hundreds of thousands of people, many from rural and peri-urban areas, blocked roundabouts and marched against a fuel tax that President Macron had framed as essential for climate action. The protests exposed a crisis of democratic legitimacy: the people most affected by climate policy had no role in shaping it. Macron's response was unprecedented in French history. He launched a Grand Débat National, and from it emerged a proposal to convene 150 randomly selected citizens — stratified by age, gender, education, geography, and urban-rural balance — to answer a single question: how can France reduce its greenhouse gas emissions by at least 40 percent by 2030, in a spirit of social justice?

The Convention Citoyenne pour le Climat met over seven weekends between October 2019 and June 2020, surviving even the disruption of COVID-19 by shifting some sessions online. Members heard from climate scientists, economists, industry representatives, and activists. They worked in thematic groups on housing, transport, food, production, and consumption. By the end, they had produced a 460-page report containing 149 concrete policy measures — from banning domestic flights where train alternatives exist, to retrofitting buildings, to enshrining climate protection in the French constitution. Macron initially embraced the work, committing at the Élysée Palace to support 146 of the 149 measures. Then the watering-down began. The climate law that eventually passed in 2021 implemented only a fraction of the convention's ambition.

The aftermath was messy and instructive. Some convention members formed an advocacy group called "Les 150" to push for full implementation. Macron, frustrated by their persistence, reportedly said: "They helped me at the start, now they want everything." The tension revealed something important about the relationship between deliberative and representative democracy: citizens who have genuinely deliberated don't simply hand over their recommendations and go home. They develop ownership, expertise, and a sense of democratic entitlement that outlasts the process itself. France's climate convention is both an inspiration — proof that 150 ordinary people can produce sophisticated, actionable climate policy — and a cautionary tale about what happens when the political system treats citizen deliberation as consultation rather than co-governance.
items.summary: After the Yellow Vest protests exposed a crisis of democratic legitimacy around climate policy, France convened 150 randomly selected citizens who produced 149 concrete policy measures — proving ordinary people can craft sophisticated climate policy, and revealing what happens when government treats deliberation as co…
items.title: France's Convention Citoyenne pour le Climat
