attribution.name: Henry Moore & the block groups of Savannah, Georgia
attribution.source: Project for Public Spaces, 'Savannah's Grants-For-Blocks Program'

items.body:
In 1993, Savannah's assistant city manager Henry Moore did something unusual with a $20,000 Ford Foundation grant: he asked residents what to do with it. The answer became **Grants for Blocks**: grants of up to $500 to groups of neighbors on a block, for improvement projects they chose and carried out themselves. Applications grew from 89 in the first year to more than 300; the city moved the program onto its own budget at $70,000 a year.

The governance details are the remixable part. A **resident review committee** — two representatives per applying neighborhood — scored applications with names, dollar amounts, and neighborhood identifiers redacted; members couldn't review their own neighborhood's bids. Early rounds skewed toward beautification, so the program learned to prefer projects that ran as ongoing community activity rather than one-day cleanups. The city's own administrator named the real product: 'the real benefit is not just in the projects themselves, it is in the collaboration they inspire.'

A block that applies for a $500 grant has to do everything this shelf teaches at miniature scale: find its people, agree on what it cares about, inventory who can do what, commit to each other, and finish something visible together. Moore went on to co-write the standard manual on combining ABCD with organizing — Savannah was his proof.

What it teaches: small money, seriously governed, is leadership development infrastructure. The grant is the excuse; the block meeting is the point.

metadata.source_note: Program design and quotes per Project for Public Spaces; whether the program still operates in this form today is unverified — the design is the durable artifact.

items.summary: A city hall practiced ABCD with $500 at a time: resident groups on a block apply for micro-grants for self-chosen projects, judged by a resident committee with names redacted. The projects mattered less than the collaboration they required.
items.title: Savannah's Grants for Blocks

attribution.name: The United Farm Workers — Larry Itliong, Cesar Chavez, Dolores Huerta, Eliseo Medina, Jessica Govea & thousands more
attribution.source: UFW history archives; Marshall Ganz, 'Why David Sometimes Wins' (Oxford, 2009)

items.body:
On September 8, 1965, Filipino-American grape workers led by Larry Itliong's generation walked out at Delano, California; Cesar Chavez's largely Latino union voted to join them eight days later. The growers could outlast a strike in the fields. So the union moved the battlefield: it sent farmworkers themselves to cities across North America to run boycott houses — organizing local committees of students, clergy, unionists, and housewives to get California grapes out of the stores.

Eliseo Medina was sent to run the Chicago boycott office in his early twenties. Jessica Govea, a 21-year-old farmworker from Bakersfield, led the boycott in Toronto and Montreal and persuaded Canadian grocery chains to drop California grapes. Dolores Huerta directed New York and sharpened the strategy: target the chains, not just the fruit. Marshall Ganz — who had left Harvard for Mississippi Freedom Summer — joined the union in 1965 and spent sixteen years learning and building this machine.

At the boycott's height an estimated seventeen million Americans stopped buying grapes. On July 29, 1970, twenty-six Delano growers signed the first real union contracts in California field agriculture, covering roughly ten thousand workers.

What it teaches: distributed organizing is what a poor constituency does when its only abundant resources are its people, their stories, and their courage. Every boycott house was a snowflake node — local leadership, real responsibility, accountable to the whole. The pattern reappeared four decades later in a presidential campaign, and it reappears any time a neighborhood realizes its people in other rooms are a resource, not a diaspora.

metadata.place: Delano, California — and boycott houses across North America
metadata.source_note: Strike and contract facts per UFW's own history pages and the National Park Service; named boycott organizers per the Walter P. Reuther Library and Facing History.

items.summary: When the strike alone couldn't win, the United Farm Workers sent farmworkers — many of whom had never left California's Central Valley — to run boycott houses in distant cities. Seventeen million Americans stopped buying grapes.
items.title: The Grape Boycott: Farmworkers in Every City

attribution.name: Referenced in Jesse Evers' guide / growfoodnorthampton.org

items.body:
Grow Food Northampton began with a community raising $670,000 to purchase 121 acres of farmland — an act of collective investment in a vision of local food sovereignty. The land now hosts a community farm where ten small farms and farming collectives lease low- and no-cost plots, including four farms owned and operated by farmers of color and refugee farmers. A 320-plot organic community garden serves hundreds of families, with roughly thirty percent receiving subsidized or no-cost plots.

The organization runs a volunteer-powered Giving Garden that grows over 6,500 pounds of fresh vegetables annually, all delivered to local soup kitchens and the Northampton Survival Center. A Tuesday Market matches the first ten dollars spent with SNAP benefits each week, resulting in $25,000 in local food purchases by low-income families. Over 1,200 public school children visit the farm each year. All of the food and land access programming is guided by a Food Access Advisory Committee comprised of people who have been harmed and marginalized by the conventional food system.

What makes Grow Food Northampton a relational technology story is the way the land itself becomes a commons — a shared resource that restructures relationships between people and their food, between long-established residents and newcomers, between those who have and those who need. The farm doesn't just grow food. It grows a web of accountability, participation, and mutual care anchored to a specific piece of ground.
items.summary: A community raised $670,000 to purchase 121 acres of farmland, creating a commons for local food sovereignty with ten small farms and a 320-plot garden.
items.title: Grow Food Northampton, Massachusetts

attribution.name: Electoral Reform Society / Involve Foundation / citizenassembly.ie

items.body:
For decades, Ireland's politicians refused to touch abortion law. The Eighth Amendment to the Constitution, passed by referendum in 1983, gave equal right to life to the mother and the unborn — making Ireland one of the most restrictive countries in Europe. Successive governments knew the issue was too divisive for parliamentary action. Polls shifted, personal stories accumulated, but the political system was frozen. Then, in 2016, the government tried something no Irish parliament had attempted on this scale: it handed the question to 99 randomly selected citizens.

The Citizens' Assembly, chaired by Supreme Court Justice Mary Laffoy, met over five weekends. Members heard from 25 expert witnesses — constitutional lawyers, obstetricians, ethicists, people who had traveled abroad for abortions, and advocates on both sides. They reviewed over 13,000 written submissions from the public. They deliberated in small groups, wrestled with competing values, and voted. The result shocked nearly everyone: 87 percent of assembly members recommended changing the amendment, and 64 percent supported access to abortion with no restriction as to reason. These were not activists or partisans — they were hairdressers, farmers, retirees, students, selected by lottery to be broadly representative of Irish society in age, gender, geography, and class.

The assembly's recommendations went to parliament, which put the question to a national referendum in May 2018. The country voted 66.4 percent in favor of repeal — almost exactly matching the assembly's own margin. The alignment was no coincidence. The assembly had demonstrated that when ordinary people are given time, information, and respectful facilitation, they arrive at positions that reflect the deeper currents of their society — currents that elected politicians, constrained by party discipline and electoral fear, cannot access. Ireland's experiment proved that deliberative democracy can break deadlocks that representative democracy cannot, and that the design of the process — random selection, expert testimony, structured small-group deliberation — is itself the most important innovation.
items.summary: When Ireland's politicians couldn't touch abortion law for decades, the government handed the question to 99 randomly selected citizens — hairdressers, farmers, retirees — whose deliberation broke the deadlock and aligned almost exactly with the national referendum that followed.
items.title: Ireland's Citizens' Assembly on the Eighth Amendment

items.body:
For a few years, Jesse Evers ran a space in Brooklyn called Highside Workshop. It was a multipurpose warehouse that hosted concerts, art galleries, motorcycle repair workshops, tattoo popups, band practices, and people just hanging out. He estimates they ran close to a hundred events. When Jesse got the warehouse, he had no plan — just a conviction that his creative and talented friends needed a place to do their thing. Space is hard to come by in New York City, and he spent the first six months gutting and rebuilding the space before inviting anyone in.

What Jesse discovered — and later wrote about in a guide that has circulated widely among community builders — is that the relationships between a community space and its members are fundamentally different from those of a business. If you build the right conditions, people show up not as customers but as co-creators. They contribute time, money, and energy in ways that don't make economic sense but make perfect relational sense. Trust, Jesse found, is the prerequisite for belonging — the feeling that you have every right to be somewhere without needing permission. Making that feeling real required making the space vulnerable, being generous beyond what was transactional.

He learned that leaving room for serendipity mattered enormously. Unstructured time in the space — people bumping into each other, unexpected encounters — was where the community grew its own ideas. A core group of deeply committed people formed organically, and Jesse found that the most important design challenge was creating a mechanism for people on the fringes to make their way inward, from casual visitors to genuine participants.
items.summary: Jesse Evers ran a multipurpose warehouse in Brooklyn hosting concerts, art, and motorcycle repair — discovering that trust is the prerequisite for belonging.
items.title: Jesse Evers and Highside Workshop, Brooklyn

attribution.name: KC Tenants — Tiana Caldwell, Tara Raghuveer & thousands of member-leaders
attribution.source: Next City; Shelterforce; WBUR On Point (Caldwell's first-person account)

items.body:
In 2019, Tara Raghuveer came home to Kansas City after researching its eviction crisis and started doing what the research couldn't: meeting tenants. Among the first was Tiana Caldwell, who with her husband and son had been evicted in late 2018 while she fought a second round of ovarian cancer. Caldwell didn't become a case study; she became a founding leader — of KC Tenants and of a national homes-guarantee campaign.

The union built itself the way this shelf teaches: base-building through shared lived experience, leaders drawn from the constituency, escalation with a strategy. Within a year, the City Council passed a **Tenants' Bill of Rights** (December 2019): notice before entry, utility-cost disclosure, and the legal right to organize. During the pandemic the union fought evictions with direct action — including chaining courthouse doors shut in October 2020. And in June 2022 Kansas City launched a citywide **right to counsel**, putting a lawyer beside every tenant facing eviction, won by the union's sustained campaign.

The union — run by poor and working-class tenants across race and neighborhood — has since moved into electoral organizing and social-housing advocacy, and helped seed a national federation of tenant unions.

What it teaches: Ganz's definition made flesh — the constituency's commitment is the decisive resource. The people with the problem ran the organization that solved it, and every campaign left the union bigger and its leaders more practiced. When the next fight comes, Kansas City's tenants won't be starting over.

metadata.source_note: Bill of Rights and right-to-counsel dates per Next City, Shelterforce, and the City of Kansas City; Caldwell's story in her own words via WBUR.

items.summary: Founded through door-knocking and 1:1s with tenants like Tiana Caldwell — evicted while fighting cancer — KC Tenants won a Tenants' Bill of Rights within a year, then a citywide right to counsel in eviction court.
items.title: KC Tenants: Evicted People Run the Union

items.body:
Daniel Marshall's grandfather, D.C. Waid, built a cabin on Lake Guntersville in the 1950s. Decades later, Daniel — a social studies teacher from Southern California who'd landed in New York — was given a book by his mentor: The Long Haul, the autobiography of Myles Horton, founder of the Highlander Folk School. The book, the cabin, a group of teacher friends with summers off, and a question — what would it look like for teenagers to practice genuine self-governance? — became the raw materials for Lamplight.

Lamplight is a free, three-week summer program in Guntersville and Birmingham, Alabama, where teenagers practice leadership by actually running the camp and doing projects for their community. Inspired by Highlander's principles and action civics, the model puts real decisions in young people's hands.

A day at Lamplight might look like this: mornings spent on labor projects — building benches, painting murals, constructing a dance floor. Lunch, then a "Pack Meeting" where campers vote on budgets with line-item proposals and quotes. They handle real money with full financial transparency, including seeing staff pay. Dinner with communal chores. A closing circle with shout-outs and occasional roasts.

Before the projects begin, campers identify problems facing their community through interviews and surveys — sometimes collecting over 100 responses at places like Walmart and local parks. They do root cause analysis and often land on something like isolation as the underlying issue. Then they vote democratically on what to build or do about it.

The learning runs deep. At one point, campers figured out how to set voting options so they'd get their preferred movie night pick — demonstrating they'd internalized how power works. At another moment, kids organized a Walmart fundraiser involving air guitar Christmas caroling, raising $300 for their projects. These aren't lessons from a textbook. They're practiced.

An unexpected ripple: Felicia Jones, mother of a first-year camper, was so moved by what she saw that she started Caring Heart Outreach to address community needs in Guntersville. The organization now funds three nonprofits including Lamplight, runs a teen pantry feeding hundreds weekly, and is acquiring a community center.

Daniel's long-term vision is patient and specific. Over many years, teenagers from Guntersville and Birmingham who know each other — trained in action civics and self-governance — might collaborate on regional change. As he puts it, if you take a really long time with something, you actually get really good at it by the time it matters.

Lamplight isn't trying to scale or replicate itself in distant places. It's trying to go deep in a particular place, with particular people, over a particular stretch of time. The results aren't quick, but the relationships are real — and the young people running the show are building muscles they'll use for life.
items.summary: A free three-week summer program in Alabama where teenagers practice self-governance by actually running the camp — voting on budgets with real money, doing root cause analysis on community problems, and building projects. One camper's mother was so inspired she started a nonprofit that now funds three organizations.
items.title: Lamplight Summer Camp

attribution.name: Demond Drummer (Teamwork Englewood), DataMade & LISC Chicago
attribution.source: Smart Chicago Collaborative; Journal of the American Planning Association (2021)

items.body:
Chicago's Large Lots program began in Englewood, where Demond Drummer at Teamwork Englewood pushed a community-planning insight to its logical end: the city owned thousands of vacant lots on Black South and West Side blocks, residents wanted them, and the purchase process was a labyrinth. With civic-tech firm DataMade and funding through LISC Chicago, largelots.org reduced the process to a **one-page application a resident could complete on a phone in under five minutes**: property owners on a block could buy up to two city-owned lots on that block for **$1 each**.

The city formally adopted the program in December 2014; the Englewood pilot drew 414 applications, and by 2019 more than 1,240 lots had sold citywide. Then came the research: a peer-reviewed evaluation found block-level crime fell about 3.5% around sold lots — and **6.8% when the buyer lived in the neighborhood**. The relational variable did the work: near neighbors mowing, fencing, gardening, watching.

What it teaches: civic tech's highest leverage is often *subtraction* — the app added nothing; it deleted friction from a right residents already had. And ownership by near neighbors, specifically, is what moved the needle — a finding the whole relational technology thesis can stand on.

metadata.source_note: Program history per Smart Chicago and DataMade; crime findings per JAPA 2021 (Univ. of Illinois research).

items.summary: Englewood residents and civic technologists reduced Chicago's byzantine land-purchase process to a one-page application for $1 lots. Over 1,240 lots sold — and crime dropped most where near neighbors became the owners.
items.title: Large Lots: The $1 Lot and the One-Page Form

items.body:
Joan Blades knows something about political intensity. In 1998, she and her husband sent an online petition urging Congress to censure President Clinton and move on to pressing issues. It went viral before viral was a word, gathering half a million signatures and spawning MoveOn.org — one of the most influential progressive organizations in American politics. But by 2004, Blades realized she had a problem. She had deep exposure to progressive viewpoints and almost no visibility into why conservatives viewed the world differently. In 2007, she connected with Michele Combs, the communications director of the Christian Coalition, at a retreat. The two became friends — and then unlikely partners, when MoveOn and the Christian Coalition teamed up to preserve net neutrality.

That improbable friendship shaped what came next. In 2011, Blades co-founded Living Room Conversations with Tea Party Patriots co-founder Mark Meckler. The concept is simple and replicable: a structured conversation, following six basic rules of discourse, held in someone's living room (or a coffee shop, or online) between people who disagree. No special training is required. No facilitators, no institutions, no budgets. Just neighbors committed to trading judgment for curiosity. Blades — a mediator and attorney by training — calls the work "a domestic peace initiative."

Over 25 conversation topics are available as open-source guides, from food to guns to voting. The model is designed to be self-organizing and horizontal: anyone can host, anyone can participate. Living Room Conversations has spread across the United States, providing a platform for people who would otherwise never talk to each other to discover they care about each other. The relational technology is the conversation guide — a few simple rules that create a container strong enough to hold disagreement. The insight is that polarization is not primarily an information problem. It's a relationship problem. And relationships are rebuilt in living rooms.
items.summary: Joan Blades, co-founder of MoveOn.org, partnered with a Tea Party co-founder to create Living Room Conversations — structured dialogues between people who disagree.
items.title: Living Room Conversations

attribution.name: Mutual Aid Medford and Somerville (Hannah Freedman, Sophia Grogan, Miriam Priven & Anna Kaplan)

items.body:
Mutual Aid Medford and Somerville (MAMAS) was started in March 2020 by a group of friends in their twenties — Hannah Freedman, Sophia Grogan, Miriam Priven, and Anna Kaplan — and became one of the Boston area's most effective COVID networks using a stack any block could copy by Friday: neighborhood **phone trees**; geographic **pods** mapping neighbors to nearby neighbors; a Google Form for help requests; shared offerings spreadsheets; and a multilingual Google Voice hotline. Grocery runs, prescription pickups, childcare, spare rooms, redistributed funds.

They published replication instructions — including how to draw pod boundaries — and open-sourced the small utilities they did write. The deliberate minimalism was the point: no accounts, no apps, nothing to install, nothing between a neighbor and help but a phone number and a nearby person. As the lead engineer of a fellow COVID network put it: 'If we were depending on an app or online form submissions we would miss a huge swath of people in need.'

What it teaches: the pod-plus-phone-tree-plus-spreadsheet architecture is the mutual aid reference design. Technology's job in it is bookkeeping; the pods — nearby neighbors bound to nearby neighbors — are the actual system. Any builder adding features should first ask what the phone tree can't already do.

metadata.source_note: Founders and stack per Boston Magazine; the anti-solutionism quote is from Invisible Hands' lead engineer Matt Schaff (Vice), not a MAMAS slogan.

items.summary: Mutual Aid Medford and Somerville ran a two-city COVID network on geographic pods, phone trees, Google Forms, and a multilingual hotline — the most remixable mutual aid architecture documented, with almost no tech at all.
items.title: MAMAS: Pods, Phone Trees, and Spreadsheets

items.body:
In 2014, Melbourne's city government faced a familiar problem: it needed to plan a decade's worth of spending — roughly five billion dollars — and the standard public consultation process was broken. Council meetings drew the same handful of vocal residents. Online surveys captured shallow preferences. The people who would actually be affected by budget decisions — commuters, small business owners, renters, students, retirees — were nowhere in the room. So Melbourne tried something new. Working with the newDemocracy Foundation, the council randomly selected 43 residents and business owners from across the city and asked them a question usually reserved for technocrats: how should Melbourne spend its money over the next ten years?

The People's Panel met over six weekends. Members received briefings from city officials, reviewed financial data, debated priorities in small groups, and drafted recommendations. The composition was deliberately balanced: a 50-50 split between residents and business owners, reflecting the fact that businesses pay 70 percent of commercial rates but residents bear the lived consequences of spending choices. The panel produced eleven recommendations covering everything from infrastructure investment to community services. The council adopted ten of them. No cherry-picking, no softening the language, no burying the findings in a report that no one reads. The Lord Mayor received the recommendations directly from panelists at a public meeting of the Future Melbourne Committee.

What made Melbourne's experiment significant was not just the quality of the recommendations — though they were widely praised — but the shift in legitimacy. A group of 43 randomly selected people, none of them elected, none of them experts, had produced a ten-year financial plan that the council trusted enough to implement. The People's Panel demonstrated that the barrier to citizen participation in complex governance is not complexity itself — it's the absence of a well-designed process. When you give ordinary people time, information, and good facilitation, they don't simplify the problem. They meet it where it is.
items.summary: Melbourne randomly selected 43 residents and business owners and asked them how to spend five billion dollars over ten years. The council adopted ten of their eleven recommendations — proving that the barrier to citizen participation in complex governance is not complexity, but the absence of a well-designed process.
items.title: Melbourne People's Panel

attribution.name: Moms 4 Housing — Dominique Walker, Carroll Fife & the mothers of Magnolia Street

items.body:
In November 2019, a group of homeless and marginally housed Black mothers — publicly led by Dominique Walker, with organizer Carroll Fife alongside — moved into a vacant house at 2928 Magnolia Street in West Oakland. The house belonged to Wedgewood Inc., a Southern California flipping firm that had bought it at foreclosure auction. The mothers' claim was a power analysis you could photograph: Oakland had more vacant homes than homeless people.

They held the house for 58 days, through an armed pre-dawn eviction in January 2020 that drew hundreds of neighbors into the street. Walker: 'We moved into that home and wanted to reclaim it back into the hands of the community.' Under public pressure brokered through the governor's office and the mayor, Wedgewood agreed to sell the house to the Oakland Community Land Trust, which renovated it for the mothers' return. The fight then scaled into law: California's SB 1079 (2020) blocked bulk purchases at foreclosure auctions and gave tenants and families a window to match investor bids. Fife was elected to Oakland's City Council that November.

What it teaches: direct action works when it *dramatizes* a power analysis rather than substituting for one — the vacant-homes-versus-homeless-mothers frame did the arguing. And escalation has a shape: occupation → negotiation → institutional fix (the land trust) → structural fix (state law). Each rung converted the previous one's attention into something durable.

metadata.source_note: Occupation, sale to the Oakland CLT, and SB 1079 per NPR, CBS, KTVU, and CalMatters coverage.

items.summary: Homeless and marginally housed Black mothers occupied an investor-owned vacant house in West Oakland for 58 days — and came out with the house in a land trust and a new state law against bulk foreclosure-flipping.
items.title: Moms 4 Housing: The Vacant House on Magnolia Street

attribution.name: The people of Montgomery, Alabama (1955–56)
attribution.source: Retold after 'Organizing: People, Power, Change' (2014) and Taylor Branch, 'Parting the Waters' (1988)

items.body:
In December 1955, Black residents of Montgomery, Alabama — forced to sit at the back of segregated buses and surrender seats to white passengers — began refusing to ride. The boycott held for 381 days, deprived the bus system of most of its riders' fares, and ended with desegregated buses.

Organizers tell this story as the cleanest illustration of what strategy *is*: turning what you have into what you need to get what you want. What the constituency had looked like almost nothing — bus fare, feet, church basements, and one another. Organized collectively, the fare became economic leverage; the feet became a daily, visible act of commitment; and weekly mass meetings renewed courage for over a year.

The theory of change fits in a sentence: if Black residents boycott the buses, the system will desegregate, because segregation will cost more than it pays.

But the boycott only looks spontaneous if you ignore the decade of organizing underneath it. The Women's Political Council — founded in 1946 by Mary Fair Burks — had documented bus abuse and threatened a boycott for years. The night of Rosa Parks's arrest, WPC president Jo Ann Robinson stayed up past midnight with two students and a colleague with mimeograph access, running off some 52,500 handbills by 4 a.m. (her memoir's estimate) — the call for the one-day boycott that became 381. E.D. Nixon — Pullman porter, union man, past NAACP president — bailed Parks out and phoned the ministers who met at Dexter Avenue Baptist Church, drafting a young Martin Luther King Jr. as spokesman. And the logistics were themselves power: a carpool of over 300 private cars running 43 dispatch and 42 pickup stations, run by the Montgomery Improvement Association's transportation committee.

What it teaches: organizing precedes mobilizing. And Montgomery's people ended those 381 days with more than desegregated buses — proof of their own power, trained leaders, and the muscle that carried the movement's next decade.

metadata.source_note: Used as the core strategy example in 'Organizing: People, Power, Change' (2014); organizing-infrastructure details per the King Institute at Stanford (Montgomery Improvement Association; Montgomery Bus Boycott), the NMAAHC on Jo Ann Robinson, and Britannica on the Women's Political Council. Handbill count 52,500 per Robinson's memoir estimate (King Institute's Jo Ann Gibson Robinson entry); some secondary accounts say 35,000.

items.summary: The Montgomery bus boycott as a strategy story: a constituency turned its humblest resource — bus fare — into the power to desegregate a bus system, by organizing to withhold it together for 381 days.
items.title: Montgomery: 381 Days of Bus Fare

items.body:
In 2016, Nate Tubbs and his family moved to The Island — a micro-neighborhood on Chicago's West Side that sits at the intersection of three large and very different communities. Nate is a communications professional and community organizer who had worked in the nonprofit sector for years, but moving to The Island was different. This wasn't about serving a community from the outside. It was about becoming a neighbor. For several years, Nate did what most institutional approaches skip: he listened. He went to local meetings, spent time on the block, and paid attention to what neighbors talked about when they talked about their streets. Two things kept coming up — the neighborhood lacked third spaces where people could simply gather, and a vacant city-owned lot on the block had become a dumping ground for weeds, garbage, and abandoned vehicles.

In the spring of 2018, Nate and his neighbors organized an Earth Day cleanup of the vacant lot. They invited the local school, city departments, and anyone on the block who wanted to show up. That single day — picking up trash, pulling weeds, imagining what the space could become — sparked something. The cleanups became regular. The sense of possibility grew. By 2020, the lot was secured as a NeighborSpace — part of a citywide land trust — and became part of the West Side Nature Play Network. Design teams from NeighborSpace and Human Scale led a community design process, involving residents young and old in shaping what the space would become.

In the fall of 2021, the Island Oasis Nature Play Garden opened. It's now used for relaxation, gardening, community meetings, movie nights, celebrations, and annual events like Taco Fest and a Halloween Spooktacular. But the garden was just the visible part of something deeper. Around the same time, Nate helped restart the Island Civic Association — a dormant neighborhood group — and has served as its president for four years. He chairs the Local School Council at the neighborhood elementary school, where he's served for eight years. And through Parish Collective, he has connected with a national network of neighborhood practitioners who share a commitment to being present in their places over the long term.
items.summary: In 2016, Nate Tubbs moved to The Island on Chicago's West Side and spent years listening before organizing neighbors to transform a vacant lot.
items.title: Nate Tubbs and The Island, Chicago

items.body:
Lawrence, Massachusetts, is a city that has been underinvested in for decades — a former mill town where civic disengagement had become the norm rather than the exception. Lawrence CommunityWorks, a community development corporation, responded with a strategy they called network organizing. At its center is a deceptively simple program called NeighborCircles. A NeighborCircle starts when a host reaches out to eight to ten unfamiliar neighbors and invites them to their home three times over the course of a month for dinner and facilitated conversation. That's it. Dinner and conversation, three times, with neighbors you didn't know before. The format is deliberately intimate — a home, not a community center. The conversation is supported by one or two facilitators but driven by the participants.

What happens after the third meeting is up to the circle. Some continue meeting regularly. Some have organized alley cleanups, playground improvements, better street lighting, and block parties. Some have become the nucleus for deeper neighborhood organizing. Since 2002, NeighborCircles have spread across Massachusetts, Connecticut, Rhode Island, Tennessee, Mississippi, Ohio, Florida, Arizona, Colorado, Virginia, and Maryland. Lawrence CommunityWorks has grown to over 5,000 members, with roughly 1,000 actively engaged each year. They've invested $175 million in Lawrence homes, neighborhoods, businesses, and education. They've been designated an Exemplary NeighborWorks affiliate and serve as technical assistance providers to other organizations adopting the model.

The relational technology is the dinner table. The practice is invitation — specifically, the act of inviting people you don't know. The insight is that civic engagement doesn't start with issues or campaigns. It starts with a meal.
items.summary: Lawrence CommunityWorks created NeighborCircles — inviting 8-10 unfamiliar neighbors to dinner three times over a month, sparking civic engagement across 11 states.
items.title: NeighborCircles, Lawrence, Massachusetts

attribution.name: Marshall Ganz & the 2008 campaign's organizers and volunteers
attribution.source: Ganz, 'Organizing Obama' (2009); Zack Exley, 'The New Organizers' (2008); McKenna & Han, 'Groundbreakers' (2014)

items.body:
In 2007, Marshall Ganz and colleagues designed a volunteer architecture for the Obama campaign that ran directly on the practices of this shelf: multi-day 'Camp Obama' trainings where volunteers learned to tell a story of self, us, and now — then organized into **neighborhood leadership teams** with defined turf and real responsibility for voter contact.

The structure was the snowflake: a team coordinator at the center of interdependent roles — canvass, phone bank, volunteer, data — each leading others, rather than staff controlling a call list. Journalist Zack Exley, embedded that fall, counted 1,231 campaign-defined neighborhoods in Ohio alone, and named the operating principle: respect the volunteers by giving them real responsibility. By Ganz's account the campaign trained roughly three thousand organizers who built thousands of neighborhood teams engaging over a million and a half volunteers; the definitive study, 'Groundbreakers,' puts the volunteer total at 2.2 million.

For this shelf, the campaign matters less as politics than as proof at scale: the house meeting, the 1:1, public narrative, testing leaders before escalating them, teams with shared purpose and ground rules — the whole toolkit held together with millions of strangers, most of whom had never organized anything. The lineage was explicit: Ganz learned the craft in the UFW, which learned it from Fred Ross's living rooms.

The question it leaves for a neighborhood: if the model works with 2.2 million people who mostly never met, what could it do with forty households who see each other every day?

metadata.place: United States (Ohio's 1,231 neighborhoods as the documented case)
metadata.source_note: Team counts and training figures per Ganz's 'Organizing Obama' and Exley's embedded reporting; 2.2M volunteer figure per 'Groundbreakers' (Oxford, 2014). Ohio figures use different units (teams vs. defined turfs) across sources.

items.summary: The 2008 Obama campaign trained volunteers in public narrative at 'Camp Obama,' structured them into neighborhood teams with real responsibility, and proved the Ganz model could hold millions of people.
items.title: Neighborhood Teams: The Snowflake at National Scale

items.body:
Casper ter Kuile had spent years studying how people — especially younger people — were leaving institutional religion but still hungering for spiritual community. As co-founder of the Sacred Design Lab, he was exploring what 21st-century spiritual well-being could look like when it wasn't tethered to a denomination. The question kept circling back to something ancient: ritual and hospitality.

The breakthrough came through an unlikely encounter. A gathering called "Nuns and Nones" brought together Catholic Sisters and unaffiliated millennial community leaders to explore what tradition might mean in an age of disaffiliation. What happened wasn't debate or negotiation — it was transmission. The Sisters shared practices, stories, and ways of being that the younger participants had been trying to invent from scratch. The millennial leaders brought fresh energy and new questions. Both groups recognized something in the other.

One moment crystallized it. Sister Mary Dacey — a woman of deep theological grounding and integrity — blessed Casper with a religious name on a Brooklyn rooftop, using oil, poetry, and liturgy. It was personal, spontaneous, and deeply rooted in tradition. Casper describes the experience as one of the most significant spiritual moments of his life — and it happened outside any church, on a roof, between people who might never have met through conventional channels.

This encounter shaped Casper's conviction that ritual works faster than conversation alone. Shared rituals — even simple ones — create a felt sense of belonging that no amount of discussion can replicate. They mark time, create rhythm, and bind people to each other and to a place.

He put this into practice with Solstice in the Park, a public gathering in Brooklyn that brings neighbors together for workshops on meditation, embroidery, bird symbolism, and seasonal reflection. The event partners with the Brooklyn Public Library and draws immigrant educators alongside lifelong residents. It's not a religious service. It's a communal marking of time — an acknowledgment that the seasons turn and that we turn together.

Casper's thinking about community centers on three practices that function as relational technology. The first is ritual — structured, repeated actions that create belonging faster and deeper than informal socializing. The second is hospitality — and not just the passive kind. Casper talks about making people feel explicitly invited and wanted, countering the assumption that an open door is enough. The third is covenant — a dynamic, relational commitment that is sustained by love rather than enforced by rules.

These ideas found a home in The Dinner Party, co-founded by Lennon Flowers, which gathers small groups of people around shared meals and shared losses. What started as a space for grief became a model for how intimate gatherings — organized around vulnerability rather than networking — can form deep bonds.

Casper's work suggests that the most powerful relational technologies may be the oldest ones: a blessing, a shared meal, a seasonal gathering, a commitment to show up again. The innovation isn't in the form but in the willingness to practice these things in places and with people that institutions have stopped reaching. On a Brooklyn rooftop, between a nun and a none, a tradition found a new carrier — and a community found its rhythm.
items.summary: A gathering called "Nuns and Nones" brought together Catholic Sisters and unaffiliated millennials. On a Brooklyn rooftop, a nun blessed a community ritualist with oil, poetry, and liturgy — one of the most significant spiritual moments of his life. The takeaway: ritual works faster than conversation alone.
items.title: Nuns, Nones, and Sacred Hospitality

items.body:
Folks in the Outer Sunset kept asking for a self-guided history walking tour. The idea showed up multiple times in neighborhood meeting notes, so one neighbor decided to stop workshopping and start building. Inspired by a local history archive and some futures-thinking work, he sketched out a past / present / future experience with his daughter on a rainy afternoon — and by the next day there was a working first version at outersunset.place.

The app organizes hyperlocal content — old photos, present-day stories, and neighbors' visions for the future — around a map of the neighborhood. The primary navigation mechanic is a "Past / Present / Future" toggle that frames each place as part of a living continuum. Within a week, neighbors were contributing photos from the 1950s, sharing stories about longtime businesses, and imagining what a vacant lot could become. A retired teacher offered to narrate audio segments; a local shop owner asked to be featured.

What started as a simple walking guide became a relational tool — a way for neighbors to see each other's knowledge, memory, and imagination layered onto the same few blocks. The builder shared daily updates with a small network of fellow builders, and the feedback loop between building, sharing, and co-creating with neighbors made the project richer at every step. It's a vivid example of what happens when you build technology that starts from a real request, stays close to home, and invites contribution rather than consumption.
items.summary: A neighbor built a walking guide app for the Outer Sunset that connects local history, present-day life, and future visions — all within a few blocks of home.
items.title: Outer Sunset Field Guide

attribution.name: Logan Square Neighborhood Association's parent mentors — and Leticia Barrera's generation of leaders
attribution.source: Parent Engagement Institute; Institute for Educational Leadership; Soo Hong, 'A Cord of Three Strands'

items.body:
In 1995, Chicago's Logan Square Neighborhood Association — schooled by years of anti-displacement fights — launched a program disarming in its simplicity: parents work two hours a day in their children's classrooms, a hundred-plus hours a semester, with a stipend, and weekly training that mixes instructional practice with community-organizing skills.

The classroom hours are real work. But the program's engine is the ladder underneath: parent mentors — mostly Latina and Black mothers, many of whom had never been asked to lead anything — went on to run campaigns for community learning centers, school annexes to relieve overcrowding, and immigrant-family protections. Many became LSNA organizers and staff; Leticia Barrera, a former parent mentor, rose to direct the program itself.

The model replicated the way good organizing does: the Southwest Organizing Project picked it up in 2004; the resulting Parent Engagement Institute won a million dollars in state funding its first year; and by spring 2019, 925 parent mentors in 117 schools across 30 organizations had won $3.5 million from the Illinois legislature to sustain the work.

What it teaches: this is the ladder of engagement built as a program — supporter to team member to leader, with a paid, structured first rung. It answers 'are we stronger now?' with a roster: every cohort leaves the neighborhood with dozens more people who know how to run a meeting, make a hard ask, and move an institution. The schools got help; the neighborhood got organizers.

metadata.source_note: Program design and replication figures per the Parent Engagement Institute's own history and the Institute for Educational Leadership profile.

items.summary: Logan Square Neighborhood Association put parents — mostly Latina and Black mothers — into classrooms two hours a day, with organizing training on the side. Many became organizers, and 925 mentors across 117 schools won millions in state funding.
items.title: Parent Mentors: The Program Where the Win Is the People

attribution.name: Alderman Joe Moore, the residents of Rogers Park & the Participatory Budgeting Project
attribution.source: Participedia; NPR; the 49th Ward's own PB record

items.body:
In November 2009, Alderman Joe Moore of Chicago's 49th Ward (Rogers Park) did something no US elected official had done: he turned his entire $1.3 million annual 'menu money' infrastructure budget over to his constituents, working with the Participatory Budgeting Project to adapt the process born in Porto Alegre, Brazil.

The process was the technology: neighborhood assemblies where anyone could propose; six resident committees that spent the winter developing 36 proposals with cost estimates; then a public vote in April 2010 — 1,652 residents — funding fourteen projects: sidewalk repairs, bike lanes, community gardens, underpass murals, street lighting, dog-friendly park areas. The digital layer stayed thin, and the documented weakness was relational, not technical: outreach missed much of the ward's Latino population, the same inclusion lesson E-Democracy learned two states away.

PB then scaled: New York City council districts have run it since 2012 — over $210 million allocated across 706 projects — with the free, open-source Stanford PB Platform (a tool on this shelf) providing multilingual digital ballots. The Participatory Budgeting Project publishes free toolkits, and People Powered maintains a global hub and atlas.

What it teaches: PB is a repeatable neighborhood-scale democratic ritual with free tooling at every step — and its failure mode is always outreach, never software. Budget for door-knocking before ballots.

metadata.source_note: Vote counts and project list per Participedia case 43; PBNYC totals per People Powered/NYC Council.

items.summary: In 2009, a Chicago alderman handed his entire $1.3M infrastructure budget to residents: assemblies, resident committees, 36 proposals, 1,652 voters, 14 projects built. The ritual mattered more than the tech.
items.title: The 49th Ward: America's First Participatory Budget

items.body:
In 2007, in Ithaca, New York, Lesley Greene and her husband were playing ukuleles on their front steps when a neighbor — Gretchen Hildreth — walked by. They got to talking about how nice it was to hear music outside. They looked around their neighborhood of Fall Creek and realized there were so many musicians living nearby that there could practically be a festival of outdoor music. After months of saying they should do it, they did. In September of that year, they gathered twenty bands and created Porchfest — a free, un-curated music festival played on the front porches, driveways, and lawns of a residential neighborhood.

There are no tickets. No stages. No paid performers. No curated lineup — anyone who signs up before the deadline and has a porch to play on is in. You don't have to prove yourself to anyone. People walk, bike, push strollers, or drive golf carts from porch to porch, discovering music they'd never seek out and meeting neighbors they'd never otherwise encounter. For years, Lesley and Gretchen funded it out of pocket. Eventually, Ithaca Neighborhood Housing Services provided sponsorship support. But Porchfest stayed stubbornly grassroots — organized by volunteers, powered by donated time, dependent on nothing but porches and people.

What started as a small event in one neighborhood has become an internationally recognized model. There are now over 230 Porchfests worldwide, including in Australia and Canada. The spread happens person to person — someone attends in Ithaca, moves somewhere else, and starts one. Porchfest is a nearly perfect piece of relational technology. It requires no special infrastructure, no budget, no permissions beyond neighborly goodwill. It turns the porch — the architectural threshold between private life and public space — into a stage for connection. The music is the medium, but the message is: we live here together.
items.summary: In 2007, two ukulele-playing neighbors in Ithaca created Porchfest — a free music festival played on front porches that has spread to over 230 locations worldwide.
items.title: Porchfest, Ithaca to Everywhere

attribution.name: Red Hook Initiative's Digital Stewards; Detroit Community Technology Project (Diana Nucera, director)
attribution.source: Technical.ly; Hour Detroit; Wikipedia (Red Hook Wi-Fi)

items.body:
The Red Hook Initiative — a youth nonprofit in a low-lying, geographically isolated Brooklyn neighborhood dominated by the Red Hook Houses — began building a small rooftop mesh network in November 2011 with the Open Technology Institute, running open-source firmware, maintained by local young people.

Eleven months later Hurricane Sandy drowned the neighborhood's power, phone, and internet. The little mesh stayed up. RHI's building became the hub where neighbors charged phones and reached relief — and FEMA connected its satellite links *into* the community's network to reach residents. In the aftermath, the improvised arrangement formalized into the **Digital Stewards** program: neighborhood young adults paid and trained to build, test, and maintain the network, which expanded with solar-powered rooftop nodes and still operates.

Detroit's Community Technology Project scaled the same model citywide: its Equitable Internet Initiative trains and pays digital stewards — residents like Monique Tate in the North End and Nyasia Valdez in Southwest Detroit — to run neighborhood wireless networks anchored by trusted local institutions, with curricula published for anyone to reuse.

What it teaches: resilience is a social outcome. The network mattered in disaster because a trusted neighborhood institution owned it and local people were paid stewards of it. The remixable unit is not the routers — it's the steward role.

metadata.source_note: Sandy events and FEMA connection per Wikipedia's sourced entry and Inverse; Detroit stewards named per Hour Detroit's profiles.

items.summary: A Brooklyn youth nonprofit started a rooftop mesh network in 2011. When Hurricane Sandy knocked out everything else, the neighborhood-owned WiFi stayed up — and FEMA plugged into it, not the other way around.
items.title: Red Hook WiFi: The Network That Held When Sandy Hit

items.body:
In 2009, Martine Postma — a Dutch journalist who had been writing about sustainability and waste reduction — attended an art exhibition on repair and was so inspired that she organized the world's first Repair Cafe in Amsterdam. The idea was simple: create a free, neighborhood gathering where people could bring broken items — toasters, lamps, bicycles, clothes, laptops — and fix them together with the help of volunteer repair specialists, all over coffee and conversation. Postma's insight was that repair had become invisible. People threw things away not because items couldn't be fixed, but because repair felt inconvenient, expensive, and socially unmoored — something your grandfather did, not something your neighborhood did together. She wanted to make repair attractive again: available around the corner, cheaper than buying new, and fun.

The first Repair Cafe's success prompted Postma to start Repair Cafe International Foundation in 2011, providing support to groups worldwide wanting to start their own. The movement grew to over 2,000 Repair Cafes across 37 countries. Together, they prevented roughly 420,000 kilograms of waste in 2019 alone — about 10 million kilograms of CO2. But the environmental numbers, while impressive, don't capture what actually happens at a Repair Cafe. A person brings in a broken coffee machine. A retired electrician opens it up, explains what went wrong, and shows the owner how to fix it. Over the course of thirty minutes, knowledge is transferred, a relationship is formed, and a person walks away not just with a working machine but with a shifted sense of what's possible.

As Postma says, "Once you have experienced the possibilities of repair yourself, you will start to think differently." The Repair Cafe is relational technology disguised as environmental activism — or perhaps it's environmental activism that works precisely because it's relational.
items.summary: In 2009, Martine Postma organized the first Repair Cafe in Amsterdam — free neighborhood gatherings where people fix broken items together over coffee.
items.title: Repair Cafe

attribution.name: De'Amon Harges & Rev. Mike Mather, Broadway United Methodist Church
attribution.source: Faith & Leadership, 'Death and resurrection of an urban church'; Mather, 'Having Nothing, Possessing Everything' (2018)

items.body:
Broadway United Methodist Church had run the programs a shrinking urban church is supposed to run — a summer program serving 250 kids a day among them. Then nine young men died violently within four blocks in nine months, some of them program alumni. Pastor Mike Mather's verdict on his own good works was blunt: 'We felt so good about it that I broke my arm patting myself on the back.' A parishioner pointed at the food pantry's intake form: it asked, in effect, *how poor are you?* — and never asked anyone what they were good at.

So the church inverted itself. It retired the pantry, the tutoring program, the summer program, and the thrift shop — thanked in worship with 'well done, good and faithful servants' — and in 2004 hired De'Amon Harges, a neighbor, as its first **roving listener**: paid not to deliver services but to walk block by block discovering what people could do. 'I was curious about what was good in people, and that was what I was going to find out.' The craft: **name** the gift, **bless** it, **connect** it.

What the listening surfaced: Adele, a pantry regular, opened a restaurant within eighteen months. Forty-five backyard gardeners, convened over dinner with no agenda, started meeting monthly and planning a farmers market in a food desert. Sunday-school rooms became a dance studio, a pottery shop, and catering startups in the church's licensed kitchen. An 'Abundance Fund' paid neighbors for their gifts — a baker paid to bake for a sick neighbor, a woman paid to sing at a bus stop, until a funeral home hired her. Since 2008, the Jubilee summer program has hired neighborhood teenagers as junior roving listeners; Harges went on to co-found The Learning Tree, applying the practice across near-northwest Indianapolis.

What it teaches: the deepest resource question isn't what a neighborhood needs — it's who has been waiting to be asked.

metadata.source_note: All named outcomes per Faith & Leadership's long profile and Mather's book excerpt; Harges is now ABCD Institute faculty.

items.summary: Broadway UMC in Indianapolis shut down its food pantry, tutoring, and summer programs — and hired neighbor De'Amon Harges to walk the blocks discovering talents instead of needs. The neighborhood answered with restaurants, gardens, and a dance studio.
items.title: The Roving Listener

attribution.name: Fred Ross Sr., Cesar Chavez & the Community Service Organization
attribution.source: Cesar Chavez Foundation; Gabriel Thompson, 'America's Social Arsonist' (UC Press, 2016)

items.body:
Fred Ross Sr. spent the late 1940s organizing Mexican-American communities across Southern California for the Community Service Organization, refining a deceptively simple instrument: the **house meeting** — a small gathering in someone's living room, hosted by a resident who invites their own people. Cycles of house meetings built toward a big organizing meeting, then a founding convention. The living room did two things a rally never could: it let an organizer talk with people inside real trust networks, and it revealed leaders — you watched who convened people, who spoke with authority in their own kitchen. The CSO's proof of power came fast: roughly a thousand members and 15,000 newly registered voters in East L.A., and in 1949 Edward Roybal became the first Mexican-American on the Los Angeles City Council since the nineteenth century.

In spring 1952, Ross arrived in Sal Si Puedes — 'get out if you can' — a barrio of East San Jose, and a public-health nurse pointed him to Cesar Chavez, a 25-year-old Navy veteran. Chavez, assuming Ross was another patronizing outsider, arranged for the June 9 house meeting in his own home to be interrupted so he'd have an exit. Instead he was captivated — by an approach built on listening to people, engaging what they actually cared about, and moving them to act together. Ross wrote in his journal that night: *'I think I've found the guy I've been looking for.'*

Chavez became a CSO organizer; Ross soon recruited Dolores Huerta in Stockton, whose CSO lobbying won pensions for some fifty thousand non-citizen farmworkers. The lineage is literal: Ross trained Chavez and Huerta; the union they built trained Marshall Ganz; Ganz's framework trained a generation. One living room at a time.

metadata.place: Sal Si Puedes, East San Jose, California
metadata.source_note: House-meeting method and Roybal registration figures per the Zinn Education Project and PBS SoCal; the June 9, 1952 meeting and Ross journal line per the Cesar Chavez Foundation and Beyond Chron; Huerta's pension win per the Dolores Huerta Foundation.

items.summary: In 1952, organizer Fred Ross came to a San Jose barrio called 'Get Out If You Can.' A 25-year-old named Cesar Chavez arranged to have the house meeting in his own home interrupted so he'd have an excuse to leave. He stayed.
items.title: Sal Si Puedes: The House Meeting That Found Cesar Chavez

items.body:
Savannah Kruger and her partner Jon Bo lived in a 31-unit apartment building in Boulder, Colorado, and knew almost nobody in it. The loneliness of proximity — surrounded by neighbors but disconnected from all of them — was the starting condition for what became a small experiment in neighborhood building. They made cute flyers with handwritten sticky notes and knocked on every door in the building. Fifteen people came to the first picnic potluck in the park. After the gathering, Jon asked the group to start a group thread — they tried Discord, then landed on WhatsApp — and what had been a one-time event became an ongoing fabric of connection.

Neighbors began coordinating events, planning impromptu hangouts, watering each other's plants, giving away things they no longer needed, and helping each other with everyday crises like getting locked out or needing a car jump-started. The simple act of knocking on doors and hosting a potluck had unlocked a small but real ecosystem of mutual support. The journey of neighborhood building can be lonely, and Savannah found that while the work was deeply rewarding, she craved peers who were doing similar things in their own places. So she created the Neighborhood Accelerator — a cohort-based program for people trying to build community where they live.

The first cohort drew participants from across the Supernuclear readership — a community of people interested in co-living and neighborhood design. When Savannah shared three case studies from the program, the response was overwhelming: fifty applications poured in for the next round, and the second cohort grew to thirty to thirty-five neighborhood stewards. What Savannah's story illustrates is that the hardest step in neighborhood building is often the first one — the willingness to knock on a door and say, essentially, "I live here too, and I'd like to know you." The technology is a flyer, a group chat, and a potluck. The innovation is the courage to use them.
items.summary: Savannah Kruger and her partner lived in a 31-unit building knowing nobody — until cute flyers and a potluck unlocked a community.
items.title: Savannah Kruger and The Neighborhood Accelerator, Boulder

items.body:
When back-to-back blizzards dropped nearly three feet of snow on Washington DC in February 2010 and shut the federal government, Ryan Ozimek — a Dupont Circle resident who ran a nonprofit-sector web firm — stood up an Ushahidi deployment to coordinate his neighborhood's dig-out. 'I really thought it was going to be just a fun experiment with my friends.'

Within a day the Washington Post had adopted and promoted it as 'Snowmageddon Cleanup.' Ozimek watched the arc every mutual aid organizer knows: the first twenty-four hours were all requests — stuck cars, unplowed streets, elderly neighbors snowed in — and then neighbors began self-organizing to answer them, claiming requests the way Bed-Stuy Strong volunteers would claim Airtable tickets a decade later.

The remix proved the pattern: during December 2010's storm, versions launched for New York, Boston, Newark, and Point Pleasant Beach, New Jersey — a new city could stand one up **in under an hour**.

What it teaches: the purest documented case of this shelf's thesis. Global open-source infrastructure (built for Kenyan election monitoring), deployed by one neighbor for one neighborhood in a weekend, made real by a trusted local channel pointing people at it. The map did the matching; the shovels were already on the block.

metadata.source_note: Quotes and remix timeline per PBS NewsHour's contemporaneous reporting.

items.summary: During DC's 2010 blizzards, one Dupont Circle resident stood up an Ushahidi map to coordinate digging out. The Washington Post pointed the city at it — and the next winter, other cities launched their own in under an hour.
items.title: Snowmageddon Cleanup: One Neighbor, One Weekend, One Map

attribution.name: newDemocracy Foundation / South Australia Nuclear Fuel Cycle Engagement

items.body:
In 2016, the government of South Australia faced a question most politicians would rather avoid: should the state accept and store nuclear waste from other countries? A Royal Commission had produced a 318-page report recommending it. But the government knew that no one would actually read the report, and that public comment would be dominated by polarized activists on both sides. So they tried something different. Working with the newDemocracy Foundation, they designed the largest citizens' jury ever attempted in Australia — randomly selecting everyday residents to do what parliaments struggle to do: deliberate honestly on a question with no easy answer.

The process unfolded in two stages. First, a jury of fifty randomly selected South Australians — drawn from 25,000 invitation letters sent to random households — spent weeks distilling the Royal Commission's dense report into a few pages of accessible summary that anyone could understand. Then a second jury of 350 randomly selected citizens convened for six days of deliberation in Adelaide. They heard from expert witnesses, asked questions, debated in small groups, and wrestled with the tradeoffs. In the end, two-thirds voted against pursuing nuclear waste storage, citing a lack of trust in government processes as their primary concern. The Premier accepted the verdict. The technical and economic arguments for storage may have been strong, but the jury had surfaced something the Royal Commission couldn't: the relational deficit between government and citizens that made the proposal untenable.

The newDemocracy Foundation was candid about what didn't work. At 350 people, the jury was far larger than the typical twelve to fifty participants. Factions formed more easily. The timeline felt compressed. Some jurors in the larger second group reported less satisfaction than those in the intimate first jury. But those honest reckonings became some of the most valuable contributions to the field. The foundation published detailed research notes on every friction point — and other practitioners around the world used them to design better processes. The South Australia jury proved that citizens, given time and good information, can grapple with enormously complex questions. It also proved that the design of deliberation matters as much as the question being deliberated — and that the willingness to say what went wrong is itself a form of democratic practice.
items.summary: When South Australia considered storing nuclear waste from other countries, the government convened the largest citizens' jury in Australian history — 350 randomly selected residents who deliberated for six days and surfaced the relational deficit between government and citizens that made the proposal untenable.
items.title: South Australia Citizens' Jury on Nuclear Waste

items.body:
In 2012, Joseph Ficalora did something improbable in Bushwick, Brooklyn. He started inviting street artists — from around the world, from the legendary New York graffiti scene, and from the neighborhood itself — to paint the walls of industrial buildings along Troutman Street and St. Nicholas Avenue. The project was personal. In 1991, when Joseph was twelve, his father Ignazio was murdered on the way home from the family steel fabrication business — killed for a few dollars and a gold chain. Years later, his mother died after a four-year battle with a brain tumor. The Bushwick Collective became Joseph's way of healing from a childhood spent in a neighborhood marked by crime and neglect — by transforming the very walls that had surrounded him.

The murals are temporary by design — each one lasts about twelve months before being replaced. Artists are not paid; these are permission murals, not commissions. What started as a personal project of healing and beautification became a catalyst for neighborhood transformation. Industrial blocks became vibrant outdoor galleries. The annual Block Party draws thousands of people and produces dozens of new installations in a single weekend. The Bushwick Collective helped shift Bushwick's identity from a place defined by its deficits to one known for creativity and vitality.

The transformation hasn't been without tension. Rising rents followed the cultural energy, pushing out longtime residents — sometimes including the artists whose work made the neighborhood attractive. The Bushwick Collective sits at the intersection of placemaking and gentrification, beauty and displacement — a tension that any community builder working in changing neighborhoods must reckon with. But at its core, the Collective demonstrates that public art, created in relationship between artists and a place, can change how a neighborhood sees itself and is seen by others.
items.summary: In 2012, Joseph Ficalora began inviting street artists to paint industrial walls in Bushwick — transforming a neighborhood marked by loss into a vibrant outdoor gallery.
items.title: The Bushwick Collective, Brooklyn

items.body:
Growing up in Pittsburgh, D.J. Trischler noticed something interesting: the entire city was dressed in black and gold. Police cars, fire trucks, sports teams, bridges. Two regular old colors creating social cohesion across a whole city. That observation planted a seed. As a graphic designer and University of Cincinnati professor, D.J. started asking: how might we use design to connect people to their local ecologies?

He'd been sitting on the idea of a one-page printed newsletter for his block for years. Then earlier this year, there was a shooting on his street in Cincinnati. He saw two paths: everyone could close up their houses and buy cameras, or they could come together. He chose together.

The Claypole Commons is a hand-designed print newsletter for 25 houses — just his block. But it's not about the people. D.J. didn't want anyone to feel pressure to perform neighborliness. Instead, the newsletter is about the land they share: the cardinals that start chirping at 6:30 in the morning, the rooster that crows at 6:00, the goldenrods about to bloom and the asters coming soon. Recently, he stamped every copy with ink made from the pokeberry bush in his backyard — connecting each neighbor to the specific ecology of their shared place.

The newsletter became an invitation for conversation. Neighbors started approaching D.J. to ask about sunflower seeds or how to grow certain plants. He and his wife began hosting monthly events on the street. For "Meet the Chickens," they made a hand-printed poster and invited neighbors over to meet three new hens. Together — no vote, just natural consensus — they named the chickens Richard, Dolly, and Penny.

The changes have been tangible. A WhatsApp group formed. One neighbor started sharing footage from a bird feeder camera. People ask for sugar, check in after storms, report loose dogs. D.J. discovered his neighbor can fix bikes — after the neighbor started bringing compost to their pile. When D.J. offered to pay him back, the neighbor said something like: "We just love being a part of the ecology here. We think we want to get bees so we can contribute to the street."

There is something radical in what's happening on Claypole Avenue: choosing slowness over efficiency, thinking small over dreaming big, designing for a particular place rather than any place. The newsletter is becoming a cohesive symbol — like Pittsburgh's black and gold, but for 25 houses. People are starting to see themselves in it. D.J. describes it simply: he's designing inside his community, for inside his community.

When asked why this slow, small, hyper-local work matters, D.J. doesn't claim to be radical. He says he's most excited about seeing monarch caterpillars on his milkweed plants, about neighbors exchanging eggs or baked goods or seeds instead of buying them. Going slow invites more people in and lets small victories build on each other.

As D.J. puts it, sometimes it feels like the commons still exist — those old shared places where you found firewood, planted a garden, met your neighbors. Maybe, on Claypole Avenue, they do.
items.summary: A hand-designed print newsletter for just 25 houses on one block in Cincinnati, focused not on the people but on the land they share — cardinals, goldenrods, a neighbor's rooster. What started as a response to a shooting became monthly events, a WhatsApp group, and neighbors exchanging eggs, seeds, and bike repairs.
items.title: The Claypole Commons
