attribution.name: Tonika Lewis Johnson, Visual Artist and Community Connector

items.body:
Chicago's North and South Sides have corresponding street addresses — the same numbers, mirrored across the city's dividing line. But the neighborhoods at those matching addresses often couldn't be more different. Decades of segregation, disinvestment, and policy created two Chicagos living side by side on paper but worlds apart in reality.

Tonika Lewis Johnson, a visual artist from the South Side's Englewood neighborhood, started the Folded Map Project to make this visible — and then to do something about it. The project begins with photography: Tonika captures side-by-side images of corresponding addresses on the North and South Sides. A house at 6700 North next to its mirror at 6700 South. The visual contrast tells a story no policy paper can: the same city, vastly unequal.

But the project doesn't stop at images. Tonika introduces the people who live at these mirrored addresses — "map twins" — to each other. They meet, visit each other's neighborhoods, share meals, and see each other's daily reality up close. The relationships that form aren't symbolic. They're real encounters between real people who happen to share a number but not a lived experience.

The Folded Map Project has been embraced by the City of Chicago, which partnered with Tonika to distribute action kits. The project has been featured at galleries, community spaces, and public events, but its core engine is intimate: two people, two neighborhoods, one conversation at a time.

What makes Folded Map a piece of relational technology is that the photographs aren't the point — the relationships are. The images create an occasion for encounter. They give people a reason to cross boundaries they'd otherwise never cross. They turn abstract inequality into something personal and proximate.

For relational technologists, the Folded Map offers a pattern: use what a place already has (its geography, its structure, its hidden symmetries) to create connection. Don't build from scratch — fold the map, and see who's been standing across from you all along.
items.summary: Chicago's North and South Sides have mirrored street addresses but vastly different realities. Artist Tonika Lewis Johnson photographs corresponding addresses side by side, then introduces the people living at those "map twin" locations to each other — turning abstract inequality into something personal and proximate.
items.title: The Folded Map

items.body:
In Brownsville, Brooklyn — home to about 100,000 people and the largest concentration of public housing in North America — Teju Ravilochan founded GatherFor on a deceptively simple belief: in community, we have everything we need.

GatherFor organizes neighbors into two kinds of teams. Neighbor teams are groups of five who form a kind of chosen family. They meet regularly, share stories, and become friends. Over time, they wind up watching each other's kids, pooling funds to pay bills, visiting each other in the hospital, helping each other find jobs. GatherFor supports them with $300 a month for in-person gatherings and a matched savings practice called Susu — a Caribbean tradition where everyone pools money and gives the whole amount to one person on a rotating basis.

Then there are action teams — groups focused on a shared neighborhood challenge like housing, mental health, childcare, or entrepreneurship, each with a $5,000 budget.

But the story that best captures GatherFor's approach is the Kindness Party.

Teju was invited to speak at a tenant association meeting for Glenmore Plaza, one of the big housing projects. The room was full of angry residents. One woman told a story about a grab bar in her bathroom that had rotted so badly it came out of the wall — she fell, hit her head, and needed brain surgery. Others nodded. Repairs hadn't been made in years.

When it was Teju's turn, he set aside his prepared remarks and just asked questions. Had they tried speaking to the housing authority with a single voice? They hadn't. Trust was low. People were afraid.

A mentor told Teju that a great way to build trust is to help people with their actual issues. So he went back and proposed they organize together to hold NYCHA accountable. Most people were skeptical. But eight residents — out of fifty — were willing to try.

They went door-to-door collecting repair requests and documented everything in a big spreadsheet. Then came the creative turn. Inspired by a friend who had organized a block party to bridge a conflict, Teju proposed: instead of yelling at NYCHA, what if they celebrated the agency for doing the right thing? They brought NYCHA the spreadsheet and said: make these repairs within three months, and we'll throw a block party in your honor, with press and community. We'll celebrate you.

NYCHA accepted. They made 1,600 repairs in 60 days — 87% of what residents had requested. Since then, they've made over 5,000 repairs. Teju calls it "accountability through celebration" — not making anyone the villain, but offering a deadline, a team, and recognition. The carrot, the stick, and the teamwork together produced something none of them could alone.

What Teju wants people to understand is that this work isn't extraordinary. It comes down to capacities we all have: being present, listening, sharing stories, asking questions. In community, we have everything we need.
items.summary: In Brownsville, Brooklyn — home to the largest concentration of public housing in North America — GatherFor organizes neighbors into chosen-family teams and action groups. When NYCHA repairs went unmade for years, they proposed "accountability through celebration": make the repairs, and we'll throw a block party in yo…
items.title: The Kindness Party

items.body:
It started as a refrain. Every time someone asked Sam Pressler, "What's one thing any community could do right now to strengthen local civic life?" he'd say some version of: every community should offer microgrants for neighbors to gather their neighbors. Block parties, barbecues, neighborhood olympics — whatever. The important thing is to get neighbors out interacting.

He said it so many times he became convinced of it himself. So in early 2024, on a bit of a whim, he launched a microgrant pilot in Charlottesville, Virginia. With $3,000 from a fellowship at UVA's Karsh Institute of Democracy and three volunteers, they built the entire initiative from scratch: a simple application (3-5 minutes to fill out), same-day funding approval, a toolkit with a checklist and facilitation guide, and a lightweight reporting form.

They distributed $100 microgrants to 30 different hosts representing 25 neighborhoods across the area. Those hosts brought together roughly 500 neighbors. A local resident had predicted they'd be lucky to get five hosts. They got 70 applications.

The variety was one of the biggest surprises. About half hosted shared meals. Others organized block parties, seed-starting events in the spirit of spring, gatherings for parents of young children, and — memorably — one beer tasting for 20+ people whose host reported three key takeaways: people like tasting beers, people like sharing food, people like doing both together.

The framework that emerged was simple but powerful: permission, accountability, commitment. The official microgrant gave hosts permission — an excuse to overcome inertia or shyness or post-pandemic withdrawal. The $100 created accountability — once you've received money, you can't easily back out. And the facilitation guide prompted hosts to close each gathering with a collective commitment, shifting the orientation from one-off event to beginning of something ongoing.

The commitments were specific. Neighbors pledged to host recurring potlucks, annual block parties, Shabbat dinners, and seasonal gatherings. Some committed to building a music stage for a neighborhood market, painting murals, or petitioning for speed bumps. Others started shared newsletters, photo albums, and neighborhood wikis. Nearly all of them followed through.

The pilot's most striking quality was its simplicity. No logic model. No five-year strategic plan. No rigorous reporting. Just a small amount of money, a basic toolkit, a few reminder emails, and trust that neighbors know how to bring their neighbors together.

The initiative has since expanded through a partnership with the Relational Tech Project, relaunching at withneighbors.org with $50 microgrants available nationally. The application is still simple: who you are, where you live, your best guess for a gathering date, and your proposed vision. The long-term hope is that local community foundations, nonprofits, and government offices will adopt and remix the model in their own places. If a self-described "goof" could make it work in a few months with $3,000, anyone can.
items.summary: With $3,000 and three volunteers, Sam Pressler launched a microgrant pilot in Charlottesville giving $100 to 30 hosts across 25 neighborhoods. They expected five applications and got 70. The framework: permission to overcome inertia, accountability from the money, and a commitment to do it again.
items.title: The Neighbor Gathering Microgrant

attribution.name: Dale King and Community, Portsmouth, OH

items.body:
Portsmouth, Ohio was ground zero of the opioid epidemic — the town where pill mills were invented. Factories had shut down, high-potency opioids were flooding in, and the community was devastated. By the mid-2000s, street corners were dangerous and hope was scarce.

Dale King grew up in Portsmouth, joined the Army after 9/11, did two tours in Iraq as a Special Forces intelligence officer, and came back around 2007. He opened a Saturday morning CrossFit workout he called "the Pain Clinic" — a play on the pill mills. Instead of coming in for oxy, you came in to throw kettlebells and barbells around. A different sort of pain.

At first, it wasn't about recovery. It was about giving people hope through something hard and shared. People from all different backgrounds — older, younger, wealthy, working-class — started showing up. The gym became a gathering space that happened to involve exercise.

Then Billy Dever appeared. Billy was a highly educated lawyer, the chief legal officer of a major recovery center in the region, a former addict himself, and an incredible athlete. He had an idea: what if the gym — which was already building community and purpose — could serve people in recovery? Billy led the charge of bringing CrossFit into the recovery center's in-patient treatment. People who had overdosed on Friday were doing workouts by Monday.

The documentary Small Town Strong, directed by veteran filmmaker Chase Millsap, captured what happened next. They filmed characters going through their transformation — from day zero in treatment, to getting sober, to getting jobs, becoming community leaders, and competing as athletes. Sarah Wilson, who had overdosed nine times, tells her own story of transformation through CrossFit and community across the film.

What made Dale's gym different was the radical mixing. Millionaires worked out alongside people who lived in trailers. People coming out of treatment joined the community gym rather than staying in recovery-only spaces. The stigma of "I used to be an addict, I can't come here" dissolved. People were no longer perceived as addicts but as members of the community. As Dale tells it, it doesn't matter where you came from — it's that you're here now, you're clean, you're sober, and you're healthy.

The tragic loss of Billy Dever to an accidental fentanyl overdose during the filming deepened the urgency of the story. Billy had been so instrumental in the community's comeback that the filmmakers knew they couldn't let it go untold.

What made Portsmouth's recovery remarkable was that the solution didn't come from Washington. Nobody from outside showed up with an answer. The town that invented the pill mills invented a way out, too. As Dale put it, you have to care that somebody in your neighborhood is dying. If you can start there, you can start seeing that we all have a responsibility for this whole thing. Community starts with a willingness to do something hard alongside someone — and saying "hi" after.
items.summary: Portsmouth, Ohio — ground zero of the opioid epidemic — found its way back through a Saturday morning CrossFit workout called "the Pain Clinic." A play on the pill mills, it became a gathering space where millionaires worked out alongside people from trailers, and people in recovery joined as community members, not pa…
items.title: The Pain Clinic

items.body:
In Philadelphia, Hillary Do runs BOLT — an organization built on a conviction that leaders already exist in every neighborhood, even (and especially) the ones that outsiders have written off.

BOLT supports grassroots leaders through two core programs. The School for Grassroots Leadership is an eight-month cohort that meets three hours every Saturday. It teaches the practical infrastructure of community work: fundraising, budgeting, fiscal sponsorship, hiring, navigating the resource ecosystem. The Youth Leaders Fellowship places 60 young people in paid summer internships, with academic-year training at partner schools where they lead peer-driven Community Action Projects.

But what makes BOLT distinctive is its ecosystem role — connecting grassroots leaders to each other and to systems of power they've often been shut out of. BOLT brings youth to City Hall to meet elected officials, many for the first time. It connects community leaders to funders who can open new financial streams. The goal isn't dependence on BOLT but building the capacity so leaders don't need BOLT long-term.

The people in BOLT's network are doing extraordinary, tangible work. Ron runs Ordinarie Heroes in North Philly. Danni leads Diamond Beauty Academy, a cosmetology program. Cleo leads A Home from Shana Foundation, helping families who've lost children to gun violence — before BOLT, she couldn't afford Ubers for grieving families to get to services; BOLT helped her get a fiscal sponsor and access real funding. Ryan runs As I Plant This Seed. These aren't programs designed in conference rooms. They're responses to real needs by people who live in the neighborhoods they serve.

Hillary pushes back against the idea that low-income neighborhoods lack leaders. The leaders are there. What they lack is infrastructure, connection, and resources. BOLT's philosophy is "going deep, not expanding" — working intensively in a small geography rather than spreading thin across a city. Scale, for BOLT, means depth.

One young person in the program — Mecca — was inspired by watching neighborhood people build from nothing. Now she wants to open an arts rec center and understands how to access the resources and support to do it. Young people in BOLT have higher school attendance than the district average.

Hillary's critique of drive-by solutions is sharp: too many programs treat communities as problems to be solved from the outside. BOLT's approach is different. If you want to understand a community, you should be invited to dinner — not parachute in with a plan. The leaders are already there, already working. The question is whether the rest of the system will recognize, resource, and connect them.
items.summary: In Philadelphia, BOLT supports grassroots leaders through an eight-month Saturday cohort and a youth fellowship placing 60 young people in paid internships. Their philosophy: low-income neighborhoods don't lack leaders — they lack infrastructure, connection, and resources. Scale means depth, not spread.
items.title: The School for Grassroots Leaders

items.body:
In 2006, Liz Joyner — a clinical social worker trained in family systems theory — had been volunteering in Tallahassee politics long enough to reach a conclusion: the way Americans work out their disagreements in public is fundamentally broken. Not because people disagree, but because they've lost the spaces and relationships that make disagreement productive. So she started the Village Square, a nonpartisan civic forum built on a deceptively simple premise: that the act of sharing a meal with someone you disagree with is itself a form of democratic infrastructure.

The signature program is Dinner at the Square, where 170 Tallahassee residents sit down together — a conservative Catholic priest and a liberal lesbian theatre owner might share the same table — and dive into structured conversations on contentious topics. Over nearly two decades, the Village Square has grown to more than thirty programs a year, partnering with local organizations across Tallahassee. Their programming ranges from "Speed Date Your Local Leaders" to the annual Tallahassee Town Hall to the "Club of Honest Citizens." The organization has expanded to six cities across America, training local teams to build their own Village Squares with ongoing support and infrastructure. Joyner's insight — rooted in her clinical training — is that political polarization behaves like a family systems problem: it escalates when people stop being in relationship, and it de-escalates when they start again.

What makes the Village Square different from most bridging organizations is its insistence on locality. It is not a national media campaign or a viral social media initiative. It is people in Tallahassee, in Sacramento, in other specific American cities, choosing to eat together and talk about hard things in the place where they actually live. Joyner often says that people are really hard to hate close up. The Village Square is a bet that deliberative democracy doesn't begin with policy papers or assemblies — it begins with proximity, a shared table, and the civic courage to stay in the room when the conversation gets uncomfortable.
items.summary: A clinical social worker in Tallahassee started a civic forum built on a simple premise: sharing a meal with someone you disagree with is itself a form of democratic infrastructure. Nearly two decades later, the Village Square has expanded to six American cities.
items.title: The Village Square, Tallahassee

items.body:
In early 2018, a local family in Granite Falls, Minnesota — a small town on the prairie — donated a vacant commercial building to the Department of Public Transformation, an artist-led nonprofit focused on rural revitalization through the arts. The family had been trying to sell the property on the private market without success. DoPT had been running a traveling nomadic theater company celebrating small-town life and was looking for a permanent home. A Granite Falls community member connected the two, and the building at 726 Prentice Street began its transformation into The Yes House.

What followed wasn't a conventional renovation. DoPT led Discovery Tours — walkthroughs of the empty space where community members were invited to dream about what it could become. Over four hundred people participated in these exercises, imagining the building as a theater venue, a youth recreation zone, an artist hub, a community gathering space. The programming and design emerged through a year-long community engagement process in which local residents collaborated with local and national artists and architects. The construction has been long and honest about its challenges. They've averaged about $130 per square foot — modest for the Upper Midwest — but COVID-era inflation pushed costs to nearly $200 per square foot. They launched a creative capital campaign in 2022, eventually raising the goal to over a million dollars. Along the way, they discovered that the space's versatility opened doors to unexpected funding — private health insurance companies funded the rock-climbing wall because of its ties to health and exercise.

In the fall of 2022, DoPT launched The Yes House Futures Committee to guide the building's operations through a community-led process, with local residents alongside staff and board members making decisions about stewardship. The Yes House is becoming what Granite Falls asked for — a place for theater, fitness, art, conversation, and gathering in a town where such spaces are rare. The project is also a case study in the messiness and beauty of community-led building: the slow timelines, the creative funding, the mistakes made and addressed, the ongoing negotiation between vision and reality. For rural communities, the Yes House suggests that the arts and community design aren't luxuries — they're infrastructure.
items.summary: A donated vacant building in a small prairie town became The Yes House — a community-designed space for theater, fitness, art, and gathering.
items.title: The Yes House, Granite Falls, Minnesota

items.body:
In 2009, a small group of people who ran a skills-sharing website called OurGoods — Rich Watts, Louise Ma, and Caroline Woolard — were given the opportunity to use a vacant shop on New York's Lower East Side. They had no budget and no institutional backing. What they had was an idea: a school where anyone could teach, and the price of attendance was a barter item the teacher requested. For just over a month, over 800 people participated in more than 70 classes. The barter items were playful and intimate — jars, music tips, vegetables, help finding an apartment. The classes ranged from sewing to sign language to web design. The only qualification for teaching was passion and knowledge. No credentials required.

What Trade School surfaced was a hunger not just for learning but for exchange that felt human. As co-founder Caroline Woolard observed, the expansion of Trade School chapters around the world may have been driven by the feeling that some things just don't work in a market economy — that people have a fundamental need for creativity, connection, and the dignity of having something to offer. The organizers insisted on horizontal governance: every Trade School chapter operated as a collective or cooperative. Trade School grew from one vacant storefront into a global network that ran for a decade, from 2009 to 2019. Chapters sprouted across the US, Canada, and beyond. They published a book documenting the project. And then they stopped.

The decision to end was as intentional as the decision to begin — a recognition that the form had run its course, and that clinging to an institution can become its own kind of extraction. What Trade School left behind is a model: that learning happens best in relationship, that everyone is an expert in something, and that the barter — the act of bringing something you have to offer — transforms a student into a participant.
items.summary: In 2009, a vacant shop on the Lower East Side became Trade School — where anyone could teach and attendance cost a barter item the teacher requested.
items.title: Trade School, New York to Everywhere

attribution.name: Radical xChange paper / CivicHall article on vTaiwan

items.body:
In 2014, Taiwan's Sunflower Movement — a wave of protests over controversial trade legislation with China — mobilized civil society in unprecedented ways. Among those who responded was g0v, a civic technology community founded in 2012 to promote digital transparency. Government minister Jaclyn Tsai attended a g0v hackathon and was so impressed that she invited the community to design a neutral platform for large-scale public deliberation. The result was vTaiwan.

At its heart was Polis — a tool developed by a Seattle-based team — which gathers, analyzes, and visually maps what large groups of people think, in real time. The design was deliberately counter to social media dynamics: users could agree or disagree with statements, or write their own, but they could not reply to each other. There were no threads, no arguments, no pile-ons. Instead, the system surfaced areas of consensus — the things people across different opinion clusters actually agreed on. Audrey Tang, a retired Silicon Valley entrepreneur and g0v cofounder, became the bridge between civic tech and government. Appointed as Minister without Portfolio in 2016 at age thirty-six — the youngest minister in Taiwan's history and the first non-binary person in cabinet — Tang championed vTaiwan as a new form of democratic infrastructure.

A defining success was Uber regulation. Initially, opinions were deeply polarized between taxi industry defenders and ride-sharing advocates. But as users revised their positions, consensus emerged around a level playing field. The government created new regulations informed by the consensus found on vTaiwan. At its peak, vTaiwan had roughly 200,000 users — about one percent of Taiwan's population — and held deliberations on 28 issues, 80 percent of which led to legislative action. The platform demonstrated that digital tools, designed with care for relational dynamics rather than engagement metrics, can help large groups of strangers find common ground. Taiwan's experiment suggests that the most important design choice in civic technology is what you don't build — no reply buttons, no virality, no outrage loops — as much as what you do.
items.summary: Taiwan's Sunflower Movement led to vTaiwan — a digital deliberation platform using Polis that surfaced consensus among 200,000 users on 28 issues.
items.title: vTaiwan and Digital Democracy

items.body:
Before prison, Gerrel Jones never thought of being beneficial to anybody. Raised in a hostile environment, he became a hedonist. When he arrived in prison with a life sentence, he attempted suicide. But a life sentence makes you contemplative. While studying psychology, he read Viktor Frankl's Man's Search for Meaning and a light came on: Frankl saved his life by investing in the people dying around him. That selflessness principle changed everything.

Gerrel started building cohorts in prison — little communities of discipleship that grew into larger communities called faith dorms. When he was released after 20 years, community-building was the only skill he had.

He bought a house in the Birmingham neighborhood with the highest number of homicides. Then he started doing what he'd learned inside: knocking on doors, hosting fish fries and yard parties, canvassing the neighborhood. His budget never exceeded $10,000 a year. But he was consistent. That consistency — from 2017 to 2022 — built Renew Birmingham.

The model works block by block. First, shrink the service area so you can actually cover it. Renew Birmingham serves about four neighborhoods, 8,000 to 12,000 people. Then aggressively bring access to people rather than waiting for them to show up. Canvass. Knock on doors. Phone bank.

The second piece is incentivizing neighbors to host. Renew will give someone $100 to invite 25 neighbors to their yard, then bring food, music, a tent, and case managers with them. The host becomes a neighborhood hero, and the yard becomes an access point for real services — housing, education, workforce development, health and wellness.

The third piece is sweat equity. Rather than just receiving services, neighbors barter volunteer effort at about $20 an hour. They earn credits they can use to pay a delinquent bill or get critical home repairs. The volunteering — canvassing, picking up trash, painting houses, attending school events — puts people in cohorts working toward a common goal. That's where accountability, responsibility, and community form.

When a drug dealer moved onto Gerrel's street, his elderly neighbor across the way raised the alarm. Gerrel went to the dealer's house, knocked on the door, introduced himself, and just talked. He didn't mention the dealing. He just let them know he was their neighbor. For a criminal, that kind of presence is uncomfortable — it disrupts the fear and intimidation they rely on. Ten days later, the dealers were gone.

Gerrel's theory is basic physics: if you mobilize the majority of people who want something good, the negative forces can't stay. You don't need a rebellion. You need positive spaces that crowd out the negative ones. As he puts it: compassion can't sit back and watch. Compassion is a participant in social change.

His advice to anyone interested in revitalizing a community: understand that it cannot be done from the outside. America has never seen a revitalization program that worked from the outside-in. You have to get your hands dirty, engage the affected population, and be consistent. It has to be done through you and the influence of your social capital — which is your time and attention.
items.summary: After 20 years in prison, Gerrel Jones bought a house in Birmingham's most violent neighborhood and started knocking on doors, hosting fish fries and yard parties. items.body:
A mobile web app for the shared bookshelf at Z-Space. Any member or anyone visiting the space can browse the ~100 book community library, borrow and return on the honor system, and grow the collection by donating their own books.

Screens
1. Browse (Home): Screen that helps you discover what’s available in the community library. It has an available/total counter and your avatar, a lime "Johnny's pick" hero card with a tilted cover, a scrollable horizontal "Recently added" cover rail, and finally the full catalog as genre bookshelves (spines on a shelf), switchable to grid or list via Tweaks.

Key decisions:
- The shelf metaphor is the default. Spines grouped by genre with a thick black shelf line mimic the real shelf in your space — browsing feels physical, not like a database. 
- Availability is ambient, not loud. A small 82/100 on shelf counter and tiny "Out" badges on covers — you can see the state of the library at a glance without it dominating.
- One featured book, hand-picked. "Johnny's pick" instead of an algorithmic carousel, it's a 100-book community library, so curation should feel personal.
- Procedural covers. Each book gets a bold typographic cover in the Z-Space palette, so the catalog looks cohesive without needing cover-art uploads.

2. Search: Screen that allows you to find a book in the library via search input (title/author, live), availability toggle (Everything / Available now / Out), scrollable genre chips.

Key decisions:
- Filters before typing. With only 100 books, most "searches" are really filters — "what design books are in right now?" is two taps, zero typing.
- "Available now" is a first-class filter. The most common real question at the shelf is "what can I actually take home today."
- Results are a list, not a grid — once you're searching, metadata (author, status, genre) matters more than visual browsing.

3. Book Detail: Screen that gives details on one Book. It shows a large tilted cover, title, author,  year, a status card, one big CTA (Borrow / Return / Checked out), genre/pages/year meta strip, a History timeline showing who has it now, everyone who has read it, and who initially donated the book.

Key decisions:
- One CTA, state-dependent. Borrow if it's in, Return if you have it, disabled "Checked out" if someone else does. No reserve/hold queue — honor system, keep it simple
- Lightly social by design. You see who has the book and who has previously taken it out (so you can walk over and ask), but there's no messaging, nudging, or due-date shaming.
- The timeline is the book's biography. Newest → oldest: current holder ("Now" badge) → past readers → the donor with a pink "+" badge. It quietly celebrates contribution and gives books provenance — and replaced reviews, which you flagged as too complex.

4. Add a Book (the FAB on the main screen): Screen that allows anyone to add a new book to the library. It shows an amber "Donate a book" banner, URL field (Goodreads/Bookshop), title, author, genre chips, "Add to library" button, a success screen ("On the shelf!") that tells you to physically drop the book off.

Key decisions:
- URL instead of photo upload, a link does the work of cover art and metadata without a camera flow.
- Can import details from link / goodreads if available
- Four fields, one screen, no wizard. Donating should take 30 seconds; the banner copy says exactly that.
- The success state bridges digital → physical: "Go drop it off at the library corner" closes the loop with the real shelf.

5. My Shelf: Screen that shows what you have read / donated in the library. It shows a dark profile card (name, "member since") · three stat tiles (Out now / Read / Added) · "Currently borrowed" cards with how long you've had each book · a rail of books you've donated · "Previously read" history.

Key decisions:
- "Currently borrowed" is the top job. The honor system has no due dates, so a gentle "Since 3 weeks ago" timestamp is the only nudge to return things — visibility instead of enforcement.
- Contribution is a stat. "Added" sits beside "Read" — donating books is as celebrated as reading them.
- No streaks or gamification. Stats are a quiet record, not a leaderboard.

items.body:
Cobudget emerged in 2014 from the Enspiral network and The Borderland's experiments in collaborative funding: give every member a slice of the group's shared money and let them allocate it across member-proposed 'buckets' (projects), in three visible stages — dream, fund, realize. It's participatory budgeting stripped of municipal ceremony: no ballots, just continuous, transparent allocation.

Deployments range from Stockholm's Blivande creative hub (members deciding together which workshop tools to buy) to WWF Switzerland's climate funding rounds in six figures. The software is AGPL-3.0-or-later, with a free hosted tier for small groups and self-hosting for the rest.

For neighborhoods, the fit is exact: block associations, garden clubs, and mutual aid funds all hold small shared money with no legible way to decide on it. Cobudget's real product is legitimacy — everyone can see every idea, every allocation, and every receipt.

**Neighborhood remix:** the block's yard-sale $500 lives in Cobudget; anyone can propose a bucket — mulch, a projector for movie night, gas money for the neighbor who drives elders to appointments — and the funding *is* the vote.

items.body:
"A guaranteed income, guaranteed by your community." Neighbors each contribute a percentage of their monthly income and redistribute it equally — directly, person to person, no pooled fund, no middleman. The app handles member onboarding, the monthly send/receive matchmaking, a roster, gatherings, and an offers-and-needs board.

The Community Guaranteed Income Club started in Baltimore in spring 2025, after watching peers lose jobs. The concept was created by Alex Zhu; the platform was co-created by Alex Zhu, Tyler Heath, Deborah Tien, and Josh Nesbit, and is stewarded and maintained as open source by the Relational Tech Project. The Baltimore pilot moved $23,000+ among 50+ members with a 100% payment completion rate — "not because of contracts; because we know each other's names." It's designed to spread, chapter by chapter.

attribution.name: CONSUL Democracy Foundation (born at Madrid City Council)

items.body:
CONSUL was built inside Madrid's city hall in 2015 to run decide.madrid.es, and grew into the most widely deployed open-source participation suite: citizen debates, proposals that advance when they clear signature thresholds, consultations, collaborative legislation, and participatory budgeting. Madrid's own participatory budget grew from €60M to €100M a year with tens of thousands of participants; the platform is used by 250+ cities and organizations from Munich to Montevideo, and is now stewarded by the CONSUL Democracy Foundation.

It's AGPL-3.0, accessibility-badged, and verified as a Digital Public Good. Like Decidim, self-hosting is an institution-sized job — but the mechanics are the remixable part.

One honest note from Madrid's record: researchers found final city outcomes only partly reflected what citizens voted for. The tool creates the channel; keeping institutions accountable to its results is organizing work, not software work — which is exactly why this shelf ships alongside the Community Organizing one.

**Neighborhood remix:** CONSUL's proposal-plus-threshold mechanic at porch scale — any neighbor's idea that collects ten door-knock endorsements automatically goes on the next potluck agenda for a yes/no decision.

attribution.name: Decidim Free Software Association (born at Barcelona City Council; Xabier Barandiaran & Arnau Monterde among the founders)

items.body:
Decidim ('we decide' in Catalan) was born at Barcelona City Council in 2016 to run the city's participatory action plan, and was rebuilt as a general framework: modular pieces for proposals, assemblies, participatory budgeting, consultations, and strategic planning. It now runs Barcelona, Helsinki's OmaStadi, New York's Participate NYC, Brasil Participativo, and the European Commission's citizen-engagement platform, and spread through Japan from the small city of Kakogawa to dozens of municipalities.

Two things make it more than software. First, its governance: Decidim is stewarded by a free-software association through its own participatory community (Metadecidim) under a published Social Contract — the tool for democracy is itself governed democratically. Second, its hybrid DNA: the best Decidim deployments pair the platform with physical assemblies and street-corner support points (see the Barcelona neighborhood-budget story on this shelf).

AGPL-3.0, Ruby on Rails, very active. Self-hosting is real work — a neighborhood would borrow a hosted instance or an ecosystem provider — but the *patterns* (proposals with thresholds, assemblies with minutes, budgets with ballots) remix at any scale.

**Neighborhood remix:** a single-neighborhood Decidim with one assembly (the block association), one budget (the yard-sale fund), and proposals capped at what's buildable in a weekend.

items.body:
Field Papers — descended from Walking Papers, built for the OpenStreetMap community, and stewarded since 2023 by OpenStreetMap US — closes the loop between paper and the world's open map: print a multi-page atlas of anywhere, walk it and annotate with a pen, photograph the pages, upload, and transcribe what you marked into OpenStreetMap, where it becomes commons data anyone can use.

Its lineage runs through the most famous community mapping story there is: Kibera in Nairobi was a blank spot on the world's maps until residents mapped it themselves in 2009 (Map Kibera), using exactly this paper-first pattern.

The tool's deeper insight is that **paper is a feature**: a printed atlas can be carried by kids, marked by elders, passed around a stoop — participation without devices. The transcription evening afterward is its own gathering.

**Neighborhood remix:** a Saturday 'map our block' walk — benches, shade trees, little libraries, step-free entrances, water taps — and by Sunday the block has contributed its own commons layer to the map everyone's apps read.

metadata.license: ISC (fp-web, fp-tiler; the umbrella fieldpapers/fieldpapers repo carries no license file)
metadata.remix_idea: The Saturday block-mapping walk, kids carrying the atlas.

items.summary: Print a paper atlas of your blocks, walk them with a pen, photograph the pages, and turn the annotations into open map data. Neighborhood mapping with no GPS, no GIS, no app.
items.title: Field Papers + OpenStreetMap

items.body:
FixMyStreet launched in the UK in 2007 with a radical simplicity: put a pin in a map, describe the broken thing, and the site figures out which authority is responsible and emails them — publishing the report, the response, and the fix (or the silence) for everyone to see. The public ledger is the point: it converts individual complaints into shared civic memory. The UK site passed its millionth report in 2017 and now carries roughly 12,000 reports a month.

The FixMyStreet Platform is AGPL-3.0 open source with 20+ installations worldwide — Zurich's 'Züri wie neu,' Sweden's FixaMinGata, Uruguay's PorMiBarrio (run by DATA Uruguay). mySociety, the UK charity behind it, sells a hosted version to councils, which funds the commons code.

One honest design lesson rides with it: reporting tools inherit the biases of who reports (research on 311-style systems finds reporting skews toward homeowners and wealthier blocks) and what gets reported *about* — the pattern is at its best pointed at conditions and infrastructure, and at its worst pointed at people.

**Neighborhood remix:** a 'FixMyBlock' where reports route not to the council but to the block's own repair crew — whoever owns the ladder, the drill, or the relationship with the alderperson — with the same public see-it-through ledger.

metadata.hosted: self-host free; paid hosting for councils (SocietyWorks)
metadata.remix_idea: FixMyBlock: the public repair ledger, routed to neighbors instead of (or alongside) city hall.

items.summary: mySociety's 'stick a pin in a map' issue-reporting pattern, running since 2007 and forked worldwide — every report public, every fix visible. The grandparent of civic reporting done in the open.

items.body:
Gathio does one thing with unusual grace: create an event page with no account, share the public link, edit it with a private password link — and the whole page auto-deletes seven days after the event ends. It federates over ActivityPub for those who want it, and ignores that entirely for those who don't.

It's GPL-3.0, maintained by Raphael Kabo with community contributors, with a free flagship instance at gath.io and Docker docs for self-hosting. The honest caveat is the bus factor of a small solo-maintainer project — mitigated by the fact that there is nothing to lose: the pages were going to delete themselves anyway.

Gathio earns its shelf spot as a design statement: most neighborhood gatherings don't need a platform, a group, a feed, or a data trail. They need a page that exists for two weeks. Tools that know how small they are, stay healthy.

**Neighborhood remix:** the potluck invite — link on a paper flyer taped to the mailboxes, gone a week after the last casserole dish goes home.

metadata.remix_idea: Event pages as ephemeral as the gatherings they announce.

items.summary: No-signup event pages that delete themselves a week after the event. The potluck invite as ephemeral as the potluck.

attribution.name: Ruby for Good & PDX Diaper Bank

items.body:
Human Essentials is what happens when a volunteer developer community (Ruby for Good) adopts an unglamorous, essential problem: diaper banks and essentials banks running their inventory on paper and memory. Built with the PDX Diaper Bank in Portland, Oregon, it now serves 200+ registered banks across the US — inventory, distributions, partner agencies, barcode scanning, reporting — free, MIT-licensed, and recognized as a Digital Public Good.

It earns its shelf spot for two reasons. As a tool: any mutual aid operation that stores and distributes *things* (a community fridge network, a supply hub, a disaster cache) eventually needs exactly this shape of software, and this one is free and maintained. As a story: it's the standing proof that volunteer open-source labor, pointed at a real operator's real workflow and sustained for years, produces civic infrastructure — the opposite of the hackathon prototype that dies by Monday.

**Neighborhood remix:** scale it down from warehouse to porch — a community fridge and pantry ledger tracking what came in, what's running low, and which partner households need a knock.

metadata.remix_idea: The community fridge ledger, scaled from warehouse to porch.

items.summary: Free, open-source inventory and distribution software built by volunteers for diaper and essentials banks — 200+ banks run on it. The warehouse version of the community pantry ledger.

attribution.name: The Karrot team & the foodsaving movement

items.body:
Karrot came out of the European foodsaving movement: volunteers rescuing surplus food needed to coordinate recurring pickups at real places, with trust-based membership and no money involved. The result generalizes startlingly well: **groups** (a block), **places** (the community fridge, the garden, the corner store that donates), **recurring activities** (Tuesday fridge cleaning, Friday stoop-sit), applications and trust karma instead of admin fiat, and discussion where the coordination happens.

It's MIT-licensed, community-governed through its own forum, very actively maintained, free to use on the hosted karrot.world instance, and self-hostable with Docker. Food-saving groups across Europe run on it daily — Gothenburg's Solikyl is the best documented.

Where most civic platforms assume a city, Karrot assumes exactly what a neighborhood is: a smallish group of semi-strangers building trust through recurring shared work.

**Neighborhood remix:** the general-purpose block engine — compost-hauling shifts, tool-library hours, fridge stewardship rotations — anywhere the unit of organizing is 'a recurring task at a real place, done by whoever signed up.'

metadata.remix_idea: Recurring shared work at real places — the block as a Karrot group.

items.summary: Groups, places, recurring pickups, and trust-based membership — built by the food-saving movement, and arguably the most neighborhood-shaped open-source codebase in civic tech.
items.title: Karrot

LittleSis — run by the nonprofit Public Accountability Initiative — is a free, collaboratively edited database of the relationships among the people and institutions that hold power: boards, donors, lobbyists, landlords, development interests. Its embedded mapping tool, **Oligrapher**, turns that data (or your own) into clear network maps of who's connected to whom.

For the organizing arc, this is question four's power tool: where the 'Tracking Down the Power' exercise maps actors on a wall, LittleSis lets a tenants union or block association research the actual interlocks — which LLC owns the buildings, who sits on which board, who funds whom — and publish the map. Neighborhood groups have used it to map local landlords and development networks.

Everything is GPL-3.0 open source, and the database itself is a commons anyone can contribute research to.

**Neighborhood remix:** the block's landlord map — every LLC on the street resolved to its owners and their other holdings, built in an evening from public records, ready for the tenants' meeting.

items.summary: 'The opposite of Big Brother': a free who-knows-who database of business and government power, with an open-source relationship-mapping tool neighborhoods use to map their landlords and developers.

LocalWiki grew out of DavisWiki (2004), where founders Philip Neustrom and Mike Ivanov built an openly editable encyclopedia of one California college town — and watched it become core infrastructure, with roughly one in seven residents contributing (the full story is on this shelf). A Knight Foundation grant generalized the software; at its 2015 peak the hosted platform served 300+ communities and ~400,000 monthly readers, all content under Creative Commons Attribution.

Honest status: the sites are online, but development has been largely dormant for years — the code (GPLv2, Python/Django) is old, and the nonprofit's energy has dispersed. It sits on this shelf anyway, for two reasons. First, the model — *every* local thing deserves a page a neighbor can edit: the history, the third places, the characters, the how-things-work — has never been beaten. Second, it's a graveyard-adjacent lesson in what actually made Davis work: not features, but resident habit and a decade of care.

**Neighborhood remix:** don't necessarily run the old software — rebuild the idea at block scale. A 'living field guide' to one neighborhood: every porch, mural, tree, elder, and unwritten rule gets a page neighbors can edit from their phones, licensed openly so it outlives any one steward.

metadata.remix_idea: A block-scale living field guide: every place and unwritten rule gets an editable page.
metadata.status_note: Sites online; development largely dormant — a proven model awaiting its next builder.

items.summary: Dead-simple editable pages and maps for one place's collective knowledge — born as DavisWiki, where one in seven residents contributed. The software is dormant; the model is undefeated.
items.title: LocalWiki

items.body:
Loomio came out of Occupy Wellington in 2011, when activists who'd experienced consensus in a plaza met the Enspiral network and asked how a group could decide things well *between* meetings. The answer: threaded discussion attached to formal proposals — consent, consensus, dot votes, time polls — each closing on a deadline and leaving a permanent record of what was decided, by whom, and why.

That decision log is the underrated feature for neighborhood groups: when the garden coordinators rotate, the log *is* the institutional memory. No more 'I think we agreed in some email thread.'

Loomio is built and run by a worker-owned cooperative in Aotearoa New Zealand — the tool for group governance is itself governed by its workers — AGPL-3.0, with paid hosting that sustains the co-op and Docker self-hosting for the determined. Groups range from the 13,000-member NYC Democratic Socialists chapter to open-source projects and co-ops in 66 countries.

**Neighborhood remix:** a community-garden Loomio where the compost proposal closes in 72 hours, quiet members vote without attending a meeting, and next year's coordinators inherit every decision ever made.

metadata.hosted: paid hosting funds the co-op; self-host via Docker
metadata.remix_idea: Garden governance with 72-hour consent rounds and a permanent decision log.

items.summary: Deliberation and formal decisions for small groups — proposals, consent rounds, time polls — from a Wellington worker co-op born out of Occupy. The decision log is the institutional memory.

items.body:
Mapeo — and its next-generation rebuild CoMapeo — is Awana Digital's answer to a hard question: how does a community map and monitor its own territory when the internet is absent, unreliable, or unsafe? The tools run entirely on phones, sync peer-to-peer between devices, and keep the data owned by the community — there is no server unless the community wants one.

The proof is consequential: the Waorani of Pastaza, Ecuador mapped twenty villages' territory with Mapeo starting in 2015, and their maps entered evidence in the 2019 lawsuit in which Ecuador's courts blocked an oil concession on Waorani land. Awana counts hundreds of frontline communities using its tools across dozens of countries.

GPL-3.0, actively developed. For neighborhoods, the offline-first, community-owned architecture matters most exactly when the cloud is the wrong place for the data.

**Neighborhood remix:** tenants photo-documenting housing-code violations building by building, syncing phone-to-phone at the tenants' meeting, and sharing only what they decide to share, when they decide to share it.

metadata.remix_idea: Tenant documentation that syncs phone-to-phone and shares only on the tenants' terms.

items.summary: Offline-first mapping and monitoring where data syncs phone-to-phone and never touches a server the community doesn't own. Built with Indigenous land defenders; evidence from it has won in court.

Mobilizon was built by Framasoft, the French free-software association, as a deliberate answer to 'all our neighborhood events live on Facebook': a federated (ActivityPub) platform for events and groups, where a group gets a page, discussions, and event listings, and attendees can RSVP without creating an account. No algorithmic feed, no data extraction, no 'people also viewed.'

Since 2024 it's been maintained by the Kaihuri association — a handoff with Framasoft's blessing, not a fork — with Framasoft still running the flagship mobilizon.fr instance for the French associative world. AGPL-3.0-or-later, Elixir, with dozens of public instances to join instead of self-hosting.

Honest status: maintained at small-association capacity — healthy, but a dependency to watch rather than bet a city on. For one neighborhood's repair cafés and porch concerts, that's plenty.

**Neighborhood remix:** one Mobilizon group as the block's events board — seed swap, stoop concert, fix-it night — with the RSVP link on the paper flyer, and the paper flyer still on the mailboxes, because the stack includes paper.

items.body:
Outer Sunset Field Guide

Build a mobile-first neighborhood walking companion for the Outer Sunset district of San Francisco, centered around 48th Avenue and Irving Street. It should feel like a calm, quiet field notebook — not a flashy app. Think of it as an adult field trip led by a knowledgeable neighbor.

Visual design:

- Maximum width of 430px, centered on larger screens, like a phone screen
- Off-white paper background with warm, muted earth tones — faded terra cotta accents, warm grays, charcoal text
- Two fonts: Lora (serif) for headings and labels, Inter (sans-serif) for body text
- Minimum 16px body text for outdoor sunlight readability
- Subtle, slow animations — gentle slides and fades, nothing flashy
- Overall aesthetic: understated, literary, like a printed field guide

Data model:

Each place in the guide has: a name, street address, latitude/longitude coordinates, a thumbnail image, an optional secondary drawing/illustration with artist credit, a prose description, a photo credit, optional audio (with label and duration), optional external links, and one or more "time layers" — past, present, or future. All place data is stored in a database and fetched on load.

Time layers:

Every place belongs to one or more of three time layers: Past (historical sites, old photos), Present (current businesses and gathering spaces), and Future (community dreams and planned projects). These are shown as three small dots — filled if active, outlined if not — next to each place entry throughout the app.

Navigation:

A fixed bottom tab bar with three tabs: Explore, Tour, and About.

Explore tab (default):

The Explore tab has three sub-views, toggled by text links in the header reading "Nearby · Map · All":

1. Nearby (default): A single large card showing one place at a time. The card has a wide thumbnail image (16:10 ratio), the place name in large serif text, the street address, walking distance and time from the user's current location (e.g. "Walk → 3 min · 0.2 mi"), and the time layer dots. Users swipe left/right or tap Back/Next buttons to move between places. Pagination dots show position. Places are sorted by distance from the user. Adjacent thumbnails are prefetched for instant transitions. If the user is within about 150 meters of a place, the card gets a subtle accent background and says "You're here." Tapping a card opens the detail view.

2. Map: A Leaflet map showing all places as colored pins — brown for past, dark charcoal for present, slate blue for future, gray for mixed. Past-only pins are outlined, future-only are dashed, present/mixed are solid. The map is grayscale-filtered. A legend explains the pin styles. Tapping a pin opens the detail view. The user's location is shown as a small blue dot.

3. All: A compact list of every place sorted by distance, showing a small thumbnail, name, address, walking time, and time layer dots. Tapping opens the detail view.

Place detail view:

Opens as a bottom sheet sliding up over the current view, scrollable, max height 92% of the screen. Contains:

- Full-width hero image (4:3 ratio) with a small expand button for a fullscreen lightbox, plus photo credit
- Optional secondary illustration below the hero, also expandable, with artist credit
- Place name, address, time layer dots, walking distance or "You're here"
- Full prose description
- Optional audio player section with play/pause button, label, and duration
- Optional external links section
- Embedded OpenStreetMap showing the location, with a "Get directions" button that opens Apple Maps on iOS or Google Maps on Android

Tour tab:

A list of four predefined walking tours: Past, Present, Future, and "Very local" (nearest 6 places). Each shows a name, description, and estimated walking time. Tapping a tour filters the Explore Nearby cards to just those places and labels the active tour in the header with a "Back to explore" link.

About tab:

A scrollable page with:

- "About this guide" section explaining what it is
- "The time layers" section with a visual key showing the three dot patterns and their meanings
- "Community credits" section
- Three collapsible form sections (each with a chevron toggle):
  - "Suggest a site" — time layer selector, details textarea, optional name and email fields
  - "Get in touch" — name, email, message fields
  - "Request a neighborhood tour" — name, email, message fields
  - All forms validate inputs and submit to the database, showing success messages after submission
- A "More neighborhood tools" section styled as a cork bulletin board with pinned cards linking to sibling neighborhood websites
- A bottom disclaimer noting it's an early prototype

Geolocation:

The app requests the user's location on load. It uses the Permissions API to distinguish between "not yet asked," "granted," and "blocked" states. If location is denied, a subtle notice appears. Walking distances and times are calculated using the Haversine formula.

Content:

The guide includes roughly 25-30 places spanning all three time layers — local cafes, surf spots, historical sites, libraries, community art spaces, planned housing projects, neighbor dreams, and historical homes of notable artists.

attribution.name: Open Food Foundation & the OFN federation

items.body:
Open Food Network began in Melbourne in 2012 as a nonprofit answer to a structural problem: the software that connects farms to eaters was owned by intermediaries whose margins were the point. OFN's AGPL-3.0 marketplace lets farmers, food hubs, and buying clubs run their own storefronts and distribution — 2,500+ enterprises now trade through a federation of national instances across Australia, the UK, France, Canada, the US, and beyond.

The governance is as instructive as the code: a foundation stewards the commons codebase while affiliated national organizations run their own instances — a working model of federated stewardship that neighborhood infrastructure keeps needing and rarely gets.

**Neighborhood remix:** a single-block buying club — one OFN storefront where fifteen households pool a weekly order from the farm twenty minutes out and split the drop-off on one porch. Food is the oldest reason neighbors organize; this is that reason with an order form.

metadata.remix_idea: Fifteen households, one storefront, one porch drop-off.

items.summary: Open-source marketplace software for farmers, food hubs, and buying clubs — 2,500+ enterprises across 15+ countries. A block's buying club is a food hub that fits on one porch.
items.title: Open Food Network

items.body:
Every neighborhood maintains the same list a dozen times: where the food pantry is, when the clinic's open, who has beds tonight. Open Referral, founded by Greg Bloom in 2013, attacks the duplication with a standard instead of a product: the **Human Services Data Specification (HSDS)** defines how to describe services, providers, and locations so any directory can be published once and consumed everywhere — by a website, a 211 line, a case worker's tool, or an AI assistant.

It's infrastructure with real adoption: piloted in Miami's county systems, adopted across UK local government as Open Referral UK, endorsed by the 211 sector's standards body. The spec and schemas are openly published on GitHub.

**Neighborhood remix:** publish the block's mutual-aid inventory — who has a truck, a spare room, jumper cables, a Narcan kit — as a tiny HSDS-shaped dataset (with consent), so the church down the street and the next tool anyone builds can both read it without asking anyone to retype it.

metadata.remix_idea: The block's who-has-what inventory as a tiny, consented HSDS dataset.

items.summary: Not an app — an open data standard for 'who provides what help, where' — so a community's resource directory can be maintained once and read by every tool, church, and hotline that needs it.
items.title: Open Referral / HSDS

attribution.name: The Computational Democracy Project (Colin Megill et al.)

items.body:
Pol.is asks participants to do two tiny things: write short statements about the question at hand, and vote agree / disagree / pass on everyone else's. Statistical clustering then reveals the real opinion groups — and, crucially, surfaces the statements that *bridge* them. No replies, no threads, no dunking; the interface simply has no button for a flame war.

Its famous outing was vTaiwan's 2015–16 Uber deliberation, where a few hundred citizens converged on near-unanimous recommendations that became regulation. But the more shelf-relevant story is Bowling Green, Kentucky: in 2018 the local civic assembly ran Pol.is with the daily newspaper, drew 2,000+ residents casting 225,000 votes, and found a town that agreed with itself about traffic and accountability far more than its Facebook comments suggested; a 2025 follow-up engaged roughly a tenth of the city.

Maintained by the Computational Democracy Project (a US nonprofit), AGPL-3.0, free hosted conversations at pol.is, fully self-hostable.

**Neighborhood remix:** a forty-person Polis for one street — 'what should happen to the empty lot?' — QR code taped to the lot's fence, results read aloud at the block party. The bridging statements become the agenda.

metadata.remix_idea: A one-street Polis about one shared question, with results read aloud in person.

items.summary: The wiki-survey that maps a group's actual opinion landscape: everyone writes short statements and votes on each other's; clustering surfaces what bridges the camps. Famous from vTaiwan, sized for a street.
items.title: Pol.is

items.body:
# The Builder's Spiral

A practice for building technology that deepens community — rooted in place, shaped by neighbors.

Software tools emerge from relationships, conversations, and dreams in the neighborhood.

## The Idea

Building technology is a relational practice, not a technical one.

This guide is for people who want to build technology that grows from their neighborhood — not from a product roadmap. The process is not linear. It's a spiral. Each time around, you widen your circle of relationships and deepen your understanding of what your community actually needs.

The tools you build are not the point. They are artifacts of something more important: the conversations you have, the trust you earn, the dreams you share with the people around you. Software is what emerges when a neighborhood imagines its own future.

### The 90 / 10 Rhythm

**90%** of your time is spent in community — listening, being present, reflecting, dreaming alongside your neighbors. **10%** is the actual building. The spiral teaches you that these aren't separate activities. The 90% is what gives the 10% its meaning and direction.

## How the Spiral Works

Instead of a step-by-step checklist, think of the build process as a series of expanding circles. You start close — with yourself and the people nearest to you. As you listen, imagine, and create together, the circle naturally widens. More voices join. More dreams surface. The tool you build gets more rooted in the real life of the place.

Each turn of the spiral passes through the same essential movements — **relating, listening, dreaming, shaping, building, and sharing** — but at a wider scale and with deeper understanding. Nothing is wasted. Every conversation feeds the next turn. Every small tool planted in the community becomes a seed for the next imagination.

> *"The process of building is itself relational. The 90% is not overhead — it's the whole point."*

## The Six Movements

Each turn of the spiral passes through these movements.

### 1. Listen & Be Present — Innermost Circle · 90%

The spiral begins where you are — in your neighborhood, in relationship. Be porous. Walk the block. Sit on porches. Show up at gatherings, schools, churches, barbershops, corner stores. Let the place teach you what it needs. This isn't preparation for the work. **This is the work.** Spend the vast majority of your time here. Let the rhythms of the neighborhood become your rhythms.

### 2. Notice & Name — Second Circle · 90%

What surfaces from being present? Dreams, needs, aspirations, frustrations, joys. Write them down — not as problems to solve, but as seeds to tend. Don't force anything into a format yet. These notes are gifts from the relationships you're building. They carry the wisdom of the neighborhood.

### 3. Imagine Together — Third Circle · 90%

Share those seeds with the people around you. What tools, spaces, or practices could make the neighborhood's vision more present in daily life? This is where dreaming becomes communal — the imagination doesn't belong to one person, it belongs to the relationships between people. What could we build, right here, with these neighbors, that would help us live more fully into the future we see?

### 4. Remix in the Studio — Fourth Circle · The 10% Begins

Bring your shared vision to the **Relational Tech Studio** at studio.relationaltechproject.org. Here you mix your neighborhood's dreams with stories, components, and patterns from relational tech builders across the country. You're not starting from scratch — you're remixing a commons. The Studio sidekick helps you shape your idea into a buildable prompt that carries your place, your culture, your aesthetic.

### 5. Shape & Build — Fifth Circle · 10%

Work with AI tools to sharpen your prompt — is it clear enough, specific enough, rooted enough for a builder like Lovable or Dyad to bring to life? Then build the thing. Open your builder of choice in Plan mode, walk through the plan, and build. **Keep it small. Keep it local. Keep it true** to the vision that came from the neighborhood.

### 6. Share & Spiral Outward — Outermost Circle · Back to 90%

Put the tool in people's hands. Share it on porches and at kitchen tables. Watch how it lives in the neighborhood. Listen again — now with something tangible between you. New conversations emerge. New dreams surface. The circle of people involved grows wider. The relationships deepen. And the spiral continues: you carry everything you've learned into the next turn, building on a wider and deeper foundation.

## Every Turn Widens the Circle

Each time you move through the spiral, something has changed. You know more people. More people know you. The dreams are sharper. The tools are more rooted. The trust is deeper.

The spiral doesn't have an end point. It's a practice — like gardening, like neighboring, like showing up. The software you build is not the goal. It's a gift that comes from living in community and paying attention to what wants to emerge.

**Remember:** 90% is listening, being present, and living in community.

**Trust the Process:** The tools will come. They emerge from the relationships.

## Start Your Spiral

1. Walk your neighborhood this week. Just listen.
2. Write down what surfaces — dreams, needs, possibilities.
3. Share those notes with someone you trust in the community.
4. When you're ready, bring your idea to the Studio.

Visit the Relational Tech Studio at **studio.relationaltechproject.org** to begin.

items.body:
The Stanford Participatory Budgeting Platform, from Stanford's Crowdsourced Democracy Team, does one democratic job extremely well: run the voting phase of a participatory budgeting process. It supports approval voting, knapsack voting (fit projects under the budget cap yourself — the most honest ballot design in civic tech), and ranked methods, in 13 languages, free and open source.

It has run digital voting for 150+ PB processes, including New York City council districts, where researchers observed that digital ballots accounted for participation growth while paper stayed flat — with the equity caveat that paper still reaches voters digital doesn't, so good deployments run both.

For a neighborhood, it's the missing piece between 'we should let everyone decide' and 'we counted hands at one meeting': a real ballot box that costs nothing and speaks your block's languages.

**Neighborhood remix:** the ballot box for the block-scale PB cycle on this shelf — every household votes, digital or paper, same weight.

items.summary: The free, open-source, multilingual digital ballot box for participatory budgeting — used in 150+ PB processes including New York City districts, where digital voting drove participation growth.

attribution.name: Streetmix (Lou Huang & collaborators; Code for America lineage)

items.body:
Streetmix began at a January 2013 Code for America hackathon, inspired by something Lou Huang saw at a San Francisco community meeting: planners handing residents paper cutouts of street elements to arrange. The web version does exactly that — drag sidewalks, bike lanes, transit, trees, and parking into a street cross-section, sized to your street's real width, and share the picture.

It's been used both by governments (San Francisco's Public Works gathered feedback on the Second Street redesign with it) and against them (Sioux Center, Iowa residents mocked up alternatives to a highway widening; Wellington cycleway advocates drew the bike lanes the council hadn't). AGPL-3.0, free at streetmix.net, maintained by a small collective.

What it teaches: giving neighbors a *drawing tool* changes the power dynamics of a planning meeting — the block arrives with twelve pictures of the same wish instead of three minutes of public comment.

**Neighborhood remix:** before the traffic-calming petition, every household mocks up 'our street, fixed' and the gallery goes to the city as one visual voice.

attribution.name: Awana Digital (née Digital Democracy) & the Terrastories community

items.body:
Terrastories ties audio and video oral histories to places on an interactive map, with community-controlled access — stories can be public, restricted, or private, because not every story is for everyone. It shipped first in 2018 for the Matawai Maroon communities mapping histories along Suriname's Saramacca River, built by Awana Digital (formerly Digital Democracy) with a volunteer developer community, and now runs from Indigenous ranger networks in the Solomon Islands to youth documentation projects in Brazil.

It's MIT-licensed, actively maintained, and ships a fully offline 'Field Kit' — the whole application can run on a Raspberry Pi with no internet and no cloud, which is both an access feature and a sovereignty feature: the community's stories live on the community's hardware.

**Neighborhood remix:** 'This corner used to be…' — elders record 90-second stories pinned to the laundromat, the old ballfield, the mural; the map runs at the branch library; the access controls mean the block decides which stories the whole internet gets.

attribution.name: Ushahidi (Ory Okolloh, Erik Hersman, Juliana Rotich & David Kobia, founders)

items.body:
Ushahidi ('testimony' in Swahili) was built in 2008 by Ory Okolloh, Erik Hersman, Juliana Rotich, and David Kobia to map eyewitness reports of violence after Kenya's disputed 2007 election. It became the template for crowdsourced civic mapping: people submit reports by SMS, web form, or email; stewards triage, categorize, and publish them to a shared map with workflows for response.

Its famous deployments are large — the 2010 Haiti earthquake response processed ~30,000 text messages, and Kenya's Uchaguzi election monitoring runs on it — but the platform scales *down* beautifully: during Washington DC's 2010 'Snowmageddon,' one resident stood up a neighborhood dig-out map in a day (a story on this shelf).

The nonprofit behind it is headquartered in Nairobi and led by Angela Oduor Lungati, who rose from within its own developer community. The platform is AGPL-3.0 open source with a hosted cloud service, and free accounts for qualifying grassroots groups.

**Neighborhood remix:** any question of the form 'what's where, according to us?' — third places, accessibility barriers, heat refuges, little free pantries, memory sites. One steward, one map, reports by text message so no one needs an app.

items.summary: The Nairobi-born, open-source crowdsourced mapping platform — reports arrive by SMS, web, or email and land on a shared map. Built for crises, remixable for anything a neighborhood wants to see together.
